Vector spaces

Arrows are not the only things you can add and scale. Polynomials, matrices, sound signals and solutions of equations follow the same rules. This chapter names those rules. Then it measures the size of any such space with one number, its dimension.

  • Decide if a set is a vector space or a subspace.
  • Test vectors for linear independence and describe their span.
  • Find a basis and the dimension of a subspace.
  • Compute the four fundamental subspaces of a matrix and use rank-nullity.
  • Change coordinates between two bases and write the matrix of a linear map.

What is a vector space?

Look at four very different things. In each case we can add two of them. We can also multiply one by a number. The result is always the same kind of thing.

Four sets with addition and scaling
SetAdd twoScale by 3
Lists of 3 numbers, \mathbb{R}^3(1, 2, 0) + (4, 0, 1) = (5, 2, 1)3(1, 2, 0) = (3, 6, 0)
Polynomials of degree at most 2(1 + x) + (2x - x^2) = 1 + 3x - x^23(1 + x) = 3 + 3x
2 \times 2 matricesAdd entry by entryScale every entry
Sound signals f(t)Play two sounds togetherMake the sound 3 times louder

All four behave like arrows. So we give them one name. A vector space is a set with an addition and a scaling that follow eight rules. Its elements are called vectors, even when they are polynomials or sounds. The numbers we scale by are scalars. In this chapter scalars are real numbers.

A set V with an addition \mathbf{u} + \mathbf{v} and a scaling c\mathbf{v} is a vector space when both results stay in V and these eight rules hold for all \mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v}, \mathbf{w} in V and all scalars c, d.

  1. \mathbf{u} + \mathbf{v} = \mathbf{v} + \mathbf{u}.
  2. (\mathbf{u} + \mathbf{v}) + \mathbf{w} = \mathbf{u} + (\mathbf{v} + \mathbf{w}).
  3. There is a zero vector \mathbf{0} with \mathbf{v} + \mathbf{0} = \mathbf{v}.
  4. Every \mathbf{v} has a negative -\mathbf{v} with \mathbf{v} + (-\mathbf{v}) = \mathbf{0}.
  5. c(d\mathbf{v}) = (cd)\mathbf{v}.
  6. 1\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{v}.
  7. c(\mathbf{u} + \mathbf{v}) = c\mathbf{u} + c\mathbf{v}.
  8. (c + d)\mathbf{v} = c\mathbf{v} + d\mathbf{v}.

These rules are called axioms. You do not need to learn them by heart. They only say: "addition and scaling work like you expect". The power comes later. Every theorem in this chapter uses only these rules. So each theorem works for arrows, polynomials, matrices and signals at once.

Take the vectors (x, y) with x \ge 0 and y \ge 0. The sum of two of them stays inside. But -1 \cdot (1, 1) = (-1, -1) falls outside. So this set is not a vector space. Always check scaling by negative numbers too.

Scalars can also be complex numbers or bits. With bits, 1 + 1 = 0. Error-correcting codes and some cryptography use vector spaces over bits. The theorems of this chapter still hold there.

Subspaces

Look at the plane x + 2y - z = 0 in \mathbb{R}^3. Take two points on it, (1, 0, 1) and (-2, 1, 0). Their sum (-1, 1, 1) is on the plane too: -1 + 2 - 1 = 0. Any multiple, like 5(1, 0, 1) = (5, 0, 5), also stays on the plane. The plane is a small vector space inside a big one.

A set W inside a vector space V is a subspace when three things are true.

  1. \mathbf{0} is in W.
  2. If \mathbf{u} and \mathbf{v} are in W, then \mathbf{u} + \mathbf{v} is in W.
  3. If \mathbf{v} is in W and c is a scalar, then c\mathbf{v} is in W.

A subspace is then a vector space by itself. The eight rules come for free from V. We say W is closed under addition and scaling.

  • The line y = 2x is a subspace of \mathbb{R}^2. It holds all multiples of (1, 2).
  • The line y = 2x + 1 is not. It does not contain (0, 0).
  • The solutions of A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{0} always form a subspace. You saw this in Linear systems and elimination.
  • The solutions of A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b} with \mathbf{b} \ne \mathbf{0} never do. Zero is not a solution.
  • The symmetric 2 \times 2 matrices form a subspace of all 2 \times 2 matrices.

Two of the three tests are not enough. Take the points (x, y) with xy \ge 0. This set holds \mathbf{0} and all multiples. But (1, 0) + (0, -1) = (1, -1), and 1 \cdot (-1) \lt 0. So it is not closed under addition.

Span

Take two vectors \mathbf{u} = (1, 0, 1) and \mathbf{v} = (0, 1, 1). Form all combinations s\mathbf{u} + t\mathbf{v} = (s, t, s + t). These points fill a plane through the origin. Its equation is z = x + y.

The span of \mathbf{v}_1, \dots, \mathbf{v}_k is the set of all linear combinations c_1\mathbf{v}_1 + \cdots + c_k\mathbf{v}_k. We write \operatorname{span}\{\mathbf{v}_1, \dots, \mathbf{v}_k\}.

A linear combination is a sum of multiples. The span is always a subspace. The sum of two combinations is again a combination. So is a multiple of one. If the span is all of V, the vectors form a spanning set of V.

  1. Is \mathbf{b} = (2, 3, 5) in the span of \mathbf{u} = (1, 0, 1) and \mathbf{v} = (0, 1, 1)? We need s\mathbf{u} + t\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{b}.
  2. This is a linear system. The vectors are the columns. \left( \begin{matrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 \end{matrix} \;\middle|\; \begin{matrix} 2 \\ 3 \\ 5 \end{matrix} \right) \to \left( \begin{matrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 \end{matrix} \;\middle|\; \begin{matrix} 2 \\ 3 \\ 0 \end{matrix} \right)
  3. No pivot in the last column. So yes: \mathbf{b} = 2\mathbf{u} + 3\mathbf{v}.
  4. Try \mathbf{b} = (2, 3, 4). The last row becomes (0 \;\; 0 \mid -1). So this \mathbf{b} is not in the span. Indeed 4 \ne 2 + 3.

This gives a key idea. The span of the columns of A is the column space C(A). The system A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b} has a solution exactly when \mathbf{b} is in C(A).

Two vectors do not always span a plane. (1, 2) and (3, 6) point along the same line. Their span is only that line.

Linear independence

Look at \mathbf{u} = (1, 0, 1), \mathbf{v} = (0, 1, 1) and \mathbf{w} = (1, 1, 2). Here \mathbf{w} = \mathbf{u} + \mathbf{v}. So \mathbf{w} adds nothing new. The span of all three is the same plane as before. We can also write this as \mathbf{u} + \mathbf{v} - \mathbf{w} = \mathbf{0}.

Vectors \mathbf{v}_1, \dots, \mathbf{v}_k are linearly independent when c_1\mathbf{v}_1 + \cdots + c_k\mathbf{v}_k = \mathbf{0} happens only for c_1 = \cdots = c_k = 0. Otherwise they are linearly dependent.

In simple words: vectors are linearly independent when none of them is a combination of the others. Each one adds a new direction. Vectors are linearly dependent when at least one is extra. The combination with all zeros is the trivial combination. Independence means it is the only way to get \mathbf{0}.

Put the vectors as the columns of a matrix A. Reduce A to echelon form. The vectors are independent exactly when every column has a pivot. A column without a pivot is a combination of the pivot columns before it.

  1. Put \mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v}, \mathbf{w} as columns. \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 & 2 \end{pmatrix} \to \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 \end{pmatrix} \to \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}
  2. Column 3 has no pivot. So the vectors are dependent.
  3. Read column 3 of the reduced form: (1, 1, 0). It says \mathbf{w} = 1\mathbf{u} + 1\mathbf{v}.

Three quick facts follow from the test.

  • A set that contains \mathbf{0} is dependent. Use weight 1 on \mathbf{0} and 0 on the rest.
  • Two vectors are dependent exactly when one is a multiple of the other.
  • More than n vectors in \mathbb{R}^n are always dependent. The matrix has more columns than rows, so some column has no pivot. This is the corollary on homogeneous systems again.

"No two of them are parallel" does not mean independent. The three vectors in Example 2 are pairwise not parallel. But all three lie in one plane, so they are dependent.

Basis and dimension

Go back to the plane x + 2y - z = 0. Solve it like a system. y = s and z = t are free, and x = -2s + t.

\begin{pmatrix} x \\ y \\ z \end{pmatrix} = s \begin{pmatrix} -2 \\ 1 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix} + t \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}

The two vectors span the plane. They are also independent: neither is a multiple of the other. So they are a perfect set. They have no gaps and nothing extra.

A basis of a vector space V is a list of vectors that is linearly independent and spans V.

A basis is like a set of building blocks. Every vector is built from them in exactly one way. The weights are the coordinates of the vector in that basis. In \mathbb{R}^n, the standard basis is \mathbf{e}_1, \dots, \mathbf{e}_n, the columns of I.

If \mathbf{v}_1, \dots, \mathbf{v}_n is a basis, each vector has exactly one list of coordinates.

Why? Suppose \mathbf{v} = \sum c_i\mathbf{v}_i = \sum d_i\mathbf{v}_i. Subtract: \sum (c_i - d_i)\mathbf{v}_i = \mathbf{0}. Independence gives c_i = d_i for every i.

All bases have the same size

The plane above has many bases. For example, (1, 0, 1) and (-1, 1, 1) is another one. But every basis of the plane has exactly 2 vectors. This is not luck. It follows from a counting lemma.

Suppose m vectors span V. Then every linearly independent list in V has at most m vectors.

Proof

Let \mathbf{w}_1, \dots, \mathbf{w}_m span V. Take \mathbf{u}_1, \dots, \mathbf{u}_k in V with k \gt m. Each \mathbf{u}_j is a combination \sum_i a_{ij}\mathbf{w}_i. The numbers a_{ij} form an m \times k matrix A.

A has more columns than rows. So A\mathbf{c} = \mathbf{0} has a solution \mathbf{c} \ne \mathbf{0}. Then \sum_j c_j\mathbf{u}_j = \sum_i (A\mathbf{c})_i\mathbf{w}_i = \mathbf{0}. This is a nontrivial combination. So the \mathbf{u}_j are dependent. An independent list can therefore have at most m vectors.

This lemma is a form of the Steinitz exchange lemma. Now the main theorem is two lines long.

If a vector space has a basis with n vectors, then every basis of it has exactly n vectors.

Proof

Let B_1 have n vectors and B_2 have k vectors. Both are bases. B_1 spans and B_2 is independent, so k \le n by the lemma. B_2 spans and B_1 is independent, so n \le k. Hence k = n.

So the size of a basis belongs to the space, not to our choice. This number is the dimension, written \dim V. The space \{\mathbf{0}\} has dimension 0.

Some dimensions
SpaceOne basisDimension
\mathbb{R}^n\mathbf{e}_1, \dots, \mathbf{e}_nn
Polynomials of degree at most 21, x, x^23
2 \times 2 matricesFour matrices, each with one entry 14
Symmetric 2 \times 2 matrices\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}, \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}, \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}3
The plane x + 2y - z = 0(-2, 1, 0), (1, 0, 1)2

Let \dim V = n. Then any n independent vectors in V form a basis. Also, any n vectors that span V form a basis.

In simple words: when the count is right, check only one property. Take (1, 0, 0), (1, 1, 0), (1, 1, 1) in \mathbb{R}^3. The matrix with these columns is upper triangular with three pivots. So they are independent. Three vectors in a space of dimension 3: they form a basis.

All polynomials together have no finite basis. Any finite list has a highest power of x. Then x to a higher power is not in its span. Such spaces are infinite-dimensional. Function spaces in analysis and signal processing are like this. See Measure and functional analysis.

Do not say "the basis" of a space. A space has many bases. Only the number of vectors in them is fixed.

The four fundamental subspaces

Take the matrix of Example 3 in Linear systems and elimination. Its reduced form R is next to it.

A = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 & 1 & 3 \\ 2 & 4 & 3 & 8 \\ 3 & 6 & 4 & 11 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad R = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}

Every m \times n matrix has four special subspaces. Here m = 3 and n = 4. The pivots are in columns 1 and 3. So the rank is r = 2.

Column space C(A), inside \mathbb{R}^3

All combinations of the columns. Basis: the pivot columns of A itself, (1, 2, 3) and (1, 3, 4). Dimension r = 2.

Null space N(A), inside \mathbb{R}^4

All solutions of A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{0}. Basis: one vector for each free variable, (-2, 1, 0, 0) and (-1, 0, -2, 1). Dimension n - r = 2.

Row space C(A^{\mathsf{T}}), inside \mathbb{R}^4

All combinations of the rows. Basis: the nonzero rows of R, (1, 2, 0, 1) and (0, 0, 1, 2). Dimension r = 2.

Left null space N(A^{\mathsf{T}}), inside \mathbb{R}^3

All \mathbf{y} with A^{\mathsf{T}}\mathbf{y} = \mathbf{0}. Here row 3 = row 1 + row 2, so \mathbf{y} = (1, 1, -1). Dimension m - r = 1.

  • The null space N(A) holds all inputs that A sends to zero.
  • The row space is the column space of A^{\mathsf{T}}.
  • The left null space holds all \mathbf{y} with \mathbf{y}^{\mathsf{T}}A = \mathbf{0}^{\mathsf{T}}. It records which rows depend on the others.
  • The dimension of the null space is the nullity.

For the column space, take the pivot columns of A, not of R. Row operations change the column space. Here the columns of R all end in 0, but C(A) contains (1, 2, 3). Row operations do keep the row space. So the rows of R are fine for the row space.

For every matrix, \dim C(A) = \dim C(A^{\mathsf{T}}) = r, the number of pivots. So \operatorname{rank}(A) = \operatorname{rank}(A^{\mathsf{T}}).

Proof

Row operations replace rows by combinations of rows, and they can be undone. So A and R have the same row space. The r nonzero rows of R are independent: each has a 1 where the others have 0. So the row space has dimension r.

Row operations keep the solutions of A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{0}. So they keep every relation between the columns. In R the pivot columns are independent, and the other columns are combinations of them. The same holds for the columns of A. So the r pivot columns of A are a basis of C(A).

For an m \times n matrix A: \operatorname{rank}(A) + \dim N(A) = n, the number of columns.

In simple words: every column is either a pivot column or a free column. Pivot columns count the rank. Free columns count the null space. For our A: 2 + 2 = 4. Apply the theorem to A^{\mathsf{T}} too: 2 + 1 = 3. So the four dimensions are r, n - r, r and m - r.

Proof

There are r pivot columns and n - r free columns. Solve A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{0}. Set one free variable to 1 and the others to 0. This gives one special solution for each free variable. Every solution is a combination of them, so they span N(A). Each special solution has a 1 where the others have 0, so they are independent. They form a basis with n - r vectors.

Right angles between the subspaces

Take a vector \mathbf{x} in the null space. Then A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{0} says: every row of A times \mathbf{x} is 0. So \mathbf{x} is at a right angle to every row. Check: (1, 2, 0, 1) \cdot (-2, 1, 0, 0) = -2 + 2 = 0. In the same way, the left null space is at right angles to the column space. Two subspaces like this are orthogonal.

Gilbert Strang calls these facts the Fundamental Theorem of Linear Algebra. Part 1 gives the four dimensions. Part 2 gives the right angles. Projections in Orthogonality and least squares build on Part 2.

from sympy import Matrix

A = Matrix([[1, 2, 1, 3], [2, 4, 3, 8], [3, 6, 4, 11]])
show = lambda vs: [list(v) for v in vs]   # print each vector as a list

print("rank      ", A.rank())
print("column    ", show(A.columnspace()))   # pivot columns of A
print("null      ", show(A.nullspace()))     # solutions of A x = 0
print("row       ", show(A.rowspace()))      # nonzero rows of an echelon form
print("left null ", show(A.T.nullspace()))   # solutions of A^T y = 0
rank       2
column     [[1, 2, 3], [1, 3, 4]]
null       [[-2, 1, 0, 0], [-1, 0, -2, 1]]
row        [[1, 2, 1, 3], [0, 0, 1, 2]]
left null  [[-1, -1, 1]]

SymPy 1.14.0 gives a different basis for the row space. It uses an echelon form that is not reduced. That is fine. A space has many bases. The left null space vector is -1 times ours, which is also fine.

Rank on a real computer

Measured data always has small errors. Then a matrix that should have rank 2 looks like rank 3. NumPy decides the rank with the singular values from The spectral theorem and the SVD. It counts only the values above a small limit.

import numpy as np

A = np.array([[1.0, 2.0, 1.0, 3.0],
              [2.0, 4.0, 3.0, 8.0],
              [3.0, 6.0, 4.0, 11.0]])
print(np.linalg.matrix_rank(A))            # exact data: rank 2

rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
B = A + 1e-10 * rng.standard_normal(A.shape)  # tiny noise, like measured data
print(np.linalg.matrix_rank(B))            # the noise adds a direction
print(np.linalg.svd(B, compute_uv=False))  # one value is almost 0
print(np.linalg.matrix_rank(B, tol=1e-6))  # ignore values below 1e-6
2
3
[1.70214801e+01 5.18859748e-01 4.02629237e-11]
2

This ran with NumPy 2.5.4. The third singular value is tiny. With a sensible limit, the rank is 2 again. Choose the limit from the size of the errors in your data.

Linear maps and their matrices

Take polynomials of degree at most 2. Send each one to its derivative.

D(a + bx + cx^2) = b + 2cx

D keeps sums and multiples. The derivative of a sum is the sum of the derivatives. So D is linear, but there is no matrix in sight. Now choose the basis 1, x, x^2. A polynomial becomes its list of coordinates (a, b, c). Then D becomes a matrix.

\begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} a \\ b \\ c \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} b \\ 2c \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}

Check with 4 + 3x + 5x^2. The matrix gives (3, 10, 0), which means 3 + 10x. Correct.

A map T: V \to W between vector spaces is linear when T(\mathbf{u} + \mathbf{v}) = T(\mathbf{u}) + T(\mathbf{v}) and T(c\mathbf{u}) = cT(\mathbf{u}) for all vectors and scalars.

Choose a basis \mathbf{v}_1, \dots, \mathbf{v}_n of V and a basis of W. Column j of the matrix is the list of coordinates of T(\mathbf{v}_j).

For D: D(1) = 0, D(x) = 1 and D(x^2) = 2x. Their coordinates (0, 0, 0), (1, 0, 0), (0, 2, 0) are the three columns. This is the same rule as in Matrix operations: the columns show where the basis vectors land.

A linear map has two subspaces of its own.

  • The kernel \ker T holds all \mathbf{v} with T(\mathbf{v}) = \mathbf{0}. It is the null space of the matrix.
  • The image \operatorname{im} T holds all outputs. It is the column space of the matrix.

Rank-nullity holds for maps too: \dim \ker T + \dim \operatorname{im} T = \dim V. For D, the kernel is the constants, with dimension 1. The image is all polynomials b + 2cx, with dimension 2. And 1 + 2 = 3.

  • T is one-to-one exactly when \ker T = \{\mathbf{0}\}.
  • T is onto exactly when \operatorname{im} T = W.
  • A linear map that is both is an isomorphism. Coordinates give an isomorphism from any n-dimensional space to \mathbb{R}^n. So, in a sense, every such space is \mathbb{R}^n in disguise.

The map T(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{x} + (1, 0) looks simple, but it is not linear. T(\mathbf{0}) = (1, 0) \ne \mathbf{0}. A linear map always sends \mathbf{0} to \mathbf{0}.

Change of basis

Take the basis B of \mathbb{R}^2 with \mathbf{b}_1 = (1, 1) and \mathbf{b}_2 = (1, -1). What are the coordinates of \mathbf{v} = (5, 1) in this basis? We need c_1(1, 1) + c_2(1, -1) = (5, 1). So c_1 + c_2 = 5 and c_1 - c_2 = 1. The answer is c_1 = 3, c_2 = 2. We write [\mathbf{v}]_B = (3, 2).

Let P have the basis vectors of B as its columns. Then \mathbf{v} = P[\mathbf{v}]_B and [\mathbf{v}]_B = P^{-1}\mathbf{v}.

P is the change-of-basis matrix. It turns B-coordinates into standard coordinates. Its inverse goes the other way. Check: P(3, 2) = 3(1, 1) + 2(1, -1) = (5, 1). P is invertible because its columns form a basis.

A map in a better basis

The mirror in the line y = x has the matrix A = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}. Look at our basis. The mirror keeps \mathbf{b}_1 = (1, 1), because it lies on the line. It flips \mathbf{b}_2 = (1, -1) to -\mathbf{b}_2. So in basis B, the mirror is very simple.

[T]_B = P^{-1}AP = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 \end{pmatrix}

Let A be the matrix of T in the standard basis. In the basis B, the matrix of T is [T]_B = P^{-1}AP.

Proof

Read P^{-1}AP from right to left. P turns B-coordinates into standard coordinates. A applies T. P^{-1} turns the result back into B-coordinates. So P^{-1}AP takes [\mathbf{v}]_B to [T\mathbf{v}]_B. That is the matrix of T in basis B.

Two matrices with A' = P^{-1}AP are called similar. They describe the same map in two bases. So they share everything that does not depend on the basis. Rank is one example. A good basis makes a matrix diagonal. Finding that basis is the main goal of Eigenvalues and eigenvectors.

[\mathbf{v}]_B = P\mathbf{v}. This gives P(5, 1) = (6, 4), which is not (3, 2).

[\mathbf{v}]_B = P^{-1}\mathbf{v} = (3, 2). Remember: P takes you from B-coordinates.

When you write a change-of-basis matrix, say in words which way it goes. Different books use different names and letters. Check your direction with one vector, like we did with (5, 1).

Why learn abstract spaces if \mathbb{R}^n is enough?

Every finite-dimensional space is like \mathbb{R}^n after you pick a basis. But the best basis depends on the problem. Thinking without a basis lets you choose it later. Fourier series, for example, choose a basis of sines and cosines for signals.

Where do embeddings fit in?

An embedding model turns a word or a document into a vector in \mathbb{R}^n, often with hundreds of entries. Then sums, spans and subspaces get a meaning. Directions in the space can carry ideas like topic or tone. See The maths of vector search and agent memory.

Can a vector space have a basis with infinitely many vectors?

Yes. The polynomials have the basis 1, x, x^2, x^3, \dots. For bigger spaces, like all functions, a basis exists only with the axiom of choice. Nobody can write one down.

A short history

  1. 1844 Grassmann. Hermann Grassmann already uses ideas like linear independence and dimension. Few readers understand him at first.
  2. 1888 Peano. Giuseppe Peano gives the first modern axioms of a vector space. He calls them "linear systems".
  3. about 1920 Function spaces. Banach and others study spaces of functions with these axioms.
  4. 1993 The big picture. Gilbert Strang publishes "The Fundamental Theorem of Linear Algebra" about the four subspaces.

Practice

Which set is a subspace of \mathbb{R}^2?

  • All (x, y) with y = x + 1
  • All (x, y) with y = -3x
  • All (x, y) with x \ge 0

The first misses the origin. The third is not closed under scaling by -1.

Are (1, 2, 3), (4, 5, 6), (7, 8, 9) linearly independent?

  • Yes, because no two are parallel.
  • No, because the matrix with these columns has rank 2.
  • No, because there are three of them.

Elimination gives only 2 pivots. In fact the first plus the third is two times the second.

A 5 \times 7 matrix has rank 3. What is the dimension of its null space?

  • 2
  • 4
  • 3

Rank-nullity uses the number of columns: 7 − 3 = 4.

Which list is a basis of \mathbb{R}^2?

  • (1, 2), (2, 4)
  • (1, 2), (2, 1)
  • (1, 0), (0, 1), (1, 1)

The first pair is dependent. The third list has three vectors, which is one too many.

The polynomials of degree at most 3 have dimension ?.

A 4 \times 6 matrix has rank 4. Its left null space has dimension ?.

In the basis (1, 1), (1, -1), the vector (4, 2) has coordinates ( ? , ? ).

  1. Is the set of 2 \times 2 matrices with trace 0 a subspace? The trace is a_{11} + a_{22}. If yes, find its dimension.
    Answer

    Yes. The zero matrix has trace 0. Traces add, and they scale. A basis is \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 \end{pmatrix}, \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}, \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}. So the dimension is 3.

  2. Find the four fundamental subspaces of A = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 & 2 \\ 1 & 2 & 3 \\ 2 & 3 & 5 \end{pmatrix}. Give a basis and the dimension of each.
    Answer

    The reduced form is \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}, so r = 2. Column space: (1, 1, 2), (1, 2, 3). Row space: (1, 0, 1), (0, 1, 1). Null space: (-1, -1, 1), dimension 1. Left null space: (-1, -1, 1) too, dimension 1, because A is symmetric.

  3. Write 3 + 2x + x^2 in the basis 1, 1 + x, (1 + x)^2.
    Answer

    (1 + x)^2 = 1 + 2x + x^2. Subtract it: 3 + 2x + x^2 - (1 + x)^2 = 2. So the polynomial is 2 \cdot 1 + 0 \cdot (1 + x) + 1 \cdot (1 + x)^2. The coordinates are (2, 0, 1).

  4. Let U and W be subspaces of V. Show that the intersection U \cap W is a subspace. Then show that the union of the x-axis and the y-axis is not a subspace of \mathbb{R}^2.
    Answer

    \mathbf{0} is in both, so it is in U \cap W. If \mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v} are in both, then \mathbf{u} + \mathbf{v} and c\mathbf{u} are in both. For the union: (1, 0) and (0, 1) are in it, but (1, 1) is on neither axis.

  5. Find the matrix of the map T(a + bx + cx^2) = a + b(x + 1) + c(x + 1)^2 in the basis 1, x, x^2. It replaces x by x + 1. Is T invertible?
    Answer

    T(1) = 1, T(x) = 1 + x, T(x^2) = 1 + 2x + x^2. The columns are (1, 0, 0), (1, 1, 0), (1, 2, 1). The matrix \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix} is triangular with three pivots, so it is invertible. The inverse map replaces x by x - 1.

  6. Prove that \operatorname{rank}(AB) \le \operatorname{rank}(A) and \operatorname{rank}(AB) \le \operatorname{rank}(B).
    Answer

    Each column of AB is A times a column of B. So it is in C(A). Then C(AB) sits inside C(A), and its dimension is at most \operatorname{rank}(A). For the second part, B\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{0} gives AB\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{0}. So N(B) sits inside N(AB). By rank-nullity, \operatorname{rank}(AB) = n - \dim N(AB) \le n - \dim N(B) = \operatorname{rank}(B).

  7. An embedding model gives 768 numbers for each sentence. You store 10 000 sentences as the rows of a matrix X. What is the largest possible rank of X? What does a rank of 50 tell you?
    Answer

    The rank is at most \min(10\,000, 768) = 768. A rank of 50 means all the sentence vectors lie in a subspace of dimension 50. You could store each one with 50 coordinates in a good basis and lose nothing.

Key takeaways

  • A vector space is any set where addition and scaling follow the usual rules.
  • A subspace contains \mathbf{0} and is closed under sums and multiples.
  • The span of some vectors is all their combinations. It is always a subspace.
  • Independent vectors each add a new direction. Test them with pivots.
  • A basis spans and is independent. Every basis of a space has the same size, the dimension.
  • Every matrix has four subspaces with dimensions r, n - r, r and m - r.
  • Rank plus nullity equals the number of columns.
  • The columns of the matrix of a linear map are the images of the basis vectors.
  • In a new basis, a map has the matrix P^{-1}AP. A good basis makes it simple.

Sources

  • Interactive Linear Algebra, section 2.7: Basis and Dimension. An open textbook. Bases of column spaces and null spaces, and the basis theorem.
  • Interactive Linear Algebra: The Rank Theorem. Rank, nullity and the proof by counting columns.
  • MIT OpenCourseWare 18.06SC: The Four Fundamental Subspaces. Gilbert Strang's course unit on the four subspaces.
  • Rank-nullity theorem. Statements for matrices and linear maps, with two proofs.
  • Steinitz exchange lemma. The counting lemma behind "all bases have the same size".
  • numpy.linalg.matrix_rank. How NumPy decides the rank with singular values and a tolerance.

Determinants

A square matrix stretches space. The determinant is one number that says by how much. Its sign says if space was flipped. When the determinant is zero, space is squashed flat, and the matrix has no inverse.

  • Read a determinant as a signed area or volume.
  • Compute 2 × 2 and 3 × 3 determinants, and use cofactor expansion for bigger ones.
  • Compute a determinant fast with row operations.
  • Use the main properties, like \det(AB) = \det A \det B.
  • Find an inverse with the adjugate and solve a small system with Cramer's rule.

Area with a sign

Take the matrix with columns (3, 1) and (1, 2). It sends the unit square to a parallelogram. The corners are (0, 0), (3, 1), (4, 3) and (1, 2). What is its area?

Put a 4 × 3 box around the parallelogram. Its area is 12. Cut away the corners: two triangles of area 1.5, two triangles of area 1, and two small squares of area 1. That leaves 12 - 3 - 2 - 2 = 5. Now look at the matrix entries: 3 \cdot 2 - 1 \cdot 1 = 5. This is no accident.

\det \begin{pmatrix} a & b \\ c & d \end{pmatrix} = \begin{vmatrix} a & b \\ c & d \end{vmatrix} = ad - bc

The determinant is written \det A or with straight bars |A|. For a 2 × 2 matrix, |\det A| is the area of the parallelogram made by the columns. The sign tells the orientation.

  • Positive: turn from column 1 to column 2 against the clock, like from (1, 0) to (0, 1).
  • Negative: the turn goes with the clock. The plane was flipped, like in a mirror. Swap the columns above: 1 \cdot 1 - 3 \cdot 2 = -5.
  • Zero: the columns lie on one line. The plane is squashed flat. Right picture: 2 \cdot 2 - 4 \cdot 1 = 0.

So \det A is a signed area. It is also the factor that scales every area. Any shape of area 2 becomes a shape of area 2 \cdot 5 = 10 under our matrix.

The formula is "main diagonal minus the other diagonal": ad - bc. Do not compute ab - cd. Also, only square matrices have a determinant. A 2 \times 3 matrix has none.

3 × 3 determinants and volume

In space, three columns make a slanted box. It is called a parallelepiped. Its volume, with a sign, is the 3 × 3 determinant. Here is the formula.

\begin{vmatrix} a & b & c \\ d & e & f \\ g & h & i \end{vmatrix} = aei + bfg + cdh - ceg - afh - bdi

There is a picture to remember it. It is called the rule of Sarrus. Copy the first two columns to the right. Add the three products going down to the right. Subtract the three products going up to the right.

  1. Take M = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 & 3 \\ 0 & 4 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 & 2 \end{pmatrix}.
  2. Down products: 2 \cdot 4 \cdot 2 = 16, 1 \cdot 1 \cdot 1 = 1, 3 \cdot 0 \cdot 0 = 0. Sum: 17.
  3. Up products: 3 \cdot 4 \cdot 1 = 12, 2 \cdot 1 \cdot 0 = 0, 1 \cdot 0 \cdot 2 = 0. Sum: 12.
  4. \det M = 17 - 12 = 5. The box made by the columns has volume 5.

Let A be n \times n. Then |\det A| is the volume of the box made by the columns of A. The matrix multiplies every volume by |\det A|.

"Volume" here means length for n = 1, area for n = 2 and normal volume for n = 3. For larger n it is the same idea in more dimensions. A proof idea comes in the section on row operations.

Sarrus works only for 3 × 3 matrices. For a 4 × 4 matrix the same picture gives a wrong answer. The full formula has 24 products, not 8. Use cofactor expansion or row operations instead.

Cofactor expansion

Bigger determinants are built from smaller ones. Look at the 3 × 3 formula again. Group it by the entries of row 1.

\det M = a(ei - fh) - b(di - fg) + c(dh - eg)

Each bracket is a 2 × 2 determinant. Delete the row and the column of the entry. The four numbers left give that small determinant.

The minor M_{ij} is the determinant of A without row i and column j. The cofactor is C_{ij} = (-1)^{i + j} M_{ij}.

A minor is a smaller determinant. A cofactor is a minor with a sign. The sign follows a chessboard pattern, starting with plus in the top left corner.

\begin{pmatrix} + & - & + & - \\ - & + & - & + \\ + & - & + & - \\ - & + & - & + \end{pmatrix}

For any row i: \det A = a_{i1}C_{i1} + a_{i2}C_{i2} + \cdots + a_{in}C_{in}. For any column j: \det A = a_{1j}C_{1j} + \cdots + a_{nj}C_{nj}. Every row and every column gives the same number.

In simple words: pick any row or column. Multiply each entry by its cofactor. Add. Choose the row or column with the most zeros. Then you have less work.

  1. Take M from Example 1. Column 2 is (1, 4, 0). Its signs are -, +, -.
  2. Entry 1: delete row 1 and column 2. The minor is \begin{vmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 \end{vmatrix} = -1. With the minus sign: -1 \cdot (-1) = 1.
  3. Entry 4: delete row 2 and column 2. The minor is \begin{vmatrix} 2 & 3 \\ 1 & 2 \end{vmatrix} = 1. With the plus sign: 4 \cdot 1 = 4.
  4. Entry 0: its term is 0. No work needed.
  5. \det M = 1 + 4 + 0 = 5. Same as before.
  1. Take B = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 & 2 & 0 \\ 3 & 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 & 0 & 3 \end{pmatrix}. Column 2 has only one nonzero entry, the 1 in row 2.
  2. Its sign is (-1)^{2 + 2} = +. Delete row 2 and column 2. \det B = +1 \cdot \begin{vmatrix} 1 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 & 3 \end{vmatrix}
  3. Expand the 3 × 3 along row 1: 1(6 - 0) - 2(0 - 1) + 0 = 8.
  4. So \det B = 8.

For a triangular matrix this is very fast. Expand along the first column again and again. Only the diagonal entry survives each time. So the determinant is the product of the diagonal entries. For example, \begin{vmatrix} 2 & 7 \\ 0 & 3 \end{vmatrix} = 6.

Proof idea for the cofactor expansion

Expand completely, down to single entries. Each final product takes one entry from each row and each column. So it belongs to a way of matching rows to columns, called a permutation. This gives the Leibniz formula below. Expanding along any row or column gives the same products with the same signs. So all expansions agree.

The full formula

Here is the formula behind everything. It is the Leibniz formula.

\det A = \sum_{\sigma} \operatorname{sgn}(\sigma)\, a_{1\sigma(1)} a_{2\sigma(2)} \cdots a_{n\sigma(n)}

The sum runs over all permutations \sigma of 1, \dots, n. The sign \operatorname{sgn}(\sigma) is +1 for an even number of swaps and -1 for an odd number. There are n! terms. For n = 3 that is 6 terms, the six products of Sarrus. For n = 10 it is 3 628 800 terms. For n = 20 it is about 2.4 \cdot 10^{18}. Nobody computes big determinants this way.

Do not forget the chessboard signs. The entry in row 1, column 2 always gets a minus sign. A missing sign is the most common error in exams.

Row operations and the determinant

The fast way uses elimination. First we need to know how each row operation changes the determinant. The area picture makes the rules easy to believe.

The identity has determinant 1

I keeps the unit square. Its area is 1. So \det I = 1.

Replace: no change

R_i \to R_i + cR_j is a shear. A shear slides a shape but keeps its area. So the determinant stays the same.

Scale: multiply by c

R_i \to cR_i stretches one side by c. The area is multiplied by c. So the determinant is multiplied by c.

Swap: change the sign

R_i \leftrightarrow R_j turns the orientation around. The area stays, but the sign flips. So the determinant is multiplied by -1.

A replace step does not change \det A. Scaling a row by c multiplies \det A by c. A swap multiplies \det A by -1. Also \det I = 1.

Proof idea

Scale. Expand along the scaled row. Every term gets the factor c.

Swap. For two neighbour rows, the minors stay the same but the chessboard signs flip. Any swap is an odd number of neighbour swaps. As a result, a matrix with two equal rows has determinant 0: swapping them changes nothing but flips the sign.

Replace. The determinant is linear in each row. So \det with row R_i + cR_j is \det A plus c times the determinant of a matrix with two equal rows. That second part is 0.

Now compute \det A by elimination. Reach an echelon form U. It is triangular, so \det U is the product of the pivots. Keep track of swaps and scalings on the way.

  1. Take C = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 & 1 \\ 2 & 1 & 3 \end{pmatrix}. The corner is 0.
  2. Swap rows 1 and 2. The sign flips. Now rows are (1, 1, 1), (0, 2, 1), (2, 1, 3).
  3. Use R_3 \to R_3 - 2R_1. No change. Row 3 is (0, -1, 1).
  4. Use R_3 \to R_3 + \tfrac{1}{2}R_2. No change. Row 3 is (0, 0, \tfrac{3}{2}).
  5. The pivots are 1, 2, \tfrac{3}{2}. Their product is 3. One swap gives \det C = -3.

\det A^{\mathsf{T}} = \det A.

Expanding A along row 1 is the same as expanding A^{\mathsf{T}} along column 1. So every rule for rows is also a rule for columns. A matrix with a zero column, or two equal columns, has determinant 0.

The same steps in code. Elimination needs about \tfrac{2}{3}n^3 steps, not n!.

# Determinant by elimination with partial pivoting.
def det(a):
    m = [row[:] for row in a]          # work on a copy
    n = len(m)
    result = 1.0
    for col in range(n):
        best = max(range(col, n), key=lambda r: abs(m[r][col]))
        if m[best][col] == 0:
            return 0.0                 # no pivot: the matrix is singular
        if best != col:
            m[col], m[best] = m[best], m[col]
            result = -result           # a swap changes the sign
        for r in range(col + 1, n):
            f = m[r][col] / m[col][col]
            for c in range(col, n):
                m[r][c] -= f * m[col][c]   # replace: no change
        result *= m[col][col]          # multiply the pivots
    return result

print(det([[0.0, 2.0, 1.0], [1.0, 1.0, 1.0], [2.0, 1.0, 3.0]]))
print(det([[2.0, 1.0, 3.0], [0.0, 4.0, 1.0], [1.0, 0.0, 2.0]]))
// Determinant by elimination with partial pivoting.
fn det(a: &[Vec<f64>]) -> f64 {
    let mut m = a.to_vec(); // work on a copy
    let n = m.len();
    let mut result = 1.0;
    for col in 0..n {
        let best = (col..n)
            .max_by(|&i, &j| m[i][col].abs().total_cmp(&m[j][col].abs()))
            .unwrap();
        if m[best][col] == 0.0 {
            return 0.0; // no pivot: the matrix is singular
        }
        if best != col {
            m.swap(col, best);
            result = -result; // a swap changes the sign
        }
        for r in col + 1..n {
            let f = m[r][col] / m[col][col];
            for c in col..n {
                m[r][c] -= f * m[col][c]; // replace: no change
            }
        }
        result *= m[col][col]; // multiply the pivots
    }
    result
}

fn main() {
    let c = vec![vec![0.0, 2.0, 1.0], vec![1.0, 1.0, 1.0], vec![2.0, 1.0, 3.0]];
    let m = vec![vec![2.0, 1.0, 3.0], vec![0.0, 4.0, 1.0], vec![1.0, 0.0, 2.0]];
    println!("{:?}", det(&c));
    println!("{:?}", det(&m));
}
-3.0
5.0
Why the determinant is the volume

Volume follows the same four rules, if we forget the sign. The unit cube has volume 1. A shear keeps volume. Stretching one edge by c multiplies the volume by |c|. Changing the order of the edges keeps the volume. Elimination reduces every matrix with these rules. So |\det A| and the volume agree on every matrix.

Scaling a row changes the determinant. If you divide a row by 2 to get a pivot 1, the new determinant is half the old one. Write the factor down. Or use only replace steps and swaps.

Properties of the determinant

Take A = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 3 & 4 \end{pmatrix} and B = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 0 \\ 1 & 3 \end{pmatrix}. Then \det A = -2 and \det B = 6. Their product is AB = \begin{pmatrix} 4 & 6 \\ 10 & 12 \end{pmatrix}. Its determinant is 48 - 60 = -12. That is exactly (-2) \cdot 6.

For n \times n matrices, \det(AB) = \det A \cdot \det B.

In simple words: B scales volumes by \det B. Then A scales them by \det A. Together they scale by the product. This is the picture from Matrix operations: a product is one move after another.

Proof

If A is singular, so is AB. Both sides are 0. Otherwise A is a product of elementary matrices E_1 \cdots E_k. For one elementary matrix, \det(EB) = \det E \cdot \det B. This is just the row operation rules, because EB is a row operation on B. Apply this k times. You get \det(AB) = \det E_1 \cdots \det E_k \cdot \det B = \det A \cdot \det B.

A square matrix A is invertible if and only if \det A \ne 0. Then \det(A^{-1}) = \dfrac{1}{\det A}.

In simple words: a matrix with determinant 0 squashes space flat. Many points land on one point, so nothing can undo it. For example, \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 2 & 4 \end{pmatrix} has determinant 0. It has no inverse. This adds one more face to the invertible matrix theorem.

Proof

Reduce A to an echelon form U with swaps and replace steps. Then \det A = \pm \det U. U is triangular, so \det U is the product of its diagonal. If A has n pivots, all diagonal entries are nonzero, so \det A \ne 0. If not, the last row of U is zero, so \det A = 0. And A is invertible exactly when it has n pivots. For the inverse: \det A \cdot \det A^{-1} = \det I = 1.

More properties (A and B are n × n)
PropertyExampleWhy
\det(cA) = c^n \det ADouble a 2 × 2 matrix: area × 4Each of the n rows gets a factor c
\det A^{\mathsf{T}} = \det A\begin{vmatrix} 1 & 3 \\ 2 & 4 \end{vmatrix} = -2Rows and columns play the same role
Two equal rows give 0\begin{vmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 1 & 2 \end{vmatrix} = 0The box is flat
Linear in each single rowSplit one row as a sum, keep the othersEach term of the formula has one entry from that row
\det(P^{-1}AP) = \det ASame map, new basis\det P^{-1} \cdot \det P = 1
\det \begin{pmatrix} A & B \\ O & D \end{pmatrix} = \det A \det DBlock triangular matricesEliminate inside each block

\det(A + B) is usually not \det A + \det B. Take A = B = I_2. Then \det(2I) = 4, but \det I + \det I = 2. The determinant is multiplicative, not additive.

On a computer, be careful with the size of a determinant. It is a bad test for "almost singular".

import numpy as np

A = 0.1 * np.eye(500)                  # a very nice matrix: 0.1 times I
print(np.linalg.det(A))                # 0.1 ** 500 is too small for a float
sign, logdet = np.linalg.slogdet(A)    # sign and log of |det|
print(sign, logdet)
print(np.linalg.cond(A))               # condition number: perfect

B = np.array([[1.0, 2.0], [1.0, 2.0 + 1e-12]])
print(np.linalg.det(B))                # tiny, and B is nearly singular
print(np.linalg.cond(B))               # huge condition number
0.0
1.0 -1151.2925464970251
1.0
1.0000889005823404e-12
9999385523069.027

This ran with NumPy 2.5.4. The matrix 0.1I is easy to invert. But its determinant 10^{-500} is too small for a float, so NumPy prints 0. slogdet returns the sign and the logarithm instead, which never overflows. To test for "almost singular", use the condition number. It is 1 for 0.1I and about 10^{13} for B. See Numerical methods.

The adjugate and Cramer's rule

Cofactors also give a formula for the inverse. Put all cofactors of A in a matrix. Then transpose it.

The adjugate \operatorname{adj}(A) is the transpose of the matrix of cofactors: \operatorname{adj}(A)_{ij} = C_{ji}.

A \operatorname{adj}(A) = \operatorname{adj}(A) A = (\det A) I. So, when \det A \ne 0, A^{-1} = \dfrac{1}{\det A}\operatorname{adj}(A).

Proof

Entry (i, i) of A \operatorname{adj}(A) is row i of A times the cofactors of row i. That is the cofactor expansion along row i. It equals \det A.

Entry (i, j) with i \ne j is row i of A times the cofactors of row j. This is the expansion of a new matrix: A with row j replaced by row i. That matrix has two equal rows. So its determinant is 0.

  1. Take M = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 & 3 \\ 0 & 4 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 & 2 \end{pmatrix} with \det M = 5.
  2. Row 1 cofactors: C_{11} = +(8 - 0) = 8, C_{12} = -(0 - 1) = 1, C_{13} = +(0 - 4) = -4.
  3. Row 2 cofactors: C_{21} = -(2 - 0) = -2, C_{22} = +(4 - 3) = 1, C_{23} = -(0 - 1) = 1.
  4. Row 3 cofactors: C_{31} = +(1 - 12) = -11, C_{32} = -(2 - 0) = -2, C_{33} = +(8 - 0) = 8.
  5. Put them in a matrix and transpose it. \operatorname{adj}(M) = \begin{pmatrix} 8 & -2 & -11 \\ 1 & 1 & -2 \\ -4 & 1 & 8 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad M^{-1} = \frac{1}{5}\begin{pmatrix} 8 & -2 & -11 \\ 1 & 1 & -2 \\ -4 & 1 & 8 \end{pmatrix}
  6. Check one entry. Row 1 of M times column 1 of \operatorname{adj}(M) is 16 + 1 - 12 = 5. Divided by 5, it is 1. Good.

For a 2 × 2 matrix, the cofactors are d, -c, -b, a. After the transpose, you get the formula from Matrix operations: \frac{1}{ad - bc}\begin{pmatrix} d & -b \\ -c & a \end{pmatrix}.

Cramer's rule

Solve 2x + y = 5 and 5x + 3y = 13. The matrix A = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 5 & 3 \end{pmatrix} has \det A = 1. Replace column 1 by the right side (5, 13). Then replace column 2 by it.

x = \frac{\begin{vmatrix} 5 & 1 \\ 13 & 3 \end{vmatrix}}{\det A} = \frac{15 - 13}{1} = 2, \qquad y = \frac{\begin{vmatrix} 2 & 5 \\ 5 & 13 \end{vmatrix}}{\det A} = \frac{26 - 25}{1} = 1

Check: 4 + 1 = 5 and 10 + 3 = 13. Correct.

Let \det A \ne 0. Let A_i be A with column i replaced by \mathbf{b}. Then the unique solution of A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b} is x_i = \dfrac{\det A_i}{\det A} for each i.

Proof

\mathbf{x} = A^{-1}\mathbf{b} = \frac{1}{\det A}\operatorname{adj}(A)\mathbf{b}. Entry i of \operatorname{adj}(A)\mathbf{b} is C_{1i}b_1 + \cdots + C_{ni}b_n. This is the cofactor expansion of \det A_i along column i. The cofactors of column i do not see column i itself, so they are the same for A and A_i.

Try it on the machine system from Linear systems and elimination. There \det A = 2. The three new determinants are 2, 4 and 6. So x = 1, y = 2 and z = 3, as before.

Cramer's rule needs n + 1 determinants. For large systems this is far slower than elimination. Use it for 2 × 2 and 3 × 3 systems, for systems with letters in them, and for proofs.

A question often asks: "For which k is the system uniquely solvable?" Compute \det A as a polynomial in k. The answer is all k where it is not zero. Then study the zeros one by one with elimination.

Where determinants appear

Eigenvalues

A number \lambda is an eigenvalue of A when A - \lambda I is singular. So we solve \det(A - \lambda I) = 0. For A = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 \end{pmatrix} this gives (2 - \lambda)^2 - 1 = \lambda^2 - 4\lambda + 3.

This polynomial is the characteristic polynomial. The chapter Eigenvalues and eigenvectors starts here.

Change of variables

A curved map is almost linear on a tiny piece. Its matrix of partial derivatives is the Jacobian matrix J. The number |\det J| says how much the map stretches tiny areas. For polar coordinates x = r\cos\theta, y = r\sin\theta, you get \det J = r. That is why dx\,dy = r\,dr\,d\theta. See Multiple integrals. Some generative models in machine learning, called normalizing flows, need \log|\det J| for every input. They use maps with triangular J, so the determinant is just the product of the diagonal.

Geometry in code

  • Left or right? Is the point C to the left of the line from A to B? Compute \det of the columns B - A and C - A. Positive means left. For A = (0, 0), B = (4, 0), C = (1, 2): 4 \cdot 2 - 1 \cdot 0 = 8 \gt 0, so C is on the left. Graphics and map software use this test all the time.
  • Triangle area. The triangle ABC has area \tfrac{1}{2}|\det(B - A, C - A)|.
  • Cross product. In Vectors and analytic geometry, \mathbf{u} \times \mathbf{v} is a "determinant" with \mathbf{i}, \mathbf{j}, \mathbf{k} in the first row.
Why is a swap a sign change, and not something else?

Look at \begin{vmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{vmatrix} = -1. This matrix is the mirror in the line y = x. A mirror keeps area but reverses the turning direction. The sign records exactly that.

Do non-square matrices have anything like a determinant?

Not a determinant. But \sqrt{\det(A^{\mathsf{T}}A)} gives the area or volume of the box made by the columns. For two vectors in space, it is the area of their parallelogram.

Is the determinant the product of the eigenvalues?

Yes, counted with multiplicity and allowing complex numbers. For \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 \end{pmatrix}: 1 \cdot 3 = 3 = 4 - 1.

A short history

  1. 1683 Seki Takakazu. In Japan, Seki works with determinants to eliminate unknowns.
  2. 1693 Leibniz. In Europe, Leibniz finds the same idea on his own.
  3. 1750 Cramer. Gabriel Cramer states his rule, without proof.
  4. 1772 Laplace. He gives the general expansion method.
  5. 1812 Binet and Cauchy. Both state the product theorem. Cauchy uses "determinant" in today's sense.
  6. 1841 Cayley. He introduces the two vertical bars, |A|.
