Practice

What is \begin{vmatrix} 4 & 1 \\ 2 & 3 \end{vmatrix}?

  • 14
  • 10
  • 2

4 \cdot 3 - 1 \cdot 2 = 12 - 2 = 10.

\det A = 3. You swap two rows of A. What is the new determinant?

  • 3
  • −3
  • 0

A swap multiplies the determinant by −1.

A is 3 × 3 with \det A = 2. What is \det(2A)?

  • 4
  • 6
  • 16

\det(2A) = 2^3 \det A = 8 \cdot 2 = 16.

Which statement is true for every square matrix?

  • \det(A + B) = \det A + \det B
  • \det(A^{\mathsf{T}}) = \det A
  • \det(-A) = -\det A

The transpose keeps the determinant. \det(-A) = (-1)^n \det A, which equals -\det A only for odd n.

\det \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 0 & 0 \\ 5 & 3 & 0 \\ 1 & 7 & -1 \end{pmatrix} = ?

If \det A = 4, then \det(A^{-1}) = ?.

The cofactor sign in row 2, column 3 is ?.

  1. Find the area of the triangle with corners (1, 1), (4, 2) and (2, 5).
    Answer

    Use the sides from (1, 1): (3, 1) and (1, 4). The determinant is 3 \cdot 4 - 1 \cdot 1 = 11. The area is half of it: 5.5.

  2. Compute \begin{vmatrix} 1 & 2 & 3 \\ 4 & 5 & 6 \\ 7 & 8 & 10 \end{vmatrix} with row operations.
    Answer

    R_2 - 4R_1 gives (0, -3, -6). R_3 - 7R_1 gives (0, -6, -11). R_3 - 2R_2 gives (0, 0, 1). No swaps, so the determinant is 1 \cdot (-3) \cdot 1 = -3.

  3. For which k is \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & k & 1 \\ 1 & 1 & k \end{pmatrix} invertible?
    Answer

    Subtract row 1 from rows 2 and 3. You get a triangular matrix with diagonal 1, k - 1, k - 1. So the determinant is (k - 1)^2. The matrix is invertible for every k \ne 1.

  4. Use Cramer's rule to solve x + 2y = 4 and 3x - y = 5.
    Answer

    \det A = -1 - 6 = -7. \det A_1 = \begin{vmatrix} 4 & 2 \\ 5 & -1 \end{vmatrix} = -14, so x = 2. \det A_2 = \begin{vmatrix} 1 & 4 \\ 3 & 5 \end{vmatrix} = -7, so y = 1. Check: 2 + 2 = 4 and 6 - 1 = 5.

  5. An orthogonal matrix satisfies Q^{\mathsf{T}}Q = I. Show that \det Q is 1 or -1.
    Answer

    \det(Q^{\mathsf{T}}Q) = \det Q^{\mathsf{T}} \det Q = (\det Q)^2. And \det I = 1. So (\det Q)^2 = 1. Rotations have +1. Mirrors have -1.

  6. Show that \begin{vmatrix} 1 & a & a^2 \\ 1 & b & b^2 \\ 1 & c & c^2 \end{vmatrix} = (b - a)(c - a)(c - b). This is a Vandermonde determinant.
    Answer

    Subtract row 1 from rows 2 and 3. They become (0, b - a, b^2 - a^2) and (0, c - a, c^2 - a^2). Take out b - a and c - a. The rows become (0, 1, b + a) and (0, 1, c + a). Expand along column 1: (c + a) - (b + a) = c - b. So the determinant is (b - a)(c - a)(c - b). It is not zero when a, b, c are all different. That is why a parabola through three points always exists.

  7. A 3 × 3 matrix has integer entries and determinant \pm 1. Why does its inverse have integer entries too?
    Answer

    The cofactors are sums of products of integers. So \operatorname{adj}(A) has integer entries. Then A^{-1} = \operatorname{adj}(A) / (\pm 1) has integer entries as well.

Key takeaways

  • The determinant is the signed area or volume factor of a square matrix.
  • For 2 × 2 it is ad - bc. Sarrus works for 3 × 3 only.
  • Cofactor expansion works along any row or column. Choose one with zeros.
  • Replace keeps it, scale multiplies it, swap flips its sign.
  • Fast method: eliminate, then multiply the pivots and fix the sign.
  • \det(AB) = \det A \det B, and \det A^{\mathsf{T}} = \det A.
  • A square matrix is invertible exactly when its determinant is not zero.
  • The adjugate gives A^{-1}. Cramer's rule gives each unknown. Both are for small matrices and proofs.
  • On a computer, use slogdet for size and the condition number for "almost singular".

Sources

  • Interactive Linear Algebra, section 4.1: Determinants, Definition. An open textbook. The four defining rules and the main properties.
  • Interactive Linear Algebra, section 4.3: Determinants and Volumes. Why the determinant measures volume.
  • Determinant. The Leibniz formula, the cost of computing, and the history.
  • Cramer's rule. The statement, the proof with cofactors and the cost.
  • numpy.linalg.slogdet. The official NumPy page for the sign and log of a determinant.

Eigenvalues and eigenvectors

A matrix turns most vectors to a new direction. A few special vectors do not turn. They only get longer or shorter. These vectors show what the matrix really does. They explain growth, the long run of a process, Google's PageRank and the stability of many systems.

  • Find eigenvalues with the characteristic polynomial and eigenvectors with elimination.
  • Decide if a matrix is diagonalisable and write it as A = PDP^{-1}.
  • Compute powers of a matrix and predict what happens in the long run.
  • Use the Perron-Frobenius theorem to explain Markov chains and PageRank.
  • Read complex eigenvalues as turns and explain the Jordan form in simple words.

Vectors that keep their direction

Take the matrix A = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 \end{pmatrix}. Multiply three vectors by it.

What A does to three vectors
Vector \mathbf{v}A\mathbf{v}What happened
(1, 0)(2, 1)It turned to a new direction.
(1, 1)(3, 3) = 3(1, 1)Same direction, 3 times longer.
(1, -1)(1, -1)It did not change at all.

The vectors (1, 1) and (1, -1) are special. The matrix keeps them on their own line. We give them a name.

Let A be an n \times n matrix. A vector \mathbf{v} \ne \mathbf{0} with A\mathbf{v} = \lambda\mathbf{v} is an eigenvector of A. The number \lambda is its eigenvalue.

An eigenvector keeps its direction. Its eigenvalue \lambda (the Greek letter lambda) says how much it stretches. "Eigen" is German for "own". An eigenvector is a direction that belongs to the matrix itself. For our A, the eigenvalues are 3 and 1. The chapter Determinants found the same two numbers.

  • \lambda \gt 1: the vector gets longer.
  • 0 \lt \lambda \lt 1: the vector gets shorter.
  • \lambda \lt 0: the vector flips to the other side.
  • \lambda = 0: the matrix sends the vector to \mathbf{0}.

\begin{pmatrix} 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 1/2 \end{pmatrix}

The x-axis stretches by 3. The y-axis shrinks by 1/2. Eigenvectors: (1, 0) with \lambda = 3, (0, 1) with \lambda = 1/2.

\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}

It drops every point onto the x-axis. Points on the axis stay: \lambda = 1. Points on the y-axis go to zero: \lambda = 0.

\begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}

The mirror in the line y = x. It keeps (1, 1): \lambda = 1. It flips (1, -1): \lambda = -1.

\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}

It slides each row of points to the right. Only the x-axis keeps its direction, with \lambda = 1. There is no second eigenvector direction.

\begin{pmatrix} 0 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}

A turn by 90 degrees. Every arrow turns. So there is no real eigenvector. The eigenvalues are complex. We meet them later in this chapter.

The zero vector is never an eigenvector. A\mathbf{0} = \lambda\mathbf{0} is true for every \lambda, so it tells us nothing. But the eigenvalue \lambda = 0 is allowed. It means A\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{0} for some \mathbf{v} \ne \mathbf{0}. So A is not invertible.

A matrix moves every arrow. Most arrows turn. Eigenvectors stay on their own line. The eigenvalue is the stretch factor. Any nonzero multiple of an eigenvector is also an eigenvector, with the same eigenvalue.

The characteristic polynomial

How do we find the eigenvalues of A = \begin{pmatrix} 4 & 1 \\ 2 & 3 \end{pmatrix}? Write A\mathbf{v} = \lambda\mathbf{v} as A\mathbf{v} - \lambda I\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{0}. So (A - \lambda I)\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{0}. We want a solution \mathbf{v} \ne \mathbf{0}. That happens exactly when A - \lambda I is not invertible.

  1. Subtract \lambda on the diagonal. A - \lambda I = \begin{pmatrix} 4 - \lambda & 1 \\ 2 & 3 - \lambda \end{pmatrix}
  2. Take the determinant. (4 - \lambda)(3 - \lambda) - 1 \cdot 2 = \lambda^2 - 7\lambda + 10
  3. Set it to zero and factor. \lambda^2 - 7\lambda + 10 = (\lambda - 2)(\lambda - 5) = 0
  4. The eigenvalues are \lambda = 2 and \lambda = 5.

A number \lambda is an eigenvalue of the square matrix A exactly when \det(A - \lambda I) = 0.

Proof

\lambda is an eigenvalue when (A - \lambda I)\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{0} has a solution \mathbf{v} \ne \mathbf{0}. By the invertible matrix theorem, that happens exactly when A - \lambda I is not invertible. By the determinant test, that happens exactly when \det(A - \lambda I) = 0.

The function p(\lambda) = \det(A - \lambda I) is the characteristic polynomial of A. For an n \times n matrix it has degree n. So A has at most n different eigenvalues. Some books use \det(\lambda I - A) instead. It differs only by the sign (-1)^n, so the roots are the same.

A shortcut for 2 × 2 matrices

The trace of a matrix is the sum of its diagonal entries. For A above, \operatorname{tr} A = 4 + 3 = 7 and \det A = 12 - 2 = 10. Look at the polynomial again: \lambda^2 - 7\lambda + 10. The trace and the determinant are its coefficients.

\det(A - \lambda I) = \lambda^2 - (\operatorname{tr} A)\,\lambda + \det A \qquad \text{for every } 2 \times 2 \text{ matrix.}

Let \lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_n be the eigenvalues of A, complex ones included, each repeated as often as it is a root. Then \lambda_1 + \cdots + \lambda_n = \operatorname{tr} A and \lambda_1 \lambda_2 \cdots \lambda_n = \det A.

Proof

By the fundamental theorem of algebra, p(\lambda) = (\lambda_1 - \lambda)(\lambda_2 - \lambda)\cdots(\lambda_n - \lambda). Put \lambda = 0. The left side is \det A. The right side is the product of the eigenvalues.

Now look at the coefficient of \lambda^{n-1}. On the right it is (-1)^{n-1}(\lambda_1 + \cdots + \lambda_n). On the left, only the product of the diagonal entries (a_{11} - \lambda)\cdots(a_{nn} - \lambda) has a \lambda^{n-1} term. It gives (-1)^{n-1}(a_{11} + \cdots + a_{nn}). So the sum of the eigenvalues is the trace.

Check with our example: 2 + 5 = 7 is the trace. 2 \cdot 5 = 10 is the determinant. This check takes five seconds. Use it every time.

A 3 × 3 example

Take S = \begin{pmatrix} 3 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 3 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 & 3 \end{pmatrix}. Cofactor expansion gives \det(\lambda I - S) = \lambda^3 - 9\lambda^2 + 24\lambda - 20 = (\lambda - 5)(\lambda - 2)^2. The root 2 appears twice. Check: 5 + 2 + 2 = 9 = \operatorname{tr} S and 5 \cdot 2 \cdot 2 = 20 = \det S.

For a triangular matrix, the eigenvalues are the diagonal entries. The determinant of a triangular matrix is the product of its diagonal. So \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 7 & 1 \\ 0 & 3 & 5 \\ 0 & 0 & -1 \end{pmatrix} has eigenvalues 2, 3 and -1. No work is needed.

Row reduce first: \begin{pmatrix} 4 & 1 \\ 2 & 3 \end{pmatrix} \to \begin{pmatrix} 4 & 1 \\ 0 & 2.5 \end{pmatrix}. Then read the diagonal: 4 and 2.5.

Row operations change the eigenvalues. Use \det(A - \lambda I) = 0 on A itself. The eigenvalues are 5 and 2.

For n \ge 5 there is no general formula for the roots of a polynomial. This is the Abel-Ruffini theorem. So computers never find eigenvalues by solving p(\lambda) = 0. They use clever repeated steps instead. You see this at the end of the chapter.

Eigenspaces and multiplicity

We know the eigenvalues of A = \begin{pmatrix} 4 & 1 \\ 2 & 3 \end{pmatrix}. Now find the eigenvectors. For each \lambda, solve (A - \lambda I)\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{0} by elimination.

  1. \lambda = 5: A - 5I = \begin{pmatrix} -1 & 1 \\ 2 & -2 \end{pmatrix}. Both rows say x = y. Take \mathbf{v}_1 = (1, 1).
  2. \lambda = 2: A - 2I = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 2 & 1 \end{pmatrix}. Both rows say 2x + y = 0. Take \mathbf{v}_2 = (1, -2).
  3. Check \mathbf{v}_2. A(1, -2) = (4 - 2,\; 2 - 6) = (2, -4) = 2(1, -2). Correct.

For an eigenvalue, the matrix A - \lambda I always loses rank. So elimination always gives at least one free variable. If you find only the zero solution, your \lambda is wrong.

The eigenspace of \lambda is E_\lambda = N(A - \lambda I). It holds all eigenvectors for \lambda and the zero vector.

An eigenspace is a null space. So it is a subspace, as in Vector spaces. Its dimension can be more than 1.

Two eigenvectors for 2. For S above, S - 2I is the matrix of all ones. Its rank is 1. So E_2 is the plane x + y + z = 0, with basis (-1, 1, 0) and (-1, 0, 1). E_5 is the line through (1, 1, 1).

Only one eigenvector for 2. Take B = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 3 \end{pmatrix}. Again 2 is a double root. But B - 2I has rank 2. So E_2 is only the line through (1, 0, 0).

So we count each eigenvalue in two ways. The algebraic multiplicity counts it as a root. The geometric multiplicity is \dim E_\lambda.

Two counts for the eigenvalue 2
MatrixAlgebraicGeometric
S22
B21
2I (size 3)33

For every eigenvalue: 1 \le geometric multiplicity \le algebraic multiplicity.

Why is this true?

Call the eigenvalue \mu and let g = \dim E_\mu. Take a basis of E_\mu and add vectors to get a basis of \mathbb{R}^n. In this basis, the first g columns of the matrix are \mu times standard vectors. Similar matrices have the same characteristic polynomial. Expand \det(A - tI) along these g columns. You get the factor (\mu - t)^g. So \mu is a root at least g times.

Let \mathbf{v}_1, \dots, \mathbf{v}_k be eigenvectors of A with eigenvalues \lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_k that are all different. Then \mathbf{v}_1, \dots, \mathbf{v}_k are linearly independent.

Proof

Suppose not. Among all zero combinations that are not trivial, take one with the fewest nonzero weights. Number the vectors so that it is c_1\mathbf{v}_1 + \cdots + c_m\mathbf{v}_m = \mathbf{0} with every c_i \ne 0. Here m \ge 2, because c_1\mathbf{v}_1 = \mathbf{0} is impossible.

Multiply by A: c_1\lambda_1\mathbf{v}_1 + \cdots + c_m\lambda_m\mathbf{v}_m = \mathbf{0}. Subtract \lambda_m times the first equation: c_1(\lambda_1 - \lambda_m)\mathbf{v}_1 + \cdots + c_{m-1}(\lambda_{m-1} - \lambda_m)\mathbf{v}_{m-1} = \mathbf{0}. The first weight c_1(\lambda_1 - \lambda_m) is not zero. So this is a shorter combination that is not trivial. That is a contradiction.

"The eigenspace" and "the eigenvectors" are not the same set. The eigenspace also holds \mathbf{0}, and \mathbf{0} is not an eigenvector. Also, a double root does not promise two eigenvectors. The matrix B shows this.

Diagonalisation

Put the two eigenvectors of A = \begin{pmatrix} 4 & 1 \\ 2 & 3 \end{pmatrix} as the columns of a matrix P. Put the eigenvalues, in the same order, on the diagonal of D.

P = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & -2 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad D = \begin{pmatrix} 5 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad AP = \begin{pmatrix} 5 & 2 \\ 5 & -4 \end{pmatrix} = PD.

The columns of AP are A\mathbf{v}_1 = 5\mathbf{v}_1 and A\mathbf{v}_2 = 2\mathbf{v}_2. That is exactly PD. P is invertible, so A = PDP^{-1}. Check it by hand with P^{-1} = \frac{1}{3}\begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 \end{pmatrix}. The first entry of PDP^{-1} is (5 \cdot 2 + 2 \cdot 1)/3 = 4. Correct.

An n \times n matrix A can be written as A = PDP^{-1} with D diagonal exactly when A has n linearly independent eigenvectors. Then the columns of P are these eigenvectors. The diagonal of D holds their eigenvalues, in the same order. This happens exactly when, for every eigenvalue, the geometric multiplicity equals the algebraic multiplicity. Here we allow complex eigenvalues and eigenvectors.

Proof

Write P = (\mathbf{v}_1 \cdots \mathbf{v}_n) and D = \operatorname{diag}(\lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_n). Column j of AP is A\mathbf{v}_j. Column j of PD is \lambda_j\mathbf{v}_j. So AP = PD says exactly that each \mathbf{v}_j is an eigenvector for \lambda_j.

If the n eigenvectors are independent, P is invertible. Then AP = PD gives A = PDP^{-1}. If A = PDP^{-1}, then AP = PD, and the columns of the invertible P are n independent eigenvectors.

For the last sentence: by the theorem above, bases of different eigenspaces together stay independent. So we can collect the sum of all geometric multiplicities. This sum reaches n exactly when each one equals its algebraic multiplicity.

A matrix like this is diagonalisable. The theorem has a meaning you already know. In Vector spaces, P^{-1}AP is the matrix of the same map in a new basis. Here the new basis is made of eigenvectors. In that basis the map only stretches each axis. That is the simplest possible matrix.

An n \times n matrix with n different eigenvalues is diagonalisable.

Why? Each eigenvalue gives one eigenvector. The n eigenvectors are independent by the theorem in the last section. Our A has two different eigenvalues, 5 and 2. So it was diagonalisable before we did any work.

Characteristic polynomial

Compute \det(A - \lambda I). Check its coefficients with the trace and the determinant.

Eigenvalues

Find the roots. Write down how often each root appears.

Eigenspaces

For each \lambda, find a basis of N(A - \lambda I) by elimination.

Count

Do you have n basis vectors in total? If not, stop. The matrix is not diagonalisable.

Build and check

Eigenvectors go into P. Eigenvalues go into D in the same order. Check AP = PD. You do not need P^{-1} for this check.

If B = P^{-1}AP, then A and B have the same characteristic polynomial. So they have the same eigenvalues, trace and determinant.

Proof

B - \lambda I = P^{-1}AP - \lambda P^{-1}P = P^{-1}(A - \lambda I)P. By the product rule for determinants, \det(B - \lambda I) = \det(P^{-1})\det(A - \lambda I)\det(P) = \det(A - \lambda I).

Two matrices like this are similar. Eigenvalues belong to the map, not to the basis.

Diagonalisable and invertible are different ideas. \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix} is diagonal but not invertible. The shear \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix} is invertible but not diagonalisable. An eigenvalue 0 kills invertibility. Missing eigenvectors kill diagonalisability.

Powers of a matrix

Compute A^{10} for A = \begin{pmatrix} 4 & 1 \\ 2 & 3 \end{pmatrix}. Multiplying ten times is slow. But look at A^2.

A^2 = PDP^{-1}\,PDP^{-1} = PD\,(P^{-1}P)\,DP^{-1} = PD^2P^{-1}.

If A = PDP^{-1}, then A^k = PD^kP^{-1} for every k \ge 1. So A^k has eigenvalues \lambda_i^k and the same eigenvectors as A.

A power of a diagonal matrix is easy: raise each diagonal entry to the power. For our A this gives a formula for every k.

A^k = \frac{1}{3}\begin{pmatrix} 2 \cdot 5^k + 2^k & 5^k - 2^k \\ 2 \cdot 5^k - 2^{k+1} & 5^k + 2^{k+1} \end{pmatrix}

For k = 1 it gives back A. For k = 10, the top left entry is (2 \cdot 9\,765\,625 + 1024)/3 = 6\,510\,758. NumPy agrees.

import numpy as np

A = np.array([[4.0, 1.0],
              [2.0, 3.0]])
P = np.array([[1.0, 1.0],
              [1.0, -2.0]])           # eigenvectors as columns
D10 = np.diag([5.0**10, 2.0**10])     # D to the power 10
print((P @ D10 @ np.linalg.inv(P)).round())
print(np.linalg.matrix_power(A, 10))  # ten multiplications
[[6510758. 3254867.]
 [6509734. 3255891.]]
[[6510758. 3254867.]
 [6509734. 3255891.]]

The largest eigenvalue wins

Write a start vector in the eigenvector basis: \mathbf{x} = c_1\mathbf{v}_1 + c_2\mathbf{v}_2. Then A^k\mathbf{x} = c_1 5^k\mathbf{v}_1 + c_2 2^k\mathbf{v}_2. The second part shrinks next to the first, by the factor (2/5)^k. So for large k, A^k\mathbf{x} points along \mathbf{v}_1 = (1, 1). The eigenvalue with the largest absolute value is the dominant eigenvalue. Its eigenvector decides the long run.

Fibonacci numbers

The Fibonacci numbers are 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13, ... Each one is the sum of the two before it. Put two of them in a vector. One step is a matrix product.

\begin{pmatrix} F_{n+1} \\ F_n \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} F_n \\ F_{n-1} \end{pmatrix}

The characteristic polynomial is \lambda^2 - \lambda - 1. Its roots are \varphi = \frac{1 + \sqrt{5}}{2} \approx 1.618 and \psi = \frac{1 - \sqrt{5}}{2} \approx -0.618. Diagonalise and read off one entry. This gives Binet's formula.

F_n = \frac{\varphi^n - \psi^n}{\sqrt{5}} 
import numpy as np

F = np.array([[1, 1],
              [1, 0]])
print(np.linalg.matrix_power(F, 10))      # holds F(11), F(10), F(9)

phi = (1 + 5 ** 0.5) / 2                   # the big eigenvalue
psi = (1 - 5 ** 0.5) / 2                   # the small eigenvalue
for n in (10, 20, 30):
    binet = (phi ** n - psi ** n) / 5 ** 0.5
    print(n, round(binet), phi ** n / 5 ** 0.5)
[[89 55]
 [55 34]]
10 55 55.00363612324743
20 6765 6765.000029563936
30 832040 832040.0000002412

The last column uses only the dominant eigenvalue. It is already almost exact, because |\psi| \lt 1 and \psi^n dies out. So the ratio F_{n+1}/F_n tends to \varphi, the golden ratio.

The power method

The long-run idea gives an algorithm. Multiply a vector by A again and again. Scale it back to length 1 each time, so the numbers stay small.

Start with any \mathbf{x}_0. Repeat \mathbf{x}_{k+1} = A\mathbf{x}_k / \|A\mathbf{x}_k\|. If one eigenvalue \lambda_1 has the largest absolute value, \mathbf{x}_k turns toward its eigenvector. The number \mathbf{x}_k^{\mathsf{T}}A\mathbf{x}_k tends to \lambda_1. The error shrinks by about |\lambda_2 / \lambda_1| per step.

The number \mathbf{x}^{\mathsf{T}}A\mathbf{x}, for \mathbf{x} of length 1, is the Rayleigh quotient. It is our best guess for \lambda_1.

import numpy as np

A = np.array([[4.0, 1.0],
              [2.0, 3.0]])
x = np.array([0.0, 1.0])            # any start that is not special
for k in range(1, 11):
    y = A @ x
    x = y / np.linalg.norm(y)       # keep the length 1
    lam = x @ A @ x                 # Rayleigh quotient: best guess for lambda
    if k in (1, 2, 5, 10):
        print(k, np.round(x, 6), round(lam, 6))
fn main() {
    let a = [[4.0_f64, 1.0], [2.0, 3.0]];
    let mut x = [0.0_f64, 1.0];
    for k in 1..=10 {
        // y = A x
        let y = [a[0][0] * x[0] + a[0][1] * x[1], a[1][0] * x[0] + a[1][1] * x[1]];
        let len = (y[0] * y[0] + y[1] * y[1]).sqrt();
        x = [y[0] / len, y[1] / len]; // keep the length 1
        // Rayleigh quotient x . (A x)
        let ax = [a[0][0] * x[0] + a[0][1] * x[1], a[1][0] * x[0] + a[1][1] * x[1]];
        let lam = x[0] * ax[0] + x[1] * ax[1];
        if [1, 2, 5, 10].contains(&k) {
            println!("{k} [{:.6} {:.6}] {:.6}", x[0], x[1], lam);
        }
    }
}
1 [0.316228 0.948683] 4.000000
2 [0.536875 0.843661] 4.647059
5 [0.696220 0.717829] 4.984021
10 [0.706996 0.707218] 4.999843

Both programs print the same numbers. Python prints fewer zeros, for example 4.0 for 4.000000. The vector tends to (0.7071, 0.7071), which is (1, 1) scaled to length 1. The guess tends to 5. From step 5 to step 10 the error drops from 0.016 to 0.00016. That is about 0.4^5 \approx 0.01, as the algorithm promised.

A matrix solves its own equation

Our A has p(\lambda) = \lambda^2 - 7\lambda + 10. Now put the matrix A in place of \lambda. Use 10I for the number 10.

A^2 - 7A + 10I = \begin{pmatrix} 18 & 7 \\ 14 & 11 \end{pmatrix} - \begin{pmatrix} 28 & 7 \\ 14 & 21 \end{pmatrix} + \begin{pmatrix} 10 & 0 \\ 0 & 10 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}

Let p(\lambda) = \det(\lambda I - A) = \lambda^n + c_{n-1}\lambda^{n-1} + \cdots + c_1\lambda + c_0. Then p(A) = A^n + c_{n-1}A^{n-1} + \cdots + c_1 A + c_0 I is the zero matrix.

Proof

Easy case. If A = PDP^{-1}, then p(A) = P\,p(D)\,P^{-1}. The matrix p(D) is diagonal with entries p(\lambda_i) = 0. So p(A) = 0.

General case. The adjugate formula says (\lambda I - A)\operatorname{adj}(\lambda I - A) = p(\lambda)I. Every entry of the adjugate is a polynomial in \lambda of degree at most n - 1. So write \operatorname{adj}(\lambda I - A) = B_0 + \lambda B_1 + \cdots + \lambda^{n-1}B_{n-1} with constant matrices B_i. Multiply out and compare the powers of \lambda:

-AB_0 = c_0 I, \quad B_0 - AB_1 = c_1 I, \quad \dots, \quad B_{n-2} - AB_{n-1} = c_{n-1}I, \quad B_{n-1} = I.

Multiply these equations from the left by I, A, A^2, \dots, A^n. Add them all. On the left every term cancels with a neighbour. On the right we get p(A). So p(A) = 0.

Two uses follow at once. First, an inverse: A^2 - 7A = -10I gives A(7I - A) = 10I. So A^{-1} = \frac{1}{10}(7I - A) = \frac{1}{10}\begin{pmatrix} 3 & -1 \\ -2 & 4 \end{pmatrix}. Second, high powers: A^2 = 7A - 10I, so A^3 = 7A^2 - 10A = 39A - 70I. Any power of an n \times n matrix is a combination of I, A, \dots, A^{n-1}.

Do not "prove" it like this: p(A) = \det(AI - A) = \det(0) = 0. The left side p(A) is a matrix. The right side is a number. They cannot be equal. The real proof needs the adjugate.

Markov chains and PageRank

A user of an app is active or idle each day. An active user stays active tomorrow with chance 0.9. An idle user becomes active with chance 0.5. Put the chances in a matrix. Column j says where a user in state j goes.

P = \begin{pmatrix} 0.9 & 0.5 \\ 0.1 & 0.5 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad \mathbf{x}_{k+1} = P\mathbf{x}_k

Here \mathbf{x}_k holds the chances of the two states on day k. A process like this is a Markov chain. The matrix P is a stochastic matrix. A probability vector has no negative entries, and its entries add up to 1.

import numpy as np

# column j = where a user in state j goes tomorrow
P = np.array([[0.9, 0.5],     # to active
              [0.1, 0.5]])    # to idle
x = np.array([0.0, 1.0])      # day 0: the user is idle
for day in range(1, 8):
    x = P @ x
    print(day, np.round(x, 4))
print(np.linalg.eigvals(P))
1 [0.5 0.5]
2 [0.7 0.3]
3 [0.78 0.22]
4 [0.812 0.188]
5 [0.8248 0.1752]
6 [0.8299 0.1701]
7 [0.832 0.168]
[1. +0.j 0.4+0.j]

The chances settle near (0.833, 0.167). The eigenvalues explain why. For \lambda = 1, solve (P - I)\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{0}: -0.1x + 0.5y = 0, so \mathbf{x} = (5, 1). Scale it so the entries add up to 1. This gives the steady state \mathbf{s} = (5/6, 1/6). The other eigenvalue is 0.4, with eigenvector (1, -1). So the exact answer is this.

\mathbf{x}_k = \begin{pmatrix} 5/6 \\ 1/6 \end{pmatrix} - \frac{5}{6}\,(0.4)^k \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ -1 \end{pmatrix}

The second part shrinks by 0.4 each day. The steady state stays. The size of the second eigenvalue sets the speed.

Here columns add up to 1, and we multiply P\mathbf{x}. Many books, and the chapter Graphs for knowledge and context, use rows that add up to 1 and write \boldsymbol{\pi}P = \boldsymbol{\pi}. It is the same idea with every matrix transposed. Always check which way a book goes.

Every stochastic matrix has the eigenvalue 1. The rows of P^{\mathsf{T}} add up to 1, so P^{\mathsf{T}}(1, \dots, 1) = (1, \dots, 1). And P has the same eigenvalues as P^{\mathsf{T}}, because a transpose keeps the determinant. But is the steady state unique? Do we always reach it? A great theorem answers this.

Let A be a square matrix with all entries positive. Let r be the largest absolute value of its eigenvalues. Then:

  1. r itself is an eigenvalue, and r \gt 0.
  2. r is a simple root of the characteristic polynomial.
  3. r has an eigenvector with all entries positive.
  4. Every other eigenvalue has |\lambda| \lt r.
  5. r lies between the smallest and the largest column sum. The same holds for row sums.

For a positive stochastic matrix, r = 1. So the steady state is unique, and P^k\mathbf{x}_0 tends to it for every probability vector \mathbf{x}_0.

Proof idea for stochastic matrices

Let P be positive with columns that add up to 1. Then P^{\mathsf{T}} has rows that add up to 1. Let P^{\mathsf{T}}\mathbf{w} = \lambda\mathbf{w} with \mathbf{w} \ne \mathbf{0}. Pick i with |w_i| as large as possible. Row i says \lambda w_i = \sum_j p_{ji}w_j. The weights p_{ji} are positive and add up to 1. By the triangle inequality, |\lambda|\,|w_i| \le \sum_j p_{ji}|w_j| \le |w_i|. So |\lambda| \le 1.

If |\lambda| = 1, both inequalities are equalities. With all weights positive, this forces all w_j to be equal. Then \lambda = 1, and the eigenspace is only the line of (1, \dots, 1). So 1 is the only eigenvalue on the unit circle, and its eigenspace is a line. The positive steady state and the simple root need more work. The sources give full proofs.

In simple words: a positive matrix has one winning direction, and it points into the positive corner. Oskar Perron proved this for positive matrices in 1907. Georg Frobenius extended it in 1912 to matrices with zeros. Then the matrix must be irreducible. The winner r is still a simple eigenvalue with a positive eigenvector. But other eigenvalues can now also have size r. Example: \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix} swaps two states each day. Its eigenvalues are 1 and -1, and the chances jump back and forth forever. If some power of the matrix is positive, the matrix is primitive, and all five statements hold again.

PageRank on three pages

Three web pages link to each other. A random surfer clicks a random link on each page. Where does the surfer spend the most time?

L = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 0 & 1 \\ 1/2 & 0 & 0 \\ 1/2 & 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix} \qquad \text{(column } j \text{ = links out of page } j\text{)}

Solve L\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{x}. Row 1 says x_A = x_C. Row 2 says x_B = x_A / 2. Scale so the sum is 1: \mathbf{x} = (0.4, 0.2, 0.4). Pages A and C share the top place.

Real webs have pages with no links. They give columns of zeros, so L is not stochastic. The usual fix puts 1/n in such a column. Real webs also have closed groups of pages. Then L is not irreducible, and Perron-Frobenius fails. Google's answer was a damping factor d, often 0.85. With chance d the surfer follows a link. Otherwise the surfer jumps to a random page. The new matrix G = dL + \frac{1 - d}{n}J has all entries positive. Here J is the matrix of all ones. So Perron-Frobenius applies directly.

import numpy as np

# three pages: A links to B and C, B links to C, C links to A
L = np.array([[0.0, 0.0, 1.0],
              [0.5, 0.0, 0.0],
              [0.5, 1.0, 0.0]])        # columns add up to 1
n, d = 3, 0.85
G = d * L + (1 - d) / n                 # the Google matrix
for M, name in ((L, "L"), (G, "G")):
    x = np.full(n, 1 / n)
    for _ in range(100):
        x = M @ x                       # power method
    print(name, np.round(x, 4), np.round(np.abs(np.linalg.eigvals(M)), 4))
L [0.4 0.2 0.4] [1.     0.7071 0.7071]
G [0.3878 0.2148 0.3974] [1.    0.601 0.601]

Look at the sizes of the eigenvalues. For L, the second largest size is 0.7071. For G it is 0.601, which is 0.85 \times 0.7071. This is no accident. If L\mathbf{v} = \lambda\mathbf{v} with \lambda \ne 1, the entries of \mathbf{v} add up to 0. Then J\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{0}, and G\mathbf{v} = d\lambda\mathbf{v}. So damping shrinks every other eigenvalue by d, and the power method speeds up. The full proof of convergence is PageRank converges to one stationary vector. Markov chains in general are in Stochastic processes.

Perron-Frobenius needs entries that are positive, or at least not negative with an irreducible pattern. A matrix with negative entries can have a dominant eigenvalue that is negative or complex. Do not use the theorem there.

Complex eigenvalues

The rotation R = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix} turns every arrow by 90 degrees. Its characteristic polynomial is \lambda^2 + 1. There is no real root. But over the complex numbers there are two: \lambda = i and \lambda = -i.

  1. For \lambda = i, solve (R - iI)\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{0}. The first row says -ix - y = 0, so y = -ix.
  2. Take x = 1. Then \mathbf{v} = (1, -i).
  3. Check. R\mathbf{v} = (0 \cdot 1 + (-1)(-i),\; 1 \cdot 1 + 0) = (i, 1). And i\mathbf{v} = (i, -i^2) = (i, 1). Correct.

The eigenvector has complex entries. It lives in \mathbb{C}^2, not in the real plane. That is why we saw no turning-free arrow in the picture.

If A has real entries and A\mathbf{v} = \lambda\mathbf{v}, then A\overline{\mathbf{v}} = \overline{\lambda}\,\overline{\mathbf{v}}. So complex eigenvalues of a real matrix come in conjugate pairs a \pm bi.

Why? Take the complex conjugate of both sides of A\mathbf{v} = \lambda\mathbf{v}. The real matrix A does not change.

Turn and stretch

A matrix of the form C = \begin{pmatrix} a & -b \\ b & a \end{pmatrix} is a rotation-scaling matrix. Its eigenvalues are a \pm bi. Write a + bi = r(\cos\theta + i\sin\theta). Then C turns by the angle \theta and stretches by r = |\lambda| = \sqrt{a^2 + b^2}. It acts like multiplication by a + bi in the complex plane.

Take A = \frac{1}{2}\begin{pmatrix} 1 & -1 \\ 1 & 1 \end{pmatrix}. Its eigenvalues are \frac{1}{2} \pm \frac{1}{2}i. So r = 1/\sqrt{2} \approx 0.707 and \theta = 45^\circ. Start at \mathbf{x}_0 = (4, 0) and apply A again and again.

After 8 steps the point has turned a full circle. Its length is 4 \cdot (1/\sqrt{2})^8 = 4/16 = 0.25. The size |\lambda| decides the long run, just like for real eigenvalues.

Let a real 2 \times 2 matrix A have eigenvalues a \pm bi with b \ne 0. Take an eigenvector \mathbf{v} for a - bi. Let P have the columns \operatorname{Re}\mathbf{v} and \operatorname{Im}\mathbf{v}. Then P^{-1}AP = \begin{pmatrix} a & -b \\ b & a \end{pmatrix}.

So every such matrix is a turn and a stretch, seen in tilted coordinates. For example, \begin{pmatrix} 2 & -1 \\ 2 & 0 \end{pmatrix} has eigenvalues 1 \pm i. It is similar to \begin{pmatrix} 1 & -1 \\ 1 & 1 \end{pmatrix}: a turn by 45 degrees and a stretch by \sqrt{2}. In Differential equations, the same eigenvalues give solutions like e^{t}\cos t. They grow and swing at the same time.

Complex eigenvalues do not mean "no eigenvectors". The eigenvectors exist. They have complex entries. Also, do not forget the partner: if 2 + 3i is an eigenvalue of a real matrix, so is 2 - 3i.

The Jordan form in simple words

Take A = \begin{pmatrix} 3 & 1 \\ -1 & 1 \end{pmatrix}. The trace is 4 and the determinant is 4. So p(\lambda) = \lambda^2 - 4\lambda + 4 = (\lambda - 2)^2. The matrix A - 2I = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ -1 & -1 \end{pmatrix} has rank 1. So there is only one eigenvector direction, \mathbf{v} = (1, -1). The matrix is not diagonalisable. Such a matrix is called defective.

We cannot get a diagonal matrix. But we can get close. Find a vector \mathbf{w} with (A - 2I)\mathbf{w} = \mathbf{v}. The equation x + y = 1 gives \mathbf{w} = (1, 0). Now look at what A does.

A\mathbf{v} = 2\mathbf{v}, \qquad A\mathbf{w} = 2\mathbf{w} + \mathbf{v}, \qquad P = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ -1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad P^{-1}AP = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 2 \end{pmatrix}.

The vector \mathbf{w} is a generalised eigenvector. Here (A - 2I)^2\mathbf{w} = \mathbf{0}, but (A - 2I)\mathbf{w} \ne \mathbf{0}. The vectors \mathbf{w} \to \mathbf{v} \to \mathbf{0} form a Jordan chain. The matrix \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 2 \end{pmatrix} is a Jordan block.

Every complex square matrix A is similar to a block diagonal matrix J = \operatorname{diag}(J_1, \dots, J_p). Each block has one eigenvalue on its diagonal, ones just above the diagonal, and zeros elsewhere.

J_i = \begin{pmatrix} \lambda_i & 1 & & \\ & \lambda_i & \ddots & \\ & & \ddots & 1 \\ & & & \lambda_i \end{pmatrix}

J is unique up to the order of the blocks. For each eigenvalue, the number of its blocks is the geometric multiplicity. The total size of its blocks is the algebraic multiplicity.

Proof idea

By the fundamental theorem of algebra, p(\lambda) splits into factors (\lambda - \lambda_i)^{m_i} over \mathbb{C}. The space splits into pieces, one for each eigenvalue: the vectors killed by some power of A - \lambda_i I. Each piece has dimension m_i. On one piece, N = A - \lambda_i I is nilpotent. A careful count of the null spaces of N, N^2, N^3, \dots gives chains of vectors. Each chain becomes one block. Those counts depend only on A, so the blocks are unique.

In simple words: every matrix is "almost diagonal" in a good basis. Diagonalisable matrices have only blocks of size 1. A defective matrix has at least one bigger block. Each block is "stretch by \lambda" plus a little push along the chain.

Why the blocks matter: powers again

Powers of a Jordan block have a new term.

\begin{pmatrix} \lambda & 1 \\ 0 & \lambda \end{pmatrix}^k = \begin{pmatrix} \lambda^k & k\lambda^{k-1} \\ 0 & \lambda^k \end{pmatrix}, \qquad \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}^k = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & k \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}.

The factor k is new. The shear has only the eigenvalue 1, but its powers still grow, like k. In differential equations the same block gives solutions like t e^{\lambda t}. So the Jordan form explains the "extra t" in those formulas.

from sympy import Matrix

A = Matrix([[3, 1], [-1, 1]])
P, J = A.jordan_form()           # A = P J P^-1
print(A.charpoly().as_expr())
print("J =", J.tolist())
print("P =", P.tolist())
print(A.is_diagonalizable())
lambda**2 - 4*lambda + 4
J = [[2, 1], [0, 2]]
P = [[1, 1], [-1, 0]]
False

SymPy 1.14.0 found the same P and J as we did by hand.

Never compute a Jordan form with decimal numbers. It jumps when an entry moves a tiny bit. Change one zero in \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 2 \end{pmatrix} to 10^{-10}. The eigenvalues become 2 \pm 10^{-5}. They are now different, so the new matrix is diagonalisable. Its Jordan form is suddenly diagonal. Exact fractions in SymPy are fine. Floating-point numbers are not.

Eigenvalues on a real computer

import numpy as np

A = np.array([[4.0, 1.0],
              [2.0, 3.0]])
vals, vecs = np.linalg.eig(A)          # columns of vecs are eigenvectors
print("eigenvalues:", vals)
print(np.round(vecs, 4))
eigenvalues: [5.+0.j 2.+0.j]
[[ 0.7071+0.j -0.4472+0.j]
 [ 0.7071+0.j  0.8944+0.j]]
  • The eigenvectors are the columns, scaled to length 1. (0.7071, 0.7071) is our (1, 1). (-0.4472, 0.8944) is -1/\sqrt{5} times our (1, -2).
  • The order of the eigenvalues is not fixed. Do not assume the largest comes first.
  • In this run with NumPy 2.5.4, the results came back as complex numbers with +0j. The documentation says real results are turned into a real type. So do not rely on the type. Use vals.real when you know the eigenvalues are real.
  • For a symmetric matrix, use np.linalg.eigh. It is faster, and it always gives real eigenvalues in order. The reason is the spectral theorem in The spectral theorem and the SVD.

NumPy calls the LAPACK routine geev. It does not solve p(\lambda) = 0. It uses the QR algorithm. John Francis and Vera Kublanovskaya found it on their own around 1961. It brings A close to a triangular matrix T = Q^{*}AQ with an orthonormal Q. This is the Schur form. The eigenvalues sit on the diagonal of T. Orthonormal matrices are the topic of Orthogonality and least squares. The details are in Numerical methods.

Where do eigenvalues appear in AI?

PCA finds the main directions of data. They are eigenvectors of a covariance matrix. Spectral clustering uses eigenvectors of the graph Laplacian, see Graph theory. PageRank and many graph scores are dominant eigenvectors. In a recurrent network, the hidden state is multiplied by a weight matrix many times. Large eigenvalues or singular values make signals explode. Small ones make them vanish.

Do AB and BA have the same eigenvalues?

Yes, for square matrices. If AB\mathbf{v} = \lambda\mathbf{v} with \lambda \ne 0, then BA(B\mathbf{v}) = \lambda(B\mathbf{v}), and B\mathbf{v} \ne \mathbf{0}. The eigenvalue 0 needs a separate small argument. But the eigenvectors are usually different.

Are the eigenvalues of A + B the sums of the eigenvalues?

No, not in general. Try A = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix} and B = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}. Both have only the eigenvalue 0. But A + B has the eigenvalues 1 and -1. It works only in special cases, for example when A and B share all their eigenvectors.

A short history

  1. 1858 Cayley. Arthur Cayley states the Cayley-Hamilton theorem. He publishes a proof only for 2 \times 2 matrices. Hamilton had found a special case for quaternions.
  2. 1870 Jordan. Camille Jordan publishes the normal form in his book on substitutions.
  3. 1878 Frobenius. Georg Frobenius gives the first general proof of the Cayley-Hamilton theorem.
  4. 1907 Perron. Oskar Perron proves his theorem for positive matrices.
  5. 1912 Frobenius again. He extends it to irreducible matrices with zeros.
  6. 1961 The QR algorithm. Francis and Kublanovskaya find the method that computers still use.
  7. 1998 PageRank. Sergey Brin and Larry Page describe their search engine. Its ranking is a dominant eigenvector.

Patterns to remember

Practice

Which vector is an eigenvector of \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 5 \end{pmatrix}?

  • (1, 1)
  • (0, 3)
  • (0, 0)

(0, 3) goes to (0, 15) = 5(0, 3). The vector (1, 1) goes to (2, 5), a new direction. The zero vector is never an eigenvector.

A 3 \times 3 matrix has the eigenvalues 1, 2 and 4. What is its determinant?

  • 7
  • 8
  • 3

The determinant is the product: 1 \cdot 2 \cdot 4 = 8. The trace is the sum, 7.

Which matrix is not diagonalisable?

  • \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}
  • \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}
  • \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1 \end{pmatrix}

The shear has the double eigenvalue 1 but only one eigenvector direction. The identity is already diagonal. The symmetric matrix has eigenvalues 3 and -1.

Markov chain X has eigenvalues 1 and 0.9. Chain Y has eigenvalues 1 and 0.2. Which one reaches its steady state faster?

  • X
  • Y
  • Both are equally fast.

The distance to the steady state shrinks like |\lambda_2|^k. 0.2^k goes to zero much faster than 0.9^k.

The eigenvalues of \begin{pmatrix} 5 & 0 \\ 3 & -1 \end{pmatrix} are 5 and ?.

A matrix has the eigenvalues 3, 3 and -2. Its trace is ?.

If A\mathbf{v} = 3\mathbf{v}, then A^2\mathbf{v} = ? \mathbf{v}.

  1. Find the eigenvalues and eigenvectors of \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1 \end{pmatrix}.
    Answer

    The trace is 2 and the determinant is -3. So \lambda^2 - 2\lambda - 3 = (\lambda - 3)(\lambda + 1). For \lambda = 3: A - 3I = \begin{pmatrix} -2 & 2 \\ 2 & -2 \end{pmatrix}, so (1, 1). For \lambda = -1: A + I = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 2 \\ 2 & 2 \end{pmatrix}, so (1, -1).

  2. Diagonalise A = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 2 \end{pmatrix}. Then find a formula for A^k.
    Answer

    It is triangular, so the eigenvalues are 1 and 2. For 1: (1, 0). For 2: A - 2I = \begin{pmatrix} -1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}, so (1, 1). Then P = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}, D = \operatorname{diag}(1, 2), P^{-1} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}. So A^k = PD^kP^{-1} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2^k - 1 \\ 0 & 2^k \end{pmatrix}. Check k = 1: it gives A.

  3. Let A be invertible with A\mathbf{v} = \lambda\mathbf{v}. Show that \lambda \ne 0 and A^{-1}\mathbf{v} = \frac{1}{\lambda}\mathbf{v}.
    Answer

    If \lambda = 0, then A\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{0} with \mathbf{v} \ne \mathbf{0}, so A is not invertible. That is a contradiction. Now multiply A\mathbf{v} = \lambda\mathbf{v} by A^{-1}: \mathbf{v} = \lambda A^{-1}\mathbf{v}. Divide by \lambda.

  4. A user moves between two states with P = \begin{pmatrix} 0.8 & 0.3 \\ 0.2 & 0.7 \end{pmatrix}. Find the steady state and the second eigenvalue.
    Answer

    (P - I)\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{0} gives -0.2x + 0.3y = 0, so \mathbf{x} = (3, 2). Scaled: (0.6, 0.4). The trace is 1.5, and one eigenvalue is 1. So the other one is 0.5.

  5. Use the Cayley-Hamilton theorem to find the inverse of A = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 \end{pmatrix}.
    Answer

    p(\lambda) = \lambda^2 - 3\lambda + 1. So A^2 - 3A + I = 0, which gives A(3I - A) = I. So A^{-1} = 3I - A = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & -1 \\ -1 & 2 \end{pmatrix}. Check: \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} 1 & -1 \\ -1 & 2 \end{pmatrix} = I.

  6. Find the Jordan form of \begin{pmatrix} 5 & 1 \\ -1 & 3 \end{pmatrix}.
    Answer

    The trace is 8 and the determinant is 15 + 1 = 16. So p(\lambda) = (\lambda - 4)^2. The matrix A - 4I = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ -1 & -1 \end{pmatrix} has rank 1. There is only one eigenvector direction. So the Jordan form is \begin{pmatrix} 4 & 1 \\ 0 & 4 \end{pmatrix}.

  7. Let A^2 = A. Show that every eigenvalue is 0 or 1, and that A is diagonalisable.
    Answer

    If A\mathbf{v} = \lambda\mathbf{v}, then \lambda\mathbf{v} = A\mathbf{v} = A^2\mathbf{v} = \lambda^2\mathbf{v}. So \lambda^2 = \lambda, and \lambda is 0 or 1. Now write any \mathbf{x} = A\mathbf{x} + (\mathbf{x} - A\mathbf{x}). The first part is in E_1, because A(A\mathbf{x}) = A\mathbf{x}. The second part is in E_0, because A(\mathbf{x} - A\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{0}. So E_1 and E_0 together span \mathbb{R}^n. Their bases give n independent eigenvectors.

  8. A recurrent network multiplies its hidden state by a diagonalisable matrix W at each step. W has the eigenvalues 1.1 and 0.5. What happens to each eigenvector part after 50 steps?
    Answer

    The first part grows by 1.1^{50} \approx 117. The second part shrinks by 0.5^{50} \approx 8.9 \times 10^{-16}. So the first direction explodes and the second one vanishes. This is the eigenvalue view of exploding and vanishing signals.

Key takeaways

  • An eigenvector keeps its direction: A\mathbf{v} = \lambda\mathbf{v} with \mathbf{v} \ne \mathbf{0}.
  • Eigenvalues are the roots of \det(A - \lambda I). Their sum is the trace, and their product is the determinant.
  • An eigenspace is N(A - \lambda I). Its dimension can be smaller than the number of times \lambda is a root.
  • A = PDP^{-1} exactly when there are n independent eigenvectors. Different eigenvalues are enough.
  • Powers are easy after diagonalising. The dominant eigenvalue decides the long run.
  • Every matrix solves its own characteristic equation: p(A) = 0.
  • A positive matrix has one positive winning eigenvalue with a positive eigenvector. This gives steady states and PageRank.
  • Complex eigenvalues mean turning. Their size decides if the spiral grows or shrinks.
  • The Jordan form is the best we can do without enough eigenvectors. It is exact maths, not something to compute with decimals.

Orthogonality and least squares

Right angles make linear algebra easy. With perpendicular directions, coordinates come from one dot product each, and the closest point is a simple drop. This chapter builds that toolbox. It ends with least squares, the method behind every fitted line and linear regression.

  • Compute inner products, lengths and angles, and use the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality.
  • Project a vector onto a line or a subspace and find the closest point.
  • Turn any basis into an orthonormal one with Gram-Schmidt and write A = QR.
  • Solve a least squares problem with the normal equations or with QR.
  • Recognise orthogonal matrices and explain why computers love them.

Inner product and length

Take \mathbf{u} = (1, 2, 2) and \mathbf{v} = (4, 0, 3). Their dot product is 1 \cdot 4 + 2 \cdot 0 + 2 \cdot 3 = 10. Their lengths are \|\mathbf{u}\| = \sqrt{1 + 4 + 4} = 3 and \|\mathbf{v}\| = \sqrt{16 + 0 + 9} = 5. From Vectors and analytic geometry we know the angle formula.

\cos\theta = \frac{\mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{v}}{\|\mathbf{u}\|\,\|\mathbf{v}\|} = \frac{10}{3 \cdot 5} = \frac{2}{3}, \qquad \theta \approx 48.2^\circ

The dot product is one example of a bigger idea. Many other "products" of two vectors follow the same rules. We give them one name.

An inner product on a real vector space gives a number \langle \mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v} \rangle for every two vectors. It follows three rules for all vectors and scalars.

  1. Symmetry: \langle \mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v} \rangle = \langle \mathbf{v}, \mathbf{u} \rangle.
  2. Linearity: \langle a\mathbf{u} + b\mathbf{w}, \mathbf{v} \rangle = a\langle \mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v} \rangle + b\langle \mathbf{w}, \mathbf{v} \rangle.
  3. Positivity: \langle \mathbf{v}, \mathbf{v} \rangle \gt 0 for every \mathbf{v} \ne \mathbf{0}.

An inner product gives every vector a norm \|\mathbf{v}\| = \sqrt{\langle \mathbf{v}, \mathbf{v} \rangle}. The distance between two vectors is \|\mathbf{u} - \mathbf{v}\|. A vector with norm 1 is a unit vector. Divide any nonzero vector by its norm to get one.

Three inner products
SpaceInner productExample
\mathbb{R}^n\mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{v} = \sum u_i v_i(1, 2, 2) \cdot (4, 0, 3) = 10
\mathbb{R}^2 with weights2u_1v_1 + 3u_2v_2\langle (1, 1), (1, -1) \rangle = 2 - 3 = -1
Functions on [0, 1]\int_0^1 f(x)g(x)\,dx\langle 1, x - \tfrac{1}{2} \rangle = 0

The last row is important later. Functions can be "perpendicular". Fourier series use exactly this idea, see Measure and functional analysis.

The Cauchy-Schwarz inequality

The angle formula needs \cos\theta between -1 and 1. Why is |\mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{v}| never bigger than \|\mathbf{u}\|\,\|\mathbf{v}\|? In our example, 10 \le 15. The next theorem says this always holds.

For all vectors \mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v} in a space with an inner product, |\langle \mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v} \rangle| \le \|\mathbf{u}\|\,\|\mathbf{v}\|. Equality holds exactly when one vector is a multiple of the other.

Proof

If \mathbf{v} = \mathbf{0}, both sides are 0. Otherwise look at f(t) = \|\mathbf{u} - t\mathbf{v}\|^2 for real t. Expand it with the rules: f(t) = \|\mathbf{v}\|^2 t^2 - 2\langle \mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v} \rangle\, t + \|\mathbf{u}\|^2. This is a quadratic in t, and it is never negative. So it has at most one real root. By the quadratic formula, its discriminant is not positive: 4\langle \mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v} \rangle^2 - 4\|\mathbf{v}\|^2\|\mathbf{u}\|^2 \le 0. Take square roots.

Equality means the discriminant is 0. Then f(t) = 0 for one t, so \mathbf{u} = t\mathbf{v}.

Check the equality case. Take \mathbf{v} = 2\mathbf{u} = (2, 4, 4). Then \mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{v} = 18 and \|\mathbf{u}\|\,\|\mathbf{v}\| = 3 \cdot 6 = 18. Equal, as promised. The triangle inequality \|\mathbf{u} + \mathbf{v}\| \le \|\mathbf{u}\| + \|\mathbf{v}\| follows in one line: expand \|\mathbf{u} + \mathbf{v}\|^2 and use Cauchy-Schwarz on the middle term.

Cosine similarity of two embeddings is \cos\theta. Cauchy-Schwarz is the reason it always lies between -1 and 1. See The maths of vector search and agent memory.

Not every formula is an inner product. Take u_1v_1 - u_2v_2 on \mathbb{R}^2. Then \langle (0, 1), (0, 1) \rangle = -1. Positivity fails. Always test \langle \mathbf{v}, \mathbf{v} \rangle \gt 0.

Orthogonal and orthonormal sets

Look at \mathbf{u}_1 = (1, 1, 0), \mathbf{u}_2 = (1, -1, 0) and \mathbf{u}_3 = (0, 0, 1). Every pair has dot product 0. Now write \mathbf{v} = (3, 1, 2) in this basis. Usually we must solve a system. Here one dot product per weight is enough.

c_1 = \frac{\mathbf{v} \cdot \mathbf{u}_1}{\mathbf{u}_1 \cdot \mathbf{u}_1} = \frac{4}{2} = 2, \qquad c_2 = \frac{\mathbf{v} \cdot \mathbf{u}_2}{\mathbf{u}_2 \cdot \mathbf{u}_2} = \frac{2}{2} = 1, \qquad c_3 = \frac{2}{1} = 2.

Check: 2(1, 1, 0) + 1(1, -1, 0) + 2(0, 0, 1) = (3, 1, 2). Correct.

Two vectors are orthogonal when \langle \mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v} \rangle = 0. A set is an orthogonal set when every two of its vectors are orthogonal. It is an orthonormal set when, in addition, every vector has norm 1.

Nonzero orthogonal vectors \mathbf{u}_1, \dots, \mathbf{u}_k are linearly independent. If they form a basis, every vector \mathbf{v} is \mathbf{v} = \sum_{i=1}^k \frac{\langle \mathbf{v}, \mathbf{u}_i \rangle}{\langle \mathbf{u}_i, \mathbf{u}_i \rangle}\,\mathbf{u}_i.

Proof

Let \mathbf{v} = c_1\mathbf{u}_1 + \cdots + c_k\mathbf{u}_k. Take the inner product with \mathbf{u}_j. All terms with i \ne j vanish. So \langle \mathbf{v}, \mathbf{u}_j \rangle = c_j\langle \mathbf{u}_j, \mathbf{u}_j \rangle. This gives the formula. For \mathbf{v} = \mathbf{0} it gives every c_j = 0. So the vectors are independent.

With an orthonormal basis the formula is even shorter: c_i = \langle \mathbf{v}, \mathbf{u}_i \rangle. Orthogonal vectors also obey Pythagoras: if \mathbf{u} \perp \mathbf{v}, then \|\mathbf{u} + \mathbf{v}\|^2 = \|\mathbf{u}\|^2 + \|\mathbf{v}\|^2. Expand the left side, and the middle term is 0. This is the Pythagorean theorem in any dimension.

Orthogonal complements

Take the plane W: x + y + z = 0. Which vectors are orthogonal to all of W? The equation says (1, 1, 1) \cdot (x, y, z) = 0. So the answer is the line through (1, 1, 1).

The orthogonal complement of a subspace W is W^{\perp} = \{\mathbf{x} : \langle \mathbf{x}, \mathbf{w} \rangle = 0 \text{ for all } \mathbf{w} \in W\}.

The orthogonal complement W^{\perp} (say "W perp") is always a subspace. In \mathbb{R}^n, \dim W + \dim W^{\perp} = n. The plane and its normal line give 2 + 1 = 3. You met two pairs in Vector spaces.

  • N(A) = C(A^{\mathsf{T}})^{\perp}: the null space is orthogonal to the row space.
  • N(A^{\mathsf{T}}) = C(A)^{\perp}: the left null space is orthogonal to the column space.

Orthogonal sets need every pair, not only neighbours. In (1, 0, 1), (0, 1, 0), (1, 0, 0), the first two are orthogonal. The second and third are orthogonal. But the first and third have dot product 1.

Projections

Take the line through \mathbf{a} = (2, 1) and the point \mathbf{b} = (3, 4). Which point \mathbf{p} of the line is closest to \mathbf{b}? Drop a perpendicular from \mathbf{b} to the line. The foot is \mathbf{p}.

  1. The point \mathbf{p} is a multiple t\mathbf{a}. The error \mathbf{b} - t\mathbf{a} must be orthogonal to \mathbf{a}.
  2. So \mathbf{a} \cdot (\mathbf{b} - t\mathbf{a}) = 0, which gives t = \dfrac{\mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{b}}{\mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{a}} = \dfrac{6 + 4}{4 + 1} = 2.
  3. \mathbf{p} = 2(2, 1) = (4, 2) and \mathbf{e} = \mathbf{b} - \mathbf{p} = (-1, 2).
  4. Check. \mathbf{e} \cdot \mathbf{a} = -2 + 2 = 0. Pythagoras: \|\mathbf{b}\|^2 = 25 = 20 + 5 = \|\mathbf{p}\|^2 + \|\mathbf{e}\|^2.

The point \mathbf{p} is the orthogonal projection of \mathbf{b} onto the line. The distance from \mathbf{b} to the line is \|\mathbf{e}\| = \sqrt{5}. In matrix form, \mathbf{p} = P\mathbf{b} with the projection matrix P = \frac{\mathbf{a}\mathbf{a}^{\mathsf{T}}}{\mathbf{a}^{\mathsf{T}}\mathbf{a}} = \frac{1}{5}\begin{pmatrix} 4 & 2 \\ 2 & 1 \end{pmatrix}.

Projection onto a subspace

Now let W be the column space of an m \times n matrix A with independent columns. The projection is \mathbf{p} = A\hat{\mathbf{x}} for some weights \hat{\mathbf{x}}. The error \mathbf{b} - A\hat{\mathbf{x}} must be orthogonal to every column of A. That is A^{\mathsf{T}}(\mathbf{b} - A\hat{\mathbf{x}}) = \mathbf{0}, or A^{\mathsf{T}}A\hat{\mathbf{x}} = A^{\mathsf{T}}\mathbf{b}. Can we always solve this?

N(A^{\mathsf{T}}A) = N(A). So the square matrix A^{\mathsf{T}}A is invertible exactly when the columns of A are independent.

Proof

If A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{0}, then A^{\mathsf{T}}A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{0}. Conversely, let A^{\mathsf{T}}A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{0}. Multiply by \mathbf{x}^{\mathsf{T}}: \mathbf{x}^{\mathsf{T}}A^{\mathsf{T}}A\mathbf{x} = \|A\mathbf{x}\|^2 = 0. So A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{0}. Independent columns mean N(A) = \{\mathbf{0}\}. Then the square matrix A^{\mathsf{T}}A has a zero null space, so it is invertible.

Let W be a subspace of \mathbb{R}^m. Every \mathbf{b} splits in exactly one way as \mathbf{b} = \mathbf{p} + \mathbf{e} with \mathbf{p} \in W and \mathbf{e} \in W^{\perp}. The point \mathbf{p} is the closest point of W to \mathbf{b}: \|\mathbf{b} - \mathbf{w}\| \gt \|\mathbf{b} - \mathbf{p}\| for every other \mathbf{w} \in W. If the columns of A are a basis of W, then \mathbf{p} = A(A^{\mathsf{T}}A)^{-1}A^{\mathsf{T}}\mathbf{b}.

Proof

Existence. Put a basis of W into the columns of A. By the proposition above, A^{\mathsf{T}}A\hat{\mathbf{x}} = A^{\mathsf{T}}\mathbf{b} has exactly one solution. Let \mathbf{p} = A\hat{\mathbf{x}} and \mathbf{e} = \mathbf{b} - \mathbf{p}. Then A^{\mathsf{T}}\mathbf{e} = \mathbf{0}, so \mathbf{e} is orthogonal to every column, and so to all of W.

Only one way. If \mathbf{p} + \mathbf{e} = \mathbf{p}' + \mathbf{e}', then \mathbf{p} - \mathbf{p}' = \mathbf{e}' - \mathbf{e} lies in W and in W^{\perp}. It is orthogonal to itself, so it is \mathbf{0}.

Closest. For \mathbf{w} \in W, write \mathbf{b} - \mathbf{w} = \mathbf{e} + (\mathbf{p} - \mathbf{w}). The two parts are orthogonal. By Pythagoras, \|\mathbf{b} - \mathbf{w}\|^2 = \|\mathbf{e}\|^2 + \|\mathbf{p} - \mathbf{w}\|^2. This is smallest exactly when \mathbf{w} = \mathbf{p}.

In simple words: to get as close as possible, go straight down. The error always stands at a right angle to the subspace. The projection matrix P = A(A^{\mathsf{T}}A)^{-1}A^{\mathsf{T}} has two marks: P^2 = P (projecting twice changes nothing) and P^{\mathsf{T}} = P. Check them on the 2 \times 2 matrix above.

With an orthonormal basis \mathbf{q}_1, \dots, \mathbf{q}_n of W, everything gets simpler. Put the \mathbf{q}_i into the columns of Q. Then Q^{\mathsf{T}}Q = I, and the formula becomes \mathbf{p} = QQ^{\mathsf{T}}\mathbf{b} = \langle \mathbf{b}, \mathbf{q}_1 \rangle\mathbf{q}_1 + \cdots + \langle \mathbf{b}, \mathbf{q}_n \rangle\mathbf{q}_n. No inverse is needed. This is why we want orthonormal bases.

The sum-of-projections formula needs an orthogonal basis. Project \mathbf{b} = (1, 1) onto the whole plane with the basis (1, 0), (1, 1). The two line projections are (1, 0) and (1, 1). Their sum (2, 1) is wrong, because \mathbf{b} itself is the right answer. The basis was not orthogonal.

The Gram-Schmidt process

Orthonormal bases are great. But most bases we meet are not orthogonal. Gram-Schmidt repairs this, one vector at a time. Take \mathbf{a}_1 = (1, 1, 0), \mathbf{a}_2 = (1, 0, 1), \mathbf{a}_3 = (0, 1, 1).

Keep the first vector

\mathbf{v}_1 = \mathbf{a}_1 = (1, 1, 0).

Remove the part along v1

\mathbf{a}_2 \cdot \mathbf{v}_1 = 1 and \mathbf{v}_1 \cdot \mathbf{v}_1 = 2. So \mathbf{a}_2 - \frac{1}{2}\mathbf{v}_1 = (\tfrac{1}{2}, -\tfrac{1}{2}, 1). Scale by 2 to avoid fractions: \mathbf{v}_2 = (1, -1, 2).

Remove the parts along v1 and v2

\mathbf{a}_3 \cdot \mathbf{v}_1 = 1 and \mathbf{a}_3 \cdot \mathbf{v}_2 = 1, with \mathbf{v}_2 \cdot \mathbf{v}_2 = 6. So \mathbf{a}_3 - \frac{1}{2}\mathbf{v}_1 - \frac{1}{6}\mathbf{v}_2 = (-\tfrac{2}{3}, \tfrac{2}{3}, \tfrac{2}{3}). Scale: \mathbf{v}_3 = (-1, 1, 1).

Check

\mathbf{v}_1 \cdot \mathbf{v}_2 = 1 - 1 + 0 = 0. \mathbf{v}_1 \cdot \mathbf{v}_3 = -1 + 1 + 0 = 0. \mathbf{v}_2 \cdot \mathbf{v}_3 = -1 - 1 + 2 = 0. All orthogonal.

Normalise

Divide by the norms: \mathbf{q}_1 = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(1, 1, 0), \mathbf{q}_2 = \frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}(1, -1, 2), \mathbf{q}_3 = \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}(-1, 1, 1).

Let \mathbf{a}_1, \dots, \mathbf{a}_n be linearly independent. Define \mathbf{v}_1 = \mathbf{a}_1, \qquad \mathbf{v}_j = \mathbf{a}_j - \sum_{i=1}^{j-1} \frac{\langle \mathbf{a}_j, \mathbf{v}_i \rangle}{\langle \mathbf{v}_i, \mathbf{v}_i \rangle}\,\mathbf{v}_i, \qquad \mathbf{q}_j = \frac{\mathbf{v}_j}{\|\mathbf{v}_j\|}. Then \mathbf{q}_1, \dots, \mathbf{q}_n are orthonormal. For every j, \operatorname{span}\{\mathbf{q}_1, \dots, \mathbf{q}_j\} = \operatorname{span}\{\mathbf{a}_1, \dots, \mathbf{a}_j\}.

Proof

Use induction on j. Suppose \mathbf{v}_1, \dots, \mathbf{v}_{j-1} are orthogonal and span W_{j-1} = \operatorname{span}\{\mathbf{a}_1, \dots, \mathbf{a}_{j-1}\}. The sum in the formula is the projection of \mathbf{a}_j onto W_{j-1}. So \mathbf{v}_j is the error part, and it is orthogonal to W_{j-1}.

Also \mathbf{v}_j \ne \mathbf{0}. Otherwise \mathbf{a}_j would lie in W_{j-1}, against independence. Finally \mathbf{v}_j is \mathbf{a}_j minus a vector of W_{j-1}. So the first j vectors \mathbf{v}_i span the same space as the first j vectors \mathbf{a}_i.

In simple words: take each new vector and remove its shadow on the earlier ones. What is left is new and perpendicular. A corollary: every finite-dimensional space with an inner product has an orthonormal basis.

import numpy as np

def gram_schmidt(A):
    """Classical Gram-Schmidt: returns Q with orthonormal columns."""
    Q = np.zeros_like(A, dtype=float)
    for j in range(A.shape[1]):
        v = A[:, j].astype(float)
        for i in range(j):
            v -= (Q[:, i] @ A[:, j]) * Q[:, i]   # remove the part along q_i
        Q[:, j] = v / np.linalg.norm(v)          # make the length 1
    return Q

A = np.array([[1, 1, 0],
              [1, 0, 1],
              [0, 1, 1]])          # columns a1, a2, a3
Q = gram_schmidt(A)
print(np.round(Q, 4))
print(np.allclose(Q.T @ Q, np.eye(3)))   # Q^T Q = I ?
print(np.round(Q.T @ A, 4) + 0.0)  # R; + 0.0 turns -0.0 into 0.0
[[ 0.7071  0.4082 -0.5774]
 [ 0.7071 -0.4082  0.5774]
 [ 0.      0.8165  0.5774]]
True
[[1.4142 0.7071 0.7071]
 [0.     1.2247 0.4082]
 [0.     0.     1.1547]]

The columns are our \mathbf{q}_1, \mathbf{q}_2, \mathbf{q}_3: for example 1/\sqrt{2} \approx 0.7071 and 2/\sqrt{6} \approx 0.8165. The last matrix is upper triangular. The next section explains why.

Use the inner product \int_{-1}^{1} f(x)g(x)\,dx. Run Gram-Schmidt on 1, x, x^2. You get 1, x and x^2 - \frac{1}{3}. These are the first Legendre polynomials, up to scaling. They are used in numerical integration.

QR decomposition

Look at the output above again. The matrix R = Q^{\mathsf{T}}A has zeros below the diagonal. Why? Entry (i, j) of Q^{\mathsf{T}}A is \mathbf{q}_i \cdot \mathbf{a}_j. Gram-Schmidt builds \mathbf{a}_j from \mathbf{q}_1, \dots, \mathbf{q}_j only. So \mathbf{q}_i \cdot \mathbf{a}_j = 0 when i \gt j.

\underbrace{\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 \end{pmatrix}}_{A} = \underbrace{\begin{pmatrix} \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{6}} & -\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & -\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \\ 0 & \frac{2}{\sqrt{6}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \end{pmatrix}}_{Q} \underbrace{\begin{pmatrix} \sqrt{2} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ 0 & \frac{3}{\sqrt{6}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{6}} \\ 0 & 0 & \frac{2}{\sqrt{3}} \end{pmatrix}}_{R}

Let A be an m \times n matrix with independent columns. Then A = QR, where Q is m \times n with orthonormal columns and R is n \times n, upper triangular and invertible. If we ask for a positive diagonal in R, then Q and R are unique.

Proof

Run Gram-Schmidt on the columns of A. It gives orthonormal \mathbf{q}_j with \mathbf{a}_j in \operatorname{span}\{\mathbf{q}_1, \dots, \mathbf{q}_j\}. So \mathbf{a}_j = r_{1j}\mathbf{q}_1 + \cdots + r_{jj}\mathbf{q}_j with r_{ij} = \mathbf{q}_i \cdot \mathbf{a}_j. These numbers form the upper triangular R. The diagonal entry r_{jj} = \|\mathbf{v}_j\| is positive, so R is invertible.

Uniqueness: let QR = Q'R'. Multiply by Q'^{\mathsf{T}} from the left and by R^{-1} from the right. This gives Q'^{\mathsf{T}}Q = R'R^{-1}, an upper triangular matrix. The columns of Q and Q' are orthonormal and span the same space C(A). So Q'^{\mathsf{T}}Q is also an orthogonal matrix. An upper triangular orthogonal matrix is diagonal with entries \pm 1. Positive diagonals in R and R' leave only +1. So R = R' and Q = Q'.

A QR decomposition is Gram-Schmidt written as matrices. The Q part holds the perpendicular directions. The R part records how to rebuild the old columns from them.

import numpy as np

A = np.array([[1.0, 1.0, 0.0],
              [1.0, 0.0, 1.0],
              [0.0, 1.0, 1.0]])
Q, R = np.linalg.qr(A)
print(np.round(R, 4))
print(np.allclose(Q @ R, A))
[[-1.4142 -0.7071 -0.7071]
 [ 0.      1.2247  0.4082]
 [ 0.      0.      1.1547]]
True

NumPy gives -1.4142 in the first row. It does not ask for a positive diagonal. It flips the signs of the first row of R and the first column of Q. The product is the same A. NumPy calls LAPACK routines (geqrf and orgqr). They do not use Gram-Schmidt at all. They use mirror matrices, which the last section of this chapter explains.

Classical Gram-Schmidt on a computer

Rounding errors hurt the formula above. Here is a hard matrix: the columns 1, t, t^2, \dots, t^{11} at 30 points. We measure how far Q^{\mathsf{T}}Q is from I.

import numpy as np

def classical(A):
    Q = np.zeros_like(A)
    for j in range(A.shape[1]):
        v = A[:, j].copy()
        for i in range(j):
            v -= (Q[:, i] @ A[:, j]) * Q[:, i]   # uses the old column a_j
        Q[:, j] = v / np.linalg.norm(v)
    return Q

def modified(A):
    Q = np.zeros_like(A)
    for j in range(A.shape[1]):
        v = A[:, j].copy()
        for i in range(j):
            v -= (Q[:, i] @ v) * Q[:, i]         # uses the new, cleaner v
        Q[:, j] = v / np.linalg.norm(v)
    return Q

A = np.vander(np.linspace(0, 1, 30), 12, increasing=True)
I = np.eye(12)
for name, Q in (("classical", classical(A)), ("modified", modified(A)),
                ("numpy qr", np.linalg.qr(A)[0])):
    print("%-9s  |Q^T Q - I| = %.1e" % (name, np.abs(Q.T @ Q - I).max()))
classical  |Q^T Q - I| = 1.0e+00
modified   |Q^T Q - I| = 1.1e-09
numpy qr   |Q^T Q - I| = 6.7e-16

Classical Gram-Schmidt lost all orthogonality: an error of size 1. Modified Gram-Schmidt changes one symbol. It projects the vector as it is now, not the original column. In exact maths both give the same result. On a computer the modified version is far better. Householder mirrors, used by NumPy, are best.

A matrix with orthonormal columns has Q^{\mathsf{T}}Q = I. But if it is not square, QQ^{\mathsf{T}} \ne I. Then QQ^{\mathsf{T}} is the projection onto the column space of Q. Only a square Q has Q^{-1} = Q^{\mathsf{T}}.

Least squares

Four measurements: at times t = 0, 1, 2, 3 we see y = 1, 2, 4, 5. We want a line y = c + mt through them. Each point gives one equation.

\begin{aligned} c + 0m &= 1 \\ c + 1m &= 2 \\ c + 2m &= 4 \\ c + 3m &= 5 \end{aligned} \qquad \Longleftrightarrow \qquad \underbrace{\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 \\ 1 & 3 \end{pmatrix}}_{A} \begin{pmatrix} c \\ m \end{pmatrix} = \underbrace{\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 2 \\ 4 \\ 5 \end{pmatrix}}_{\mathbf{b}}

Four equations, two unknowns. No line passes through all four points. The system A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b} has no solution. So we ask for the next best thing: make the error \|A\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{b}\| as small as possible. That means the sum of the squared misses is as small as possible.

A vector \hat{\mathbf{x}} makes \|A\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{b}\| as small as possible exactly when A^{\mathsf{T}}A\,\hat{\mathbf{x}} = A^{\mathsf{T}}\mathbf{b}. If the columns of A are independent, there is exactly one such \hat{\mathbf{x}} = (A^{\mathsf{T}}A)^{-1}A^{\mathsf{T}}\mathbf{b}.

Proof

The vectors A\mathbf{x} fill the column space C(A). By the projection theorem, the closest point of C(A) to \mathbf{b} is the projection \mathbf{p}. It is the only point where \mathbf{b} - \mathbf{p} is orthogonal to C(A). So A\hat{\mathbf{x}} is closest exactly when A^{\mathsf{T}}(\mathbf{b} - A\hat{\mathbf{x}}) = \mathbf{0}. With independent columns, A^{\mathsf{T}}A is invertible.

The solution \hat{\mathbf{x}} is the least squares solution. The equations A^{\mathsf{T}}A\hat{\mathbf{x}} = A^{\mathsf{T}}\mathbf{b} are the normal equations. Here "normal" means "perpendicular": the error is normal to the column space.

  1. Compute A^{\mathsf{T}}A = \begin{pmatrix} 4 & 6 \\ 6 & 14 \end{pmatrix} and A^{\mathsf{T}}\mathbf{b} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 + 2 + 4 + 5 \\ 0 + 2 + 8 + 15 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 12 \\ 25 \end{pmatrix}.
  2. Solve. The determinant is 56 - 36 = 20. So c = (14 \cdot 12 - 6 \cdot 25)/20 = 0.9 and m = (4 \cdot 25 - 6 \cdot 12)/20 = 1.4.
  3. The best line is y = 0.9 + 1.4t.
  4. The misses \mathbf{e} = \mathbf{b} - A\hat{\mathbf{x}} are 0.1, -0.3, 0.3, -0.1. Their squares add up to 0.2.
  5. Check orthogonality. The misses add up to 0, so \mathbf{e} is orthogonal to the column of ones. Also 0(0.1) + 1(-0.3) + 2(0.3) + 3(-0.1) = 0. Correct.

Why is this the best slope? Keep c = 0.9 and try other slopes m. The sum of squared misses is a parabola in m: 14m^2 - 39.2m + 27.64. Its lowest point is at m = 39.2/28 = 1.4, with the value 0.2.

This picture also shows another road to the normal equations. Set the gradient of \|A\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{b}\|^2 to zero. You get 2A^{\mathsf{T}}(A\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{b}) = \mathbf{0}. The chapter Matrix calculus does this derivation in full.

Linear regression in practice

Fitting a line is linear regression. "Linear" means linear in the unknowns c and m, not in t. To fit a parabola y = c_0 + c_1t + c_2t^2, just add a column t^2 to A. The method stays the same. Many features work the same way: one column per feature.

import numpy as np

t = np.array([0.0, 1.0, 2.0, 3.0])
y = np.array([1.0, 2.0, 4.0, 5.0])
A = np.column_stack([np.ones_like(t), t])   # columns: 1 and t

x_ne = np.linalg.solve(A.T @ A, A.T @ y)    # normal equations
Q, R = np.linalg.qr(A)
x_qr = np.linalg.solve(R, Q.T @ y)          # R x = Q^T y
x_ls, res, rank, sv = np.linalg.lstsq(A, y) # NumPy does it for you
print(x_ne, x_qr, x_ls)
print("residuals:", y - A @ x_ls, "sum of squares:", res)
[0.9 1.4] [0.9 1.4] [0.9 1.4]
residuals: [ 0.1 -0.3  0.3 -0.1] sum of squares: [0.2]

Three methods, one answer. The QR road works like this. Put A = QR into the normal equations: R^{\mathsf{T}}Q^{\mathsf{T}}QR\hat{\mathbf{x}} = R^{\mathsf{T}}Q^{\mathsf{T}}\mathbf{b}. Since Q^{\mathsf{T}}Q = I and R^{\mathsf{T}} is invertible, this becomes R\hat{\mathbf{x}} = Q^{\mathsf{T}}\mathbf{b}. That is a triangular system. Solve the last equation first, then go up. This is back substitution. The misses are called residuals.

Why experts avoid the normal equations

import numpy as np

t = np.linspace(0, 1, 30)
A = np.vander(t, 12, increasing=True)    # columns 1, t, t^2, ..., t^11
x_true = np.ones(12)
b = A @ x_true                           # data that fits exactly

x_ne = np.linalg.solve(A.T @ A, A.T @ b) # normal equations
Q, R = np.linalg.qr(A)
x_qr = np.linalg.solve(R, Q.T @ b)       # QR
print("cond(A)     %.1e" % np.linalg.cond(A))
print("cond(A^T A) %.1e" % np.linalg.cond(A.T @ A))
print("error, normal equations %.1e" % np.abs(x_ne - x_true).max())
print("error, QR               %.1e" % np.abs(x_qr - x_true).max())
cond(A)     1.2e+08
cond(A^T A) 1.4e+16
error, normal equations 7.9e-01
error, QR               5.5e-09

The condition number measures how much small errors can grow. Forming A^{\mathsf{T}}A squares it: (1.2 \times 10^8)^2 \approx 1.4 \times 10^{16}. That is beyond the about 16 digits of a float. So the normal equations lost every digit, and QR kept about 9. The condition number comes from the singular values in The spectral theorem and the SVD. NumPy's lstsq also uses singular values. In NumPy 2.0 its default cut-off rcond changed to machine precision times the larger side of A.

Fit y = c + mt and minimise the sum of the misses \sum (y_i - c - mt_i).

Minimise the sum of the squared misses. Plain misses can cancel: a terrible line can have a sum of 0. Squares are never negative, so they cannot cancel.

After any least squares answer, check A^{\mathsf{T}}\mathbf{e} = \mathbf{0}. For a line y = c + mt with a constant term c, this says two things. The residuals add up to 0, and the residuals weighted by t add up to 0. If not, you made an arithmetic error.

Least squares is also the start of statistics. Under some assumptions about the noise, it is the best linear unbiased estimator. That is the Gauss-Markov theorem in Statistical inference. Adding \lambda I to A^{\mathsf{T}}A gives ridge regression, see The maths of machine learning.

Orthogonal matrices

Take the rotation Q = \begin{pmatrix} \cos\theta & -\sin\theta \\ \sin\theta & \cos\theta \end{pmatrix}. Its columns are unit vectors, and they are orthogonal. So Q^{\mathsf{T}}Q = I. The inverse of a rotation is just its transpose. A turn by \theta is undone by a turn by -\theta.

For a square matrix Q, these three statements are equivalent.

  1. Q^{\mathsf{T}}Q = I, so Q^{-1} = Q^{\mathsf{T}}.
  2. \|Q\mathbf{x}\| = \|\mathbf{x}\| for every \mathbf{x}.
  3. Q\mathbf{x} \cdot Q\mathbf{y} = \mathbf{x} \cdot \mathbf{y} for all \mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y}.

Then \det Q = 1 or \det Q = -1.

Proof

From 1 to 3: (Q\mathbf{x})^{\mathsf{T}}(Q\mathbf{y}) = \mathbf{x}^{\mathsf{T}}Q^{\mathsf{T}}Q\mathbf{y} = \mathbf{x}^{\mathsf{T}}\mathbf{y}. From 3 to 2: take \mathbf{y} = \mathbf{x}. From 2 to 3: use \mathbf{x} \cdot \mathbf{y} = \frac{1}{4}(\|\mathbf{x} + \mathbf{y}\|^2 - \|\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{y}\|^2). From 3 to 1: entry (i, j) of Q^{\mathsf{T}}Q is Q\mathbf{e}_i \cdot Q\mathbf{e}_j = \mathbf{e}_i \cdot \mathbf{e}_j, which is the entry of I.

For the determinant: 1 = \det(Q^{\mathsf{T}}Q) = \det(Q^{\mathsf{T}})\det(Q) = (\det Q)^2.

A square matrix with orthonormal columns is an orthogonal matrix. The name is strange: the columns must be orthonormal, not only orthogonal. Orthogonal matrices are the rigid moves of space that keep the origin. They never stretch anything. So every eigenvalue has |\lambda| = 1, as in Eigenvalues and eigenvectors.

Householder mirrors

Can we send \mathbf{x} = (3, 4) to (5, 0) with a mirror? Both have length 5, so yes. Mirror in the line that is perpendicular to \mathbf{w} = \mathbf{x} - (5, 0) = (-2, 4).

H = I - 2\frac{\mathbf{w}\mathbf{w}^{\mathsf{T}}}{\mathbf{w}^{\mathsf{T}}\mathbf{w}} = I - \frac{2}{20}\begin{pmatrix} 4 & -8 \\ -8 & 16 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 0.6 & 0.8 \\ 0.8 & -0.6 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad H\begin{pmatrix} 3 \\ 4 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 5 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}.

A matrix H = I - 2\mathbf{u}\mathbf{u}^{\mathsf{T}} with a unit vector \mathbf{u} is a Householder reflection. It is symmetric and orthogonal, and \det H = -1. One mirror can make all entries of a column zero below the first. Apply one mirror per column, and A becomes the triangular R. The product of the mirrors gives Q. This is how LAPACK computes QR. Mirrors keep lengths, so rounding errors cannot grow.

Why do computers love orthogonal matrices?

Multiplying by Q keeps the length of every vector, and of every error too. So errors never grow. The condition number of an orthogonal matrix is 1, the best possible value. Inverting it costs nothing: just transpose.

Where are rotations used in AI?

Rotary position embeddings (RoPE) in many language models rotate pairs of query and key coordinates. The angle depends on the position of the token. Rotations keep lengths, and the dot product of two rotated vectors depends only on the difference of the angles. So attention sees the distance between tokens. See The maths of deep learning.

What is the "best" orthogonal matrix near a given matrix?

This is the orthogonal Procrustes problem. It appears when you align two sets of embeddings or two 3D scans. The answer comes from the SVD: if M = U\Sigma V^{\mathsf{T}}, the closest orthogonal matrix is UV^{\mathsf{T}}.

\det Q = \pm 1 does not make Q orthogonal. The shear \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix} has determinant 1, but it changes lengths: (0, 1) goes to (1, 1). Check Q^{\mathsf{T}}Q = I instead.

A short history

  1. 1801 Ceres. Giuseppe Piazzi finds the dwarf planet Ceres and then loses it. Young Gauss uses least squares to predict where it is.
  2. 1805 Legendre. Adrien-Marie Legendre publishes the first clear description of least squares.
  3. 1809 Gauss. Carl Friedrich Gauss publishes his method and says he used it since 1795. A famous priority dispute begins.
  4. 1821 Cauchy. Augustin-Louis Cauchy proves the inequality for sums.
  5. 1859 and 1888 Bunyakovsky and Schwarz. They prove the version for integrals.
  6. 1883 and 1907 Gram and Schmidt. Jørgen Gram and Erhard Schmidt publish the orthogonalisation process. Laplace had used the idea earlier.
