Practice

Which pair of vectors is orthogonal?

  • (1, 2) and (2, 1)
  • (2, -3, 1) and (1, 1, 1)
  • (1, 1, 1) and (1, 1, -1)

2 - 3 + 1 = 0. The other dot products are 4 and 1.

\|\mathbf{u}\| = 2 and \|\mathbf{v}\| = 5. Which value is impossible for \mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{v}?

  • -10
  • 7
  • 11

Cauchy-Schwarz gives |\mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{v}| \le 10. The value -10 happens when \mathbf{v} points opposite to \mathbf{u}.

Q is 5 \times 3 with orthonormal columns. Which statement is true?

  • QQ^{\mathsf{T}} = I
  • Q^{\mathsf{T}}Q = I
  • Q^{-1} = Q^{\mathsf{T}}

Q^{\mathsf{T}}Q is 3 \times 3 and holds the dot products of the columns. QQ^{\mathsf{T}} is a 5 \times 5 projection, not I. A non-square matrix has no inverse.

At the least squares solution, the error \mathbf{e} = \mathbf{b} - A\hat{\mathbf{x}} lies in which subspace?

  • The column space C(A)
  • The left null space N(A^{\mathsf{T}})
  • The null space N(A)

The normal equations say A^{\mathsf{T}}\mathbf{e} = \mathbf{0}. That is the left null space, which is C(A)^{\perp}.

The norm of (2, 3, 6) is ?.

The projection of (5, 5) onto the x-axis is ( ? , 0).

An orthogonal matrix has determinant 1 or ?.

  1. Project \mathbf{b} = (1, 2, 3) onto the line through \mathbf{a} = (1, 1, 1). Find the error and check it.
    Answer

    t = \frac{1 + 2 + 3}{3} = 2, so \mathbf{p} = (2, 2, 2). The error is \mathbf{e} = (-1, 0, 1). Check: \mathbf{e} \cdot \mathbf{a} = -1 + 0 + 1 = 0.

  2. Run Gram-Schmidt on \mathbf{a}_1 = (3, 4) and \mathbf{a}_2 = (1, 0). Give \mathbf{q}_1, \mathbf{q}_2.
    Answer

    \mathbf{q}_1 = (0.6, 0.8). Then \mathbf{a}_2 - (\mathbf{a}_2 \cdot \mathbf{q}_1)\mathbf{q}_1 = (1, 0) - 0.6(0.6, 0.8) = (0.64, -0.48). Its norm is 0.8. So \mathbf{q}_2 = (0.8, -0.6).

  3. Find the least squares line y = c + mt through (0, 0), (1, 1), (2, 1).
    Answer

    A^{\mathsf{T}}A = \begin{pmatrix} 3 & 3 \\ 3 & 5 \end{pmatrix} and A^{\mathsf{T}}\mathbf{b} = (2, 3). The determinant is 6. So c = (5 \cdot 2 - 3 \cdot 3)/6 = 1/6 and m = (3 \cdot 3 - 3 \cdot 2)/6 = 1/2. The residuals are -1/6, 1/3, -1/6. They add up to 0. Check.

  4. Show that P = A(A^{\mathsf{T}}A)^{-1}A^{\mathsf{T}} satisfies P^2 = P and P^{\mathsf{T}} = P.
    Answer

    P^2 = A(A^{\mathsf{T}}A)^{-1}(A^{\mathsf{T}}A)(A^{\mathsf{T}}A)^{-1}A^{\mathsf{T}} = A(A^{\mathsf{T}}A)^{-1}A^{\mathsf{T}} = P. For the transpose, A^{\mathsf{T}}A is symmetric, so its inverse is symmetric too. Then P^{\mathsf{T}} = A\left((A^{\mathsf{T}}A)^{-1}\right)^{\mathsf{T}}A^{\mathsf{T}} = P.

  5. With the inner product \int_{-1}^{1} f(x)g(x)\,dx, show that x and x^2 - \frac{1}{3} are orthogonal to 1. Are they orthogonal to each other?
    Answer

    \int_{-1}^{1} x\,dx = 0, because x is odd. \int_{-1}^{1} (x^2 - \frac{1}{3})\,dx = \frac{2}{3} - \frac{2}{3} = 0. And \int_{-1}^{1} x(x^2 - \frac{1}{3})\,dx = 0, because the function is odd. So all three are orthogonal.

  6. Let \mathbf{u} be a unit vector and H = I - 2\mathbf{u}\mathbf{u}^{\mathsf{T}}. Show that H^{\mathsf{T}}H = I and H\mathbf{u} = -\mathbf{u}.
    Answer

    H is symmetric. H^2 = I - 4\mathbf{u}\mathbf{u}^{\mathsf{T}} + 4\mathbf{u}(\mathbf{u}^{\mathsf{T}}\mathbf{u})\mathbf{u}^{\mathsf{T}} = I, because \mathbf{u}^{\mathsf{T}}\mathbf{u} = 1. Also H\mathbf{u} = \mathbf{u} - 2\mathbf{u}(\mathbf{u}^{\mathsf{T}}\mathbf{u}) = -\mathbf{u}. So \mathbf{u} is flipped, and vectors orthogonal to \mathbf{u} stay.

  7. A model predicts house prices from size and age with y \approx w_0 + w_1 \cdot \text{size} + w_2 \cdot \text{age}. You have 500 houses. What is the shape of A? When is the least squares solution not unique?
    Answer

    A is 500 \times 3: a column of ones, a column of sizes and a column of ages. The solution is unique when the three columns are independent. It fails if, for example, every house has the same age. Then the age column is a multiple of the column of ones.

Key takeaways

  • An inner product gives lengths, distances and angles. Cauchy-Schwarz bounds it by the product of the lengths.
  • Orthogonal vectors are independent. Their coordinates come from one inner product each.
  • The closest point of a subspace is the orthogonal projection. The error is perpendicular to the subspace.
  • Gram-Schmidt turns any independent list into an orthonormal one with the same spans.
  • Gram-Schmidt in matrix form is A = QR. Computers build it with Householder mirrors.
  • Least squares solves A^{\mathsf{T}}A\hat{\mathbf{x}} = A^{\mathsf{T}}\mathbf{b}. It fits lines, curves and linear models.
  • On a computer, prefer QR or lstsq to the normal equations. A^{\mathsf{T}}A squares the condition number.
  • Orthogonal matrices keep lengths and angles. Their inverse is their transpose.

Sources

  • Interactive Linear Algebra: The Method of Least Squares. An open textbook section on least squares solutions, their geometry and best-fit curves.
  • Cauchy-Schwarz inequality. Statement, equality case, several proofs and the history from Cauchy to Schwarz.
  • Gram-Schmidt process. The algorithm, the link to QR, and why the modified version and Householder mirrors are more stable.
  • Least squares. The method and its history: Ceres, Legendre in 1805 and Gauss in 1809.
  • numpy.linalg.lstsq. The NumPy 2.5 reference: return values and the default rcond that changed in NumPy 2.0.
  • numpy.linalg.qr. Modes of the QR function and the LAPACK routines it calls.

The spectral theorem and the SVD

Symmetric matrices are the best-behaved matrices. Their eigenvectors are perpendicular, and their eigenvalues are real. The singular value decomposition gives every matrix, even a rectangular one, the same kind of picture. It powers PCA, compression, recommendation systems and the numerical rank of data.

  • Diagonalise a symmetric matrix with an orthogonal matrix and read its quadratic form.
  • Test a matrix for positive definiteness in four different ways.
  • Compute and draw the singular value decomposition of a small matrix.
  • Use the best low-rank approximation and run PCA on data.
  • Use the pseudoinverse and judge a problem by its condition number.

Symmetric matrices and the spectral theorem

Take the symmetric matrix S = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 \end{pmatrix}. Its eigenvalues are 3 and 1, with eigenvectors (1, 1) and (1, -1). Look at the eigenvectors: (1, 1) \cdot (1, -1) = 0. They are perpendicular. Compare the matrix \begin{pmatrix} 4 & 1 \\ 2 & 3 \end{pmatrix} from Eigenvalues and eigenvectors. It is not symmetric. Its eigenvectors (1, 1) and (1, -2) have dot product -1.

A matrix is symmetric when S^{\mathsf{T}} = S. Covariance matrices, Hessians, graph Laplacians and Gram matrices A^{\mathsf{T}}A are all symmetric. That is why this chapter matters so much.

Let S be a real symmetric matrix. Then every eigenvalue of S is real. Eigenvectors for different eigenvalues are orthogonal.

Proof

Real. Let S\mathbf{v} = \lambda\mathbf{v} with a complex \mathbf{v} \ne \mathbf{0}. Multiply by \overline{\mathbf{v}}^{\mathsf{T}}: \overline{\mathbf{v}}^{\mathsf{T}}S\mathbf{v} = \lambda\,\overline{\mathbf{v}}^{\mathsf{T}}\mathbf{v} = \lambda\|\mathbf{v}\|^2. The number \overline{\mathbf{v}}^{\mathsf{T}}S\mathbf{v} equals its own complex conjugate, because S is real and symmetric. So it is real. And \|\mathbf{v}\|^2 \gt 0 is real. So \lambda is real.

Orthogonal. Let S\mathbf{v}_1 = \lambda_1\mathbf{v}_1 and S\mathbf{v}_2 = \lambda_2\mathbf{v}_2. Then \lambda_1\,\mathbf{v}_1 \cdot \mathbf{v}_2 = (S\mathbf{v}_1) \cdot \mathbf{v}_2 = \mathbf{v}_1 \cdot (S\mathbf{v}_2) = \lambda_2\,\mathbf{v}_1 \cdot \mathbf{v}_2. The middle step uses S^{\mathsf{T}} = S. With \lambda_1 \ne \lambda_2, this forces \mathbf{v}_1 \cdot \mathbf{v}_2 = 0.

Every real symmetric n \times n matrix S can be written as S = Q\Lambda Q^{\mathsf{T}} = \lambda_1\mathbf{q}_1\mathbf{q}_1^{\mathsf{T}} + \cdots + \lambda_n\mathbf{q}_n\mathbf{q}_n^{\mathsf{T}}, where Q is an orthogonal matrix with columns \mathbf{q}_i, and \Lambda is diagonal with the real eigenvalues \lambda_i. Conversely, every matrix of this form is symmetric.

Proof idea

Use induction on n. By the fundamental theorem of algebra, S has an eigenvalue. By the lemma it is real, so it has a real unit eigenvector \mathbf{q}_1. Let W be all vectors orthogonal to \mathbf{q}_1. If \mathbf{x} \in W, then \mathbf{q}_1 \cdot S\mathbf{x} = S\mathbf{q}_1 \cdot \mathbf{x} = \lambda_1\,\mathbf{q}_1 \cdot \mathbf{x} = 0. So S maps W into W.

In an orthonormal basis of W, S acts as a symmetric matrix of size n - 1. By induction it has an orthonormal basis of eigenvectors \mathbf{q}_2, \dots, \mathbf{q}_n in W. Together with \mathbf{q}_1 they form Q. The converse: (Q\Lambda Q^{\mathsf{T}})^{\mathsf{T}} = Q\Lambda Q^{\mathsf{T}}.

In simple words: a symmetric matrix is a pure stretch along perpendicular axes. The axes are the eigenvectors. The stretch factors are the eigenvalues. No shear and no turning are hidden inside. Each term \mathbf{q}_i\mathbf{q}_i^{\mathsf{T}} is the projection onto one axis, as in Orthogonality and least squares. This sum is the spectral decomposition. The set of eigenvalues is often called the spectrum.

  1. Normalise the eigenvectors: \mathbf{q}_1 = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(1, 1) and \mathbf{q}_2 = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(1, -1).
  2. Build the projections: \mathbf{q}_1\mathbf{q}_1^{\mathsf{T}} = \frac{1}{2}\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 \end{pmatrix} and \mathbf{q}_2\mathbf{q}_2^{\mathsf{T}} = \frac{1}{2}\begin{pmatrix} 1 & -1 \\ -1 & 1 \end{pmatrix}.
  3. Add with weights 3 and 1: \frac{3}{2}\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 \end{pmatrix} + \frac{1}{2}\begin{pmatrix} 1 & -1 \\ -1 & 1 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 \end{pmatrix}. Correct.

Repeated eigenvalues

Take S = \begin{pmatrix} 3 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 3 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 & 3 \end{pmatrix} with eigenvalues 5, 2, 2. Inside the eigenspace of 2, the plane x + y + z = 0, elimination gives (-1, 1, 0) and (-1, 0, 1). They are not orthogonal: the dot product is 1. Gram-Schmidt inside the plane fixes this: (-1, 0, 1) - \frac{1}{2}(-1, 1, 0) = (-\frac{1}{2}, -\frac{1}{2}, 1), or (-1, -1, 2).

Q = \begin{pmatrix} \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} & -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & -\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & -\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} & 0 & \frac{2}{\sqrt{6}} \end{pmatrix}, \qquad \Lambda = \begin{pmatrix} 5 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 2 \end{pmatrix} 
import numpy as np

S = np.array([[3.0, 1.0, 1.0],
              [1.0, 3.0, 1.0],
              [1.0, 1.0, 3.0]])
lam, Q = np.linalg.eigh(S)        # for symmetric matrices
print(lam)                        # real, in increasing order
print(np.allclose(Q.T @ Q, np.eye(3)))           # Q is orthogonal
print(np.allclose(Q @ np.diag(lam) @ Q.T, S))    # S = Q Lambda Q^T
[2. 2. 5.]
True
True

Use eigh, not eig, for symmetric matrices. It returns real eigenvalues in increasing order and an orthogonal Q. Its Q may differ from ours inside the plane of the eigenvalue 2. Any orthonormal basis of that plane is correct.

For a repeated eigenvalue, elimination gives a basis of the eigenspace, but not an orthogonal one. Run Gram-Schmidt inside each eigenspace before you build Q. Different eigenspaces are already orthogonal, so leave them alone.

For complex matrices the right idea is a Hermitian matrix, with \overline{S}^{\mathsf{T}} = S. The same theorem holds with a unitary Q. Quantum mechanics is built on this version.

Quadratic forms

Expand \mathbf{x}^{\mathsf{T}}S\mathbf{x} for S = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 \end{pmatrix} and \mathbf{x} = (x, y).

\begin{pmatrix} x & y \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} x \\ y \end{pmatrix} = 2x^2 + 2xy + 2y^2

A function like this is a quadratic form. Each diagonal entry s_{ii} gives s_{ii}x_i^2. Each pair of off-diagonal entries gives 2s_{ij}x_ix_j. So the cross term 2xy comes from the two entries 1.

Now change to the eigenvector coordinates u = \frac{x + y}{\sqrt{2}} and v = \frac{x - y}{\sqrt{2}}. The spectral theorem says the cross term disappears.

2x^2 + 2xy + 2y^2 = 3u^2 + 1v^2

So the curve 2x^2 + 2xy + 2y^2 = 3 is the ellipse 3u^2 + v^2 = 3. Its half-axes are 1 along (1, 1) and \sqrt{3} along (1, -1).

This is the principal axes idea. It works in any dimension: a quadratic form is a sum of squares \lambda_1y_1^2 + \cdots + \lambda_ny_n^2 in the right coordinates. The half-axes of \mathbf{x}^{\mathsf{T}}S\mathbf{x} = 1 are 1/\sqrt{\lambda_i}.

Let S be symmetric with smallest eigenvalue \lambda_{\min} and largest eigenvalue \lambda_{\max}. For every \mathbf{x} \ne \mathbf{0}, \lambda_{\min} \le \frac{\mathbf{x}^{\mathsf{T}}S\mathbf{x}}{\mathbf{x}^{\mathsf{T}}\mathbf{x}} \le \lambda_{\max}. The bounds are reached at the matching eigenvectors.

Proof

Write \mathbf{x} = Q\mathbf{y}. Then \mathbf{x}^{\mathsf{T}}\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{y}^{\mathsf{T}}\mathbf{y} and \mathbf{x}^{\mathsf{T}}S\mathbf{x} = \sum \lambda_i y_i^2. This is a weighted average of the \lambda_i with weights y_i^2 / \sum y_j^2. An average lies between the smallest and the largest value.

Check with our S: at \mathbf{x} = (1, 0), the quotient is 2/1 = 2. That is between 1 and 3. At (1, 1) it is 6/2 = 3, the maximum. So the largest eigenvalue answers the question "in which direction does the form grow fastest?". PCA asks exactly this question, later in this chapter.

Do not put the whole cross coefficient into one entry. For x^2 + 6xy + y^2, the matrix is \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 3 \\ 3 & 1 \end{pmatrix}, not \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 6 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}. Split it in half, so the matrix is symmetric.

Positive definite matrices

The form 2x^2 + 2xy + 2y^2 = 3u^2 + v^2 is positive for every (x, y) \ne (0, 0). Its graph is a bowl. The form x^2 + 4xy + y^2 from \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1 \end{pmatrix} is different. Its eigenvalues are 3 and -1. It goes up in one direction and down in another.

A symmetric matrix S is positive definite when \mathbf{x}^{\mathsf{T}}S\mathbf{x} \gt 0 for every \mathbf{x} \ne \mathbf{0}. It is positive semidefinite when \mathbf{x}^{\mathsf{T}}S\mathbf{x} \ge 0 for every \mathbf{x}.

A positive definite matrix is the matrix version of a positive number. A positive semidefinite matrix is like a number that is at least 0. A form that takes both signs is indefinite.

For a real symmetric n \times n matrix S, these five statements are equivalent.

  1. Energy: \mathbf{x}^{\mathsf{T}}S\mathbf{x} \gt 0 for every \mathbf{x} \ne \mathbf{0}.
  2. Eigenvalues: all eigenvalues of S are positive.
  3. Minors: the determinants of the upper-left 1 \times 1, 2 \times 2, \dots, n \times n corners are all positive.
  4. Pivots: elimination without row swaps gives n positive pivots.
  5. Factor: S = R^{\mathsf{T}}R for some matrix R with independent columns.
Proof

1 ⇔ 2: with \mathbf{x} = Q\mathbf{y}, \mathbf{x}^{\mathsf{T}}S\mathbf{x} = \sum \lambda_i y_i^2. This is positive for every \mathbf{y} \ne \mathbf{0} exactly when every \lambda_i \gt 0.

2 ⇒ 5: take R = \Lambda^{1/2}Q^{\mathsf{T}}. Then R^{\mathsf{T}}R = Q\Lambda Q^{\mathsf{T}} = S. 5 ⇒ 1: \mathbf{x}^{\mathsf{T}}R^{\mathsf{T}}R\mathbf{x} = \|R\mathbf{x}\|^2, and R\mathbf{x} \ne \mathbf{0} for \mathbf{x} \ne \mathbf{0}.

1 ⇒ 3: the upper-left k \times k corner S_k also passes the energy test. Use vectors whose last n - k entries are 0. So its eigenvalues are positive, and \det S_k, their product, is positive. 3 ⇒ 4: pivot k is \det S_k / \det S_{k-1}. 4 ⇒ 5: elimination gives S = LDL^{\mathsf{T}} with the pivots in D. Take R = D^{1/2}L^{\mathsf{T}}.

  1. Take K = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & -1 & 0 \\ -1 & 2 & -1 \\ 0 & -1 & 2 \end{pmatrix}. It appears in physics and in numerical methods for differential equations.
  2. Minors: 2, then 4 - 1 = 3, then \det K = 4. All positive.
  3. Pivots: 2, 3/2, 4/3. They are the ratios of the minors. All positive.
  4. Eigenvalues: 2 - \sqrt{2}, 2, 2 + \sqrt{2}. All positive.
  5. So K is positive definite, and K = R^{\mathsf{T}}R with an upper triangular R.
import numpy as np

K = np.array([[2.0, -1.0, 0.0],
              [-1.0, 2.0, -1.0],
              [0.0, -1.0, 2.0]])
print(np.round([np.linalg.det(K[:k, :k]) for k in (1, 2, 3)], 6))  # minors
print(np.round(np.linalg.eigvalsh(K), 4))                        # eigenvalues
R = np.linalg.cholesky(K, upper=True)       # K = R^T R
print(np.round(R, 4))
try:
    np.linalg.cholesky(np.array([[1.0, 2.0], [2.0, 1.0]]))
except np.linalg.LinAlgError as err:
    print("not positive definite:", err)
[2. 3. 4.]
[0.5858 2.     3.4142]
[[ 1.4142 -0.7071  0.    ]
 [ 0.      1.2247 -0.8165]
 [ 0.      0.      1.1547]]
not positive definite: Matrix is not positive definite

The factor S = R^{\mathsf{T}}R with upper triangular R and a positive diagonal is the Cholesky factorisation. The diagonal of R holds the square roots of the pivots: \sqrt{2} \approx 1.4142, \sqrt{3/2} \approx 1.2247, \sqrt{4/3} \approx 1.1547. Trying a Cholesky factorisation is the fastest positive definite test on a computer. It fails exactly when the matrix is not positive definite.

Where do positive definite matrices come from?

  • Every Gram matrix A^{\mathsf{T}}A is positive semidefinite, because \mathbf{x}^{\mathsf{T}}A^{\mathsf{T}}A\mathbf{x} = \|A\mathbf{x}\|^2. It is positive definite exactly when the columns of A are independent.
  • Every covariance matrix is positive semidefinite. A variance can never be negative.
  • If the Hessian of a smooth function is positive definite at a critical point, that point is a strict local minimum. This is the second derivative test of Multivariable optimisation.
  • The graph Laplacian is positive semidefinite, because its form is a sum of squares. See the Laplacian quadratic form.
  • Kernel matrices in machine learning must be positive semidefinite. This is the idea behind Mercer's theorem in The maths of machine learning.

Positive entries do not make a matrix positive definite. \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1 \end{pmatrix} has only positive entries but the eigenvalue -1. Also, for semidefinite matrices the corner minors are not enough. \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 \end{pmatrix} has corner minors 0 and 0, but \mathbf{x} = (0, 1) gives -1.

The singular value decomposition

Symmetric matrices are stretches along perpendicular axes. What about a general matrix, like A = \begin{pmatrix} 4 & 0 \\ 3 & 5 \end{pmatrix}? Its eigenvectors are not perpendicular. But there is a different trick. Look for perpendicular input directions that A sends to perpendicular output directions.

Form A transpose A

A^{\mathsf{T}}A = \begin{pmatrix} 25 & 15 \\ 15 & 25 \end{pmatrix}. It is symmetric and positive semidefinite.

Its eigenvalues

The trace is 50 and the determinant is 625 - 225 = 400. So the eigenvalues are 40 and 10. Their square roots are the singular values: \sigma_1 = \sqrt{40} = 2\sqrt{10} \approx 6.32 and \sigma_2 = \sqrt{10} \approx 3.16.

Input directions

The unit eigenvectors of A^{\mathsf{T}}A are \mathbf{v}_1 = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(1, 1) and \mathbf{v}_2 = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(-1, 1).

Output directions

\mathbf{u}_i = A\mathbf{v}_i / \sigma_i. This gives \mathbf{u}_1 = \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}(1, 2) and \mathbf{u}_2 = \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}(-2, 1). They are perpendicular.

Check

\sigma_1\mathbf{u}_1\mathbf{v}_1^{\mathsf{T}} + \sigma_2\mathbf{u}_2\mathbf{v}_2^{\mathsf{T}} = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 2 \\ 4 & 4 \end{pmatrix} + \begin{pmatrix} 2 & -2 \\ -1 & 1 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 4 & 0 \\ 3 & 5 \end{pmatrix}. Correct.

Every real m \times n matrix A of rank r can be written as A = U\Sigma V^{\mathsf{T}} = \sigma_1\mathbf{u}_1\mathbf{v}_1^{\mathsf{T}} + \cdots + \sigma_r\mathbf{u}_r\mathbf{v}_r^{\mathsf{T}}. Here U (m \times m) and V (n \times n) are orthogonal. \Sigma is m \times n with \sigma_1 \ge \sigma_2 \ge \cdots \ge \sigma_r \gt 0 on its diagonal and zeros elsewhere. The \sigma_i are the square roots of the nonzero eigenvalues of A^{\mathsf{T}}A.

Proof

A^{\mathsf{T}}A is symmetric and positive semidefinite. By the spectral theorem it has orthonormal eigenvectors \mathbf{v}_1, \dots, \mathbf{v}_n with eigenvalues \lambda_1 \ge \cdots \ge \lambda_n \ge 0. By the null space fact, N(A^{\mathsf{T}}A) = N(A). So exactly r eigenvalues are positive. Put \sigma_i = \sqrt{\lambda_i} and \mathbf{u}_i = A\mathbf{v}_i / \sigma_i for i \le r.

These \mathbf{u}_i are orthonormal: \mathbf{u}_i \cdot \mathbf{u}_j = \mathbf{v}_i^{\mathsf{T}}A^{\mathsf{T}}A\mathbf{v}_j / (\sigma_i\sigma_j) = \lambda_j\,\mathbf{v}_i \cdot \mathbf{v}_j / (\sigma_i\sigma_j). That is 1 for i = j and 0 otherwise. Extend them to an orthonormal basis of \mathbb{R}^m with Gram-Schmidt. Now A\mathbf{v}_i = \sigma_i\mathbf{u}_i for i \le r and A\mathbf{v}_i = \mathbf{0} for i \gt r. In matrix form, AV = U\Sigma. Multiply by V^{\mathsf{T}} on the right.

The numbers \sigma_i are the singular values. The \mathbf{v}_i and \mathbf{u}_i are the right and left singular vectors. This factorisation is the singular value decomposition, or SVD.

The picture: turn, stretch, turn

Read A\mathbf{x} = U\Sigma V^{\mathsf{T}}\mathbf{x} from right to left. First V^{\mathsf{T}} turns the plane. Then \Sigma stretches along the axes. Then U turns again. So every matrix sends the unit circle to an ellipse.

The SVD also gives clean bases for the four fundamental subspaces. The first r vectors \mathbf{v}_i are an orthonormal basis of the row space. The other \mathbf{v}_i span the null space. The first r vectors \mathbf{u}_i span the column space. The other \mathbf{u}_i span the left null space. And A sends each \mathbf{v}_i to \sigma_i\mathbf{u}_i.

import numpy as np

A = np.array([[4.0, 0.0],
              [3.0, 5.0]])
U, s, Vt = np.linalg.svd(A)       # A = U diag(s) Vt
print(np.round(s, 4), np.round(s ** 2, 4))
print(np.round(U, 4))
print(np.round(Vt, 4))
A1 = s[0] * np.outer(U[:, 0], Vt[0])   # keep only the first term
print(np.round(A1, 4))
print(round(np.linalg.norm(A - A1, 2), 4))   # spectral norm of the error
[6.3246 3.1623] [40. 10.]
[[-0.4472 -0.8944]
 [-0.8944  0.4472]]
[[-0.7071 -0.7071]
 [-0.7071  0.7071]]
[[2. 2.]
 [4. 4.]]
3.1623
  • NumPy returns V^{\mathsf{T}}, not V. The rows of Vt are the \mathbf{v}_i.
  • NumPy chose -\mathbf{u}_1 and -\mathbf{v}_1. Flipping both signs keeps \sigma_1\mathbf{u}_1\mathbf{v}_1^{\mathsf{T}} the same. Singular vectors are only fixed up to such a pair of signs.
  • The singular values come sorted from large to small, and they are never negative.

The largest singular value is the largest stretch: \sigma_1 = \max \|A\mathbf{x}\| over unit vectors \mathbf{x}. This number is the spectral norm \|A\|_2. The Frobenius norm \|A\|_F = \sqrt{\sum a_{ij}^2} also comes from the singular values: \|A\|_F^2 = \sigma_1^2 + \cdots + \sigma_r^2. For our A: 16 + 0 + 9 + 25 = 50 = 40 + 10.

Singular values are not the absolute values of the eigenvalues, except for symmetric matrices. Our A is triangular, so its eigenvalues are 4 and 5. Its singular values are 6.32 and 3.16. Their product is the same, |\det A| = 20. The individual numbers differ.

Low-rank approximation

The SVD writes A as a sum of simple pieces \sigma_i\mathbf{u}_i\mathbf{v}_i^{\mathsf{T}}. Each piece has rank 1. The pieces come in order of importance, because the \sigma_i decrease. So keep only the first k pieces.

A_k = \sigma_1\mathbf{u}_1\mathbf{v}_1^{\mathsf{T}} + \cdots + \sigma_k\mathbf{u}_k\mathbf{v}_k^{\mathsf{T}}

For our 2 \times 2 example, A_1 = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 2 \\ 4 & 4 \end{pmatrix}. The error A - A_1 = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & -2 \\ -1 & 1 \end{pmatrix} has spectral norm \sigma_2 = \sqrt{10} \approx 3.1623. The code above printed this number.

Let A have singular values \sigma_1 \ge \cdots \ge \sigma_r \gt 0, and let k \lt r. Among all matrices B of rank at most k, the truncated SVD A_k is closest to A: \|A - B\|_2 \ge \|A - A_k\|_2 = \sigma_{k+1}, \qquad \|A - B\|_F \ge \|A - A_k\|_F = \sqrt{\sigma_{k+1}^2 + \cdots + \sigma_r^2}.

Proof for the spectral norm

Let B have rank at most k. By rank-nullity, N(B) has dimension at least n - k. The span of \mathbf{v}_1, \dots, \mathbf{v}_{k+1} has dimension k + 1. The two dimensions add up to more than n. So the two subspaces share a unit vector \mathbf{x}.

Then B\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{0}, and \mathbf{x} = \sum_{i \le k+1} c_i\mathbf{v}_i with \sum c_i^2 = 1. So \|A\mathbf{x}\|^2 = \sum_{i \le k+1} \sigma_i^2c_i^2 \ge \sigma_{k+1}^2. Hence \|A - B\|_2 \ge \|(A - B)\mathbf{x}\| = \|A\mathbf{x}\| \ge \sigma_{k+1}. The Frobenius case uses a similar but longer argument.

In simple words: to squeeze a matrix into rank k, keep its k biggest pieces. Nothing else does better. Carl Eckart and Gale Young published this in 1936 for the Frobenius norm. Leon Mirsky extended it to many other norms in 1960. So the result is often called the Eckart-Young-Mirsky theorem.

Low rank in real data

Imagine 200 users rating 50 films. Suppose people really have only 3 hidden tastes, plus small random noise. The ratings form a 200 \times 50 matrix. Its singular values show the hidden structure.

import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
users, items, tastes = 200, 50, 3
X = rng.standard_normal((users, tastes)) @ rng.standard_normal((tastes, items))
X += 0.1 * rng.standard_normal((users, items))   # small noise, like real data

U, s, Vt = np.linalg.svd(X, full_matrices=False)
print(np.round(s[:6], 2))
total = np.linalg.norm(X)                        # Frobenius norm
for k in (1, 2, 3, 4):
    Xk = U[:, :k] * s[:k] @ Vt[:k]               # best rank-k matrix
    err = np.linalg.norm(X - Xk) / total
    print(k, "relative error %.4f" % err, "numbers stored", k * (users + items + 1))
print("full matrix stores", users * items)
[113.62 102.07  78.45   2.04   2.     1.96]
1 relative error 0.7507 numbers stored 251
2 relative error 0.4596 numbers stored 502
3 relative error 0.0561 numbers stored 753
4 relative error 0.0548 numbers stored 1004
full matrix stores 10000

After three pieces, the error drops to about 5.6%. The rest is noise, and more pieces barely help. Rank 3 needs 753 numbers instead of 10 000. This is the core idea of recommendation systems, image compression and noise removal. LoRA uses the same idea to fine-tune large language models. It learns a low-rank update of a big weight matrix instead of the full matrix.

Plot the singular values and look for a sharp drop, often called an "elbow". The number of values before the drop is a good guess for the true rank. NumPy's matrix_rank counts singular values above a small cut-off, as in Vector spaces.

Principal component analysis

Five measurements have two features each: (1, 3), (2, 2), (3, 4), (4, 6), (5, 5). They lie roughly along a line. Which direction holds most of the spread?

  1. Put the samples in the rows of X, one column per feature.
  2. Subtract the mean of each column. Call the result X_c.
  3. Compute the SVD X_c = U\Sigma V^{\mathsf{T}}.
  4. The rows of V^{\mathsf{T}} are the principal axes. The variance along axis i is \sigma_i^2 / (n - 1).
  5. To reduce to k dimensions, keep the coordinates X_cV_k on the first k axes.

Here the mean is (3, 4). The centred rows are (-2, -1), (-1, -2), (0, 0), (1, 2), (2, 1). The covariance matrix is C = \frac{1}{n - 1}X_c^{\mathsf{T}}X_c = \frac{1}{4}\begin{pmatrix} 10 & 8 \\ 8 & 10 \end{pmatrix}. Its eigenvalues are 4.5 and 0.5, with eigenvectors along (1, 1) and (1, -1).

import numpy as np

X = np.array([[1.0, 3.0], [2.0, 2.0], [3.0, 4.0],
              [4.0, 6.0], [5.0, 5.0]])       # 5 samples, 2 features
Xc = X - X.mean(axis=0)                      # centre each column
U, s, Vt = np.linalg.svd(Xc, full_matrices=False)
var = s ** 2 / (len(X) - 1)                  # variance along each axis
print("mean      ", X.mean(axis=0))
print("components", np.round(Vt, 4))         # rows = principal axes
print("variances ", np.round(var, 4))
print("ratio     ", np.round(var / var.sum(), 4))
print("scores    ", np.round(Xc @ Vt[0], 4)) # 1D coordinates on axis 1
mean       [3. 4.]
components [[ 0.7071  0.7071]
 [-0.7071  0.7071]]
variances  [4.5 0.5]
ratio      [0.9 0.1]
scores     [-2.1213 -2.1213  0.      2.1213  2.1213]
import numpy as np
import sklearn
from sklearn.decomposition import PCA

X = np.array([[1.0, 3.0], [2.0, 2.0], [3.0, 4.0],
              [4.0, 6.0], [5.0, 5.0]])
pca = PCA(n_components=1).fit(X)             # centres X for you
print(sklearn.__version__)
print(np.round(pca.components_, 4), np.round(pca.explained_variance_ratio_, 4))
print(np.round(pca.transform(X).ravel(), 4))
1.9.1
[[0.7071 0.7071]] [0.9]
[-2.1213 -2.1213  0.      2.1213  2.1213]

Both give the same axis (0.7071, 0.7071) and the same ratio 0.9. One number per point keeps 90% of the variance. The scikit-learn documentation says that PCA centres the data but does not scale it. Why does this method find the best direction?

Among all unit vectors \mathbf{w}, the variance of the projected data X_c\mathbf{w} is largest for \mathbf{w} = \mathbf{v}_1. Its value is \lambda_{\max}(C) = \sigma_1^2 / (n - 1).

The variance of X_c\mathbf{w} is \frac{1}{n-1}\|X_c\mathbf{w}\|^2 = \mathbf{w}^{\mathsf{T}}C\mathbf{w}. By the Rayleigh bounds, this is at most \lambda_{\max}(C), reached at its eigenvector. The eigenvectors of C = \frac{1}{n-1}X_c^{\mathsf{T}}X_c are the right singular vectors of X_c. So the SVD and the covariance matrix give the same axes. The SVD is more accurate on a computer, because it never forms X_c^{\mathsf{T}}X_c.

PCA depends on units. Measure one feature in metres and another in millimetres, and the millimetre feature wins only because its numbers are bigger. When features have different units, divide each column by its standard deviation first. Also, never forget to centre. Without centring, the first axis mostly points at the mean.

PCA is also linked to Eckart-Young. Keeping k axes gives the best rank-k approximation of the centred data. The chapter The maths of machine learning uses PCA as a tool among many others.

The pseudoinverse and the condition number

Take A = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 \end{pmatrix} and \mathbf{b} = (2, 4). The system A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b} asks for x_1 + x_2 = 2 and x_1 + x_2 = 4. There is no solution. The least squares solutions satisfy x_1 + x_2 = 3, the average. That is a whole line of answers. Which one should we take? A natural choice is the shortest one: (1.5, 1.5).

Let A = U\Sigma V^{\mathsf{T}}. Define A^{+} = V\Sigma^{+}U^{\mathsf{T}}, where \Sigma^{+} is n \times m with 1/\sigma_1, \dots, 1/\sigma_r on its diagonal. Then \mathbf{x}^{+} = A^{+}\mathbf{b} is a least squares solution of A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}. Among all least squares solutions, it has the smallest norm. If the columns of A are independent, A^{+} = (A^{\mathsf{T}}A)^{-1}A^{\mathsf{T}}. If A is invertible, A^{+} = A^{-1}.

Proof

Use the coordinates \mathbf{y} = V^{\mathsf{T}}\mathbf{x} and \mathbf{c} = U^{\mathsf{T}}\mathbf{b}. Orthogonal matrices keep lengths, so \|A\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{b}\|^2 = \|\Sigma\mathbf{y} - \mathbf{c}\|^2 = \sum_{i \le r}(\sigma_iy_i - c_i)^2 + \sum_{i \gt r} c_i^2. The smallest value needs y_i = c_i/\sigma_i for i \le r. The other y_i do not matter, so take them 0 for the shortest \mathbf{y}. Also \|\mathbf{x}\| = \|\mathbf{y}\|. That choice is exactly \mathbf{y} = \Sigma^{+}\mathbf{c}, so \mathbf{x} = V\Sigma^{+}U^{\mathsf{T}}\mathbf{b}.

The matrix A^{+} is the pseudoinverse, also called the Moore-Penrose inverse. It inverts what can be inverted and sends the rest to zero. For our A: \sigma_1 = 2, \mathbf{u}_1 = \mathbf{v}_1 = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(1, 1). So A^{+} = \frac{1}{2}\mathbf{v}_1\mathbf{u}_1^{\mathsf{T}} = \frac{1}{4}\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 \end{pmatrix}, and A^{+}\mathbf{b} = (1.5, 1.5).

import numpy as np

A = np.array([[1.0, 1.0],
              [1.0, 1.0]])          # rank 1: no inverse
b = np.array([2.0, 4.0])            # no exact solution
Ap = np.linalg.pinv(A)
print(Ap)
print(Ap @ b)                       # shortest least squares solution
print(np.linalg.lstsq(A, b)[0])     # lstsq gives the same x
[[0.25 0.25]
 [0.25 0.25]]
[1.5 1.5]
[1.5 1.5]

NumPy's pinv treats singular values up to rcond times \sigma_1 as zero. The default rcond is 10^{-15}. Without such a cut-off, a tiny \sigma_i would give a huge 1/\sigma_i and blow up the noise.

The condition number

That last remark leads to a key number. Take A = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1.0001 \end{pmatrix}. Its columns are almost parallel. Solve A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b} twice, with \mathbf{b} changed only in the fifth digit.

import numpy as np

A = np.array([[1.0, 1.0],
              [1.0, 1.0001]])       # columns almost parallel
s = np.linalg.svd(A, compute_uv=False)
print("singular values", s)
print("condition number %.1f" % (s[0] / s[-1]), "%.1f" % np.linalg.cond(A))
print(np.round(np.linalg.solve(A, [2.0, 2.0001]), 6))  # answer (1, 1)
print(np.round(np.linalg.solve(A, [2.0, 2.0002]), 6))  # b moved a tiny bit
singular values [2.000050e+00 4.999875e-05]
condition number 40002.0 40002.0
[1. 1.]
[0. 2.]

A change of 0.0001 in \mathbf{b} moved the answer from (1, 1) to (0, 2). The reason is the tiny second singular value. The condition number \kappa(A) = \sigma_{\max}/\sigma_{\min} measures this danger. Here it is about 40 000.

Let A be invertible, A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b} and A(\mathbf{x} + \delta\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{b} + \delta\mathbf{b}. Then \frac{\|\delta\mathbf{x}\|}{\|\mathbf{x}\|} \le \kappa(A)\,\frac{\|\delta\mathbf{b}\|}{\|\mathbf{b}\|}.

Proof

\delta\mathbf{x} = A^{-1}\delta\mathbf{b}, and A^{-1} stretches by at most 1/\sigma_{\min}. So \|\delta\mathbf{x}\| \le \|\delta\mathbf{b}\| / \sigma_{\min}. Also \|\mathbf{b}\| = \|A\mathbf{x}\| \le \sigma_{\max}\|\mathbf{x}\|. Divide the first inequality by \|\mathbf{x}\| \ge \|\mathbf{b}\|/\sigma_{\max}.

Check with our numbers. The relative change in \mathbf{b} is 0.0001 / 2.83 \approx 3.5 \times 10^{-5}. The relative change in \mathbf{x} is \|(-1, 1)\| / \|(1, 1)\| = 1. The ratio is about 28 000, below the bound 40 000. A rule of thumb: with \kappa \approx 10^k, you may lose about k correct digits. Doubles carry about 16 digits.

  • An orthogonal matrix has \kappa = 1, the best value.
  • \kappa(A^{\mathsf{T}}A) = \kappa(A)^2. That is why the normal equations lose twice as many digits as QR.
  • A singular matrix has \sigma_{\min} = 0, so \kappa = \infty.

A small determinant does not mean a bad condition number. 0.1I of size 10 has determinant 10^{-10}, but \kappa = 1. It is perfectly safe. The determinant changes with scaling. The condition number does not. Always use \kappa, never \det, to judge sensitivity. More about this is in Numerical methods.

How do computers compute the SVD?

They do not form A^{\mathsf{T}}A, because that squares the condition number. Gene Golub and William Kahan published a method in 1965. It first uses Householder mirrors to make A bidiagonal: only the main diagonal and the one above it stay nonzero. A variant by Golub and Christian Reinsch from 1970 is still widely used. For huge matrices, randomised methods find only the top singular values.

What is the polar decomposition?

Group the SVD as A = (UV^{\mathsf{T}})(V\Sigma V^{\mathsf{T}}). The first factor is orthogonal: a turn or a mirror. The second is symmetric positive semidefinite: a pure stretch. So every square matrix is a stretch followed by a turn, like a complex number re^{i\theta}.

Why is the SVD called the most important factorisation?

It exists for every matrix, square or not. Its factors U and V are orthogonal, so it is stable on a computer. It shows the rank, the four subspaces, the norm, the condition number and the best low-rank approximation at once.

A short history

  1. 1873 and 1874 Beltrami and Jordan. Eugenio Beltrami and Camille Jordan find singular values on their own.
  2. 1889 Sylvester. James Joseph Sylvester derives the SVD for real square matrices.
  3. 1901 Pearson. Karl Pearson fits lines and planes of closest fit to data. This is the start of PCA.
  4. 1933 Hotelling. Harold Hotelling develops principal components further and gives them their name.
  5. 1936 Eckart and Young. They prove the SVD for rectangular matrices and the best low-rank approximation.
  6. 1965 and 1970 Golub, Kahan and Reinsch. They give stable algorithms to compute the SVD.

Patterns to remember
