Practice

Which statement is true for every real symmetric matrix?

  • All its eigenvalues are real.
  • All its eigenvalues are positive.
  • It is invertible.

The lemma gives real eigenvalues. But \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1 \end{pmatrix} has the eigenvalue -1, and the zero matrix is symmetric but not invertible.

The singular values of A are the square roots of the eigenvalues of which matrix?

  • A
  • A^{\mathsf{T}}A
  • A + A^{\mathsf{T}}

A^{\mathsf{T}}A = V\Sigma^{\mathsf{T}}\Sigma V^{\mathsf{T}} has the eigenvalues \sigma_i^2. The matrix AA^{\mathsf{T}} works too.

Which matrix is positive definite?

  • \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1 \end{pmatrix}
  • \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 \end{pmatrix}
  • \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}

The corner minors of the second matrix are 2 and 3. The first has minors 1 and -3. The third is only semidefinite: (1, 0) gives 0.

You run PCA on height in metres and weight in grams. What should you do first?

  • Nothing. PCA does not care about units.
  • Centre each column and divide it by its standard deviation.
  • Only remove the first row.

The weight numbers are much bigger, so they would take over the first axis. Standardising puts both features on the same scale.

The largest singular value of \begin{pmatrix} 3 & 0 \\ 0 & -7 \end{pmatrix} is ?.

A matrix has the singular values 4, 2 and 0. Its rank is ?.

The condition number of \begin{pmatrix} 8 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 \end{pmatrix} is ?.

  1. Diagonalise S = \begin{pmatrix} 5 & 2 \\ 2 & 2 \end{pmatrix} with an orthogonal matrix.
    Answer

    The trace is 7 and the determinant is 6, so \lambda = 6 and \lambda = 1. For 6: S - 6I = \begin{pmatrix} -1 & 2 \\ 2 & -4 \end{pmatrix} gives (2, 1). For 1: \begin{pmatrix} 4 & 2 \\ 2 & 1 \end{pmatrix} gives (1, -2). They are orthogonal. So Q = \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & -2 \end{pmatrix} and \Lambda = \operatorname{diag}(6, 1).

  2. For which numbers c is \begin{pmatrix} 1 & c \\ c & 4 \end{pmatrix} positive definite?
    Answer

    The first minor is 1, which is positive. The second is 4 - c^2. It is positive exactly when -2 \lt c \lt 2.

  3. Find an SVD of A = \begin{pmatrix} 3 & 0 \\ 0 & -2 \end{pmatrix}.
    Answer

    A\mathbf{e}_1 = 3\mathbf{e}_1 and A\mathbf{e}_2 = 2(-\mathbf{e}_2). So \sigma_1 = 3, \sigma_2 = 2, V = I and U = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 \end{pmatrix}. The minus sign goes into U. Singular values are never negative.

  4. A matrix has the singular values 5, 3 and 1. Find the error of its best rank-1 approximation in the spectral norm and in the Frobenius norm.
    Answer

    By Eckart-Young, the spectral error is \sigma_2 = 3. The Frobenius error is \sqrt{3^2 + 1^2} = \sqrt{10} \approx 3.16.

  5. A grey image is a 1000 \times 1000 matrix. How many numbers does a rank-50 approximation need? What fraction is that?
    Answer

    Each term needs \mathbf{u}_i (1000 numbers), \mathbf{v}_i (1000 numbers) and \sigma_i (1 number). So 50 \cdot 2001 = 100\,050 numbers, about 10% of the 1\,000\,000 pixels.

  6. Find the pseudoinverse of the column \mathbf{a} = (1, 2, 2), seen as a 3 \times 1 matrix.
    Answer

    The columns are independent, so \mathbf{a}^{+} = (\mathbf{a}^{\mathsf{T}}\mathbf{a})^{-1}\mathbf{a}^{\mathsf{T}} = \frac{1}{9}(1, 2, 2) as a row. Then \mathbf{a}^{+}\mathbf{b} is the best multiple t in t\mathbf{a} \approx \mathbf{b}, as in projection onto a line.

  7. Show that \|A\|_F^2 = \sigma_1^2 + \cdots + \sigma_r^2.
    Answer

    \|A\|_F^2 is the trace of A^{\mathsf{T}}A, the sum of the squared lengths of the columns. The trace is the sum of the eigenvalues of A^{\mathsf{T}}A. Those eigenvalues are \sigma_1^2, \dots, \sigma_r^2 and zeros.

  8. An embedding model gives 768 numbers per document. You run PCA on 100 000 documents and find that 64 axes keep 95% of the variance. What does this mean for storage and search?
    Answer

    You can store 64 numbers per document instead of 768, about 8% of the space, and lose only 5% of the variance. Distances in the 64-dimensional space approximate the original ones, so search gets faster. Check the search quality on real queries before you switch, because 5% of the variance can still matter for some queries.

Key takeaways

  • A real symmetric matrix has real eigenvalues and orthonormal eigenvectors: S = Q\Lambda Q^{\mathsf{T}}.
  • A quadratic form becomes a sum of squares on the eigenvector axes. For a positive definite matrix, its level curves are ellipses.
  • Positive definite means positive energy. Equivalent tests: eigenvalues, corner minors, pivots, R^{\mathsf{T}}R.
  • Every matrix has an SVD A = U\Sigma V^{\mathsf{T}}: turn, stretch, turn. It sends the unit circle to an ellipse.
  • Keeping the top k singular values gives the best rank-k approximation. This is the Eckart-Young theorem.
  • PCA is the SVD of centred data. The first axis carries the most variance.
  • The pseudoinverse gives the shortest least squares solution.
  • The condition number \sigma_{\max}/\sigma_{\min} says how much input errors can grow.

Sources

  • MIT OpenCourseWare 18.06SC: Singular Value Decomposition. Gilbert Strang's unit on the SVD and its link to positive definite matrices.
  • Singular value decomposition. Statement, geometry, pseudoinverse, condition number and the history from Beltrami to Golub.
  • Low-rank approximation. The Eckart-Young-Mirsky theorem with its proofs for the spectral and Frobenius norms.
  • Sylvester's criterion. The corner minor test for positive definite matrices and its limits for semidefinite ones.
  • sklearn.decomposition.PCA. The scikit-learn 1.9.1 reference: centring without scaling, solvers and explained variance.
  • numpy.linalg.pinv. The NumPy 2.5 reference: the pseudoinverse through the SVD and the rcond cut-off.

Matrix calculus

Machine learning needs derivatives of functions with many inputs. Often the inputs form a vector or a whole matrix. Matrix calculus gives you a few rules for these derivatives. With them you can find any gradient by hand, check its shape, and test it with code.

  • Name the shape of a gradient, a Jacobian and a Hessian, and spot a layout mix-up.
  • Find gradients of linear and quadratic forms, trace, determinant and inverse with the differential method.
  • Use the chain rule as a product of Jacobians, in the right order.
  • Derive the least squares equations and the gradients of a neural network layer.
  • Check any matrix gradient with finite differences in Python.

Shapes first: gradient, Jacobian, Hessian

Take f(\mathbf{x}) = 3x_1 + 5x_2 - x_3. Add 0.01 to x_1. Then f grows by 0.03. Add 0.01 to x_2. Then f grows by 0.05. The three partial derivatives are 3, 5 and -1. Put them in one column, and you have the gradient.

That is the whole idea of this chapter. We collect many partial derivatives in a vector or a matrix. Then we compute with the whole object at once. The chapter Partial derivatives and the gradient built these objects one entry at a time. Here we learn rules that skip the entries.

  • For f : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}, the gradient \nabla f(\mathbf{x}) is the column with entries \partial f / \partial x_j. It has the same shape as \mathbf{x}.
  • For \mathbf{f} : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^m, the Jacobian J is the m \times n matrix with entry \partial f_i / \partial x_j. One row per output, one column per input.
  • For f : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}, the Hessian H is the n \times n matrix with entry \partial^2 f / \partial x_i \partial x_j.
  • For f : \mathbb{R}^{p \times q} \to \mathbb{R}, the gradient \nabla_X f is the p \times q matrix with entry \partial f / \partial x_{ij}. It has the same shape as X.
What the derivative looks like
The function takesand givesExampleDerivativeShape
a numbera numberx^2f'(x)1 \times 1
a vector in \mathbb{R}^na numbera loss of n weightsgradientn \times 1
a vector in \mathbb{R}^na vector in \mathbb{R}^mone layer of a networkJacobianm \times n
a matrix p \times qa numbera loss of a weight matrixgradientp \times q
a matrixa matrixX \mapsto X^{-1}a linear mapuse differentials
a vector in \mathbb{R}^na numbercurvature of a lossHessiann \times n

Two layouts

Books do not agree on one detail. Is the derivative of a number by a column vector a row or a column? Both choices exist. Each one is called a layout.

The two layouts, for x with n entries and y with m entries
DerivativeNumerator layoutDenominator layout
number by vectorrow, 1 \times ncolumn, n \times 1
vector by vectorm \times nn \times m
number by matrix p \times qq \times pp \times q

The two layouts give transposes of each other. This book makes one fixed choice. The Jacobian is m \times n, as in the numerator layout. A gradient of a number always has the shape of its variable. So \nabla f = J^\top for a function with one output. PyTorch does the same: w.grad has the shape of w.

Do not take one formula from a book with one layout and the next formula from a book with the other. You get a transposed answer, or shapes that do not fit. Before you copy a formula, check which layout the source uses.

Write the shape under every symbol, like \underset{n \times 1}{\mathbf{x}}. A product only works if the inner sizes match. Most errors in matrix calculus show up as a shape that does not fit.

The differential: one rule for every shape

Here is a trap. For a number, the derivative of x^2 is 2x. Is the derivative of X^2 for a matrix also 2X? Try X = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}. Change it by a small \varepsilon E with E = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}.

  1. Multiply out: (X + \varepsilon E)^2 = X^2 + \varepsilon(XE + EX) + \varepsilon^2 E^2.
  2. Compute XE = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix} and EX = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}.
  3. The first-order change is \varepsilon(XE + EX) = \varepsilon I.
  4. The guess 2X \cdot \varepsilon E gives \varepsilon \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}. That is wrong.

Matrices do not commute: XE \ne EX. So we need a method that keeps the order. That method is the differential.

The differential df is the part of f(X + dX) - f(X) that is linear in the small change dX. We write df = f'(X)[dX]. The derivative f'(X) is the linear map that turns dX into df.

You compute differentials with a few rules. They look like the rules for numbers. The only new thing is that the order stays fixed.

  • A constant matrix A has dA = 0.
  • Sum: d(X + Y) = dX + dY. Scaling: d(cX) = c\,dX.
  • Product: d(XY) = (dX)\,Y + X\,(dY). Keep X on the left of Y.
  • Transpose: d(X^\top) = (dX)^\top. Trace: d \operatorname{tr} X = \operatorname{tr} dX.

With the product rule, d(X^2) = dX\,X + X\,dX. That is exactly XE + EX from Example 1.

From the differential to the gradient

The trace of a square matrix is the sum of its diagonal. For example \operatorname{tr} \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 3 & 4 \end{pmatrix} = 5. The trace gives a dot product for matrices.

For two matrices of the same shape, \langle A, B \rangle = \operatorname{tr}(A^\top B) = \sum_{i,j} a_{ij} b_{ij}. It multiplies matching entries and adds them up. This is the Frobenius inner product.

Example: A = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 3 & 4 \end{pmatrix} and B = \begin{pmatrix} 5 & 6 \\ 7 & 8 \end{pmatrix}. Then \langle A, B \rangle = 5 + 12 + 21 + 32 = 70. The trace of A^\top B is also 70.

Now the key fact. A small change in a scalar function is a sum of "partial derivative times change" over all entries. That sum is an inner product.

df = \sum_{i,j} \frac{\partial f}{\partial x_{ij}}\, dx_{ij} = \operatorname{tr}\big( (\nabla_X f)^\top dX \big).

So if you bring df to the form \operatorname{tr}(M\,dX), the gradient is M^\top. To get there, you move matrices around inside the trace.

When the products are defined, \operatorname{tr}(AB) = \operatorname{tr}(BA), and \operatorname{tr}(ABC) = \operatorname{tr}(CAB) = \operatorname{tr}(BCA). Also \operatorname{tr}(A^\top) = \operatorname{tr}(A), and a number is its own trace.

Proof

Let A be m \times n and B be n \times m. The diagonal entry i of AB is \sum_j a_{ij} b_{ji}. So \operatorname{tr}(AB) = \sum_i \sum_j a_{ij} b_{ji}. The same double sum, in the other order, is \sum_j \sum_i b_{ji} a_{ij} = \operatorname{tr}(BA). For three factors, take A as one block and BC as the other: \operatorname{tr}(A(BC)) = \operatorname{tr}((BC)A).

You may rotate the factors. You may not swap two of them. In general \operatorname{tr}(ABC) \ne \operatorname{tr}(ACB). Also, \operatorname{tr}(AB) = \operatorname{tr}(A)\operatorname{tr}(B) is false. Try A = B = I_2: the left side is 2, the right side is 4.

Write the shapes

Write the size of every matrix and vector. The gradient will have the shape of the variable.

Take the differential

Apply d to the formula. Use the product rule. Keep every factor in its place.

Make it a trace

A scalar df equals its own trace. Write df = \operatorname{tr}(\dots).

Move dX to the end

Rotate the factors and use transposes until you have df = \operatorname{tr}(M\,dX).

Read off the gradient

The gradient is M^\top. Check that it has the shape of X.

Test with numbers

Change one entry by a tiny step h. Compare the change of f with h times the gradient entry.

Linear and quadratic forms

Go back to f(\mathbf{x}) = 3x_1 + 5x_2 - x_3. With \mathbf{a} = (3, 5, -1)^\top this is f = \mathbf{a}^\top \mathbf{x}, a linear form. Its gradient is \mathbf{a}. Now take f(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{x}^\top A \mathbf{x}, a quadratic form. With A = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 3 \end{pmatrix} it is x_1^2 + 2x_1x_2 + 3x_2^2.

Let \mathbf{a} be a fixed vector and A a fixed matrix.

  • \nabla (\mathbf{a}^\top \mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{a}, and the Jacobian of \mathbf{x} \mapsto A\mathbf{x} is A.
  • \nabla (\mathbf{x}^\top A \mathbf{x}) = (A + A^\top)\mathbf{x}. Its Hessian is A + A^\top.
  • If A is symmetric, these become 2A\mathbf{x} and 2A. In particular \nabla \|\mathbf{x}\|^2 = 2\mathbf{x}.
Proof with differentials

For the linear form, d(\mathbf{a}^\top \mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{a}^\top d\mathbf{x}. This is \operatorname{tr}(\mathbf{a}^\top d\mathbf{x}), so the gradient is (\mathbf{a}^\top)^\top = \mathbf{a}.

For the quadratic form, the product rule gives d(\mathbf{x}^\top A \mathbf{x}) = d\mathbf{x}^\top A \mathbf{x} + \mathbf{x}^\top A\, d\mathbf{x}. The first term is a number, so it equals its transpose: d\mathbf{x}^\top A \mathbf{x} = \mathbf{x}^\top A^\top d\mathbf{x}. Together, df = \mathbf{x}^\top (A + A^\top)\, d\mathbf{x}. The gradient is the transpose of the row in front of d\mathbf{x}: (A + A^\top)\mathbf{x}. The gradient is linear in \mathbf{x}, so its Jacobian, the Hessian, is the constant A + A^\top.

  1. A = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 3 \end{pmatrix}, so A + A^\top = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 2 \\ 2 & 6 \end{pmatrix}.
  2. At \mathbf{x} = (1, 1)^\top: \nabla f = (2 + 2,\ 2 + 6)^\top = (4, 8)^\top.
  3. Check by hand. \partial f / \partial x_1 = 2x_1 + 2x_2 = 4 and \partial f / \partial x_2 = 2x_1 + 6x_2 = 8. Correct.
  4. The wrong formula 2A\mathbf{x} gives (6, 6)^\top. It fails because A is not symmetric.

What does the gradient tell us along a line? Walk from (1, 1) in the direction \mathbf{v} = (1, 1). The slice is g(t) = f(1 + t, 1 + t) = 6(1 + t)^2. Its slope at t = 0 is 12. The gradient predicts the same: \nabla f \cdot \mathbf{v} = 4 + 8 = 12.

The Hessian and the second-order picture

The Hessian holds the curvature. By Clairaut's theorem, mixed partials are equal for smooth functions. So the Hessian is symmetric. Near a point, a smooth function looks like a quadratic form:

f(\mathbf{x} + \mathbf{h}) \approx f(\mathbf{x}) + \nabla f(\mathbf{x})^\top \mathbf{h} + \tfrac{1}{2}\, \mathbf{h}^\top H(\mathbf{x})\, \mathbf{h}.

For Example 2, f(1.1, 1.1) = 6 \cdot 1.21 = 7.26. The formula gives 6 + 1.2 + \tfrac{1}{2}(0.02 + 0.04 + 0.06) = 7.26. It is exact here, because f is itself quadratic. The chapter Optimisation in many variables uses the Hessian to tell minima from saddle points.

\nabla(\mathbf{x}^\top A \mathbf{x}) = 2A\mathbf{x} is true only for a symmetric A. In general use (A + A^\top)\mathbf{x}. A safe habit: first replace A by its symmetric part \tfrac{1}{2}(A + A^\top). The quadratic form does not change.

Trace, determinant and inverse

Take f(X) = \operatorname{tr}(AX) with A = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 3 & 4 \end{pmatrix}. Write it out: f = x_{11} + 2x_{21} + 3x_{12} + 4x_{22}. So \partial f / \partial x_{12} = 3 and \partial f / \partial x_{21} = 2. The gradient is \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 3 \\ 2 & 4 \end{pmatrix} = A^\top. Note the transpose.

For fixed matrices A, B of fitting shapes:

  • \nabla_X \operatorname{tr}(A^\top X) = A and \nabla_X \operatorname{tr}(AX) = A^\top.
  • \nabla_X \operatorname{tr}(AXB) = A^\top B^\top.
  • \nabla_X \operatorname{tr}(X^\top A X) = (A + A^\top)X, and \nabla_X \|X\|_F^2 = 2X.
Proof

d \operatorname{tr}(AXB) = \operatorname{tr}(A\,dX\,B) = \operatorname{tr}(BA\,dX) by rotation. The gradient is (BA)^\top = A^\top B^\top. Put B = I for \operatorname{tr}(AX).

For the last rule: d \operatorname{tr}(X^\top A X) = \operatorname{tr}(dX^\top A X) + \operatorname{tr}(X^\top A\, dX). The first trace equals the trace of its transpose, \operatorname{tr}(X^\top A^\top dX). So df = \operatorname{tr}(X^\top (A + A^\top)\, dX), and the gradient is (A + A^\top)X. With A = I this is \|X\|_F^2 = \operatorname{tr}(X^\top X).

The determinant

For a 2 \times 2 matrix, \det X = x_{11}x_{22} - x_{12}x_{21}. The four partial derivatives are easy:

\nabla_X \det X = \begin{pmatrix} x_{22} & -x_{21} \\ -x_{12} & x_{11} \end{pmatrix}.

This is the cofactor matrix from the chapter Determinants. Take X = \begin{pmatrix} 3 & 1 \\ 2 & 4 \end{pmatrix}, with \det X = 10. Change x_{22} from 4 to 4.01. The cofactor of that entry is 3. So the determinant should grow by 3 \cdot 0.01 = 0.03. Indeed 3 \cdot 4.01 - 2 = 10.03.

For a square matrix X, d(\det X) = \operatorname{tr}\big(\operatorname{adj}(X)\, dX\big). So \nabla_X \det X is the cofactor matrix C. If X is invertible, d(\det X) = \det X \, \operatorname{tr}(X^{-1} dX), and

\nabla_X \det X = \det(X)\, X^{-\top}, \qquad \nabla_X \ln|\det X| = X^{-\top}.
Proof

Expand the determinant along row i: \det X = \sum_j x_{ij} C_{ij}. The cofactor C_{ij} uses only entries outside row i and column j. So it does not contain x_{ij}. Then \partial \det X / \partial x_{ij} = C_{ij}. This proves \nabla \det X = C.

The adjugate is \operatorname{adj}(X) = C^\top, and X^{-1} = \operatorname{adj}(X) / \det X. So C = \det(X)\, X^{-\top}. For the logarithm, use the chain rule for numbers: d \ln|\det X| = d(\det X) / \det X = \operatorname{tr}(X^{-1} dX).

The formula is named after Carl Gustav Jacob Jacobi. The log-determinant shows up often in machine learning. The likelihood of a Gaussian with covariance \Sigma contains -\tfrac{1}{2}\ln\det\Sigma. Normalising flows, a kind of generative model, add \ln|\det J| for every layer.

The inverse

If X is invertible, then d(X^{-1}) = -X^{-1}\, dX\, X^{-1}.

Proof

Start from X X^{-1} = I. Take the differential of both sides. The right side is constant, so dX\, X^{-1} + X\, d(X^{-1}) = 0. Multiply by X^{-1} on the left: d(X^{-1}) = -X^{-1}\, dX\, X^{-1}.

For a 1 \times 1 matrix this is the old rule d(1/x) = -dx/x^2. Here is a check with numbers. Take Y = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 \end{pmatrix}. Change only its bottom-right entry by a tiny step.

import numpy as np

Y = np.array([[2.0, 1.0], [1.0, 1.0]])
E = np.array([[0.0, 0.0], [0.0, 1.0]])   # change only the bottom-right entry
eps = 1e-4
true_change = np.linalg.inv(Y + eps * E) - np.linalg.inv(Y)
predicted = -eps * np.linalg.inv(Y) @ E @ np.linalg.inv(Y)
print(np.round(true_change / eps, 4))
print(np.round(predicted / eps, 4))
[[-0.9998  1.9996]
 [ 1.9996 -3.9992]]
[[-1.  2.]
 [ 2. -4.]]

The two results agree to about 10^{-4}. The small gap is the \varepsilon^2 part, which the differential ignores.

d(X^{-1}) = -X^{-2}\, dX

d(X^{-1}) = -X^{-1}\, dX\, X^{-1}

The first form is true only when X and dX commute. In general they do not. Keep dX in the middle.

Here a short script checks four rules of this chapter at random matrices. It changes one entry at a time by \pm h. This is the method of central differences.

import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(1)

def num_grad(f, X, h=1e-6):
    """Central differences: change one entry at a time."""
    G = np.zeros_like(X)
    for idx in np.ndindex(X.shape):
        E = np.zeros_like(X); E[idx] = h
        G[idx] = (f(X + E) - f(X - E)) / (2 * h)
    return G

A = rng.standard_normal((3, 3))         # not symmetric
x = rng.standard_normal(3)
X = rng.standard_normal((3, 3))

checks = {
    "x^T A x  -> (A + A^T) x": (lambda v: v @ A @ v, x, (A + A.T) @ x),
    "tr(A^T X) -> A":         (lambda M: np.trace(A.T @ M), X, A),
    "det X    -> det(X) X^-T": (np.linalg.det, X, np.linalg.det(X) * np.linalg.inv(X).T),
    "ln|det X| -> X^-T":      (lambda M: np.log(abs(np.linalg.det(M))), X, np.linalg.inv(X).T),
}
for name, (f, P, exact) in checks.items():
    err = np.abs(num_grad(f, P) - exact).max()
    print(f"{name:26} max error {err:.1e}")
x^T A x  -> (A + A^T) x    max error 1.4e-11
tr(A^T X) -> A             max error 1.5e-10
det X    -> det(X) X^-T    max error 1.9e-11
ln|det X| -> X^-T          max error 2.3e-10

The chain rule with matrices

Let \mathbf{y} = A\mathbf{x} with A = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 \end{pmatrix}. Let L = \|\mathbf{y}\|^2. So \mathbf{x} has 2 entries, \mathbf{y} has 3, and L is a number. What is \nabla_{\mathbf{x}} L at \mathbf{x} = (1, 1)^\top?

  1. Inner map: \mathbf{y} = A\mathbf{x} = (1, 2, 3)^\top. Its Jacobian is A, shape 3 \times 2.
  2. Outer map: L = \|\mathbf{y}\|^2. Its Jacobian is the row 2\mathbf{y}^\top = (2, 4, 6), shape 1 \times 3.
  3. Multiply in this order: (2, 4, 6)\, A = (2 + 4 + 6,\ 0 + 4 + 12) = (12, 16). Shape 1 \times 2.
  4. The gradient is the transpose: \nabla_{\mathbf{x}} L = 2A^\top A\mathbf{x} = (12, 16)^\top.

Let \mathbf{g} : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^k and \mathbf{f} : \mathbb{R}^k \to \mathbb{R}^m be differentiable. Then

\underset{m \times n}{J_{\mathbf{f} \circ \mathbf{g}}(\mathbf{x})} = \underset{m \times k}{J_{\mathbf{f}}\big(\mathbf{g}(\mathbf{x})\big)}\ \underset{k \times n}{J_{\mathbf{g}}(\mathbf{x})}.

For a chain of maps, J = J_L J_{L-1} \cdots J_1, with the last map on the left. If the final output L is a number and \mathbf{y} = \mathbf{g}(\mathbf{x}), then \nabla_{\mathbf{x}} L = J_{\mathbf{g}}(\mathbf{x})^\top\, \nabla_{\mathbf{y}} L.

Proof

Look at entry (i, j) of the product. It is \sum_{r=1}^{k} \frac{\partial f_i}{\partial y_r} \frac{\partial y_r}{\partial x_j}. The multivariable chain rule says this sum is \partial f_i / \partial x_j. So every entry is right.

With differentials it is one line: d\mathbf{y} = J_{\mathbf{g}}\, d\mathbf{x} and d\mathbf{z} = J_{\mathbf{f}}\, d\mathbf{y}, so d\mathbf{z} = J_{\mathbf{f}} J_{\mathbf{g}}\, d\mathbf{x}. For a scalar L, J_{\mathbf{f}} is the row (\nabla_{\mathbf{y}} L)^\top. Transpose the product to get the gradient.

A deep network is a long chain. For a scalar loss, the leftmost Jacobian is a single row. So the cheapest order multiplies from the left: row times matrix, again and again. This is reverse mode. The chapter The maths of deep learning shows that this is backpropagation. We do not repeat it here.

For a gradient, \nabla_{\mathbf{x}} L = J^\top \nabla_{\mathbf{y}} L. Writing J \nabla_{\mathbf{y}} L gives a shape error in Example 3: (3 \times 2) times (3 \times 1) is not defined. If the shapes fit only after a transpose, you probably need that transpose.

Matrix inputs: vec and the Kronecker product

What is the Jacobian of X \mapsto AXB? The input is a matrix, so stack its columns into one long vector. This is \operatorname{vec}(X), the vectorisation of X. The Kronecker product P \otimes Q is the block matrix with blocks p_{ij} Q.

For matrices of fitting shapes, \operatorname{vec}(AXB) = (B^\top \otimes A)\, \operatorname{vec}(X). So the Jacobian of X \mapsto AXB, in vec form, is B^\top \otimes A.

import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(2)
A = rng.standard_normal((2, 3))
X = rng.standard_normal((3, 4))
B = rng.standard_normal((4, 5))

vec = lambda M: M.reshape(-1, order="F")      # stack the columns
left = vec(A @ X @ B)
right = np.kron(B.T, A) @ vec(X)
print("vec(AXB) has", left.size, "entries")
print("Jacobian (B^T kron A) has shape", np.kron(B.T, A).shape)
print("max difference:", f"{abs(left - right).max():.1e}")
vec(AXB) has 10 entries
Jacobian (B^T kron A) has shape (10, 12)
max difference: 7.8e-16

The Kronecker form is good for proofs. It is bad for computing. A 1000 \times 1000 weight matrix has a million entries. A full Jacobian from it to a million outputs would have 10^{12} entries. Real code almost never builds it. It uses products like A^\top G B^\top instead. Note also order="F": NumPy stacks rows by default, but vec stacks columns.

Least squares by calculus

Three measured points are (0, 1), (1, 3) and (2, 4). No line goes through all three. Which line y = c + mx fits best? "Best" means the smallest sum of squared errors.

Write the unknowns as \mathbf{x} = (c, m)^\top. Each row of A is (1, x_i), and \mathbf{b} holds the y_i.

A = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 \end{pmatrix}, \quad \mathbf{b} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 3 \\ 4 \end{pmatrix}, \quad f(\mathbf{x}) = \|A\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{b}\|^2.

The vector A\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{b} is the residual. We want the smallest residual.

  1. Expand: f = \mathbf{x}^\top A^\top A \mathbf{x} - 2\,\mathbf{b}^\top A \mathbf{x} + \mathbf{b}^\top \mathbf{b}.
  2. A^\top A is symmetric. By the quadratic form rule, the first term has gradient 2A^\top A\mathbf{x}.
  3. The middle term is a linear form with \mathbf{a} = -2A^\top \mathbf{b}. The last term is constant.
  4. So \nabla f = 2A^\top A\mathbf{x} - 2A^\top \mathbf{b} = 2A^\top (A\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{b}).
  5. Set it to zero: A^\top A\, \mathbf{x} = A^\top \mathbf{b}. These are the normal equations.
  6. Numbers: A^\top A = \begin{pmatrix} 3 & 3 \\ 3 & 5 \end{pmatrix} and A^\top \mathbf{b} = \begin{pmatrix} 8 \\ 11 \end{pmatrix}. Solve: m = 1.5 and c = 7/6 \approx 1.167.

Is this point really a minimum? The Hessian is 2A^\top A. For every vector \mathbf{v}, \mathbf{v}^\top A^\top A \mathbf{v} = \|A\mathbf{v}\|^2 \ge 0. So the Hessian is positive semidefinite, and f is a bowl. Every point with zero gradient is a lowest point. If the columns of A are independent, the bowl has exactly one lowest point.

The chapter Orthogonality and least squares gets the same equations from geometry, with projections. Calculus and geometry agree. Here is the check in code, plus a common variant.

import numpy as np

A = np.array([[1, 0], [1, 1], [1, 2]], dtype=float)   # columns: 1 and x
b = np.array([1, 3, 4], dtype=float)                  # the y values

x_normal = np.linalg.solve(A.T @ A, A.T @ b)          # gradient = 0
x_lstsq = np.linalg.lstsq(A, b, rcond=None)[0]        # library answer
print("normal equations:", x_normal)
print("np.linalg.lstsq: ", x_lstsq)
print("gradient there:  ", 2 * A.T @ (A @ x_normal - b))

lam = 1.0                                             # ridge penalty
x_ridge = np.linalg.solve(A.T @ A + lam * np.eye(2), A.T @ b)
print("ridge, lambda=1: ", x_ridge)
normal equations: [1.16666667 1.5       ]
np.linalg.lstsq:  [1.16666667 1.5       ]
gradient there:   [-1.77635684e-15 -2.66453526e-15]
ridge, lambda=1:  [1.         1.33333333]

The gradient is not exactly 0. It is about 10^{-15}, the size of rounding errors. The last line is ridge regression. It minimises \|A\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{b}\|^2 + \lambda \|\mathbf{x}\|^2. The penalty adds 2\lambda\mathbf{x} to the gradient. So the equations become (A^\top A + \lambda I)\mathbf{x} = A^\top \mathbf{b}. For \lambda = 1: \begin{pmatrix} 4 & 3 \\ 3 & 6 \end{pmatrix} \mathbf{x} = \begin{pmatrix} 8 \\ 11 \end{pmatrix}, so \mathbf{x} = (1, 4/3)^\top. The penalty pulls the slope down from 1.5.

Do not compute inv(A.T @ A) @ A.T @ b in real code. The product A^\top A squares the condition number of A. So you can lose twice as many digits. Use np.linalg.lstsq, which uses a stable factorisation. The normal equations are for thinking, not for computing.

The gradient of a neural network layer

A dense layer takes a batch of N examples. Each example is a row with d numbers. The layer computes Z = HW + \mathbf{1}\mathbf{b}^\top. Here \mathbf{1}\mathbf{b}^\top just adds the bias row \mathbf{b}^\top to every row.

The shapes in one layer
SymbolMeaningShape
Hinputs, one example per rowN \times d
Wweightsd \times k
\mathbf{b}biask
ZoutputsN \times k
G = \partial L / \partial Zgradient that comes from the layers aboveN \times k

The loss L is one number. The layers above give us G. We want the gradients for W, for \mathbf{b} and for H. The last one is the message for the layer below.

  1. Differential of the layer: dZ = dH\, W + H\, dW + \mathbf{1}\, d\mathbf{b}^\top.
  2. Change of the loss: dL = \operatorname{tr}(G^\top dZ). This is the definition of G.
  3. Weights: \operatorname{tr}(G^\top H\, dW). The gradient is (G^\top H)^\top = H^\top G.
  4. Input: \operatorname{tr}(G^\top dH\, W) = \operatorname{tr}(W G^\top dH). The gradient is (W G^\top)^\top = G W^\top.
  5. Bias: \operatorname{tr}(G^\top \mathbf{1}\, d\mathbf{b}^\top) = d\mathbf{b}^\top G^\top \mathbf{1}. The gradient is G^\top \mathbf{1}, the sum of the rows of G.
  6. Shapes: H^\top G is (d \times N)(N \times k) = d \times k, like W. G W^\top is N \times d, like H. Both fit.

Let Z = HW + \mathbf{1}\mathbf{b}^\top and G = \partial L / \partial Z. Then

\frac{\partial L}{\partial W} = H^\top G, \qquad \frac{\partial L}{\partial \mathbf{b}} = G^\top \mathbf{1}, \qquad \frac{\partial L}{\partial H} = G W^\top.

For an activation applied to each entry, A = \sigma(Z), the rule is \partial L / \partial Z = (\partial L / \partial A) \odot \sigma'(Z).

The symbol \odot is the Hadamard product. It multiplies entry by entry. Why? An entrywise function has a diagonal Jacobian. A diagonal matrix times a vector is an entrywise product. So code never builds that Jacobian.

The script below checks all three rules with central differences. It uses the loss L = \tfrac{1}{2}\|Z - T\|_F^2, so G = Z - T.

import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
H = rng.standard_normal((4, 3))        # batch of 4 rows, 3 inputs each
W = rng.standard_normal((3, 2))        # 3 inputs -> 2 outputs
b = rng.standard_normal(2)
T = rng.standard_normal((4, 2))        # targets

def loss(H, W, b):
    Z = H @ W + b                      # b is added to every row
    return 0.5 * np.sum((Z - T) ** 2)  # a simple scalar loss

# the three rules from the differential
G = H @ W + b - T                      # G = dL/dZ, same shape as Z
dW, db, dH = H.T @ G, G.sum(axis=0), G @ W.T

def num_grad(f, P, h=1e-6):
    out = np.zeros_like(P)
    for i in np.ndindex(P.shape):
        E = np.zeros_like(P); E[i] = h
        out[i] = (f(P + E) - f(P - E)) / (2 * h)
    return out

print("dW shape", dW.shape, "error", f"{abs(dW - num_grad(lambda P: loss(H, P, b), W)).max():.1e}")
print("db shape", db.shape, "error", f"{abs(db - num_grad(lambda P: loss(H, W, P), b)).max():.1e}")
print("dH shape", dH.shape, "error", f"{abs(dH - num_grad(lambda P: loss(P, W, b), H)).max():.1e}")
dW shape (3, 2) error 3.0e-09
db shape (2,) error 2.9e-09
dH shape (4, 3) error 2.5e-09

These three rules are exactly what The maths of deep learning uses in its XOR network. There they run in a loop from the last layer to the first.

PyTorch's nn.Linear stores the weight the other way round. Its weight has shape (out_features, in_features), and the layer computes HW^\top + \mathbf{b}^\top. So in PyTorch the weight gradient is G^\top H. It is the same rule, transposed. Always check how a library stores its weights.

The bias is shared by all N rows. So its gradient is a sum over the batch. If you forget the sum, you get an N \times k matrix where a vector of length k belongs. And if the loss is a mean over the batch, the factor 1/N must already be inside G.

In an interview you may not remember H^\top G or G H^\top. Use shapes. The gradient of W must be d \times k. From H (N \times d) and G (N \times k), the only product with that shape is H^\top G.

Patterns to remember

Patterns for matrix derivatives
PatternPurposeModelNote
df = \operatorname{tr}(M\,dX) \Rightarrow \nabla f = M^\topRead off any gradient of a numberdf = \operatorname{tr}(BA\,dX) gives A^\top B^\topThe gradient has the shape of X. Check it.
d(XY) = dX\,Y + X\,dYProduct rule for matricesd(X^2) = dX\,X + X\,dXNever write 2X\,dX. Keep the order.
\operatorname{tr}(ABC) = \operatorname{tr}(CAB)Move dX to the end\operatorname{tr}(A\,dX\,B) = \operatorname{tr}(BA\,dX)Rotate only. Never swap two factors.
\nabla(\mathbf{a}^\top\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{a}Linear scores and penalties3x_1 + 5x_2 - x_3 has gradient (3, 5, -1)^\topA column, like \mathbf{x}.
\nabla(\mathbf{x}^\top A\mathbf{x}) = (A + A^\top)\mathbf{x}Energies, variances, curvatureA = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 3 \end{pmatrix}, \mathbf{x} = (1,1)^\top gives (4, 8)^\top2A\mathbf{x} only if A is symmetric.
\nabla\|A\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{b}\|^2 = 2A^\top(A\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{b})Least squares and regressionZero gives A^\top A\mathbf{x} = A^\top \mathbf{b}Solve with lstsq, not with an inverse.
\nabla_X \operatorname{tr}(AX) = A^\topLinear functions of a matrixA = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 3 & 4 \end{pmatrix} gives \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 3 \\ 2 & 4 \end{pmatrix}Note the transpose.
\nabla_X \det X = \det(X)\,X^{-\top}Volumes and likelihoods\det \begin{pmatrix} 3 & 1 \\ 2 & 4 \end{pmatrix} grows by 0.03 when 4 becomes 4.01It is the cofactor matrix.
\nabla_X \ln|\det X| = X^{-\top}Gaussian likelihood, normalising flowsX = 2I_3 gives \tfrac{1}{2} I_3Needs \det X \ne 0.
d(X^{-1}) = -X^{-1}\,dX\,X^{-1}Sensitivity of an inverseAt X = I: d(X^{-1}) = -dXdX stays in the middle.
J_{\mathbf{f} \circ \mathbf{g}} = J_{\mathbf{f}} J_{\mathbf{g}}Chain rule for maps between vectors(1 \times 3)(3 \times 2) = 1 \times 2Outer map on the left. Gradient: J_{\mathbf{g}}^\top \nabla_{\mathbf{y}} L.
Z = HW + \mathbf{1}\mathbf{b}^\topGradients of a dense layerH^\top G, G^\top\mathbf{1}, G W^\topSum the bias gradient over the batch.
A = \sigma(Z) \Rightarrow G_Z = G_A \odot \sigma'(Z)Entrywise activationsReLU: keep G_A where Z \gt 0Never build the diagonal Jacobian.
\operatorname{vec}(AXB) = (B^\top \otimes A)\operatorname{vec}XWrite a matrix map as one big Jacobian2 \times 3, 3 \times 4, 4 \times 5 give a 10 \times 12 JacobianFor proofs. Too big for real code.

Practice

A loss L depends on a weight matrix W of shape 64 \times 10. What is the shape of \nabla_W L in this book?

  • 10 \times 64
  • 64 \times 10
  • 640 \times 1
  • 1 \times 1

A gradient of a number has the shape of its variable.

\mathbf{g} : \mathbb{R}^5 \to \mathbb{R}^3 and \mathbf{f} : \mathbb{R}^3 \to \mathbb{R}^2. What is the shape of the Jacobian of \mathbf{f} \circ \mathbf{g}?

  • 3 \times 3
  • 5 \times 2
  • 2 \times 5
  • 2 \times 3

(2 \times 3)(3 \times 5) = 2 \times 5: outputs by inputs.

A is symmetric. What is \nabla(\mathbf{x}^\top A \mathbf{x})?

  • A\mathbf{x}
  • 2A\mathbf{x}
  • \mathbf{x}^\top A
  • 2\mathbf{x}^\top \mathbf{x}

(A + A^\top)\mathbf{x} = 2A\mathbf{x} when A^\top = A.

Which formula is correct for an invertible matrix X?

  • d(X^{-1}) = -X^{-2}\,dX
  • d(X^{-1}) = X^{-1}\,dX\,X^{-1}
  • d(X^{-1}) = -X^{-1}\,dX\,X^{-1}
  • d(X^{-1}) = -dX\,X^{-2}

Differentiate XX^{-1} = I. The minus sign stays, and dX stays in the middle.

\operatorname{tr}\begin{pmatrix} 7 & 1 \\ 2 & -3 \end{pmatrix} = ?

For X = \begin{pmatrix} 3 & 1 \\ 2 & 4 \end{pmatrix}, the entry of \nabla_X \det X at position (1, 1) is ?.

A layer has H of shape 32 \times 100 and W of shape 100 \times 10. The gradient \partial L / \partial W has ? entries.

The gradient of f(\mathbf{x}) = \|\mathbf{x}\|^2 at \mathbf{x} = (1, -2, 2)^\top is (2, ? , 4)^\top.

  1. Write f = x_1^2 + 4x_1x_2 + x_2^2 as \mathbf{x}^\top A\mathbf{x} with a symmetric A. Then find \nabla f.
    Answer

    A = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1 \end{pmatrix}. Split the cross term evenly: 2 and 2. Then \nabla f = 2A\mathbf{x} = (2x_1 + 4x_2,\ 4x_1 + 2x_2)^\top. Check: \partial f/\partial x_1 = 2x_1 + 4x_2. Correct.

  2. Find the gradient of f(\mathbf{x}) = \tfrac{1}{2}\|\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{c}\|^2 for a fixed vector \mathbf{c}. Where is the minimum?
    Answer

    df = (\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{c})^\top d\mathbf{x}, so \nabla f = \mathbf{x} - \mathbf{c}. It is zero only at \mathbf{x} = \mathbf{c}. A gradient descent step with step size 1 jumps straight to \mathbf{c}.

  3. Use the recipe to show \nabla_X \operatorname{tr}(X^\top X) = 2X.
    Answer

    d\operatorname{tr}(X^\top X) = \operatorname{tr}(dX^\top X) + \operatorname{tr}(X^\top dX). The first trace equals the trace of its transpose, \operatorname{tr}(X^\top dX). So df = \operatorname{tr}(2X^\top dX), and the gradient is (2X^\top)^\top = 2X.

  4. For fixed vectors \mathbf{a} \in \mathbb{R}^m and \mathbf{b} \in \mathbb{R}^n, find \nabla_X (\mathbf{a}^\top X \mathbf{b}).
    Answer

    df = \mathbf{a}^\top dX\, \mathbf{b} = \operatorname{tr}(\mathbf{b}\mathbf{a}^\top dX). The gradient is (\mathbf{b}\mathbf{a}^\top)^\top = \mathbf{a}\mathbf{b}^\top. It is m \times n, like X. Entry (i, j) is a_i b_j, which is clear from \mathbf{a}^\top X \mathbf{b} = \sum_{i,j} a_i x_{ij} b_j.

  5. Derive the ridge equations: minimise \|A\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{b}\|^2 + \lambda\|\mathbf{x}\|^2. Why is A^\top A + \lambda I always invertible for \lambda \gt 0?
    Answer

    The gradient is 2A^\top(A\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{b}) + 2\lambda\mathbf{x}. Zero gives (A^\top A + \lambda I)\mathbf{x} = A^\top \mathbf{b}. For \mathbf{v} \ne 0, \mathbf{v}^\top (A^\top A + \lambda I)\mathbf{v} = \|A\mathbf{v}\|^2 + \lambda\|\mathbf{v}\|^2 \gt 0. So no nonzero \mathbf{v} is sent to zero, and the matrix is invertible.

  6. Show that the Hessian of \|A\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{b}\|^2 is positive semidefinite. When is it positive definite?
    Answer

    The Hessian is 2A^\top A. For any \mathbf{v}, \mathbf{v}^\top 2A^\top A\mathbf{v} = 2\|A\mathbf{v}\|^2 \ge 0. It is positive definite when A\mathbf{v} = 0 only for \mathbf{v} = 0. That means the columns of A are independent.

  7. Hard. A layer uses Z = HW and the loss L = \tfrac{1}{2}\|HW - T\|_F^2. Find \partial L/\partial W and set it to zero. What do you get?
    Answer

    G = HW - T, so \partial L/\partial W = H^\top (HW - T). Zero gives H^\top H W = H^\top T. These are the normal equations again, one for each column of T. A linear layer with squared loss is least squares.

  8. Hard. For a symmetric invertible \Sigma and a fixed vector \mathbf{x}, let f(\Sigma) = \ln\det\Sigma + \mathbf{x}^\top \Sigma^{-1}\mathbf{x}. Find \nabla_\Sigma f. Ignore the symmetry constraint.
    Answer

    Jacobi: d\ln\det\Sigma = \operatorname{tr}(\Sigma^{-1} d\Sigma). Inverse rule: d(\mathbf{x}^\top\Sigma^{-1}\mathbf{x}) = -\mathbf{x}^\top\Sigma^{-1}d\Sigma\,\Sigma^{-1}\mathbf{x} = -\operatorname{tr}(\Sigma^{-1}\mathbf{x}\mathbf{x}^\top\Sigma^{-1}d\Sigma). Transpose what stands before d\Sigma and use symmetry: \nabla f = \Sigma^{-1} - \Sigma^{-1}\mathbf{x}\mathbf{x}^\top\Sigma^{-1}. With many samples, setting the average to zero gives \Sigma = the average of \mathbf{x}\mathbf{x}^\top. This is the maximum likelihood covariance of a Gaussian with mean 0.

Key takeaways

  • The gradient of a number has the shape of its variable. The Jacobian is outputs by inputs. The Hessian is the matrix of second partials.
  • Books use two layouts that are transposes of each other. Pick one and check every shape.
  • The differential method works for every shape: take d, keep the order, bring df to \operatorname{tr}(M\,dX), and read off M^\top.
  • Key results: (A + A^\top)\mathbf{x}, \nabla \det X = \det(X)X^{-\top}, d(X^{-1}) = -X^{-1}dX\,X^{-1}.
  • The chain rule multiplies Jacobians, outer map first. For a scalar loss, transpose to get the gradient.
  • Setting the gradient of \|A\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{b}\|^2 to zero gives the normal equations. A dense layer has gradients H^\top G, G^\top \mathbf{1} and G W^\top.
  • Always test a new gradient with central differences.

Sources

  • Matrix Calculus for Machine Learning and Beyond, MIT OpenCourseWare 18.S096. Lecture notes from the course by Alan Edelman and Steven G. Johnson: derivatives as linear maps, the determinant and the inverse.
  • Bright, Edelman and Johnson, Matrix Calculus (for Machine Learning and Beyond), arXiv 2501.14787. The full course notes: differentials, the product rule, the determinant gradient as the cofactor matrix.
  • Matrix calculus (Wikipedia). The numerator and denominator layouts side by side, with tables of identities.
  • Petersen and Pedersen, The Matrix Cookbook (DTU). A classic reference of matrix identities and derivatives, version of November 2012.
  • Jacobi's formula (Wikipedia). The derivative of the determinant and its log-determinant corollary.
  • torch.nn.Linear (PyTorch documentation). The layer formula and the (out_features, in_features) weight shape.

Logic and proofs

A proof is a chain of steps. Each step follows from the steps before it by logic. This chapter teaches the logic first: statements, truth tables and quantifiers. Then it teaches the main ways to prove, from direct proof to strong induction and the pigeonhole principle.

  • Write statements with connectives and quantifiers, and check them with truth tables.
  • Negate any statement correctly, even one with three quantifiers.
  • Choose a proof method: direct, contrapositive, contradiction, cases or induction.
  • Use strong induction, the well-ordering principle and the pigeonhole principle.
  • Find the error in a wrong proof.

Statements and connectives

"7 is a prime number" is true. "10 is a prime number" is false. "Close the door" is neither true nor false. "x \gt 3" is true or false only when we know x.

A statement is a sentence that is true or false, not both. The first two sentences above are statements. A sentence with a variable, like x \gt 3, is a predicate. We write it P(x). It becomes a statement when x gets a value.

We join statements with connectives. Let P and Q be statements.

The five connectives
SymbolRead asTrue whenExample
\neg Pnot PP is falsenot (7 is even): true
P \land QP and Qboth are true2 is even and 2 is prime: true
P \lor QP or Qat least one is true2 is even or 2 is odd: true
P \to Qif P, then Qnot (P true and Q false)if 4 is odd, then 4 is prime: true
P \leftrightarrow QP if and only if Qboth have the same valuen is even iff n^2 is even

The "if, then" connective

The implication P \to Q is a promise. "If it rains, I take an umbrella." When is the promise broken? Only when it rains and I take no umbrella. If it does not rain, I keep the promise, whatever I do.

So P \to Q is false in exactly one case: P true and Q false. When P is false, P \to Q is true. This is called vacuously true. "If 4 is odd, then 4 is prime" is true, because 4 is not odd.

From one implication P \to Q we can build three more.

  • The converse: Q \to P.
  • The inverse: \neg P \to \neg Q.
  • The contrapositive: \neg Q \to \neg P.

Example: "If a shape is a square, it has four sides." True. Converse: "If a shape has four sides, it is a square." False: a rectangle 1 by 2 is a counterexample. Contrapositive: "If a shape does not have four sides, it is not a square." True. The next section proves that this is no accident.

In maths, "or" is inclusive: "P or Q" is true when both are true. In daily English, "tea or coffee?" often means one, not both. That is the exclusive or, written P \oplus Q. In Python it is p != q for booleans, and ^ for bits.

Truth tables

A truth table lists every case. With two statements there are four cases: TT, TF, FT, FF. With n statements there are 2^n rows.

Truth table of the connectives (T = true, F = false)
PQ¬PP ∧ QP ∨ QP → QP ↔ Q
TTFTTTT
TFFFTFF
FTTFTTF
FFTFFTT

Two statements are logically equivalent if they agree in every row. We write \equiv. A statement that is true in every row is a tautology, like P \lor \neg P.

For all statements P and Q:

\neg(P \land Q) \equiv \neg P \lor \neg Q, \qquad \neg(P \lor Q) \equiv \neg P \land \neg Q.

For predicates over a domain, the same idea holds for quantifiers: \neg\, \forall x\, P(x) \equiv \exists x\, \neg P(x) and \neg\, \exists x\, P(x) \equiv \forall x\, \neg P(x).

Proof

Check the four rows for the first law. Row TT: \neg(P \land Q) is F, and \neg P \lor \neg Q is F or F, so F. Row TF: left is \neg F = T, right is F or T, so T. Row FT: T and T. Row FF: T and T. They agree in all rows. The second law has the same kind of check.

For quantifiers: "not every x has P" means some x fails P. That is "there is an x with \neg P(x)". On a finite domain \{x_1, \dots, x_n\}, \forall x\, P(x) is P(x_1) \land \dots \land P(x_n). Then the quantifier law is the first law used many times.

In words: "not (A and B)" means "not A, or not B". Example: "The server is fast and cheap" is false. Then the server is slow, or it is expensive, or both. Augustus De Morgan stated these laws in his book Formal Logic in 1847. Logicians in the Middle Ages already knew the idea in words. The chapter Sets, relations and infinity uses them for sets: the complement of A \cup B is A^c \cap B^c.

P \to Q \equiv \neg Q \to \neg P. Also P \to Q \equiv \neg P \lor Q. The converse Q \to P is not equivalent to P \to Q.

Proof

P \to Q is false only in row TF. Now look at \neg Q \to \neg P. It is false only when \neg Q is true and \neg P is false. That means Q is false and P is true: again row TF. Both are false in the same single row. So they are equivalent. \neg P \lor Q is also false only in row TF.

The converse Q \to P is false in row FT, where P \to Q is true. So they differ.

A computer can check such laws. A truth table is just a loop over all rows.

from itertools import product

def implies(p, q):
    return (not p) or q          # P -> Q is false only when P is true and Q is false

def equivalent(f, g):
    """True if f and g agree on every row of the truth table."""
    return all(f(p, q) == g(p, q) for p, q in product([True, False], repeat=2))

print("De Morgan (and):", equivalent(lambda p, q: not (p and q),
                                     lambda p, q: (not p) or (not q)))
print("De Morgan (or): ", equivalent(lambda p, q: not (p or q),
                                     lambda p, q: (not p) and (not q)))
print("contrapositive: ", equivalent(lambda p, q: implies(p, q),
                                     lambda p, q: implies(not q, not p)))
print("converse:       ", equivalent(lambda p, q: implies(p, q),
                                     lambda p, q: implies(q, p)))
De Morgan (and): True
De Morgan (or):  True
contrapositive:  True
converse:        False

De Morgan helps you clean up code. if not (user and user.active): is the same as if not user or not user.active:. Flip each part and change and to or.

A truth table with n letters has 2^n rows. With 60 letters that is more than 10^{18} rows. No one knows a fast method that always decides if a formula is a tautology. This is linked to the famous P versus NP question. Real tools called SAT solvers still handle huge formulas in practice. They are used to check computer chips.

Quantifiers

"Every real number has a square that is zero or more." In symbols: \forall x \in \mathbb{R},\ x^2 \ge 0. "Some integer is even and prime." In symbols: \exists n \in \mathbb{Z},\ n \text{ is even} \land n \text{ is prime}. Here n = 2 works.

The symbol \forall means "for all". It is the universal quantifier. The symbol \exists means "there exists". It is the existential quantifier. The set the variable runs over is the domain. The domain matters: \exists x,\ x^2 = 2 is true in \mathbb{R} but false in \mathbb{Q}.

  • To prove \forall x\, P(x), take an arbitrary x and prove P(x). Examples are not enough.
  • To prove \exists x\, P(x), one example is enough. Show it and check it.
  • To disprove \forall x\, P(x), one counterexample is enough.
  1. Claim: n^2 + n + 41 is prime for every whole number n \ge 0.
  2. n = 0 gives 41, n = 1 gives 43, n = 2 gives 47. All prime.
  3. A computer checks n = 0, 1, \dots, 39. All 40 values are prime.
  4. But n = 40 gives 1600 + 40 + 41 = 1681 = 41^2. Not prime.
  5. One counterexample kills the claim. Euler studied this polynomial in the 1700s.
def is_prime(m):
    return m > 1 and all(m % d for d in range(2, int(m ** 0.5) + 1))

first_bad = next(n for n in range(1000) if not is_prime(n * n + n + 41))
print(first_bad, first_bad**2 + first_bad + 41, "= 41 *", (first_bad**2 + first_bad + 41) // 41)
print(all(is_prime(n * n + n + 41) for n in range(40)))   # the first 40 values
40 1681 = 41 * 41
True

Python's all is \forall and any is \exists, but only on a finite domain. A program can check a million cases. It cannot check infinitely many. That is why we need proofs.

The order of quantifiers

Compare two sentences about whole numbers.

  • \forall x\ \exists y,\ y \gt x. For every number there is a bigger one. True: take y = x + 1.
  • \exists y\ \forall x,\ y \gt x. There is one number bigger than all numbers. False.

In the first sentence, y may depend on x. In the second, one y must work for every x. The same words in another order say something very different. "Everyone has a mother" is not "someone is the mother of everyone".

Never swap \forall and \exists to "simplify". \forall\varepsilon\, \exists\delta is the definition of continuity. \exists\delta\, \forall\varepsilon is a much stronger claim. Read quantifiers from left to right. Each one may depend on the ones before it.

Negation

A monitoring tool says: "Every server is up." When is that report false? Not when every server is down. It is false when at least one server is down. So the negation is: "Some server is not up."

The rule: to negate, move \neg from left to right. Each \forall becomes \exists, and each \exists becomes \forall. At the end, negate the inner statement. These are the quantifier forms of De Morgan's laws.

How to negate
StatementIts negation
P \land Q\neg P \lor \neg Q
P \lor Q\neg P \land \neg Q
P \to QP \land \neg Q
\forall x\, P(x)\exists x\, \neg P(x)
\exists x\, P(x)\forall x\, \neg P(x)
x \gt 3x \le 3

Why is the negation of P \to Q equal to P \land \neg Q? Because P \to Q \equiv \neg P \lor Q. De Morgan turns \neg(\neg P \lor Q) into P \land \neg Q. The negation of an implication is not another implication.

  1. Statement: \forall \varepsilon \gt 0\ \exists \delta \gt 0\ \forall x:\ |x - a| \lt \delta \to |f(x) - L| \lt \varepsilon.
  2. Flip the first quantifier: \exists \varepsilon \gt 0\ \neg\big(\exists \delta \gt 0 \dots\big).
  3. Flip the second: \exists \varepsilon \gt 0\ \forall \delta \gt 0\ \neg\big(\forall x \dots\big).
  4. Flip the third: \exists \varepsilon \gt 0\ \forall \delta \gt 0\ \exists x:\ \neg\big(|x - a| \lt \delta \to |f(x) - L| \lt \varepsilon\big).
  5. Negate the implication: |x - a| \lt \delta \land |f(x) - L| \ge \varepsilon.
  6. In words: there is a bad \varepsilon. For every \delta, some x close to a still has f(x) far from L.

The chapter Limits and continuity uses this negation to prove that a limit does not exist. Note one detail. The domains \varepsilon \gt 0 and \delta \gt 0 do not change. Only the quantifiers flip.

Not every test passed. So every test failed.

The negation of x \gt 3 is x \lt 3.

The negation of "if it rains, the road is wet" is "if it rains, the road is dry".

Not every test passed. So at least one test failed.

The negation of x \gt 3 is x \le 3.

The negation of "if it rains, the road is wet" is "it rains and the road is not wet".

Direct proof and the contrapositive

Claim: the sum of two odd numbers is even. Try 3 + 5 = 8 and 7 + 11 = 18. It looks true. Now prove it for all odd numbers.

First we need clear definitions. An integer n is even if n = 2k for some integer k. It is odd if n = 2k + 1 for some integer k.

  1. Let a and b be odd. By definition, a = 2k + 1 and b = 2m + 1 for some integers k, m.
  2. Add them: a + b = 2k + 2m + 2 = 2(k + m + 1).
  3. k + m + 1 is an integer. So a + b is even, by definition.

To prove P \to Q: assume P. Use definitions and known facts, step by step, until you reach Q.

Note the letters. We used k for a and a new letter m for b. With the same letter, we would prove the claim only for a = b.

When the direct way is hard

Claim: if ab is even, then a is even or b is even. Starting from "ab is even" gives ab = 2k. Then what? It is hard to split 2k into a and b.

Use the contrapositive instead. By De Morgan, "not (a even or b even)" is "a odd and b odd". So the contrapositive is: if a and b are odd, then ab is odd.

  1. Assume a = 2k + 1 and b = 2m + 1.
  2. Then ab = 4km + 2k + 2m + 1 = 2(2km + k + m) + 1.
  3. That is odd. So the contrapositive is true.
  4. A statement equals its contrapositive. So the original claim is true.

Rule. Use the contrapositive when "not Q" gives you an equation to work with, and P does not. Statements with "or" in the conclusion, or "not" in them, are good candidates.

If and only if

"P if and only if Q" means P \to Q and Q \to P. So it needs two proofs. Example: n is odd if and only if n^2 is odd. One direction is Example 4 with a = b = n. For the other, use the contrapositive: if n is even, n = 2k, then n^2 = 4k^2 is even.

Do not prove the converse by accident. Claim: "if n is divisible by 6, then n is even". Some people start from "n is even" and stop. That proves the converse, which is false: 4 is even, but 4 is not divisible by 6. Always write your first line as "Assume P".

Proof by contradiction and by cases

Claim: \log_2 3 is irrational. A calculator says 1.58496... and the digits go on. But digits do not prove anything. Assume the opposite and look for something impossible.

  1. Assume \log_2 3 = p/q with whole numbers p, q \ge 1. It is positive, since 3 \gt 1.
  2. Then 2^{p/q} = 3. Raise both sides to the power q: 2^p = 3^q.
  3. The left side is even, because p \ge 1. The right side is odd: a product of odd numbers.
  4. An even number cannot equal an odd number. This is a contradiction.
  5. So the assumption is false. \log_2 3 is irrational.

To prove P: assume \neg P. Derive a statement R and also \neg R. Since R \land \neg R is always false, \neg P must be false. So P is true.

The proofs that \sqrt{2} is irrational and that there are infinitely many primes work this way. A proof by contrapositive is a special, tidy kind of proof by contradiction.

Proof by cases

Claim: a square leaves remainder 0 or 1 when you divide it by 4. Test: 3^2 = 9 = 2 \cdot 4 + 1, 6^2 = 36 = 9 \cdot 4 + 0. Every integer is even or odd. So split into two cases.

  • Case 1: n = 2k. Then n^2 = 4k^2, remainder 0.
  • Case 2: n = 2k + 1. Then n^2 = 4(k^2 + k) + 1, remainder 1.

The cases cover all integers, so the claim is proved. Now a nice result follows. A sum of two squares leaves remainder 0 + 0, 0 + 1 or 1 + 1 after division by 4. That is 0, 1 or 2, never 3. So 2027 = 4 \cdot 506 + 3 is not a sum of two squares.

The cases must cover every possibility. Sometimes two cases are the same up to names. Then we write without loss of generality and treat only one of them.

A proof can show that something exists without showing which thing it is. Claim: there are irrational a, b with a^b rational. Look at \sqrt{2}^{\sqrt{2}}. If it is rational, take a = b = \sqrt{2}. If it is irrational, take a = \sqrt{2}^{\sqrt{2}} and b = \sqrt{2}. Then a^b = \sqrt{2}^2 = 2. One of the two cases works, but this proof does not say which. That is a non-constructive proof.

Induction, strong induction and well-ordering

The chapter Sequences, series and induction teaches ordinary induction with four examples. Here we look at its foundation and at a stronger form.

The well-ordering principle

Take any set of whole numbers, like \{17, 4, 9\} or the set of all even numbers above 100. It always has a smallest member: 4 and 102. This seems obvious. It is still a real principle, and it fails for other sets. The positive fractions have no smallest member.

Every non-empty set of natural numbers 0, 1, 2, \dots has a smallest element.

Why we accept it

In most foundations, the well-ordering principle and induction can each be proved from the other. One of them must be taken as a basic rule about \mathbb{N}. Here is the proof from induction. Let S have no smallest element. Prove by strong induction that no n is in S. If 0, \dots, n - 1 are not in S and n were in S, then n would be the smallest element. That is impossible. So n \notin S. Then S is empty. So a non-empty set must have a smallest element.

It gives a proof method: the smallest counterexample. Assume the claim fails. Take the smallest number where it fails. Then show an even smaller failure. That is a contradiction.

  1. Claim: every n \ge 1 is a sum of different powers of 2. For example, 13 = 8 + 4 + 1.
  2. Assume not. By well-ordering there is a smallest bad number m.
  3. Let 2^j be the largest power of 2 with 2^j \le m. Then m \lt 2^{j+1}.
  4. m is bad, so it is not itself a power of 2. So r = m - 2^j is between 1 and m - 1.
  5. r \lt m, so r is good: a sum of different powers of 2. Also r \lt 2^{j+1} - 2^j = 2^j. So those powers are all smaller than 2^j.
  6. Then m = 2^j + r is a sum of different powers of 2. This contradicts "m is bad".

Strong induction

Stamps come in values 4 and 5. Can you pay every amount of 12 or more? 12 = 4 + 4 + 4, 13 = 4 + 4 + 5, 14 = 4 + 5 + 5, 15 = 5 + 5 + 5. For 16, take the stamps for 12 and add a 4. For 17, take 13 and add a 4. The step from k + 1 goes back four places, not one. Ordinary induction only looks back one place. We need a stronger tool.

Let P(n) be a statement for whole numbers n \ge n_0. Suppose

  1. P(n_0) is true, and
  2. for every k \ge n_0: if P(n_0), P(n_0 + 1), \dots, P(k) are all true, then P(k + 1) is true.

Then P(n) is true for every n \ge n_0.

Proof

Let Q(k) say "P(n_0), \dots, P(k) are all true". Use ordinary induction on Q. Base: Q(n_0) is P(n_0), which is true. Step: assume Q(k). Condition 2 gives P(k + 1). Together with Q(k) this is Q(k + 1). So Q(n) holds for all n \ge n_0, and Q(n) contains P(n).

  1. P(n): the amount n can be paid with stamps of 4 and 5. We prove it for n \ge 12.
  2. Base cases: 12, 13, 14 and 15, shown above. We need four, because the step goes back four places.
  3. Step: let k \ge 15 and assume P(12), \dots, P(k). Then k + 1 - 4 = k - 3 \ge 12, so P(k - 3) is true.
  4. Add one stamp of 4 to the stamps for k - 3. That pays k + 1.
  5. By strong induction, P(n) is true for all n \ge 12. And 11 fails: no mix of 4s and 5s makes 11.

Strong induction is natural when a case depends on cases far back. Two more classic uses:

  • Fibonacci: F_1 = F_2 = 1 and F_{n+1} = F_n + F_{n-1}. Claim: F_n \lt 2^n. Step: F_{k+1} = F_k + F_{k-1} \lt 2^k + 2^{k-1} \lt 2^{k+1}. The step uses two earlier cases, so we check two base cases.
  • Primes: every n \ge 2 is a product of primes. If n is not prime, n = ab with 2 \le a, b \lt n. Both a and b are products of primes by the strong hypothesis. This is the first half of the fundamental theorem of arithmetic.

Strong induction still needs enough base cases. In the stamp proof, the step from k + 1 uses k - 3. With only the base case 12, the step for 13 would need the amount 9, which fails. Check that the step only uses cases you already have.

The pigeonhole principle

A team has 13 people. Two of them must have a birthday in the same month. Why? There are only 12 months. If each month had at most one birthday, there would be at most 12 people.

Put n objects into k boxes. If n \gt k, some box holds at least two objects. More generally, some box holds at least \lceil n / k \rceil objects.

Proof

Use the contrapositive. Suppose every box holds at most \lceil n/k \rceil - 1 objects. Since \lceil n/k \rceil \lt n/k + 1, each box holds fewer than n/k objects. Then the k boxes hold fewer than k \cdot n/k = n objects in total. But there are n objects. So some box holds at least \lceil n/k \rceil.

The symbol \lceil x \rceil is the ceiling of x: round up. Example: 100 files go into 7 folders. Some folder holds at least \lceil 100/7 \rceil = \lceil 14.3 \rceil = 15 files. Peter Dirichlet used the idea in 1834. He called it the drawer principle.

The hard part is always the same: choose the boxes. Here are four examples.

  • Points in a square. Put 5 points in a square of side 1. Cut it into 4 small squares of side \tfrac{1}{2}. Two points share a small square. So their distance is at most the small diagonal, \tfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2} \approx 0.71.
  • Compression. No lossless program makes every file shorter. There are 2^n files of n bits. There are only 2^n - 1 bit strings shorter than n. Two files would get the same short form, and then one could not be restored.
  • Hash tables. A table with 1000 buckets and 1001 keys must have a collision. No hash function can avoid it.
  • Divisors. Choose any n + 1 numbers from 1, 2, \dots, 2n. Then one of them divides another.
  1. Write each chosen number as 2^a \cdot m with m odd. For example, 12 = 2^2 \cdot 3.
  2. The odd part m is one of 1, 3, 5, \dots, 2n - 1. These are n boxes.
  3. We have n + 1 numbers. So two of them have the same odd part: 2^a m and 2^b m with a \lt b.
  4. Then 2^a m divides 2^b m. Done.
  5. n + 1 is the best possible. The n numbers n + 1, \dots, 2n contain no such pair.
from itertools import combinations

def has_divisor_pair(nums):
    return any(b % a == 0 for a, b in combinations(sorted(nums), 2))

for n in range(1, 9):
    pool = range(1, 2 * n + 1)
    always = all(has_divisor_pair(s) for s in combinations(pool, n + 1))
    top_half = list(range(n + 1, 2 * n + 1))       # n numbers, no pair
    print(n, always, has_divisor_pair(top_half))
1 True False
2 True False
3 True False
4 True False
5 True False
6 True False
7 True False
8 True False

The code checks every choice for n \le 8. The proof covers every n. The chapter Graph theory uses the pigeonhole principle for Dirac's and Ramsey's theorems.

The principle says that some box has two objects. It does not say which box. It also says nothing when n \le k. With 365 days and 30 people, pigeonhole gives nothing. Shared birthdays there are a question of probability. See Probability basics.

Writing proofs and finding mistakes

A good proof is written for a reader. Every step has a reason. Here is a simple way to build one.

Write the claim in logic

Find the quantifiers and the "if, then". For example: \forall a, b \in \mathbb{Z}, ab even \to a even \lor b even.

Choose a method

A for-all claim about whole numbers: induction. A "not" or "irrational" claim: contradiction. An "or" in the conclusion: contrapositive.

Write the first line

"Let a, b be integers. Assume ...". Write exactly what you may use.

Write the last line

Write the goal at the bottom of the page. Now you know where the steps must go.

Fill the middle

Unpack the definitions on both ends. Work forward from the top and backward from the bottom until they meet.

Check every step

Give each line a reason: a definition, an earlier step, or a theorem. Test the smallest and the strangest cases.

Common proof mistakes

Here is a famous wrong proof that 2 = 1. Find the error before you open the list below.

  1. Let a = b. Multiply both sides by a: a^2 = ab.
  2. Take b^2 away: a^2 - b^2 = ab - b^2.
  3. Factor: (a + b)(a - b) = b(a - b).
  4. Divide by a - b: a + b = b.
  5. Since a = b: 2b = b, so 2 = 1.
Dividing by zero

In Example 9, a = b, so a - b = 0. Step 4 divides by zero. Before you divide or cancel, check that the number is not 0.

Assuming what you want to prove

A proof that uses its own conclusion is circular. A common form: start from the equation you want, change both sides until you get 0 = 0, and stop. That shows "claim implies true", which proves nothing. Write the steps in the other direction, and check that each one can be reversed.

Checking examples instead of all cases

Example 1 had 40 good cases and still failed. Examples help you guess. Only an argument for an arbitrary n proves a for-all claim.

Proving the converse

You were asked for P \to Q but you showed Q \to P. Start your proof with "Assume P".

A wrong negation

In a proof by contradiction, the assumption must be the exact negation. The negation of "all are even" is "some is odd", not "all are odd".

Reusing a letter

"Let a = 2k + 1 and b = 2k + 1" makes a = b. Each new number needs a new letter.

An induction step that fails for the smallest case

The step must work for every k \ge n_0. Test it with k = n_0. This is where most wrong induction proofs break.

Squaring both sides

From x = -2 we get x^2 = 4, which also allows x = 2. Squaring keeps the true answers but can add false ones. After squaring, check every answer in the original equation.

Computers can now check proofs. In a proof assistant such as Lean or Isabelle, you write each step in a formal language. The program accepts only valid steps. In 2024 Google DeepMind's AlphaProof wrote proofs in Lean for problems of the International Mathematical Olympiad. Together with AlphaGeometry 2 it solved 4 of the 6 problems, a silver medal score.

Examiners look for the frame. Write the method in the first line: "We prove the contrapositive", "Assume, for contradiction, that ...", "By strong induction on n". Then mark where you use the key assumption. End with a clear sentence: "This contradicts ..." or "This proves the claim."

Patterns to remember

Patterns for logic and proof
PatternPurposeModelNote
Assume P. ... Therefore Q.Direct proof of P \to QOdd + odd: 2k + 1 + 2m + 1 = 2(k + m + 1)Use a new letter for each number.
Prove \neg Q \to \neg PWhen "not Q" is easier to usea, b odd \Rightarrow ab odd, so ab even \Rightarrow one is evenNot the converse Q \to P.
Assume \neg P. ... Contradiction."Not", "no", "irrational", "infinitely many"\log_2 3 = p/q \Rightarrow 2^p = 3^q: even = oddNegate exactly.

Prove P \to Q and Q \to P"If and only if"n odd \leftrightarrow n^2 oddTwo directions, two proofs.
\neg\forall x\, P \equiv \exists x\, \neg PNegate quantifiers"Not every test passed" = "some test failed"Domains stay the same.

Practice

P is false and Q is true. What is the value of P \to Q?

  • True
  • False
  • Not defined

An implication is false only when P is true and Q is false. Here it is vacuously true.

What is the contrapositive of "if a number is divisible by 4, then it is even"?

  • If a number is even, then it is divisible by 4.
  • If a number is not divisible by 4, then it is not even.
  • If a number is not even, then it is not divisible by 4.
  • A number is divisible by 4 and not even.

The contrapositive is \neg Q \to \neg P. The first option is the converse, the second the inverse, the last the negation.

Which is the negation of \forall x\ \exists y:\ x + y = 0?

  • \forall x\ \exists y:\ x + y \ne 0
  • \exists x\ \forall y:\ x + y \ne 0
  • \exists x\ \exists y:\ x + y \ne 0
  • \forall x\ \forall y:\ x + y \ne 0

Each quantifier flips, then the inner statement is negated.

Which method fits best for "there is no largest prime"?

  • A direct check of examples
  • Proof by contradiction
  • One counterexample
  • Proof by cases on even and odd

"No" statements are natural for contradiction: assume a largest prime exists.

A truth table with 4 letters has ? rows.

By De Morgan, \neg(P \lor Q) \equiv \neg P ? \neg Q.

50 emails go into 8 folders. Some folder holds at least ? emails.

The smallest n \ge 0 where n^2 + n + 41 is not prime is ?.

  1. Show with a truth table that P \to Q and \neg P \lor Q are equivalent.
    Answer

    Rows TT, TF, FT, FF. P \to Q: T, F, T, T. \neg P \lor Q: F∨T = T, F∨F = F, T∨T = T, T∨F = T. The columns match in every row.

  2. Negate: "Every user who logs in sees the dashboard." Write it in symbols first.
    Answer

    \forall u:\ \text{login}(u) \to \text{sees}(u). Negation: \exists u:\ \text{login}(u) \land \neg\text{sees}(u). In words: some user logs in and does not see the dashboard.

  3. Prove directly: if a \mid b and b \mid c, then a \mid c. (a \mid b means b = ak for some integer k.)
    Answer

    Assume b = ak and c = bm for integers k, m. Then c = (ak)m = a(km). km is an integer, so a \mid c.

  4. Prove by contrapositive: if n^2 + 2n is odd, then n is odd. (n is an integer.)
    Answer

    Contrapositive: if n is even, then n^2 + 2n is even. Let n = 2k. Then n^2 + 2n = 4k^2 + 4k = 2(2k^2 + 2k), which is even.

  5. Prove by cases: n^3 - n is divisible by 3 for every integer n.
    Answer

    n^3 - n = (n - 1)n(n + 1). Write n = 3k, 3k + 1 or 3k + 2. In case 1, n is divisible by 3. In case 2, n - 1 = 3k. In case 3, n + 1 = 3(k + 1). In every case one factor is divisible by 3, so the product is.

  6. Use strong induction: every amount n \ge 8 can be paid with coins of 3 and 5.
    Answer

    Base cases: 8 = 3 + 5, 9 = 3 + 3 + 3, 10 = 5 + 5. Step: let k \ge 10 and assume all amounts from 8 to k. Then k + 1 - 3 = k - 2 \ge 8 can be paid. Add one coin of 3. By strong induction every n \ge 8 works.

  7. Hard. Show that among any 6 integers, two have a difference divisible by 5.
    Answer

    Boxes: the 5 possible remainders 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 after division by 5. Six integers, five boxes. Two integers a, b share a remainder r. Then a - b = (5s + r) - (5t + r) = 5(s - t).

  8. Hard. Find the error: "Claim: every n \ge 1 has n = n + 1. Step: assume k = k + 1. Add 1 to both sides: k + 1 = k + 2. So the claim holds for k + 1."
    Answer

    The step is correct as logic: if k = k + 1, then k + 1 = k + 2. But there is no base case. P(1) says 1 = 2, which is false. Without a true base case, the chain never starts.

  9. Hard. Prove that \sqrt{3} is irrational. Use the fact from this chapter about squares and remainders, but for 3.
    Answer

    First, by cases n = 3k, 3k \pm 1: if 3 does not divide n, then n^2 = 9k^2 \pm 6k + 1 is not divisible by 3. So if 3 \mid n^2, then 3 \mid n (contrapositive). Now assume \sqrt{3} = p/q in lowest terms. Then p^2 = 3q^2, so 3 \mid p^2 and 3 \mid p. Write p = 3r: 9r^2 = 3q^2, so q^2 = 3r^2 and 3 \mid q. Both are divisible by 3, which contradicts lowest terms.

Key takeaways

  • A statement is true or false. Connectives build bigger statements. P \to Q is false only when P is true and Q is false.
  • Truth tables prove equivalences. De Morgan: \neg(P \land Q) \equiv \neg P \lor \neg Q. A statement equals its contrapositive, not its converse.
  • To negate, flip every \forall and \exists from left to right, then negate the inside. The order of quantifiers matters.
  • Choose the method by the shape of the claim: direct, contrapositive, contradiction, cases, or induction.
  • Well-ordering gives the smallest counterexample method. Strong induction may use all earlier cases, with enough base cases.
  • Pigeonhole: n objects in k boxes put at least \lceil n/k \rceil in one box. The skill is choosing the boxes.
  • Many examples never prove a for-all claim. One counterexample disproves it.
