  3. 1905 Albert Einstein explains Brownian motion by hits from water molecules.
  4. 1906 Andrey Markov publishes his first paper on chains of dependent events.
  5. 1913 Markov counts vowels and consonants in 20,000 letters of the poem Eugene Onegin.
  6. 1921 George Pólya proves when a random walk comes home.
  7. 1923 Norbert Wiener builds Brownian motion as an exact mathematical object.
  8. 1953 Metropolis, the Rosenbluths and the Tellers publish the first MCMC method.
  9. 1970 W. K. Hastings makes the method general.

Markov chains and transition matrices

Here are the server's habits, learned from old logs. From Up, it stays Up with probability 0.90. It turns Slow with 0.08 and Down with 0.02. Each row below lists the chances for the next minute.

P = \begin{pmatrix} 0.90 & 0.08 & 0.02 \\ 0.50 & 0.40 & 0.10 \\ 0.60 & 0 & 0.40 \end{pmatrix} \qquad \begin{matrix} \text{from Up} \\ \text{from Slow} \\ \text{from Down} \end{matrix}

A process X_0, X_1, \ldots on a finite set of states is a Markov chain if

P(X_{n+1} = y \mid X_n = x, X_{n-1}, \ldots, X_0) = P(X_{n+1} = y \mid X_n = x) = P(x, y) .

This is the Markov property. The matrix P is the transition matrix. Its entries are not negative, and each row adds up to 1. Such a matrix is called stochastic.

In simple words: the chain has no memory beyond "where am I now". What is the chance that an Up server is Down two minutes later? Add over the state in between.

P^2(\text{Up}, \text{Down}) = 0.90 \cdot 0.02 + 0.08 \cdot 0.10 + 0.02 \cdot 0.40 = 0.034 .

This is row Up times column Down. So it is an entry of the matrix product P^2.

Let P^n(x, y) = P(X_n = y \mid X_0 = x). Then P^n is the n-th power of the matrix P, and P^{m+n} = P^m P^n. If the start has the row vector of probabilities \mu_0, then the distribution at time n is \mu_n = \mu_0 P^n.

Proof

Use the law of total probability over the state z at time m: P(X_{m+n} = y \mid X_0 = x) = \sum_z P(X_m = z \mid X_0 = x)\,P(X_{m+n} = y \mid X_m = z). The Markov property says the second factor does not care about X_0. It is P^n(z, y). The sum is exactly the matrix product. With m = n = 1 and induction, P^n is the n-th power.

The whole matrix for two steps is

P^2 = \begin{pmatrix} 0.862 & 0.104 & 0.034 \\ 0.710 & 0.200 & 0.090 \\ 0.780 & 0.048 & 0.172 \end{pmatrix} .

This is the same idea as in Graphs for knowledge and context. There, powers of the adjacency matrix count walks. Here, powers of P add up the chances of walks.

Rows add up to 1, not columns. Row x holds the chances of leaving x. Also, a distribution is a row vector and multiplies P from the left: \mu_{n+1} = \mu_n P. Some books use columns and P^T. Check which one a text uses.

In 1913 Markov tested his idea on text. He sorted 20,000 letters of a Pushkin poem into vowels and consonants. The next letter type depended on the one before. A simple next-word model that looks at the last k words is also a Markov chain. Its state is those k words.

Classes of states

A product has four user states: New, Free, Pro and Gone. A New user becomes Free (0.7) or Gone (0.3). Free users upgrade to Pro (0.2) or stay Free (0.8). Pro users go back to Free (0.1) or stay Pro (0.9). Gone users never come back.

Some states can reach each other and some cannot. New can reach Free, but Free can never reach New. Free and Pro reach each other. Gone reaches only itself.

  • State y is accessible from x if P^n(x, y) \gt 0 for some n \ge 0. Two states communicate if each is accessible from the other.
  • Communicating states form classes. A class is closed if the chain cannot leave it. A chain with one class is irreducible.
  • A state is recurrent if the chain returns to it with probability 1. Otherwise it is transient. A state with P(x, x) = 1 is absorbing.
  • The period of x is the greatest common divisor of all n with P^n(x, x) \gt 0. Period 1 means aperiodic.

For the user chain:

  • \{\text{New}\} is a class that is not closed. New is transient. A user is New only once.
  • \{\text{Free}, \text{Pro}\} is a closed class. Both states are recurrent and aperiodic, because Free can stay Free for one step.
  • \{\text{Gone}\} is closed. Gone is absorbing.

The chain is not irreducible. The server chain is irreducible: every state reaches every other one. It is also aperiodic, because P(\text{Up}, \text{Up}) \gt 0.

In a finite chain, all states of one class are of the same type: all recurrent or all transient, and all with the same period. A class is recurrent exactly when it is closed. So every finite chain has at least one recurrent class.

Do not think that a chain "settles" just because it is finite. Take two states that swap every step: P = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}. The period is 2. Started in state 1, P^n(1, 1) goes 0, 1, 0, 1 for ever. It has no limit. A random walk on a bipartite graph has the same problem.

Stationary distributions and the long run

Start the server in Down. Compute \mu_n = \mu_0 P^n minute by minute.

The numbers settle at about (0.841, 0.112, 0.047). If you start there, you stay there. That is a stationary distribution.

A row vector \pi with \pi(x) \ge 0 and \sum_x \pi(x) = 1 is a stationary distribution if \pi P = \pi. So \pi is a left eigenvector of P for the eigenvalue 1.

  1. Slow column: \pi_S = 0.08\pi_U + 0.40\pi_S. So 0.6\pi_S = 0.08\pi_U and \pi_S = \frac{2}{15}\pi_U.
  2. Down column: 0.6\pi_D = 0.02\pi_U + 0.10\pi_S = \frac{1}{30}\pi_U. So \pi_D = \frac{1}{18}\pi_U.
  3. Sum to 1: \pi_U\left(1 + \frac{2}{15} + \frac{1}{18}\right) = \pi_U \cdot \frac{107}{90} = 1.
  4. \pi = \left(\frac{90}{107}, \frac{12}{107}, \frac{5}{107}\right) \approx (0.841, 0.112, 0.047).

If a Markov chain on a finite set is irreducible, it has exactly one stationary distribution \pi. All entries of \pi are positive.

Proof idea

Existence: average the rows of P, P^2, \ldots, P^n. The averages stay in a closed and bounded set, so some of them converge. The limit satisfies \pi P = \pi. Uniqueness: suppose Ph = h for a column vector h. Take a state where h is largest. Its value is an average of its neighbours, so they are all equally large. Irreducibility spreads this to every state, so h is constant. So the eigenvalue 1 has a one-dimensional eigenspace, and \pi is unique. This also follows from the Perron-Frobenius theorem.

Let P be irreducible and aperiodic on a finite set, with stationary distribution \pi. Then there are constants C \gt 0 and 0 \lt \alpha \lt 1 with

\max_x \big\| P^t(x, \cdot) - \pi \big\|_{TV} \le C\alpha^t \quad \text{for all } t .

Here \|\mu - \nu\|_{TV} = \frac{1}{2}\sum_y |\mu(y) - \nu(y)| is the total variation distance. So every row of P^t goes to \pi, fast.

In simple words: a good chain forgets where it started. With numbers: from Down, the distance is 0.953, 0.353, 0.125, 0.042, 0.014 after 0 to 4 minutes. Each minute it shrinks by a factor of about 0.36.

Proof idea

Irreducible and aperiodic together give a power P^r with all entries positive. Then P^r(x, y) \ge \delta\,\pi(y) for some \delta \gt 0 and all x, y. So each block of r steps can be read as: with chance \delta, forget the start and jump to \pi. Otherwise, do something else. After k blocks, the chance of never forgetting is (1 - \delta)^k. That bounds the distance. The PageRank proof uses the same trick, with the random jump as the forgetting step.

The speed comes from the eigenvalues. The server's P has eigenvalues 1 and 0.35 \pm 0.074i. Their size is \sqrt{0.35^2 + 0.074^2} \approx 0.358. That is the factor 0.36 we saw. In general the distance falls like |\lambda_2|^t, where \lambda_2 is the second largest eigenvalue in size.

Time averages: the ergodic theorem

The convergence theorem talks about one future moment. Often we want averages over a long run. What fraction of minutes is the server Down?

Let (X_t) be an irreducible Markov chain on a finite set with stationary distribution \pi. For every function f on the states and every start, with probability 1,

\frac{1}{t}\sum_{s=0}^{t-1} f(X_s) \;\longrightarrow\; \sum_x f(x)\,\pi(x) \quad \text{as } t \to \infty .

In simple words: the long-run average along one path equals the average under \pi. With f = 1 on Down and 0 elsewhere, the server is Down in about 4.7% of all minutes. Aperiodicity is not needed here. The swapping chain spends half its time in each state.

Proof idea

Fix a state x. Cut the path at each visit to x. Each piece starts afresh at x, so the pieces are independent copies of one another. Apply the strong law of large numbers to the sums of f over the pieces and to their lengths. The ratio of the two averages is the time average. Then check that this limit defines a stationary distribution. By uniqueness it is \pi.

For an irreducible finite chain, \pi(x) = \dfrac{1}{E_x[\tau_x^+]}, where \tau_x^+ = \min\{t \ge 1 : X_t = x\} is the first return time to x.

In simple words: if you visit a place every 20 days on average, you are there 1/20 of the time. With numbers: \pi(\text{Down}) = 5/107, so a Down server comes back to Down every 107/5 = 21.4 minutes on average. Let us check both results with a seeded simulation. It uses the SplitMix generator from Statistical inference, saved as prng.py or prng.rs.

# Run the Up/Slow/Down server chain for 1,000,000 minutes.
from prng import SplitMix  # the seeded generator from the inference chapter

P = [[0.90, 0.08, 0.02],   # from Up
     [0.50, 0.40, 0.10],   # from Slow
     [0.60, 0.00, 0.40]]   # from Down
names = ["Up", "Slow", "Down"]

def step(state: int, u: float) -> int:  # pick the next state with one uniform
    total = 0.0
    for nxt, p in enumerate(P[state]):
        total += p
        if u < total:
            return nxt
    return len(P) - 1

rng, state, steps = SplitMix(1906), 2, 1_000_000  # start in Down
visits = [0, 0, 0]
returns, last_down = [], 0
for t in range(1, steps + 1):
    state = step(state, rng.uniform())
    visits[state] += 1
    if state == 2:                       # back in Down: record the return time
        returns.append(t - last_down)
        last_down = t
for i, name in enumerate(names):
    print(f"time in {name:4}: {visits[i] / steps:.4f}")
print(f"mean return time to Down: {sum(returns) / len(returns):.2f} minutes")
// Run the Up/Slow/Down server chain for 1,000,000 minutes.
include!("prng.rs"); // the seeded generator from the inference chapter

const P: [[f64; 3]; 3] = [
    [0.90, 0.08, 0.02], // from Up
    [0.50, 0.40, 0.10], // from Slow
    [0.60, 0.00, 0.40], // from Down
];

fn step(state: usize, u: f64) -> usize { // pick the next state with one uniform
    let mut total = 0.0;
    for (next, p) in P[state].iter().enumerate() {
        total += p;
        if u < total { return next; }
    }
    P.len() - 1
}

fn main() {
    let (mut rng, mut state, steps) = (SplitMix(1906), 2, 1_000_000); // start in Down
    let mut visits = [0u64; 3];
    let (mut returns, mut last_down) = (Vec::new(), 0);
    for t in 1..=steps {
        state = step(state, rng.uniform());
        visits[state] += 1;
        if state == 2 { // back in Down: record the return time
            returns.push(t - last_down);
            last_down = t;
        }
    }
    for (i, name) in ["Up", "Slow", "Down"].iter().enumerate() {
        println!("time in {:4}: {:.4}", name, visits[i] as f64 / steps as f64);
    }
    println!("mean return time to Down: {:.2} minutes", returns.iter().sum::<u64>() as f64 / returns.len() as f64);
}
time in Up  : 0.8410
time in Slow: 0.1123
time in Down: 0.0467
mean return time to Down: 21.41 minutes

Both programs print these lines. Rust may warn that normal is unused. That warning is harmless. The fractions match \pi = (0.841, 0.112, 0.047), and the mean return time matches 21.4.

A quick test: detailed balance

If a distribution \pi satisfies \pi(x)P(x, y) = \pi(y)P(y, x) for all states x, y, then \pi P = \pi. Such a chain is called reversible.

Proof

Sum both sides over x: \sum_x \pi(x)P(x, y) = \pi(y)\sum_x P(y, x) = \pi(y), because row y adds up to 1.

In simple words: the flow from x to y equals the flow back, for every pair. The random walk on a graph is reversible with \pi proportional to the degree. See random walks on graphs. MCMC below is built on this test.

Detailed balance is enough for stationarity, but it is not needed. The server chain is not reversible: \pi_U P(U, D) = 0.841 \cdot 0.02 = 0.017, but \pi_D P(D, U) = 0.047 \cdot 0.6 = 0.028. Its \pi is still stationary. Flows balance around cycles, not pair by pair.

The random surfer of PageRank is an irreducible, aperiodic Markov chain on web pages. Its stationary distribution is the PageRank vector. The chapter Graphs for knowledge and context works it out with code.

Random walks and gambler's ruin

Toss a fair coin. Step up 1 for heads and down 1 for tails. After n steps your position is S_n = \xi_1 + \cdots + \xi_n, where each \xi_i is +1 or -1 with chance \frac{1}{2}. This is the simple random walk.

Each step has mean 0 and variance 1. So E[S_n] = 0 and \operatorname{Var}(S_n) = n. The walk does not drift. But its typical distance from 0 grows like \sqrt{n}. After 400 steps it is usually within \pm 40.

Does the walk come back to 0? On a line, the chance of being at 0 after 2n steps is \binom{2n}{n} / 4^n. That is 0.5, 0.375 and 0.3125 for n = 1, 2, 3. For large n it is about 1/\sqrt{\pi n}.

The simple symmetric random walk on the grid \mathbb{Z}^d returns to its start with probability 1 when d = 1 or d = 2. When d \ge 3, the probability of ever returning is less than 1.

In simple words: on a line or a flat map you always get home. In space you may be lost for ever. With numbers: in three dimensions the chance of ever returning is only about 0.34.

Proof idea

A state is recurrent exactly when the expected number of returns, \sum_n P(S_{2n} = 0), is infinite. In d dimensions, P(S_{2n} = 0) behaves like c\,n^{-d/2}. The comparison test with \sum n^{-d/2} gives an infinite sum for d \le 2 and a finite sum for d \ge 3.

Gambler's ruin

You have 10 euros. You bet 1 euro per round on a fair coin. You stop when you reach 20 euros or 0. What is the chance that you reach 20? This question goes back to letters between Pascal and Fermat in 1656.

A player starts with i units, 0 \le i \le N. Each round she wins 1 unit with probability p and loses 1 unit with probability q = 1 - p, independently. She stops at 0 or at N. The probability to reach N first is

P_i = \begin{cases} \dfrac{i}{N} & \text{if } p = \frac{1}{2}, \\[2ex] \dfrac{1 - (q/p)^i}{1 - (q/p)^N} & \text{if } p \ne \frac{1}{2}. \end{cases}

For p = \frac{1}{2}, the expected number of rounds is i(N - i).

In simple words: in a fair game your chance is your share of the total money. In an unfair game the house wins far more often. With numbers: from 10 with target 20, a fair coin gives 0.5 and about 100 rounds. Betting on red at roulette, p = 18/38 \approx 0.474, gives only 0.259.

Proof (first-step analysis)

Look at the first round. By the law of total probability, P_i = pP_{i+1} + qP_{i-1}, with P_0 = 0 and P_N = 1. Write P_i = pP_i + qP_i and rearrange: p(P_{i+1} - P_i) = q(P_i - P_{i-1}). So each difference is q/p times the one before, and P_{i+1} - P_i = (q/p)^i P_1. Add the differences: P_i = P_1 \sum_{k=0}^{i-1} (q/p)^k. If p = q, this is iP_1, and P_N = 1 gives P_1 = 1/N. If p \ne q, sum the geometric series and use P_N = 1.

For the duration D_i with p = \frac{1}{2}: D_i = 1 + \frac{1}{2}D_{i+1} + \frac{1}{2}D_{i-1}, with D_0 = D_N = 0. Check that D_i = i(N - i) solves it. The solution is unique.

# Gambler's ruin: start with 10, stop at 0 or 20. Bet 1 each round.
from prng import SplitMix

def play(rng: SplitMix, p: float, start: int, goal: int) -> tuple[bool, int]:
    money, rounds = start, 0
    while 0 < money < goal:
        money += 1 if rng.uniform() < p else -1  # win or lose one unit
        rounds += 1
    return money == goal, rounds

rng, games = SplitMix(1657), 20_000
for p in (0.5, 18 / 38):                     # a fair coin, then red at roulette
    wins = total_rounds = 0
    for _ in range(games):
        won, rounds = play(rng, p, 10, 20)
        wins += won
        total_rounds += rounds
    print(f"p = {p:.4f}: reached 20 in {wins / games:.4f} of games, "
          f"mean length {total_rounds / games:.1f} rounds")
// Gambler's ruin: start with 10, stop at 0 or 20. Bet 1 each round.
include!("prng.rs");

fn play(rng: &mut SplitMix, p: f64, start: i32, goal: i32) -> (bool, u64) {
    let (mut money, mut rounds) = (start, 0);
    while 0 < money && money < goal {
        money += if rng.uniform() < p { 1 } else { -1 }; // win or lose one unit
        rounds += 1;
    }
    (money == goal, rounds)
}

fn main() {
    let (mut rng, games) = (SplitMix(1657), 20_000);
    for p in [0.5, 18.0 / 38.0] { // a fair coin, then red at roulette
        let (mut wins, mut total_rounds) = (0, 0);
        for _ in 0..games {
            let (won, rounds) = play(&mut rng, p, 10, 20);
            if won { wins += 1; }
            total_rounds += rounds;
        }
        println!("p = {:.4}: reached 20 in {:.4} of games, mean length {:.1} rounds",
            p, wins as f64 / games as f64, total_rounds as f64 / games as f64);
    }
}
p = 0.5000: reached 20 in 0.4956 of games, mean length 100.4 rounds
p = 0.4737: reached 20 in 0.2595 of games, mean length 91.6 rounds

Theory says 0.5 and 100 rounds for the fair coin. For roulette it says 0.2585 and 91.8 rounds. The simulation agrees to about two digits, as expected from 20,000 games.

A small edge looks harmless. With p = 0.49, the chance to double 10 euros is already down to 0.40. With a larger target it falls much faster. For the unfair game, P_i shrinks roughly like (p/q)^{N - i} when the target is far away.

Poisson processes

Requests reach an API at random moments, about 3 per second on average. They do not come in a fixed rhythm. Each moment is as likely as any other. This is the standard model for arrivals.

A Poisson process with rate \lambda \gt 0 is a counting process N(t), the number of arrivals in [0, t], with:

  1. N(0) = 0.
  2. Independent increments: counts in time ranges that do not overlap are independent.
  3. N(s + t) - N(s) has a Poisson distribution with mean \lambda t: P(k \text{ arrivals}) = e^{-\lambda t}\dfrac{(\lambda t)^k}{k!}.
  1. No request in one second: P(N(1) = 0) = e^{-3} \approx 0.050.
  2. Exactly 4 requests in two seconds: e^{-6}\,6^4/4! \approx 0.134.
  3. At least 10 requests in two seconds: about 0.084. So a burst of 10 is not rare.

In a Poisson process with rate \lambda, the waiting times between arrivals T_1, T_2, \ldots are independent. Each has the exponential distribution with mean 1/\lambda: P(T_k \gt t) = e^{-\lambda t}. The other way round, independent exponential gaps always give a Poisson process.

Proof idea

The first gap is longer than t exactly when there is no arrival in [0, t]. So P(T_1 \gt t) = P(N(t) = 0) = e^{-\lambda t}. After each arrival, independent increments mean the process starts again, with no memory of the past. So the next gap has the same law and does not depend on the earlier ones.

Why Poisson counts? Cut one second into many tiny slots. Each slot holds an arrival with a tiny chance. The count is then binomial with many trials and a small chance, and that is close to Poisson. See the Poisson limit in Random variables.

The exponential distribution has no memory: P(T \gt s + t \mid T \gt s) = P(T \gt t). If no request came in the last second, the wait from now is still exponential with mean 1/3 second.

  • Merge two independent Poisson processes with rates \lambda and \mu. You get a Poisson process with rate \lambda + \mu.
  • Keep each arrival with probability p, independently. The kept arrivals form a Poisson process with rate p\lambda. The removed ones form another, independent one.

With numbers: 10% of the requests fail. Then failures form a Poisson process with rate 0.3 per second. The chance of 10 seconds without a failure is e^{-3} \approx 0.05.

Buses come as a Poisson process, one every 10 minutes on average. You arrive at a random time. Your mean wait is 10 minutes, not 5. You are more likely to arrive during a long gap than a short one. So the gap you land in is longer than average, 20 minutes on average.

Let requests arrive as a Poisson process with rate \lambda = 8 per second. One server handles them with exponential service times at rate \mu = 10 per second. This is the M/M/1 queue, a Markov chain in continuous time. Its load is \rho = \lambda/\mu = 0.8. In the long run there are on average \rho/(1 - \rho) = 4 requests in the system. By Little's law L = \lambda W, the mean time in the system is W = 4/8 = 0.5 seconds. At \lambda = 9.5, so \rho = 0.95, it is already 19 requests and 2 seconds each. Queues explode near full load.

Martingales in simple words

Your money in a fair game is the classic example. After each round, your expected money next round equals your money now. The past does not help you predict a gain. That is a martingale.

A process M_0, M_1, \ldots with E|M_n| \lt \infty is a martingale with respect to a process X_0, X_1, \ldots if M_n depends only on X_0, \ldots, X_n and

E[M_{n+1} \mid X_0, \ldots, X_n] = M_n .

A stopping time \tau is a random time where the event \{\tau = n\} depends only on X_0, \ldots, X_n. You cannot look into the future to decide to stop.

Three martingales for the simple random walk S_n started at i:

  • S_n itself, when p = \frac{1}{2}.
  • S_n^2 - n, when p = \frac{1}{2}. Check: E[(S_n + \xi)^2 - (n + 1) \mid S_n] = S_n^2 + 2S_n \cdot 0 + 1 - n - 1 = S_n^2 - n.
  • (q/p)^{S_n}, for any p. Check: p \cdot \frac{q}{p} + q \cdot \frac{p}{q} = q + p = 1.

"Stop when the money first hits 0 or 20" is a stopping time. "Stop just before the next loss" is not, because it needs the future.

Let (M_n) be a martingale and \tau a stopping time. Then E[M_\tau] = E[M_0] if at least one of these holds:

  1. \tau \le c for a constant c.
  2. E[\tau] \lt \infty, and the steps are bounded: |M_{n+1} - M_n| \le c.
  3. The stopped process is bounded: |M_{\min(n, \tau)}| \le c for all n, and \tau \lt \infty with probability 1.

In simple words: with a fair game and a stopping rule that cannot see the future, you cannot win on average. You need limited time, limited bets or a limited range.

Proof idea

Case 1: write M_\tau = M_0 + \sum_{k=0}^{c-1} (M_{k+1} - M_k)\,\mathbf{1}\{\tau \gt k\}. The event \{\tau \gt k\} is known at time k. So each term has mean E[\mathbf{1}\{\tau \gt k\}\,E[M_{k+1} - M_k \mid X_0, \ldots, X_k]] = 0. Cases 2 and 3: apply case 1 to the bounded time \min(\tau, n). Then let n \to \infty. The conditions let you swap the limit and the expectation, by the dominated convergence theorem.

  1. Fair game from i, stop at 0 or N. The stopped walk stays in [0, N], so case 3 holds. E[S_\tau] = i. But S_\tau is N with chance P_i and 0 otherwise. So N P_i = i, and P_i = i/N.
  2. Use S_n^2 - n (case 2, since E[\tau] \lt \infty). E[S_\tau^2] - E[\tau] = i^2. And E[S_\tau^2] = N^2 \cdot \frac{i}{N} = iN. So E[\tau] = iN - i^2 = i(N - i).
  3. Unfair game: (q/p)^{S_\tau} gives P_i (q/p)^N + (1 - P_i) = (q/p)^i. Solve for P_i. It is the formula of the theorem.

Bet 1. After a loss, double the bet. Stop at the first win. You always end exactly 1 unit up. Is that free money? No. The bets grow without limit, and none of the three conditions holds. With a budget of 1023 units you can lose 10 times in a row. Then you win 1 with chance 1 - 2^{-10} and lose 1023 with chance 2^{-10}. The mean is \frac{1023}{1024} \cdot 1 - \frac{1}{1024} \cdot 1023 = 0.

Brownian motion: the idea

Shrink the random walk. Take steps every 1/n seconds, each of size 1/\sqrt{n}. Why \sqrt{n}? Because after one second the variance is n \cdot \frac{1}{n} = 1. As n grows, the zigzag path looks like a continuous curve that never becomes smooth.

A Brownian motion is a process (W_t)_{t \ge 0} with:

  1. W_0 = 0.
  2. Independent increments.
  3. W_t - W_s is normal with mean 0 and variance t - s, for s \lt t.
  4. Continuous paths.

Let S_k be a random walk with steps of mean 0 and variance 1. Then the scaled path t \mapsto S_{\lfloor nt \rfloor}/\sqrt{n} approaches Brownian motion in distribution as n \to \infty. This is Donsker's theorem. It is the central limit theorem for whole paths.

Some facts, each with a number:

  • Scaling: W_{ct} has the same law as \sqrt{c}\,W_t. After 4 seconds the typical distance is 2, not 4.
  • The path is continuous everywhere but has a slope nowhere. A change over time h has size about \sqrt{h}. So the ratio \sqrt{h}/h blows up as h \to 0.
  • Quadratic variation: cut [0, t] into small pieces and add the squared changes. The sum goes to t, not 0. For a smooth curve it would go to 0.
  • W_t and W_t^2 - t are martingales, as S_n and S_n^2 - n were. So W hits a \gt 0 before -b \lt 0 with probability b/(a + b). This is gambler's ruin again.

Uses: in physics, particles in a fluid. In finance, prices are often modelled as S_t = S_0 e^{\mu t + \sigma W_t}, a geometric Brownian motion. In AI, the forward process of a diffusion model adds small Gaussian noise step by step. It is a discrete Brownian-type process. See The maths of deep learning.

Do not use normal calculus on Brownian paths. Because the squared changes add up to t, the chain rule gets an extra term. For example, d(W_t^2) = 2W_t\,dW_t + dt, not 2W_t\,dW_t. This is Itô's rule. It is the start of stochastic calculus, which is beyond this chapter.

Monte Carlo and MCMC

Throw 10,000 random points into the unit square. Count the points inside the quarter circle x^2 + y^2 \le 1. About \pi/4 \approx 78.5\% of them land inside. Multiply the fraction by 4 and you have an estimate of \pi. This is Monte Carlo.

To estimate \theta = E[f(X)], draw independent X_1, \ldots, X_n with the law of X. Use \hat{\theta}_n = \frac{1}{n}\sum f(X_i). By the law of large numbers, \hat{\theta}_n \to \theta. By the central limit theorem, its standard error is about \sigma/\sqrt{n}, where \sigma^2 = \operatorname{Var} f(X).

With numbers: for the quarter circle, f is 1 inside and 0 outside. Then \sigma = \sqrt{0.785 \cdot 0.215} \approx 0.41. With n = 10{,}000, the standard error of the fraction is 0.0041. For \pi it is 4 \times 0.0041 \approx 0.016. The error does not depend on the dimension. That is why Monte Carlo works for integrals in 1000 dimensions. But each extra digit costs 100 times more samples.

When you cannot sample directly

In Statistical inference, a click rate had a posterior proportional to p^8(1 - p)^{20}. For big models we know the posterior only up to a constant, and we cannot draw from it directly. The trick: build a Markov chain whose stationary distribution is the posterior. Run it. By the ergodic theorem, its time averages are posterior averages. This is MCMC.

Target: a density \pi(x), known up to a constant. Proposal: a rule q(x, y) to suggest a move from x to y. From the current state x:

  1. Draw a proposal y from q(x, \cdot).
  2. Compute the acceptance probability a(x, y) = \min\!\left(1, \dfrac{\pi(y)\,q(y, x)}{\pi(x)\,q(x, y)}\right).
  3. With probability a(x, y) move to y. Otherwise stay at x.

For a symmetric proposal, such as y = x + small normal noise, the q terms cancel. That is the original Metropolis rule.

The Metropolis-Hastings chain satisfies detailed balance with respect to \pi. So \pi is stationary. If the chain is also irreducible and aperiodic, its distribution converges to \pi, and its time averages converge to averages under \pi.

Proof

For x \ne y, the chain moves from x to y with probability q(x, y)\,a(x, y). So \pi(x)\,q(x, y)\,a(x, y) = \min\big(\pi(x)q(x, y),\ \pi(y)q(y, x)\big). This expression does not change if you swap x and y. That is detailed balance. The unknown constant in \pi cancels in the ratio, so we never need it. The rest follows from the convergence and ergodic theorems.

# Random-walk Metropolis for a click rate p with density proportional to p^8 (1-p)^20.
import math
from prng import SplitMix

def log_target(p: float) -> float:          # log of the unnormalised density
    if not 0.0 < p < 1.0:
        return -math.inf                     # outside (0, 1): impossible
    return 8 * math.log(p) + 20 * math.log(1 - p)

rng, p, step = SplitMix(1953), 0.9, 0.1      # a bad start on purpose
burn_in, keep = 1_000, 50_000
samples, accepted = [], 0
for t in range(burn_in + keep):
    proposal = p + step * rng.normal()        # a small random move
    diff = log_target(proposal) - log_target(p)
    if diff >= 0 or rng.uniform() < math.exp(diff):
        p, accepted = proposal, accepted + 1  # accept the move
    if t >= burn_in:
        samples.append(p)                     # keep only after burn-in
samples.sort()
mean = sum(samples) / keep
above = sum(s > 0.25 for s in samples) / keep
print(f"acceptance rate: {accepted / (burn_in + keep):.3f}")
print(f"posterior mean:  {mean:.4f}   exact 0.3000")
print(f"P(p > 0.25):     {above:.4f}   exact 0.7125")
print(f"95% interval:    {samples[int(0.025 * keep)]:.3f} to {samples[int(0.975 * keep)]:.3f}"
      f"   exact 0.153 to 0.472")
// Random-walk Metropolis for a click rate p with density proportional to p^8 (1-p)^20.
include!("prng.rs");

fn log_target(p: f64) -> f64 { // log of the unnormalised density
    if !(0.0 < p && p < 1.0) { return f64::NEG_INFINITY; } // outside (0, 1): impossible
    8.0 * p.ln() + 20.0 * (1.0 - p).ln()
}

fn main() {
    let (mut rng, mut p, step) = (SplitMix(1953), 0.9, 0.1); // a bad start on purpose
    let (burn_in, keep) = (1_000, 50_000);
    let (mut samples, mut accepted) = (Vec::new(), 0);
    for t in 0..burn_in + keep {
        let proposal = p + step * rng.normal(); // a small random move
        let diff = log_target(proposal) - log_target(p);
        if diff >= 0.0 || rng.uniform() < diff.exp() {
            p = proposal; // accept the move
            accepted += 1;
        }
        if t >= burn_in { samples.push(p); } // keep only after burn-in
    }
    samples.sort_by(|a, b| a.partial_cmp(b).unwrap());
    let mean = samples.iter().sum::<f64>() / keep as f64;
    let above = samples.iter().filter(|&&s| s > 0.25).count() as f64 / keep as f64;
    println!("acceptance rate: {:.3}", accepted as f64 / (burn_in + keep) as f64);
    println!("posterior mean:  {:.4}   exact 0.3000", mean);
    println!("P(p > 0.25):     {:.4}   exact 0.7125", above);
    println!("95% interval:    {:.3} to {:.3}   exact 0.153 to 0.472",
        samples[(0.025 * keep as f64) as usize], samples[(0.975 * keep as f64) as usize]);
}
acceptance rate: 0.651
posterior mean:  0.3005   exact 0.3000
P(p > 0.25):     0.7114   exact 0.7125
95% interval:    0.151 to 0.474   exact 0.153 to 0.472

Both programs print these lines. The sampler never used the constant of the Beta density. Still, it finds the exact Beta(9, 21) answers to two or three digits.

Burn in

The chain starts at 0.9, far from the target. It reaches the bulk near 0.2 to 0.3 after about 13 steps. Throw away an early part, here 1,000 steps.

Tune the step

Tiny steps are almost always accepted but crawl. Huge steps are almost always rejected. Common targets: about 50% acceptance in one dimension and about 23% in many dimensions. Ours is 65%, so a larger step would explore faster.

Count the real samples

Neighbouring samples are correlated. Here the lag-1 correlation is 0.73. The effective sample size is about 7,700, not 50,000. Use it for standard errors.

Run several chains

Start chains from different points. If they disagree, the chain has not converged yet. Tools report this as the R-hat number.

Use better proposals

For many parameters, random-walk steps are slow. Gibbs sampling updates one part at a time. Hamiltonian Monte Carlo uses gradients. Stan and PyMC use it by default.

MCMC samples are not independent. Do not divide by \sqrt{50000} for the standard error. Divide by the square root of the effective sample size. Also, a chain can look stable while it is stuck in one mode of a target with two peaks. A long run does not prove convergence.

Practice

Which matrix can be a transition matrix?

  • \begin{pmatrix} 0.5 & 0.6 \\ 0.5 & 0.4 \end{pmatrix}
  • \begin{pmatrix} 0.3 & 0.7 \\ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}
  • \begin{pmatrix} 1.2 & -0.2 \\ 0.5 & 0.5 \end{pmatrix}

Each row must add up to 1 with no negative entries. The first matrix has columns that add to 1, not rows.

A chain goes A → B → C → A with probability 1 at each step. What is the period of A?

  • 1
  • 2
  • 3
  • It has no period.

The chain returns to A only at times 3, 6, 9 and so on. Their greatest common divisor is 3.

Emails arrive as a Poisson process with rate 2 per minute. No email came in the last 5 minutes. What is the expected wait for the next one?

  • Less than 0.5 minutes, because one is "due".
  • 0.5 minutes
  • 5 minutes

Exponential gaps have no memory. The wait from now is still exponential with mean 1/2 minute.

For P = \begin{pmatrix} 0.9 & 0.1 \\ 0.3 & 0.7 \end{pmatrix}, the stationary probability of the first state is ?

A fair gambler starts with 3 and stops at 0 or 10. The chance to reach 10 is ?

In the same game, the expected number of rounds is ?

  1. For the server chain, compute P^2(\text{Slow}, \text{Down}).
    Answer

    Row Slow times column Down: 0.50 \cdot 0.02 + 0.40 \cdot 0.10 + 0.10 \cdot 0.40 = 0.01 + 0.04 + 0.04 = 0.09. This matches the matrix P^2 above.

  2. A two-state chain moves from A to B with probability a and from B to A with probability b, with 0 \lt a, b \lt 1. Find \pi and the mean return time to A.
    Answer

    Balance of flows: \pi_A a = \pi_B b. With \pi_A + \pi_B = 1: \pi = \left(\frac{b}{a + b}, \frac{a}{a + b}\right). Mean return time to A: 1/\pi_A = (a + b)/b. For a = 0.1, b = 0.3: \pi_A = 0.75 and return time 4/3.

  3. States 1, 2, 3, 4. From 1: to 2 with 0.5, to 3 with 0.5. From 2: to 1 with 1. From 3: to 4 with 1. From 4: to 3 with 1. Find the classes. Which are closed? Which states are recurrent? What are the periods?
    Answer

    Classes \{1, 2\} and \{3, 4\}. From 1 the chain can go to 3 and never come back, so \{1, 2\} is not closed, and 1 and 2 are transient. \{3, 4\} is closed, so 3 and 4 are recurrent. All four states have period 2: returns happen only at even times.

  4. A player wins each round with p = 0.6. She starts with 2 and stops at 0 or 5. Find the chance to reach 5.
    Answer

    q/p = 2/3. P_2 = \frac{1 - (2/3)^2}{1 - (2/3)^5} = \frac{0.5556}{0.8683} \approx 0.640. With a fair coin it would be 2/5 = 0.4.

  5. Support tickets arrive as a Poisson process with 6 per hour. Find the chance of at least one ticket in 10 minutes, and the expected time to the third ticket.
    Answer

    In 10 minutes the mean count is 1. P(N \ge 1) = 1 - e^{-1} \approx 0.632. The third arrival is the sum of three exponential gaps with mean 10 minutes each, so 30 minutes on average.

  6. A fair random walk starts at 0 and stops when it first reaches +3 or -3. Use optional stopping to find the expected stopping time.
    Answer

    S_n^2 - n is a martingale. E[\tau] \lt \infty and the steps are bounded, so E[S_\tau^2] - E[\tau] = 0. But S_\tau^2 = 9 always. So E[\tau] = 9. In general the answer is m^2 for the range \pm m.

  7. Hard. Target \pi = (0.5, 0.3, 0.2) on states 1, 2, 3. The proposal picks one of the two other states with chance \frac{1}{2} each. Write the Metropolis transition matrix and check detailed balance.
    Answer

    From 1: to 2 with \frac{1}{2}\min(1, 0.3/0.5) = 0.3, to 3 with \frac{1}{2} \cdot 0.4 = 0.2, stay 0.5. From 2: to 1 with \frac{1}{2}, to 3 with \frac{1}{2} \cdot \frac{2}{3} = \frac{1}{3}, stay \frac{1}{6}. From 3: to 1 with \frac{1}{2}, to 2 with \frac{1}{2}, stay 0. Check: 0.5 \cdot 0.3 = 0.3 \cdot 0.5 = 0.15. 0.5 \cdot 0.2 = 0.2 \cdot 0.5 = 0.1. 0.3 \cdot \frac{1}{3} = 0.2 \cdot 0.5 = 0.1. Detailed balance holds, so \pi is stationary.

  8. Hard. You estimate a probability near 0.05 by Monte Carlo. How many independent samples give a standard error of 0.001? An MCMC chain for the same number has an effective sample size of 15% of its length. How long must the chain be?
    Answer

    \sigma^2 = 0.05 \cdot 0.95 = 0.0475. We need \sqrt{0.0475/n} = 0.001, so n = 47{,}500. The chain must give 47,500 effective samples, so its length must be about 47{,}500 / 0.15 \approx 317{,}000 steps.

Key takeaways

  • A Markov chain forgets everything except its present state. Its transition matrix has rows that add up to 1, and \mu_n = \mu_0 P^n.
  • States form classes. In a finite chain, closed classes are recurrent and the others are transient. Period 2 or more blocks convergence.
  • A finite irreducible chain has one stationary distribution \pi with \pi P = \pi. If it is also aperiodic, every start converges to \pi at a geometric rate set by |\lambda_2|.
  • Ergodic theorem: long-run time averages equal averages under \pi. Also \pi(x) = 1/E_x[\tau_x^+].
  • Gambler's ruin: a fair game gives i/N and i(N - i) rounds. A small house edge makes ruin much more likely.
  • A Poisson process has independent Poisson counts and exponential gaps with no memory. Merging adds rates, thinning multiplies them.
  • A martingale is a fair game. Optional stopping says you cannot beat it with limited time, bets or range.
  • Brownian motion is the scaled limit of a random walk: continuous, nowhere smooth, with size \sqrt{t}.
  • Monte Carlo error is \sigma/\sqrt{n}. MCMC builds a chain with the target as its stationary distribution. Watch burn-in and the effective sample size.

Sources

  • Levin and Peres, Markov Chains and Mixing Times, 2nd edition (free PDF). Classes, stationary distributions, detailed balance, the convergence theorem (Theorem 4.9) and the ergodic theorem (Theorem C.1).
  • Optional stopping theorem (Wikipedia). The three conditions, gambler's ruin, the expected exit time m^2 and the doubling counterexample.
  • Gambler's ruin (Wikipedia). The fair and unfair formulas, and the history from Pascal and Fermat in 1656 to Huygens in 1657.
  • Random: The Poisson Process. Open course pages on exponential gaps, Poisson counts, thinning and merging.
  • Wiener process (Wikipedia). The definition of Brownian motion, scaling, quadratic variation and the random-walk limit.
  • Metropolis-Hastings algorithm (Wikipedia). The 1953 and 1970 papers, the acceptance rule, burn-in, correlation and acceptance-rate advice.

Real analysis

Calculus tells you how to compute. Real analysis tells you why the computing is correct. It starts from one fact about the real numbers: they have no gaps. From that fact it proves the big theorems of calculus, and it shows exactly when they fail.

  • Use the completeness axiom and the supremum in short proofs.
  • Prove limits of sequences with \varepsilon and N, and use Bolzano-Weierstrass and Cauchy sequences.
  • Tell open, closed and compact sets apart, and use the Heine-Borel theorem.
  • Explain uniform continuity and uniform convergence, and say why they matter.
  • State and use the fixed-point, inverse function, Arzela-Ascoli and Stone-Weierstrass theorems.

The real numbers have no gaps

Look at the fractions q with q^2 \lt 2. Some of them are 1, 1.4, 1.41 and 1.414. They grow, but they never pass 1.5. Is there a smallest fraction that sits above all of them? No. That number would be \sqrt{2}, and \sqrt{2} is not a fraction. The rational numbers have a hole at \sqrt{2}.

We need words for this. Let A be a set of real numbers.

  • An upper bound of A is a number u with a \le u for every a \in A.
  • The supremum \sup A is the smallest upper bound.
  • The infimum \inf A is the largest lower bound.

Example: A = \{ 1 - \frac{1}{n} : n = 1, 2, 3, \dots \} = \{0, 0.5, 0.67, 0.75, \dots\}. Every member is below 1. Any number below 1, like 0.999, is passed by some member. So \sup A = 1. But 1 is not in A. The set has no largest member.

Every set of real numbers that is not empty and has an upper bound has a supremum in \mathbb{R}.

In simple words: the real line has no holes. The set \{ q : q^2 \lt 2 \} has the supremum \sqrt{2} in \mathbb{R}. This is the one property that makes \mathbb{R} different from \mathbb{Q}. Every proof in this chapter uses it somewhere.

1. Archimedean property. For every real x there is a natural number n \gt x. So \frac{1}{n} \to 0.

2. Approximation. If s = \sup A and \varepsilon \gt 0, then some a \in A has a \gt s - \varepsilon.

Proof

1. Assume no natural number is bigger than x. Then x is an upper bound of \mathbb{N}. So s = \sup \mathbb{N} exists. The number s - 1 is not an upper bound. So some n \gt s - 1. Then n + 1 \gt s, and n + 1 is in \mathbb{N}. This is a contradiction.

2. The number s - \varepsilon is smaller than s. So it is not an upper bound. So some member of A is bigger than it.

Do not mix up the supremum and the maximum. The set (0, 1) has supremum 1 but no maximum. A maximum must be in the set. A supremum need not be. When a set has a maximum, the two are equal.

Sequences and limits done carefully

Take a_n = \frac{2n + 1}{n + 3}. The terms are 0.75, 1, 1.17, 1.29, and later 1.95 at n = 100. They seem to go to 2. How do we prove it? We must show that the terms get as close to 2 as anyone asks, and stay there.

  1. Compute the distance. |a_n - 2| = \left| \frac{2n + 1 - 2n - 6}{n + 3} \right| = \frac{5}{n + 3}.
  2. We want \frac{5}{n + 3} \lt 0.01. That means n + 3 \gt 500.
  3. So every n \ge 498 works. Take N = 498.
  4. For any \varepsilon \gt 0, the same steps give n \gt \frac{5}{\varepsilon} - 3. The Archimedean property gives such an N.

a_n \to L means: for every \varepsilon \gt 0 there is an N such that |a_n - L| \lt \varepsilon for all n \ge N.

The number \varepsilon is the tolerance. The number N may depend on \varepsilon. A smaller tolerance usually needs a bigger N. A sequence with a limit is convergent. Two facts follow quickly. A limit is unique. A convergent sequence is bounded.

Simplify the distance

Write |a_n - L| as a simple expression in n. In Example 1 it is \frac{5}{n + 3}.

Bound it from above

Make it bigger but simpler. For example \frac{5}{n + 3} \lt \frac{5}{n}. You may throw away helpful terms.

Solve for n

\frac{5}{n} \lt \varepsilon holds when n \gt \frac{5}{\varepsilon}. This is scratch work. It is not the proof yet.

Write the proof forwards

"Let \varepsilon \gt 0. Choose N \gt 5 / \varepsilon. For n \ge N: |a_n - 2| = \frac{5}{n + 3} \lt \frac{5}{n} \le \frac{5}{N} \lt \varepsilon."

Check the order

\varepsilon comes first and is arbitrary. N comes second and depends on \varepsilon. Then n is any index from N on.

Monotone sequences

Newton's rule for \sqrt{2} is a_1 = 2, a_{n+1} = \frac{1}{2}\left(a_n + \frac{2}{a_n}\right). The terms are 2, 1.5, 1.4167, 1.41422. They only go down, and they stay above 1. Each term is a fraction. The limit is not. So the next theorem cannot hold in \mathbb{Q}.

A sequence that is monotone and bounded is convergent. If it goes up, its limit is \sup \{ a_n \}. If it goes down, its limit is \inf \{ a_n \}.

Proof

Let a_n go up and be bounded. By completeness, s = \sup \{a_n\} exists. Let \varepsilon \gt 0. By the approximation property, some a_N \gt s - \varepsilon. The sequence goes up, so a_n \ge a_N \gt s - \varepsilon for all n \ge N. Also a_n \le s. So |a_n - s| \lt \varepsilon for all n \ge N.

For Newton's sequence the limit L satisfies L = \frac{1}{2}(L + 2/L). So L^2 = 2 and L = \sqrt{2}.

Subsequences and Bolzano-Weierstrass

The sequence (-1)^n is -1, 1, -1, 1, \dots. It has no limit. But the even terms form the sequence 1, 1, 1, \dots, which converges. A subsequence keeps infinitely many terms in their order. We write it a_{n_1}, a_{n_2}, \dots with n_1 \lt n_2 \lt \dots.

Every bounded sequence of real numbers has a convergent subsequence. The same holds in \mathbb{R}^n.

Proof

Call n a peak if a_n \ge a_m for every m \gt n. Think of a mountain view: from a peak you see all later terms below you.

Case 1: there are infinitely many peaks n_1 \lt n_2 \lt \dots. Then a_{n_1} \ge a_{n_2} \ge \dots. This subsequence goes down.

Case 2: there are finitely many peaks. Pick n_1 after the last peak. It is not a peak, so some n_2 \gt n_1 has a_{n_2} \gt a_{n_1}. Repeat. This subsequence goes up.

In both cases we have a monotone bounded subsequence. The monotone convergence theorem finishes the proof. In \mathbb{R}^n, take a subsequence for the first coordinate, then a subsequence of that for the second, and so on.

In simple words: you cannot put infinitely many points into a bounded box without a crowd forming somewhere. The proof of the extreme value theorem in the chapter Limits and continuity uses exactly this.

Cauchy sequences

Often we do not know the limit. Then we test whether the terms get close to each other. A sequence is Cauchy if for every \varepsilon \gt 0 there is an N with |a_m - a_n| \lt \varepsilon for all m, n \ge N.

A sequence of real numbers converges if and only if it is a Cauchy sequence.

Proof

If a_n \to L, take N with |a_n - L| \lt \varepsilon / 2 for n \ge N. Then |a_m - a_n| \le |a_m - L| + |L - a_n| \lt \varepsilon.

Now let a_n be Cauchy. With \varepsilon = 1, all terms after some N lie within 1 of a_N. So the sequence is bounded. By Bolzano-Weierstrass a subsequence converges to some L. Let \varepsilon \gt 0. Choose N from the Cauchy condition for \varepsilon / 2. Choose an index n_k \ge N of the subsequence with |a_{n_k} - L| \lt \varepsilon / 2. For n \ge N: |a_n - L| \le |a_n - a_{n_k}| + |a_{n_k} - L| \lt \varepsilon.

A space where every Cauchy sequence converges is called complete. \mathbb{R} is complete. \mathbb{Q} is not: Newton's sequence is Cauchy, but its limit is missing from \mathbb{Q}.

"The steps get small" is not the Cauchy condition. Take a_n = \sqrt{n}. Then a_{n+1} - a_n = \frac{1}{\sqrt{n+1} + \sqrt{n}} \to 0. But a_n goes to infinity. The Cauchy condition talks about all pairs m, n \ge N, not only neighbours.

Open, closed and compact sets

Stand at 0.999 inside the interval (0, 1). You can step a little left or right and stay inside. Now stand at 1 inside [0, 1]. Any step to the right leaves the set. This small difference controls a lot of analysis.

  • A set U is open if every point x \in U has some r \gt 0 with (x - r, x + r) \subseteq U.
  • A set F is closed if its complement is open. The same thing: if x_n \in F and x_n \to x, then x \in F.

Examples: (0, 1) is open. [0, 1] is closed. [0, 1) is neither. \mathbb{R} and the empty set are both. In \mathbb{R}^n, replace intervals by balls \{ y : |y - x| \lt r \}.

"Not open" does not mean "closed". Sets are not doors. The set [0, 1) is not open, because of the point 0. It is not closed either, because 1 - \frac{1}{n} \to 1 \notin [0, 1).

Covers and compactness

An open cover of K is a family of open sets whose union contains K. A finite subcover is a finite part of it that still covers K. A set K is compact if every open cover has a finite subcover.

Look at (0, 1) and the open sets U_n = (\frac{1}{n}, 1) for n = 2, 3, \dots. Every x \in (0, 1) is in some U_n: take n \gt 1/x. So they cover (0, 1). But any finite choice has a largest n, and it misses (0, \frac{1}{n}]. So (0, 1) is not compact.

A subset of \mathbb{R}^n is compact if and only if it is closed and bounded.

Proof idea

Compact gives closed and bounded. The balls of radius 1, 2, 3, \dots around 0 cover K. A finite subcover means one big ball holds K. So K is bounded. If a point p outside K were a limit of points of K, the open sets \{ x : |x - p| \gt \frac{1}{n} \} would cover K with no finite subcover.

Closed and bounded gives compact. First take [a, b]. Assume some open cover has no finite subcover. Cut [a, b] in half. One half also has no finite subcover. Cut that half again, and so on. The intervals shrink and are nested. Their left ends go up and are bounded, so they converge to a point c. The point c lies in some open set U of the cover. U contains a small interval around c. This interval holds one of the small halves. Then one set covers that half. This is a contradiction. For a closed bounded set in \mathbb{R}^n, put it in a big closed box and cut boxes into 2^n parts.

In \mathbb{R}^n there is a third way to say compact. A set K is compact exactly when every sequence in K has a subsequence with a limit in K. This is Bolzano-Weierstrass plus "closed". The history is long. Dirichlet used the idea for intervals in lectures in 1852. Borel proved a version for countable covers in 1895. Cousin and Lebesgue gave the general form a few years later.

In other spaces, closed and bounded is not enough. Take infinite sequences x = (x_1, x_2, \dots) with \sum x_k^2 finite. The unit vectors e_1 = (1, 0, 0, \dots), e_2 = (0, 1, 0, \dots) all have length 1. Any two are \sqrt{2} apart. So no subsequence converges. The unit ball there is closed and bounded but not compact. The chapters Topology and Measure and functional analysis go further.

Continuity and uniform continuity

Let f(x) = x^2 and a = 3. We want |f(x) - 9| \lt \varepsilon. Write |x^2 - 9| = |x - 3|\,|x + 3|. If |x - 3| \lt 1, then |x + 3| \lt 7. So |x^2 - 9| \lt 7|x - 3|. The choice \delta = \min(1, \varepsilon / 7) works. At a = 100 the same steps give \delta = \min(1, \varepsilon / 201). The steeper the graph, the smaller \delta must be.

\forall a\ \forall \varepsilon \gt 0\ \exists \delta \gt 0\ \forall x:\ |x - a| \lt \delta \Rightarrow |f(x) - f(a)| \lt \varepsilon

Here \delta may depend on \varepsilon and on the point a.

\forall \varepsilon \gt 0\ \exists \delta \gt 0\ \forall a\ \forall x:\ |x - a| \lt \delta \Rightarrow |f(x) - f(a)| \lt \varepsilon

Here one \delta works at every point. It depends on \varepsilon only.

The only change is the place of "\forall a". That small move changes the meaning a lot. The definition of continuity at a point is in Limits and continuity. A useful equal form is the sequence test: f is continuous at a if and only if x_n \to a always gives f(x_n) \to f(a).

Some examples of uniform continuity:

  • f(x) = 3x + 1 on \mathbb{R}: yes. Take \delta = \varepsilon / 3 everywhere.
  • f(x) = x^2 on \mathbb{R}: no. Take x = n and y = n + \frac{1}{n}. They are \frac{1}{n} apart, but y^2 - x^2 = 2 + \frac{1}{n^2} \gt 2.
  • f(x) = \frac{1}{x} on (0, 1]: no. Near 0 the graph is too steep.
  • f(x) = \sqrt{x} on [0, \infty): yes, because |\sqrt{x} - \sqrt{y}| \le \sqrt{|x - y|}. Take \delta = \varepsilon^2.

A function is Lipschitz if |f(x) - f(y)| \le L|x - y| for one constant L. Every Lipschitz function is uniformly continuous with \delta = \varepsilon / L. By the mean value theorem, a function with |f'| \le L is Lipschitz.

A continuous function on a compact set is uniformly continuous. In particular, every continuous f : [a, b] \to \mathbb{R} is uniformly continuous.

Proof

Assume f is not uniformly continuous on the compact set K. Then some \varepsilon \gt 0 has no good \delta. So for \delta = \frac{1}{n} there are x_n, y_n \in K with |x_n - y_n| \lt \frac{1}{n} and |f(x_n) - f(y_n)| \ge \varepsilon.

By Bolzano-Weierstrass, a subsequence x_{n_k} \to c, and c \in K because K is closed. Then also y_{n_k} \to c. By continuity, f(x_{n_k}) - f(y_{n_k}) \to f(c) - f(c) = 0. That contradicts |f(x_{n_k}) - f(y_{n_k})| \ge \varepsilon.

Why care? Uniform continuity lets one step size work everywhere. The next sections use it to prove that continuous functions have integrals and can be approximated by polynomials.

Compactness is needed. \frac{1}{x} is continuous on (0, 1] but not uniformly continuous. The set (0, 1] is bounded but not closed. x^2 on \mathbb{R} fails because \mathbb{R} is closed but not bounded.

Derivatives, fixed points and inverse functions

The chapters Derivatives and Using derivatives already prove a chain of results. The extreme value theorem gives a maximum. Fermat's theorem says the slope is 0 there. Rolle's theorem and the mean value theorem follow. Each link needs completeness through Bolzano-Weierstrass. Now we use the mean value theorem to solve equations.

A machine that shrinks distances

Type 1 into a calculator in radians. Press cos again and again. The display settles at 0.739085. This number solves \cos x = x. Why does pressing a button solve an equation?

On [0, 1], \cos maps the interval into itself. Its slope is -\sin x, and |\sin x| \le \sin 1 \approx 0.84. By the mean value theorem, |\cos x - \cos y| \le 0.84\,|x - y|. Each press brings any two points closer by the factor 0.84.

Let X be a set with a distance d. A map T : X \to X is a contraction if there is a q \lt 1 with d(T(x), T(y)) \le q\, d(x, y) for all x, y. A fixed point is a point with T(x) = x.

Let X be a complete space with a distance, not empty, and let T : X \to X be a contraction with factor q \lt 1. Then T has exactly one fixed point x^*. For any start x_0, the iterates x_{n+1} = T(x_n) converge to x^*, and

d(x_n, x^*) \le \frac{q^n}{1 - q}\, d(x_1, x_0).
Proof

Each step shrinks the distance: d(x_{k+1}, x_k) \le q^k d(x_1, x_0). For m \gt n, add the steps from n to m and use the geometric series:

d(x_m, x_n) \le (q^n + q^{n+1} + \dots)\, d(x_1, x_0) = \frac{q^n}{1 - q}\, d(x_1, x_0).

This goes to 0, so the sequence is Cauchy. The space is complete, so x_n \to x^*. A contraction is continuous, so T(x^*) = \lim T(x_n) = \lim x_{n+1} = x^*. Let m \to \infty to get the error bound. If y is another fixed point, d(x^*, y) = d(Tx^*, Ty) \le q\, d(x^*, y). Since q \lt 1, d(x^*, y) = 0.

import math

q = math.sin(1)              # contraction factor of cos on [0, 1]
x0 = 1.0
x1 = math.cos(x0)
star = 0.7390851332151607    # the fixed point, from 200 steps
x = x0
for n in range(1, 41):
    x = math.cos(x)          # one step: x_n = T(x_{n-1})
    if n in (1, 10, 20, 30, 40):
        bound = q**n / (1 - q) * abs(x1 - x0)   # the error bound from the theorem
        print(f"n={n:2d}  x={x:.10f}  error={abs(x - star):.1e}  bound={bound:.1e}")
n= 1  x=0.5403023059  error=2.0e-01  bound=2.4e+00
n=10  x=0.7442373549  error=5.2e-03  bound=5.2e-01
n=20  x=0.7391843998  error=9.9e-05  bound=9.2e-02
n=30  x=0.7390870427  error=1.9e-06  bound=1.6e-02
n=40  x=0.7390851699  error=3.7e-08  bound=2.9e-03

The bound is always true, but it is careful. The real error is much smaller, because near the fixed point the factor is \sin(0.739) \approx 0.67, not 0.84. The theorem also works when the points are whole functions. That is how the Picard-Lindelof theorem in Differential equations gets one solution and only one.

The inverse function theorem

Start in one variable. Let f(x) = x^3 + x. Its slope 3x^2 + 1 is never 0. So near any point the graph can be read backwards, and (f^{-1})'(f(a)) = \frac{1}{f'(a)}. At a = 1: f(1) = 2 and (f^{-1})'(2) = \frac{1}{4}. Now take g(x) = x^2 at a = 0. Its slope is 0. The values near 0 come from both x and -x, so no inverse exists there.

Let f : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^n have continuous partial derivatives near a. Assume the Jacobian matrix Df(a) is invertible. Then there are open sets U \ni a and V \ni f(a) such that f : U \to V is one-to-one and onto. Its inverse is also continuously differentiable, and

D(f^{-1})(f(a)) = \big(Df(a)\big)^{-1}.
Proof idea

Let A = Df(a). To solve f(x) = y, look at \varphi(x) = x + A^{-1}(y - f(x)). A fixed point of \varphi is a solution. The derivative of \varphi is I - A^{-1}Df(x), which is 0 at a. By continuity it stays small, say below \frac{1}{2}, on a small closed ball. By the mean value inequality, \varphi is a contraction there. For y close to f(a), it maps the ball into itself. Banach gives exactly one solution x. So the inverse exists. More estimates show it is differentiable, and the chain rule gives its matrix.

Example: polar coordinates f(r, \theta) = (r\cos\theta,\ r\sin\theta). The Jacobian determinant is r. So for r \gt 0 you can go back from (x, y) to (r, \theta) near each point. At r = 0 you cannot: every \theta gives the origin.

The theorem is local. Take f(x, y) = (e^x \cos y,\ e^x \sin y). Its Jacobian determinant is e^{2x}, never 0. But f(x, y) = f(x, y + 2\pi). So f is not one-to-one on the whole plane. An invertible Jacobian everywhere does not give one global inverse.

The implicit function theorem

The circle x^2 + y^2 = 25 is not the graph of one function. Near (3, 4), though, it is the graph of y = \sqrt{25 - x^2}. Near (5, 0) it is not: the circle is vertical there. The test is the partial derivative in y: F_y = 2y. It is 8 at (3, 4) and 0 at (5, 0).

Let F : \mathbb{R}^{n} \times \mathbb{R}^{m} \to \mathbb{R}^m have continuous partial derivatives, and let F(a, b) = 0. Assume the m \times m matrix D_y F(a, b) of derivatives in y is invertible. Then near (a, b) the solutions of F(x, y) = 0 are exactly the points (x, g(x)) for one continuously differentiable g with g(a) = b, and

Dg(a) = -\big(D_y F(a, b)\big)^{-1} D_x F(a, b).
Proof idea

Build a square map G(x, y) = (x, F(x, y)). Its Jacobian matrix has the block form \begin{pmatrix} I & 0 \\ D_x F & D_y F \end{pmatrix}. This is invertible because D_y F is. By the inverse function theorem, G has a local inverse. Solve G(x, y) = (x, 0). The second part of the answer is g(x). The formula for Dg comes from the chain rule on F(x, g(x)) = 0.

For the circle with n = m = 1: g'(3) = -\frac{F_x}{F_y} = -\frac{2 \cdot 3}{2 \cdot 4} = -\frac{3}{4}. This matches the answer from implicit differentiation in Partial derivatives and the gradient. The theorem also explains why constraint sets in Optimisation in many variables are smooth when the gradient is not zero.

The Riemann integral with proofs

How much area lies under f(x) = x^2 on [0, 1]? Cut the interval into n equal pieces. On each piece the function is smallest at the left end and largest at the right end. Low boxes give a lower sum L. High boxes give an upper sum U. The true area is between them.

from fractions import Fraction

def sums(n):
    """Lower and upper sums of x^2 on [0, 1] with n equal pieces."""
    h = Fraction(1, n)
    lower = sum((k * h) ** 2 * h for k in range(n))         # left ends: smallest value
    upper = sum(((k + 1) * h) ** 2 * h for k in range(n))   # right ends: largest value
    return lower, upper

for n in (10, 100, 1000):
    L, U = sums(n)
    print(f"n={n:4d}  L={float(L):.6f}  U={float(U):.6f}  U-L={float(U - L):.6f}")
n=  10  L=0.285000  U=0.385000  U-L=0.100000
n= 100  L=0.328350  U=0.338350  U-L=0.010000
n=1000  L=0.332834  U=0.333834  U-L=0.001000

The gap U - L is exactly \frac{1}{n}. Both sums close in on \frac{1}{3}. Now the general rule.

Let f be bounded on [a, b]. A partition is P : a = x_0 \lt x_1 \lt \dots \lt x_n = b. On piece k let m_k = \inf f and M_k = \sup f. Then

L(f, P) = \sum_{k=1}^n m_k (x_k - x_{k-1}), \qquad U(f, P) = \sum_{k=1}^n M_k (x_k - x_{k-1}).

f is integrable if \sup_P L(f, P) = \inf_P U(f, P). This common value is \int_a^b f(x)\,dx.

Adding cut points makes L bigger or equal and U smaller or equal. So every lower sum is below every upper sum. This gives a practical test.

A bounded f is integrable on [a, b] if and only if for every \varepsilon \gt 0 there is a partition P with U(f, P) - L(f, P) \lt \varepsilon.

Every continuous function on [a, b] is Riemann integrable.

Proof

Let \varepsilon \gt 0. By Heine-Cantor, f is uniformly continuous. So there is a \delta with |f(x) - f(y)| \lt \frac{\varepsilon}{b - a} whenever |x - y| \lt \delta. Take a partition with all pieces shorter than \delta. On each piece, M_k - m_k \le \frac{\varepsilon}{b - a}, because the max and min are reached at two close points. Then

U - L = \sum (M_k - m_k)(x_k - x_{k-1}) \le \frac{\varepsilon}{b - a} \sum (x_k - x_{k-1}) = \varepsilon.

By the Riemann criterion, f is integrable. Notice the key point: one \delta for all pieces. Plain continuity would not give that.

Monotone functions are integrable too, even with jumps. The proofs of the fundamental theorem of calculus in Integrals rest on this theory and the mean value theorem.

Here is a function with no Riemann integral. Let D(x) = 1 for rational x and D(x) = 0 for irrational x. It is called the Dirichlet function. Every piece of every partition holds both kinds of number. So every m_k = 0 and every M_k = 1. On [0, 1], L = 0 and U = 1 for every partition.

"Bounded" does not give "integrable". The Dirichlet function is bounded by 1. Worse, list the rationals as r_1, r_2, \dots. Let f_n be 1 at r_1, \dots, r_n and 0 elsewhere. Each f_n is integrable with integral 0. But f_n \to D at every point. The Riemann integral does not survive this limit. The Lebesgue integral in Measure and functional analysis repairs it.

Sequences of functions and uniform convergence

Let f_n(x) = x^n on [0, 1]. For x \lt 1, x^n \to 0. At x = 1, 1^n = 1. So the limit function is 0 on [0, 1) and 1 at the point 1. Each f_n is continuous. The limit is not. Something went wrong. What?

Pointwise convergence: f_n(x) \to f(x) for each x. The N may depend on \varepsilon and on x.

Uniform convergence: for every \varepsilon \gt 0 there is one N with |f_n(x) - f(x)| \lt \varepsilon for all n \ge N and all x. The same: \sup_x |f_n(x) - f(x)| \to 0.

The number \|g\|_\infty = \sup_x |g(x)| is the sup norm. Uniform convergence means \| f_n - f \|_\infty \to 0. In the picture: the whole graph of f_n lies in a thin band around f.

# f_n(x) = x^n. The limit is 0 for every x in [0, 1).
for n in (1, 10, 100, 1000):
    x = 1 - 1 / n                  # a point that moves towards 1
    print(f"n={n:4d}  f_n(1 - 1/n) = {x**n:.4f}   sup on [0, 0.9] = {0.9**n:.2e}")
n=   1  f_n(1 - 1/n) = 0.0000   sup on [0, 0.9] = 9.00e-01
n=  10  f_n(1 - 1/n) = 0.3487   sup on [0, 0.9] = 3.49e-01
n= 100  f_n(1 - 1/n) = 0.3660   sup on [0, 0.9] = 2.66e-05
n=1000  f_n(1 - 1/n) = 0.3677   sup on [0, 0.9] = 1.75e-46

At the moving point 1 - \frac{1}{n}, the value tends to \frac{1}{e} \approx 0.368, not to 0. So the sup on [0, 1) never falls below 0.36. The convergence is not uniform there. On [0, 0.9] the sup is 0.9^n \to 0, so there it is uniform.

If each f_n is continuous and f_n \to f uniformly, then f is continuous.

Proof (the epsilon over 3 trick)

Fix a point a and \varepsilon \gt 0. Choose n with \|f_n - f\|_\infty \lt \varepsilon / 3. The function f_n is continuous at a, so some \delta gives |f_n(x) - f_n(a)| \lt \varepsilon / 3 for |x - a| \lt \delta. By the triangle inequality:

|f(x) - f(a)| \le |f(x) - f_n(x)| + |f_n(x) - f_n(a)| + |f_n(a) - f(a)| \lt \tfrac{\varepsilon}{3} + \tfrac{\varepsilon}{3} + \tfrac{\varepsilon}{3} = \varepsilon.

Integrals behave well too. If f_n \to f uniformly on [a, b], then \left| \int_a^b f_n - \int_a^b f \right| \le (b - a)\, \|f_n - f\|_\infty \to 0. With only pointwise convergence this fails. Picture tents with base [0, \frac{2}{n}] and height n. Each tent has area 1. At every point the tents go to 0, but the areas stay 1.

Derivatives need even more care. Let f_n(x) = \frac{\sin(nx)}{\sqrt{n}}. Then \|f_n\|_\infty = \frac{1}{\sqrt{n}} \to 0, so f_n \to 0 uniformly. But f_n'(0) = \sqrt{n} \to \infty. The safe rule is this. Work on a bounded interval. If the derivatives f_n' converge uniformly, and f_n(x_0) converges at one point, then f_n converges uniformly and the limit of f_n' is the derivative of the limit.

The Weierstrass M-test

A series of functions \sum u_k(x) converges uniformly when its partial sums do. The uniform Cauchy criterion says this happens exactly when \| \sum_{k=n}^{m} u_k \|_\infty \to 0 as n, m \to \infty. It comes from the Cauchy criterion used at each point. The easiest way to check it is this test.

Let |u_k(x)| \le M_k for all x in a set S, and let \sum M_k converge. Then \sum u_k(x) converges uniformly (and absolutely) on S.

Proof

For m \gt n and every x: \left| \sum_{k=n}^m u_k(x) \right| \le \sum_{k=n}^m M_k. The right side does not depend on x. It goes to 0 by the Cauchy criterion for the number series \sum M_k. So the partial sums are uniformly Cauchy. At each point they converge, and the bound passes to the limit. That bound shows the convergence is uniform.

Example: \sum_{k=1}^\infty \frac{\sin(kx)}{k^2} converges uniformly on \mathbb{R}, with M_k = \frac{1}{k^2}. Each term is continuous, so the sum is continuous. A stronger example is the Weierstrass function W(x) = \sum_{k=0}^\infty a^k \cos(b^k \pi x) with 0 \lt a \lt 1. The M-test with M_k = a^k shows that W is continuous. Weierstrass showed in 1872 that W has no derivative anywhere for odd whole b with ab \gt 1 + \frac{3\pi}{2}. Hardy relaxed this to ab \ge 1 in 1916.

The same test gives the uniform convergence of power series on any closed interval inside the radius of convergence. See Infinite series and Taylor series.

Compact families and approximation

Bolzano-Weierstrass says: bounded sequences of numbers have convergent subsequences. Is the same true for functions? Take f_n(x) = \sin(nx) on [0, \pi]. All of them lie between -1 and 1. But they wiggle faster and faster. No subsequence converges uniformly. Being bounded is not enough. We also need a control on the wiggles.

  • A family of functions is uniformly bounded if one M has |f(x)| \le M for every f in the family and every x.
  • It is equicontinuous if for every \varepsilon \gt 0 one \delta works for all members: |x - y| \lt \delta \Rightarrow |f(x) - f(y)| \lt \varepsilon.

Example: all functions with |f| \le 1 and |f'| \le 5 form such a family. Take \delta = \varepsilon / 5 for all of them. The family \sin(nx) is not equicontinuous, because |f_n'| = n|\cos(nx)| can be as large as n.

Let (f_n) be a sequence of continuous functions on [a, b] that is uniformly bounded and equicontinuous. Then some subsequence converges uniformly on [a, b]. The same holds on any compact set.

Proof idea (the diagonal trick)

List the rational points of [a, b] as r_1, r_2, \dots. The numbers f_n(r_1) are bounded. By Bolzano-Weierstrass, a subsequence converges at r_1. From that subsequence, take a further one that converges at r_2. Go on forever. Now take the first function of the first list, the second of the second list, and so on. This "diagonal" sequence converges at every rational point.

Now use equicontinuity. Fix \varepsilon. Choose \delta for \varepsilon / 3. By compactness, finitely many rational points are within \delta of every point of [a, b]. At those finitely many points the sequence is Cauchy. With the \varepsilon / 3 trick, it is uniformly Cauchy everywhere. So it converges uniformly.

Ascoli found the sufficient condition in 1883 to 1884. Arzela proved the converse in 1895. A main use is in Differential equations. The Peano theorem says y' = F(x, y) has a solution when F is only continuous. Its proof builds rough solutions with Euler's method. The rough solutions are uniformly bounded and equicontinuous. Arzela-Ascoli picks a subsequence that converges to a true solution. Uniqueness can fail then: y' = 3y^{2/3}, y(0) = 0 has the solutions y = 0 and y = x^3.

Approximation by polynomials

Computers evaluate sums and products quickly. So we want to replace a hard function by a polynomial. Can every continuous function be replaced? Weierstrass proved yes in 1885.

For every continuous f : [a, b] \to \mathbb{R} and every \varepsilon \gt 0 there is a polynomial p with |f(x) - p(x)| \lt \varepsilon for all x \in [a, b].

Proof idea (Bernstein polynomials)

Work on [0, 1]. Define B_n f(x) = \sum_{k=0}^n f\!\left(\frac{k}{n}\right) \binom{n}{k} x^k (1 - x)^{n-k}. Read it with probability. Toss a coin with heads chance x for n times. Let K be the number of heads. Then B_n f(x) is the expected value of f(K/n).

The variance of K/n is \frac{x(1 - x)}{n} \le \frac{1}{4n}. So K/n is usually close to x. Where it is close, uniform continuity makes f(K/n) close to f(x). Where it is far, the chance is small and f is bounded. Both parts are small for large n, at every x at once.

from math import comb

def f(x):
    return abs(x - 0.5)                    # continuous, with a corner at 0.5

def bernstein(n, x):
    """B_n f(x) = sum of f(k/n) C(n,k) x^k (1-x)^(n-k)."""
    return sum(f(k / n) * comb(n, k) * x**k * (1 - x)**(n - k) for k in range(n + 1))

grid = [i / 1000 for i in range(1001)]
for n in (10, 100, 1000):
    err = max(abs(bernstein(n, x) - f(x)) for x in grid)
    print(f"n={n:4d}  max error on [0, 1] = {err:.4f}")
n=  10  max error on [0, 1] = 0.1230
n= 100  max error on [0, 1] = 0.0398
n=1000  max error on [0, 1] = 0.0126

The error goes to 0, but slowly. Ten times more terms give only about three times less error. The worst place is the corner at 0.5. Bernstein polynomials prove the theorem well. Other methods compute better in practice.

Let K be compact, for example a closed bounded set in \mathbb{R}^n. Let \mathcal{A} be a set of continuous real functions on K that is closed under sums, products and multiplication by numbers. Assume \mathcal{A} contains the constants and separates points. Then every continuous function on K is a uniform limit of members of \mathcal{A}.

Proof idea

First, |x| can be approximated by polynomials on [-1, 1]. So the closure of \mathcal{A} contains |g| for each member g. Then it contains \max(g, h) = \frac{g + h + |g - h|}{2} and \min(g, h). Separation lets us match any target f at any two points. Then take the max and min of finitely many such functions. Compactness makes "finitely many" possible. The result is within \varepsilon of f everywhere.

Stone published the general theorem in 1937 and a simpler proof in 1948. It has many uses.

  • Polynomials in x and y approximate any continuous function on a closed square.
  • Trigonometric sums \sum (a_k \cos kx + b_k \sin kx) approximate any continuous function on a circle.
  • Even polynomials on [-1, 1] do not separate x from -x. Indeed they cannot approximate f(x) = x.

The universal approximation theorem for neural networks has the same shape: a family of simple functions is dense in C(K). See The maths of machine learning.

The approximation is on a compact set. No polynomial is uniformly close to \sin x on all of \mathbb{R}. A polynomial that is not constant goes to infinity, but \sin x stays between -1 and 1.

Patterns to remember

Patterns for real analysis
PatternPurposeModelNote
Let \varepsilon \gt 0. Choose N ... For n \ge N ...Prove a limit of a sequence\frac{5}{n + 3} \lt \varepsilon for n \gt 5/\varepsilonFind N in scratch work, then write forwards.
s - \varepsilon is not an upper boundUse a supremumSome a_N \gt s - \varepsilonThe sup need not be in the set.
Monotone + boundedGet a limit you cannot computeNewton's sequence for \sqrt{2}Find the limit after from L = T(L).
