Practice

What is \sup \{ 1 - \frac{1}{n} : n \ge 1 \}, and is it a maximum?

  • 0, and it is a maximum
  • 1, and it is not a maximum
  • 1, and it is a maximum
  • It has no supremum

Every member is below 1, and members get as close to 1 as we like. But 1 is not a member.

Which set is compact?

  • (0, 1)
  • [0, \infty)
  • [0, 1] \cup [2, 3]
  • \mathbb{Q} \cap [0, 1]

By Heine-Borel we need closed and bounded. (0,1) is not closed, [0,\infty) is not bounded, and \mathbb{Q} \cap [0,1] misses limits like \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}.

Which function is uniformly continuous on the given set?

  • x^2 on \mathbb{R}
  • 1/x on (0, 1)
  • \sin x on \mathbb{R}
  • \sin(1/x) on (0, 1)

|\sin x - \sin y| \le |x - y|, so \sin is Lipschitz with L = 1. The others get too steep.

f_n(x) = x^n on [0, 1]. Which statement is true?

  • It converges uniformly to 0.
  • It converges pointwise, but not uniformly.
  • It does not converge at x = 1.
  • The limit is continuous.

The limit jumps to 1 at x = 1. A uniform limit of continuous functions would be continuous.

For a_n = \frac{2n + 1}{n + 3} and \varepsilon = 0.1, the smallest whole N that works is ?.

The contraction factor of \cos on [0, 1] is \sin ?.

For x^2 on [0, 1] with n equal pieces, U - L = ?.

The Jacobian determinant of polar coordinates (r, \theta) \mapsto (r\cos\theta, r\sin\theta) is ?.

  1. Prove from the definition that \frac{n}{n^2 + 1} \to 0.
    Answer

    Scratch: \frac{n}{n^2 + 1} \lt \frac{n}{n^2} = \frac{1}{n}. Proof: let \varepsilon \gt 0. Choose N \gt 1/\varepsilon. For n \ge N, \left|\frac{n}{n^2 + 1} - 0\right| \lt \frac{1}{n} \le \frac{1}{N} \lt \varepsilon.

  2. Show that a_1 = 1, a_{n+1} = \sqrt{2 + a_n} converges, and find the limit.
    Answer

    By induction a_n \lt 2: if a_n \lt 2 then a_{n+1} \lt \sqrt{4} = 2. Also a_{n+1}^2 - a_n^2 = 2 + a_n - a_n^2 = (2 - a_n)(1 + a_n) \gt 0, so the sequence goes up. Monotone and bounded, so it converges to some L. Then L = \sqrt{2 + L}, so L^2 - L - 2 = 0 and L = 2, since L \gt 0.

  3. Give an open cover of [0, \infty) with no finite subcover. Which part of Heine-Borel fails?
    Answer

    U_n = (-1, n) for n = 1, 2, \dots. Any finite choice lies inside (-1, N) and misses N. The set is closed but not bounded.

  4. Prove that f(x) = \frac{1}{x} is not uniformly continuous on (0, 1].
    Answer

    Take \varepsilon = 1. Let x = \frac{1}{n} and y = \frac{1}{n + 1}. Then |x - y| = \frac{1}{n(n+1)}, which is smaller than any \delta for large n. But |f(x) - f(y)| = |n - (n + 1)| = 1. So no \delta works for \varepsilon = 1.

  5. Show that T(x) = \frac{1}{2}\cos x has exactly one fixed point in \mathbb{R}. How many steps from x_0 = 0 guarantee an error below 10^{-6}?
    Answer

    |T'(x)| = \frac{1}{2}|\sin x| \le \frac{1}{2}, so T is a contraction with q = \frac{1}{2} on the complete space \mathbb{R}. Banach gives exactly one fixed point. x_1 = 0.5, so the bound is \frac{(1/2)^n}{1/2} \cdot 0.5 = (1/2)^n. We need 2^n \gt 10^6, so n = 20 steps are enough.

  6. Near which points of the curve x^3 + y^3 = 6xy does the implicit function theorem give y = g(x)? Find g'(3) at the point (3, 3).
    Answer

    F = x^3 + y^3 - 6xy, F_y = 3y^2 - 6x. The theorem works where 3y^2 \ne 6x, that is y^2 \ne 2x. At (3, 3): F_y = 27 - 18 = 9 \ne 0. F_x = 3x^2 - 6y = 27 - 18 = 9. So g'(3) = -\frac{9}{9} = -1.

  7. Hard. Show that \sum_{k=1}^\infty \frac{x^k}{k^2} is continuous on [-1, 1].
    Answer

    For |x| \le 1, \left|\frac{x^k}{k^2}\right| \le \frac{1}{k^2} = M_k, and \sum \frac{1}{k^2} converges. By the M-test the series converges uniformly on [-1, 1]. Each partial sum is a polynomial, so it is continuous. A uniform limit of continuous functions is continuous.

  8. Hard. Let f_n(x) = \frac{x}{1 + n x^2} on \mathbb{R}. Find \|f_n\|_\infty. Does f_n \to 0 uniformly? Does f_n' \to 0 at every point?
    Answer

    f_n'(x) = \frac{1 - n x^2}{(1 + n x^2)^2}. It is zero at x = \frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}, where f_n = \frac{1}{2\sqrt{n}}. So \|f_n\|_\infty = \frac{1}{2\sqrt{n}} \to 0: uniform convergence to 0. But f_n'(0) = 1 for every n, while the derivative of the limit is 0. Uniform convergence of f_n says nothing about f_n'.

Key takeaways

  • The completeness axiom says the real line has no gaps. Monotone convergence, Bolzano-Weierstrass and the Cauchy criterion all come from it.
  • A limit proof gives an N for every \varepsilon. The order of the quantifiers is the whole meaning.
  • In \mathbb{R}^n, compact means closed and bounded (Heine-Borel). Compactness turns "near each point" into "near all points at once".
  • Continuous on a compact set gives uniformly continuous (Heine-Cantor). That is why continuous functions have integrals.
  • Contractions on complete spaces have one fixed point (Banach). This proves the inverse and implicit function theorems and the existence of ODE solutions.
  • Uniform convergence keeps continuity and integrals. The M-test is the quick way to prove it. Derivatives need a separate check.
  • Arzela-Ascoli gives compactness for families of functions. Stone-Weierstrass says simple functions can approximate every continuous function on a compact set.

Sources

  • Basic Analysis: Introduction to Real Analysis (Jiri Lebl). A free open textbook, version 6.3 of May 2026, used for the order of topics and the proofs.
  • MIT OpenCourseWare 18.100A Real Analysis (Fall 2020). A full university course with lecture notes on sequences, continuity, the Riemann integral and uniform convergence.
  • Heine-Borel theorem (Wikipedia). Statement, the bisection proof and the history with Dirichlet, Borel, Cousin and Lebesgue.
  • Banach fixed-point theorem (Wikipedia). Statement, the error bound and the link to Picard iteration.
  • Arzela-Ascoli theorem (Wikipedia). Equicontinuity, the diagonal proof and the dates of Ascoli and Arzela.
  • Stone-Weierstrass theorem (Wikipedia). The 1885 Weierstrass theorem and Stone's 1937 and 1948 papers.

Complex analysis

Complex analysis studies functions of a complex variable that have a derivative. That one condition is much stronger than it looks. Such functions are fixed by a few values, they have power series, and their integrals around loops can be computed by a simple count. Engineers and physicists use this to compute hard real integrals and to map shapes onto each other.

  • Test a function for a complex derivative with the Cauchy-Riemann equations.
  • Compute contour integrals with Cauchy's theorem and Cauchy's integral formula.
  • Use Liouville's theorem, the identity theorem and the maximum modulus principle.
  • Find poles and residues, and compute real integrals with the residue theorem.
  • Count zeros with Rouche's theorem and explain conformal maps and the Riemann mapping theorem.

Complex functions as maps

Take f(z) = z^2. Put z = x + iy. Then z^2 = (x^2 - y^2) + i(2xy). So one complex function is two real functions: u(x, y) = x^2 - y^2 and v(x, y) = 2xy. The point 1 + i goes to 2i. In polar form, z^2 doubles the angle and squares the length. The quarter plane x \gt 0, y \gt 0 goes onto the upper half-plane.

A complex function sends a complex number z to a complex number f(z) = u + iv. We cannot draw its graph, because that needs four dimensions. Instead we draw it as a map from one plane to another. The basics of i, the modulus and the polar form are in Complex numbers.

Four functions appear everywhere.

  • Polynomials, like z^3 - 2z + 1.
  • \frac{1}{z}. It turns the inside of the unit circle into the outside.
  • e^z = e^x(\cos y + i \sin y). It never takes the value 0. It repeats: e^{z + 2\pi i} = e^z.
  • \operatorname{Log} z = \ln|z| + i \operatorname{Arg} z with -\pi \lt \operatorname{Arg} z \le \pi. It undoes e^z, but it jumps across the negative real axis.

Limits and continuity work as in the plane. z \to a means |z - a| \to 0, from any direction.

There is no "bigger" or "smaller" between complex numbers. 3i \gt 2i means nothing. Only moduli are compared: |3i| = 3 \gt 2 = |2i|. So a sentence like "|f| has a maximum" makes sense, but "f has a maximum" does not.

Holomorphic functions and the Cauchy-Riemann equations

The derivative is defined as in one variable: f'(a) = \lim_{h \to 0} \frac{f(a + h) - f(a)}{h}. But now h is complex. It can go to 0 along the real axis, the imaginary axis or a spiral. The limit must be the same for all paths.

  1. For f(z) = z^2: \frac{(a + h)^2 - a^2}{h} = 2a + h \to 2a. This works for every path. So f'(a) = 2a.
  2. For g(z) = \overline{z} = x - iy, the conjugate: \frac{\overline{a + h} - \overline{a}}{h} = \frac{\overline{h}}{h}.
  3. Real h: \overline{h}/h = 1. Imaginary h = it: \overline{h}/h = -it/(it) = -1.
  4. Two paths, two answers. So \overline{z} has no complex derivative anywhere.

A function is holomorphic on an open set if it has a complex derivative at every point. A function holomorphic on all of \mathbb{C} is entire. Polynomials, e^z, \sin z and \cos z are entire. \frac{1}{z} is holomorphic on \mathbb{C} \setminus \{0\}.

Let f = u + iv. If f has a complex derivative at a, then at a:

u_x = v_y, \qquad u_y = -v_x, \qquad f'(a) = u_x + i v_x.

Conversely, if u and v have continuous partial derivatives near a that satisfy these equations, then f has a complex derivative at a.

Proof

Let h = t be real. The quotient is \frac{u(x + t, y) - u + i(v(x + t, y) - v)}{t} \to u_x + i v_x.

Let h = it be imaginary. The quotient is \frac{u(x, y + t) - u + i(v(x, y + t) - v)}{it} \to \frac{u_y + i v_y}{i} = v_y - i u_y.

Both limits equal f'(a). Compare real parts: u_x = v_y. Compare imaginary parts: v_x = -u_y. For the converse, continuous partials give a linear approximation of (u, v). The equations say this linear map is "multiply by u_x + i v_x". That is a complex derivative.

Check z^2: u_x = 2x = v_y and u_y = -2y = -v_x. Check e^z: u = e^x \cos y, v = e^x \sin y. Then u_x = e^x \cos y = v_y and u_y = -e^x \sin y = -v_x. Also f' = u_x + i v_x = e^z. For \overline{z}: u_x = 1 but v_y = -1. The test fails, as Example 1 showed.

The equations have a picture. Near a, a holomorphic f acts like multiplication by the number f'(a). Multiplying by a complex number rotates and stretches. It never squashes a circle into an ellipse.

If f = u + iv is holomorphic, then u_{xx} + u_{yy} = 0 and v_{xx} + v_{yy} = 0. Functions with this property are called harmonic. They describe heat at rest, electric potential and ideal fluid flow.

Why? u_{xx} = (v_y)_x = (v_x)_y = (-u_y)_y = -u_{yy}. This uses that u, v have second derivatives. The next sections show that holomorphic functions have derivatives of every order. Example: u = x^2 - y^2 has u_{xx} + u_{yy} = 2 - 2 = 0.

Smooth as a map of the plane is not enough. \overline{z} is just a mirror, as smooth as can be. But it fails Cauchy-Riemann. A complex derivative needs the special link between u and v.

Contour integrals and Cauchy's theorem

Integrate \frac{1}{z} once around the unit circle. Write the circle as z = e^{it} for 0 \le t \le 2\pi. Then dz = ie^{it}\,dt, and

\oint_{|z| = 1} \frac{dz}{z} = \int_0^{2\pi} \frac{ie^{it}}{e^{it}}\,dt = \int_0^{2\pi} i\,dt = 2\pi i.

Do the same with z^n for a whole number n \ne -1. You get \int_0^{2\pi} i e^{i(n+1)t}\,dt = 0. Only the power -1 survives. This one fact is the seed of the whole theory.

A contour is a path \gamma : [a, b] \to \mathbb{C} made of smooth pieces. The integral of f along it is

\int_\gamma f(z)\,dz = \int_a^b f(\gamma(t))\,\gamma'(t)\,dt.

It does not depend on how fast we move along the path. It changes sign if we go backwards. A closed contour ends where it starts. We write \oint.

Two tools follow at once.

  • The ML bound. If |f| \le M on \gamma and \gamma has length L, then \left|\int_\gamma f\,dz\right| \le ML.
  • Antiderivatives. If F' = f along \gamma, then \int_\gamma f\,dz = F(\text{end}) - F(\text{start}). On a closed contour that is 0.

So \oint z^n\,dz = 0 for n \ne -1, because \frac{z^{n+1}}{n+1} is an antiderivative. \frac{1}{z} has no antiderivative on \mathbb{C} \setminus \{0\}. The candidate \operatorname{Log} z jumps by 2\pi i once around 0.

Let f be holomorphic on a simply connected open set D. Then \oint_\gamma f(z)\,dz = 0 for every closed contour \gamma in D.

Proof idea

Assume also that f' is continuous, and let \gamma bound a region R. Write f\,dz = (u + iv)(dx + i\,dy). Then

\oint_\gamma f\,dz = \oint_\gamma (u\,dx - v\,dy) + i \oint_\gamma (v\,dx + u\,dy).

By Green's theorem, the first part is \iint_R (-v_x - u_y)\,dA. The second is \iint_R (u_x - v_y)\,dA. By Cauchy-Riemann, both integrands are 0. Goursat later proved the theorem without assuming f' is continuous. His proof cuts triangles into smaller and smaller triangles.

"Simply connected" means: no holes. A disk, a half-plane and a star shape qualify. The ring 1 \lt |z| \lt 2 and the punctured plane \mathbb{C} \setminus \{0\} do not. A useful form of the theorem is the deformation rule. You may move a closed contour inside the region where f is holomorphic, and the integral stays the same. So every circle around 0 gives \oint \frac{dz}{z} = 2\pi i, whatever its radius.

Check for holes. \frac{1}{z} is holomorphic at every point of the unit circle. But \oint \frac{dz}{z} = 2\pi i \ne 0. The theorem does not apply because the region inside the circle contains 0, where \frac{1}{z} is not defined.

Cauchy's integral formula and what follows

Here is a surprise. The values of a holomorphic function on a circle fix all its values inside.

Let f be holomorphic on an open set that contains the closed disk |z - a| \le r. Let C be its boundary circle, traced once counterclockwise. Then for every w inside the circle

f(w) = \frac{1}{2\pi i} \oint_C \frac{f(z)}{z - w}\,dz, \qquad f^{(n)}(w) = \frac{n!}{2\pi i} \oint_C \frac{f(z)}{(z - w)^{n+1}}\,dz.
Proof

By the deformation rule, replace C by a tiny circle C_\varepsilon of radius \varepsilon around w. Split the integrand: \frac{f(z)}{z - w} = \frac{f(w)}{z - w} + \frac{f(z) - f(w)}{z - w}. The first part gives f(w) \cdot 2\pi i. In the second part the fraction stays bounded near w, say by K, because f has a derivative. By the ML bound its integral is at most K \cdot 2\pi\varepsilon \to 0. So \oint_C \frac{f(z)}{z - w}\,dz = 2\pi i\, f(w). For the derivatives, differentiate under the integral sign in w.

Two examples on the circle |z| = 2:

  • \oint \frac{e^z}{z - 1}\,dz = 2\pi i \cdot e^1 = 2\pi i e. Here f = e^z and w = 1.
  • \oint \frac{\cos z}{z^3}\,dz = \frac{2\pi i}{2!} \cos''(0) = \pi i \cdot (-1) = -\pi i. Here n = 2.

The second formula says something deep. If f has one complex derivative, it has derivatives of every order. Real functions are very different: x|x| has one derivative but not two.

If |f| \le M on the circle |z - a| = r, then |f^{(n)}(a)| \le \frac{n!\, M}{r^n}.

Proof: use the ML bound on the formula. The length is 2\pi r and the integrand is at most M / r^{n+1}. So |f^{(n)}(a)| \le \frac{n!}{2\pi} \cdot \frac{M}{r^{n+1}} \cdot 2\pi r.

Every entire function that is bounded is constant.

Proof

Let |f(z)| \le M for all z. Fix any point a. Cauchy's estimate with n = 1 gives |f'(a)| \le \frac{M}{r} for every radius r. Let r \to \infty. Then f'(a) = 0. This holds at every a, so f is constant.

So \sin z cannot be bounded on \mathbb{C}. Indeed \sin(iy) = i \sinh y, which grows without limit. On the real line, \sin x is bounded. In the complex plane it is not.

  1. Let p(z) = z^n + \dots with n \ge 1. Assume p has no root.
  2. Then g(z) = \frac{1}{p(z)} is entire.
  3. For large |z|, |p(z)| \ge \frac{1}{2}|z|^n, so |g(z)| \to 0. A continuous function on a closed disk is bounded. So g is bounded on all of \mathbb{C}.
  4. By Liouville, g is constant. Then p is constant. This contradicts n \ge 1.
  5. So every polynomial of degree n \ge 1 has a complex root. This is the fundamental theorem of algebra.

Let f be holomorphic and not constant on a connected open set D. Then |f| has no maximum inside D. If D is bounded and f is continuous up to the edge, the maximum of |f| on the closure is reached only on the edge.

Proof idea

Put z = a + re^{it} into Cauchy's formula. It becomes f(a) = \frac{1}{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi} f(a + re^{it})\,dt. So f(a) is the average of f on every small circle around a. Now let |f(a)| be the largest value. An average cannot be larger than all the values it averages. So |f| = |f(a)| on each small circle. Then |f| is constant near a, and with Cauchy-Riemann f is constant near a. The identity theorem below spreads this to all of D.

Example: f(z) = z^2 + 1 on the closed unit disk. On the edge, |z^2 + 1| \le 2, with equality at z = \pm 1. Inside, the value is smaller. At the centre it is only 1.

Power series, zeros and the identity theorem

The real function \frac{1}{1 + x^2} is smooth on the whole line. Yet its Taylor series 1 - x^2 + x^4 - \dots works only for |x| \lt 1. Why stop at 1? Look in the complex plane. \frac{1}{1 + z^2} blows up at z = \pm i. They are at distance 1 from 0. The series cannot pass them.

Let f be holomorphic on the open disk |z - a| \lt R. Then f is equal to its Taylor series there:

f(z) = \sum_{n=0}^\infty \frac{f^{(n)}(a)}{n!} (z - a)^n \quad \text{for all } |z - a| \lt R.

So the radius of convergence is at least the distance from a to the nearest bad point.

Proof idea

In Cauchy's formula, expand \frac{1}{z - w} as a geometric series in \frac{w - a}{z - a}. On a circle where \left|\frac{w - a}{z - a}\right| \le q \lt 1, the M-test makes the convergence uniform. So we may integrate term by term. Each term gives one coefficient \frac{f^{(n)}(a)}{n!}.

A function given by a power series near each point is called analytic. For complex functions, holomorphic and analytic mean the same. Power series themselves are covered in Infinite series and Taylor series.

Zeros are isolated

Let f(a) = 0 and f not be zero near a. The first nonzero coefficient tells the order m of the zero. Then f(z) = (z - a)^m g(z) with g(a) \ne 0. Since g is continuous, g \ne 0 near a. So a has a small disk with no other zero. Example: \sin z = z - \frac{z^3}{6} + \dots has a zero of order 1 at 0. 1 - \cos z = \frac{z^2}{2} - \dots has a zero of order 2.

Let f and g be holomorphic on a connected open set D. If f = g on a set that has a limit point in D, then f = g on all of D.

Proof idea

Let h = f - g. Its zeros crowd around a point c \in D. Zeros of a nonzero power series are isolated. So all Taylor coefficients of h at c are 0, and h = 0 near c. Let S be the set of points where h is 0 on a whole small disk. S is open, not empty, and also closed in D. Since D is connected, S = D.

In simple words: a holomorphic function is like a crystal. A small piece fixes the whole. For example \sin^2 z + \cos^2 z = 1 holds for real z. Both sides are entire. So it holds for every complex z. Every real identity of this kind carries over for free.

The limit point must be inside D. \sin(1/z) is holomorphic on \mathbb{C} \setminus \{0\}. It has zeros \frac{1}{n\pi} that crowd around 0. But it is not the zero function. The point 0 is not in the domain, so the theorem says nothing.

Singularities, residues and counting zeros

Look at three functions near z = 0.

  • \frac{\sin z}{z} = 1 - \frac{z^2}{6} + \dots. Set its value to 1 at 0, and the problem is gone.
  • \frac{1}{z^2}. It goes to infinity in a regular way.
  • e^{1/z} = 1 + \frac{1}{z} + \frac{1}{2!\,z^2} + \dots. Along the positive real axis it explodes. Along the negative axis it goes to 0. It is wild.

Each is holomorphic near 0 but not at 0. Such a point is an isolated singularity. Near it, f has a Laurent series \sum_{n=-\infty}^{\infty} c_n (z - a)^n. The negative powers decide the kind.

Near an essential singularity, f comes as close as we like to every complex value. This is the Casorati-Weierstrass theorem. Picard's great theorem says more: f takes every value, with at most one exception, infinitely often.

Residues

Integrate a Laurent series around a small circle. Every power gives 0 except (z - a)^{-1}, which gives 2\pi i. So only c_{-1} survives. It is called the residue, written \operatorname{Res}(f, a).

1. Simple pole: \operatorname{Res}(f, a) = \lim_{z \to a} (z - a) f(z). If f = \frac{g}{h} with g(a) \ne 0, h(a) = 0 and h'(a) \ne 0, then \operatorname{Res}(f, a) = \frac{g(a)}{h'(a)}.

2. Pole of order m: \operatorname{Res}(f, a) = \frac{1}{(m - 1)!} \lim_{z \to a} \frac{d^{m-1}}{dz^{m-1}} \big[(z - a)^m f(z)\big].

Example: f(z) = \frac{e^z}{z(z - 1)}. At 0: \lim z f(z) = \frac{e^0}{0 - 1} = -1. At 1: \lim (z - 1) f(z) = \frac{e^1}{1} = e.

Let f be holomorphic inside and on a simple closed contour \gamma, traced counterclockwise, except at finitely many points a_1, \dots, a_k inside. Then

\oint_\gamma f(z)\,dz = 2\pi i \sum_{j=1}^{k} \operatorname{Res}(f, a_j).
Proof idea

Draw a tiny circle around each a_j. Join them to \gamma with thin cuts. The new contour encloses no bad point, so by Cauchy's theorem its integral is 0. The two sides of each cut cancel. So the integral over \gamma equals the sum over the tiny circles. Each tiny circle gives 2\pi i\,c_{-1}.

So for f(z) = \frac{e^z}{z(z - 1)} on |z| = 2: \oint f\,dz = 2\pi i(-1 + e) \approx 10.796i. A computer can check this by adding up many small steps on the circle.

import cmath, math

def contour(f, radius=1.0, n=2000):
    """Integral of f over the circle |z| = radius (sum of small steps)."""
    total = 0
    for k in range(n):
        t = 2 * math.pi * k / n
        z = radius * cmath.exp(1j * t)
        dz = 1j * z * (2 * math.pi / n)        # z'(t) dt
        total += f(z) * dz
    return total

f = lambda z: cmath.exp(z) / (z * (z - 1))     # poles at 0 and 1
print("numeric :", contour(f, radius=2))
print("residues:", 2j * math.pi * (math.e - 1))

p = lambda z: z**5 - 6*z + 2                   # used in the next example
dp = lambda z: 5*z**4 - 6
for r in (1, 2):
    zeros = contour(lambda z: dp(z) / p(z), radius=r) / (2j * math.pi)
    print(f"zeros of p inside |z| < {r}: {zeros.real:.6f}")
numeric : (-1.170802821012784e-16+10.79628313816755j)
residues: 10.796283138167546j
zeros of p inside |z| < 1: 1.000000
zeros of p inside |z| < 2: 5.000000

Counting zeros

Apply the residue theorem to \frac{f'}{f}. Near a zero of order m, f = (z - a)^m g, so \frac{f'}{f} = \frac{m}{z - a} + \frac{g'}{g}. The residue is m. Near a pole of order m it is -m.

Let f be holomorphic inside and on \gamma except for poles inside, with no zeros or poles on \gamma. Let Z and P be the numbers of zeros and poles inside, counted with order. Then \frac{1}{2\pi i}\oint_\gamma \frac{f'(z)}{f(z)}\,dz = Z - P. This number is how many times f(\gamma) winds around 0.

Let f and g be holomorphic inside and on a simple closed contour \gamma. If |g(z)| \lt |f(z)| at every point of \gamma, then f and f + g have the same number of zeros inside \gamma, counted with order.

Proof idea

Picture a person who walks around a tree with a dog on a leash. The person's path is f(\gamma), and the tree is the point 0. The dog's path is (f + g)(\gamma). The leash has length |g|. It is always shorter than the person's distance |f| from the tree. So the dog cannot go around the tree a different number of times. By the argument principle, the winding numbers count the zeros.

  1. On |z| = 1, take f = -6z and g = z^5 + 2. Then |g| \le 1 + 2 = 3 \lt 6 = |f|. The function -6z has one zero inside. So p has exactly one root with |z| \lt 1.
  2. On |z| = 2, take f = z^5 and g = -6z + 2. Then |g| \le 12 + 2 = 14 \lt 32 = |f|. So p has all five roots in |z| \lt 2.
  3. So four roots lie in the ring 1 \le |z| \lt 2. The program above confirms the counts 1 and 5.

Eugene Rouche published the theorem in 1862. Engineers use the same winding idea in the Nyquist test, which checks if a feedback system is stable.

Real integrals with residues

Here is the famous trick. To compute a real integral, leave the real line. Close the path in the complex plane, and let residues do the work.

Choose f(z)

Replace x by z. For \cos x or \sin x, use e^{iz} and take the real or imaginary part at the end.

Choose a contour

Usually the segment [-R, R] plus the upper half circle C_R of radius R.

Find the poles inside

Solve for the zeros of the denominator. Keep only those with positive imaginary part.

Kill the arc

Show \int_{C_R} f\,dz \to 0 as R \to \infty. Use the ML bound, or Jordan's lemma for e^{iz}.

Read off the answer

The real integral equals 2\pi i times the sum of residues in the upper half-plane.

  1. f(z) = \frac{1}{1 + z^2} = \frac{1}{(z - i)(z + i)}. The pole in the upper half-plane is i.
  2. Residue at i: \frac{1}{i + i} = \frac{1}{2i}.
  3. On the arc, |1 + z^2| \ge R^2 - 1. So \left|\int_{C_R}\right| \le \frac{\pi R}{R^2 - 1} \to 0.
  4. Answer: \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \frac{dx}{1 + x^2} = 2\pi i \cdot \frac{1}{2i} = \pi. This matches \arctan(\infty) - \arctan(-\infty) = \pi.
  1. The poles solve z^4 = -1. In the upper half-plane: a_1 = e^{i\pi/4} and a_2 = e^{3i\pi/4}.
  2. Simple pole rule: \operatorname{Res} = \frac{1}{4a^3} = \frac{a}{4a^4} = -\frac{a}{4}, since a^4 = -1.
  3. Sum: -\frac{1}{4}(a_1 + a_2) = -\frac{1}{4} \cdot i\sqrt{2}. Here a_1 + a_2 = \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}(1 + i) + \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}(-1 + i) = i\sqrt{2}.
  4. Answer: 2\pi i \cdot \left(-\frac{i\sqrt{2}}{4}\right) = \frac{\pi\sqrt{2}}{2} = \frac{\pi}{\sqrt{2}} \approx 2.2214.

Integrals over a full turn of an angle use the unit circle instead. Put z = e^{i\theta}. Then \cos\theta = \frac{1}{2}\left(z + \frac{1}{z}\right) and d\theta = \frac{dz}{iz}.

  1. Substitute: \int_0^{2\pi} \frac{d\theta}{2 + \cos\theta} = \oint_{|z|=1} \frac{1}{2 + \frac{1}{2}(z + 1/z)} \cdot \frac{dz}{iz} = \oint \frac{2\,dz}{i(z^2 + 4z + 1)}.
  2. Poles: z = -2 \pm \sqrt{3}. Only z_1 = -2 + \sqrt{3} \approx -0.27 is inside the circle.
  3. Residue: \frac{2}{i(z_1 - z_2)} = \frac{2}{i \cdot 2\sqrt{3}} = \frac{1}{i\sqrt{3}}.
  4. Answer: 2\pi i \cdot \frac{1}{i\sqrt{3}} = \frac{2\pi}{\sqrt{3}} \approx 3.6276.

With \cos x on top we use e^{iz}, not \cos z. In the upper half-plane |e^{iz}| = e^{-y} \le 1. But \cos z grows like e^{|y|}. For \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \frac{\cos x}{1 + x^2}\,dx, the residue of \frac{e^{iz}}{1 + z^2} at i is \frac{e^{-1}}{2i}. So the integral is the real part of 2\pi i \cdot \frac{e^{-1}}{2i} = \frac{\pi}{e}. A numerical check of all four answers:

from mpmath import mp, quad, quadosc, cos, sqrt, pi, e, inf

mp.dps = 15
print("1/(1+x^2)  :", quad(lambda x: 1 / (1 + x**2), [-inf, inf]), " pi      =", pi)
print("1/(1+x^4)  :", quad(lambda x: 1 / (1 + x**4), [-inf, inf]), " pi/sqrt2 =", pi / sqrt(2))
print("1/(2+cos t):", quad(lambda t: 1 / (2 + cos(t)), [0, 2 * pi]), " 2pi/sqrt3 =", 2 * pi / sqrt(3))
osc = 2 * quadosc(lambda x: cos(x) / (1 + x**2), [0, inf], period=2 * pi)   # even function
print("cos/(1+x^2):", osc, " pi/e    =", pi / e)
1/(1+x^2)  : 3.14159265358979  pi      = 3.14159265358979
1/(1+x^4)  : 2.22144146907918  pi/sqrt2 = 2.22144146907918
1/(2+cos t): 3.62759872846844  2pi/sqrt3 = 3.62759872846844
cos/(1+x^2): 1.15572734979092  pi/e    = 1.15572734979092

Always check that the arc integral goes to 0. For \frac{P(x)}{Q(x)} the ML bound works when \deg Q \ge \deg P + 2. For \frac{x}{1 + x^2} it fails, and indeed that real integral does not converge. Also, a pole on the real line needs a small detour around it.

Conformal maps

Draw two curves that cross at z = 1 at a right angle. Apply f(z) = z^2. Here f'(1) = 2. Near 1, f acts like "multiply by 2". That stretches but does not rotate the crossing. The image curves still meet at a right angle. At z = 0 the story changes: f'(0) = 0, and the angle doubles. The two axes, at 90^\circ, go to rays at 180^\circ.

If f is holomorphic and f'(a) \ne 0, then f keeps the angle and the orientation between any two curves through a. Such a map is called conformal at a. Small circles become nearly circles. Their size is multiplied by |f'(a)|.

The most useful conformal maps are the Mobius maps w = \frac{az + b}{cz + d} with ad - bc \ne 0. They send circles and lines to circles and lines. One of them, the Cayley map, sends the upper half-plane onto the unit disk:

w = \frac{z - i}{z + i}.

Check: z = i goes to 0. For real z, the points z and i and -i give |z - i| = |z + i|. So |w| = 1: the real line goes to the unit circle.

Why do engineers care? A conformal map sends harmonic functions to harmonic functions. So you can solve the heat or flow problem on a simple disk, then map the answer to a hard shape. The Joukowski map z + \frac{1}{z} sends some circles to wing-like shapes. It was an early tool to study the air flow around a wing.

Let D be a simply connected open set, not empty and not all of \mathbb{C}. Then there is a holomorphic map from D onto the unit disk that is one-to-one, with a holomorphic inverse. It is unique if we also fix one point a \in D with f(a) = 0 and f'(a) \gt 0.

Proof idea

Look at all one-to-one holomorphic maps g from D into the disk with g(a) = 0. Choose the one that stretches most at a: the largest |g'(a)|. Why does a best map exist? Cauchy's estimate makes the family bounded and equicontinuous on compact sets. Arzela-Ascoli then gives a limit of a maximising sequence (Montel's theorem). A Rouche-type argument (Hurwitz's theorem) keeps the limit one-to-one. If the best map missed a point of the disk, a square-root trick would build a map that stretches even more. So the best map is onto. Uniqueness comes from the Schwarz lemma, a form of the maximum modulus principle.

Riemann stated the theorem in his thesis in 1851. His proof had a gap, because it used the Dirichlet principle without full justification. Osgood gave the first complete proof in 1900. Carathéodory and Koebe gave the function theory proofs around 1912 to 1914. The proof shows that the map exists, but it gives no formula. Even the map from a disk onto a square has no formula in simple functions. In practice it is computed with numerical methods.

The whole plane \mathbb{C} is simply connected, but it is excluded. A holomorphic map \mathbb{C} \to disk is a bounded entire function. By Liouville it is constant. So no such map can be onto.
