Practice

Which function is holomorphic on all of \mathbb{C}?

  • |z|^2
  • \overline{z}
  • z^3 e^z
  • \operatorname{Re} z

Products of entire functions are entire. The others fail Cauchy-Riemann. For \operatorname{Re} z: u_x = 1 but v_y = 0.

What is \oint_{|z| = 3} \frac{dz}{z - 1}?

  • 0
  • 2\pi i
  • 2\pi
  • 6\pi i

Cauchy's formula with f = 1 and w = 1, which is inside the circle.

What kind of singularity does \frac{1 - \cos z}{z^2} have at 0?

  • Removable
  • Simple pole
  • Pole of order 2
  • Essential

1 - \cos z = \frac{z^2}{2} - \frac{z^4}{24} + \dots. Divide by z^2: \frac{1}{2} - \frac{z^2}{24} + \dots. No negative powers.

An entire function satisfies |f(z)| \le 7 for all z. What can you say?

  • f is a polynomial of degree at most 7.
  • f is constant.
  • f has a root.
  • Nothing.

This is Liouville's theorem.

The residue of \frac{1}{z^2 + 4} at z = 2i is \frac{1}{4i}. So it equals -\frac{i}{k} with k = ?.

\oint_{|z|=1} \frac{\sin z}{z^2}\,dz = 2\pi i \cdot ?.

By Rouche, z^7 + 10z^3 + 1 has ? zeros in |z| \lt 1.

The Cayley map \frac{z - i}{z + i} sends z = i to ?.

  1. Use Cauchy-Riemann to show that f(z) = z^3 is holomorphic.
    Answer

    z^3 = (x^3 - 3xy^2) + i(3x^2y - y^3). u_x = 3x^2 - 3y^2 = v_y. u_y = -6xy and v_x = 6xy, so u_y = -v_x. The partials are continuous, so f is holomorphic everywhere.

  2. Compute \oint_{|z| = 1} \bar{z}\,dz. Why does Cauchy's theorem not give 0?
    Answer

    On the circle \bar{z} = e^{-it} and dz = ie^{it}dt. The integral is \int_0^{2\pi} i\,dt = 2\pi i. Cauchy's theorem does not apply, because \bar{z} is not holomorphic.

  3. Compute \oint_{|z| = 2} \frac{z^2}{(z - 1)^3}\,dz.
    Answer

    Cauchy's formula with n = 2, f = z^2, w = 1: \frac{2\pi i}{2!} f''(1) = \pi i \cdot 2 = 2\pi i.

  4. Find the residues of f(z) = \frac{z}{(z - 1)(z + 2)} and compute \oint_{|z| = 3} f\,dz and \oint_{|z| = 3/2} f\,dz.
    Answer

    At 1: \frac{1}{1 + 2} = \frac{1}{3}. At -2: \frac{-2}{-2 - 1} = \frac{2}{3}. On |z| = 3 both are inside: 2\pi i(\frac{1}{3} + \frac{2}{3}) = 2\pi i. On |z| = 3/2 only 1 is inside: \frac{2\pi i}{3}.

  5. Compute \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \frac{dx}{(x^2 + 1)(x^2 + 4)}.
    Answer

    Poles in the upper half-plane: i and 2i. Residue at i: \frac{1}{2i \cdot 3} = \frac{1}{6i}. Residue at 2i: \frac{1}{(-4 + 1) \cdot 4i} = -\frac{1}{12i}. Sum: \frac{1}{12i}. Answer: 2\pi i \cdot \frac{1}{12i} = \frac{\pi}{6}.

  6. Find \max |e^z| on the closed square 0 \le x \le 1, 0 \le y \le 1, and say where it is reached.
    Answer

    |e^z| = e^x. It is largest when x = 1: the maximum is e, reached on the right edge x = 1. This is on the boundary, as the maximum modulus principle says.

  7. Hard. Show that z^4 + 6z + 3 has exactly 3 roots in the ring 1 \lt |z| \lt 2.
    Answer

    On |z| = 2: |z^4| = 16 \gt 15 \ge |6z + 3|. So all 4 roots are in |z| \lt 2. On |z| = 1: |6z| = 6 \gt 4 \ge |z^4 + 3|. So exactly 1 root is in |z| \lt 1. No root has |z| = 1, because there |6z| \gt |z^4 + 3|. So 4 - 1 = 3 roots lie in the open ring.

  8. Hard. Let f be entire with |f(z)| \le 5|z|^2 for all z. Show that f is a polynomial of degree at most 2.
    Answer

    Cauchy's estimate on the circle |z| = r around 0: |f'''(0)| \le \frac{3! \cdot 5r^2}{r^3} = \frac{30}{r} \to 0. The same works at any point a: on |z - a| = r, |f| \le 5(|a| + r)^2, so |f'''(a)| \le \frac{30(|a| + r)^2}{r^3} \to 0. So f''' = 0 everywhere, and f is a polynomial of degree at most 2.

Key takeaways

  • A complex derivative must be the same from every direction. This gives the Cauchy-Riemann equations u_x = v_y, u_y = -v_x.
  • Holomorphic functions have zero integral around loops in regions with no holes (Cauchy). Their values inside a circle come from the values on it (integral formula).
  • One complex derivative gives all derivatives and a power series. Bounded entire functions are constant (Liouville). This proves the fundamental theorem of algebra.
  • Holomorphic functions are rigid. A small piece fixes the whole (identity theorem). |f| has its maximum on the edge (maximum modulus).
  • A loop integral is 2\pi i times the sum of the residues inside. This computes many real integrals and counts zeros (argument principle, Rouche).
  • Holomorphic maps with f' \ne 0 keep angles. Every simply connected region except \mathbb{C} maps onto the disk (Riemann mapping theorem), but usually with no formula.

Sources

  • A First Course in Complex Analysis (Beck, Marchesi, Pixton, Sabalka). An open textbook, version 1.6, CC BY 4.0, used for the order of topics and the proofs.
  • MIT OpenCourseWare 18.04 Complex Variables with Applications (Spring 2018). Course notes on Cauchy's theorems, residues, real integrals and conformal maps.
  • Rouche's theorem (Wikipedia). The statement, the dog-on-a-leash picture and the 1862 paper.
  • Riemann mapping theorem (Wikipedia). The statement, the 1851 thesis, the proofs by Osgood, Carathéodory and Koebe, and the normal families proof.

Groups

A group is the mathematics of symmetry. It is a set of moves that you can combine and undo. The same few rules describe the turns of a square, clock arithmetic, shuffles of cards and invertible matrices. This chapter builds the theory from the rules up to the counting tricks and the structure theorems.

  • Check the group axioms and work with the main examples: integers mod n, permutations, matrices and the symmetries of a square.
  • Find subgroups and cosets, and use Lagrange's theorem.
  • Use homomorphisms, quotient groups and the first isomorphism theorem.
  • Count objects up to symmetry with the orbit-stabiliser theorem and Burnside's lemma.
  • Use the Sylow theorems and list all finite abelian groups of a given order.

Symmetry is the starting idea

Put a square tile in a square hole. In how many ways can you pick it up and put it back so that it fits? You can turn it by 0, 90, 180 or 270 degrees. You can also flip it over a mirror line. A square has four mirror lines: one vertical, one horizontal and two diagonals. That makes 8 moves in total.

Watch what happens when you combine moves.

  • Two moves in a row give another of the 8 moves. A flip followed by a flip is a turn.
  • The "do nothing" move is one of them.
  • Every move can be undone by one of the moves. A 90° turn is undone by a 270° turn. A flip undoes itself.
  • The order matters. Turn then flip is not the same as flip then turn.

These four observations are the definition of a group. A symmetry of an object is a move that leaves it looking the same. The symmetries of any object always form a group. Group theory studies that structure on its own, without the object.

Agree on the order of writing. In this chapter gh means "first do h, then do g". This is the order of function composition g(h(x)). Some books use the other order. Both work, but you must not mix them in one calculation.

The group axioms

A group is a set G with an operation \ast that has these four properties.

  1. Closure. If a, b \in G, then a \ast b \in G.
  2. Associativity. (a \ast b) \ast c = a \ast (b \ast c).
  3. Identity. There is an e \in G with e \ast a = a \ast e = a for all a.
  4. Inverses. Each a has an a^{-1} \in G with a \ast a^{-1} = a^{-1} \ast a = e.

If also a \ast b = b \ast a for all a, b, the group is abelian.

Is it a group?
Set and operationGroup?Reason
\mathbb{Z} with +yes, abelianidentity 0, inverse of a is -a
\mathbb{N} = \{0, 1, 2, \dots\} with +no3 has no inverse in \mathbb{N}
\mathbb{Q} \setminus \{0\} with \timesyes, abelianidentity 1, inverse 1/a
\mathbb{Z} with -no(5 - 3) - 1 \ne 5 - (3 - 1): not associative
Invertible 2 \times 2 real matrices with \timesyes, not abelianidentity I, inverse A^{-1}
Strings with joining ("ab" + "cd")noidentity "" exists, but no inverses

1. The identity is unique. 2. Each element has exactly one inverse. 3. (ab)^{-1} = b^{-1}a^{-1}. 4. Cancellation: if ab = ac, then b = c.

Proof

1. If e and e' are identities, then e = ee' = e'. 2. If b and c are inverses of a, then b = b(ac) = (ba)c = c. 3. (ab)(b^{-1}a^{-1}) = a(bb^{-1})a^{-1} = aa^{-1} = e. 4. Multiply ab = ac on the left by a^{-1}.

Fact 3 is like socks and shoes. You put on socks, then shoes. To undo it, you take off the shoes first, then the socks.

The order of a group |G| is its number of elements. The order of an element g is the smallest n \ge 1 with g^n = e. In the square group, a 90° turn has order 4 and every flip has order 2.

Check all four axioms, and check them in G. The integers with \times look like a group: closed, associative, identity 1. But 2 has no inverse among the integers, since \frac{1}{2} \notin \mathbb{Z}.

Examples to know

Integers mod n

On a 12-hour clock, 9 + 5 = 2. This is \mathbb{Z}_{12} = \{0, 1, \dots, 11\} with addition mod 12. In general \mathbb{Z}_n with + mod n is an abelian group of order n. The element 8 in \mathbb{Z}_{12} has order 3, because 8 + 8 + 8 = 24 \equiv 0. In general the order of a in \mathbb{Z}_n is \frac{n}{\gcd(a, n)}.

The numbers coprime to n form a group U(n) under multiplication mod n. For example U(8) = \{1, 3, 5, 7\}. Here 3^2 = 9 \equiv 1, 5^2 = 25 \equiv 1 and 7^2 = 49 \equiv 1. This group is studied in Number theory.

Permutations

A permutation of \{1, \dots, n\} is a shuffle: a bijection of the set to itself. All of them form the symmetric group S_n, with composition. It has n! elements. We write permutations in cycle notation: (1\,2\,3) sends 1 \to 2 \to 3 \to 1.

  1. Let \sigma = (1\,2\,3) and \tau = (1\,2). Compute \sigma\tau: first \tau, then \sigma.
  2. 1 \xrightarrow{\tau} 2 \xrightarrow{\sigma} 3. 2 \xrightarrow{\tau} 1 \xrightarrow{\sigma} 2. 3 \xrightarrow{\tau} 3 \xrightarrow{\sigma} 1. So \sigma\tau = (1\,3).
  3. Now \tau\sigma: 1 \to 2 \to 1, 2 \to 3 \to 3, 3 \to 1 \to 2. So \tau\sigma = (2\,3).
  4. \sigma\tau \ne \tau\sigma. So S_3 is not abelian. It is the smallest group that is not abelian.

The order of a permutation is the least common multiple of its cycle lengths. For example (1\,2\,3)(4\,5) has order \operatorname{lcm}(3, 2) = 6. Every permutation is a product of swaps. The number of swaps is always even or always odd for a given permutation. The even permutations form the alternating group A_n, of order \frac{n!}{2}.

Matrices and the square again

  • GL_n(\mathbb{R}): invertible n \times n matrices. SL_n(\mathbb{R}): those with determinant 1.
  • SO(2): rotation matrices \begin{pmatrix} \cos\theta & -\sin\theta \\ \sin\theta & \cos\theta \end{pmatrix}. They form an infinite abelian group.
  • Finite examples also exist. GL_2(\mathbb{Z}_2), the invertible 2 \times 2 matrices with entries 0 and 1 mod 2, has 6 elements.

The square group is the dihedral group D_4. Let r be the 90° turn and s one flip. Then the 8 elements are e, r, r^2, r^3, s, rs, r^2s, r^3s. The rules are r^4 = e, s^2 = e and srs = r^{-1}. In general D_n, the symmetries of a regular n-gon, has 2n elements. A computer can build D_4 from r and s alone.

# Symmetries of a square as permutations of its corners 0, 1, 2, 3.
def compose(p, q):
    """p after q: first do q, then p."""
    return tuple(p[q[i]] for i in range(len(q)))

r = (1, 2, 3, 0)          # turn by 90 degrees: corner i goes to i + 1
s = (0, 3, 2, 1)          # mirror in the diagonal through corners 0 and 2
e = (0, 1, 2, 3)

group, frontier = {e}, [e]
while frontier:           # keep multiplying until nothing new appears
    g = frontier.pop()
    for h in (r, s):
        new = compose(h, g)
        if new not in group:
            group.add(new)
            frontier.append(new)

def order(g):
    n, x = 1, g
    while x != e:
        x, n = compose(g, x), n + 1
    return n

print("size:", len(group))
print("r s == s r ?", compose(r, s) == compose(s, r))
print("orders:", sorted(order(g) for g in group))
size: 8
r s == s r ? False
orders: [1, 2, 2, 2, 2, 2, 4, 4]

The orders match the picture: one identity, five elements of order 2 (four flips and the 180° turn), and two quarter turns of order 4.

A group is cyclic if one element g makes all elements as powers g^k. \mathbb{Z}_n is cyclic with g = 1. Every cyclic group is a copy of \mathbb{Z} or of some \mathbb{Z}_n.

Subgroups, cosets and Lagrange's theorem

Inside the square group, the four turns \{e, r, r^2, r^3\} form a group of their own. Inside \mathbb{Z}_{12}, the set \{0, 4, 8\} is closed under addition mod 12. Groups inside groups are everywhere.

A subgroup H \le G is a subset that is a group with the same operation. A subset H that is not empty is a subgroup if and only if a, b \in H gives ab^{-1} \in H. If H is finite, closure under the operation is enough.

The powers of one element form the subgroup \langle g \rangle = \{ g^k \}. Its size is the order of g. The subgroups of \mathbb{Z}_{12} are \langle 1 \rangle, \langle 2 \rangle, \langle 3 \rangle, \langle 4 \rangle, \langle 6 \rangle and \{0\}. Their sizes are 12, 6, 4, 3, 2 and 1. They are all divisors of 12. That is no accident.

Now shift a subgroup. Take H = \{0, 4, 8\} in \mathbb{Z}_{12}. Add 1 to each member: 1 + H = \{1, 5, 9\}. Also 2 + H = \{2, 6, 10\} and 3 + H = \{3, 7, 11\}. These four sets have the same size. They do not overlap. Together they fill \mathbb{Z}_{12}.

A left coset of H is a set gH = \{ gh : h \in H \}. Two cosets are equal or disjoint, because "a^{-1}b \in H" is an equivalence relation. So the cosets split G into equal blocks, as in equivalence classes form a partition. The number of cosets is the index [G : H].

If G is finite and H \le G, then |H| divides |G|. More exactly, |G| = [G : H] \cdot |H|.

Proof

The left cosets of H form a partition of G. Each coset has |H| elements: the map h \mapsto gh is a bijection from H to gH, by cancellation. So G is cut into [G : H] blocks of size |H|. Count the elements: |G| = [G : H] \cdot |H|.

Lagrange saw a form of this idea in 1771, while he studied how permutations act on polynomials. Gauss, Cauchy and Jordan proved more and more general cases. Three results follow at once.

  • The order of every element divides |G|. (Apply Lagrange to \langle g \rangle.)
  • So g^{|G|} = e for every g.
  • A group of prime order p is cyclic. Any g \ne e has order dividing p, so order p.

Apply the second result to U(n), which has \varphi(n) elements. You get a^{\varphi(n)} \equiv 1 \pmod n. That is Euler's theorem, and Fermat's little theorem is the case of a prime n.

The converse of Lagrange is false. A divisor of |G| need not be the size of a subgroup. The group A_4 has 12 elements but no subgroup with 6 elements. The program in the last section checks this.

Homomorphisms and isomorphisms

The exponential function turns sums into products: e^{a + b} = e^a e^b. The determinant turns matrix products into number products: \det(AB) = \det A \det B. Both maps respect the group operation. Such maps let us compare groups.

A homomorphism is a map \varphi : G \to H with \varphi(ab) = \varphi(a)\varphi(b). Its kernel is \ker\varphi = \{ g : \varphi(g) = e_H \}. Its image is \varphi(G). A homomorphism that is one-to-one and onto is an isomorphism. We then write G \cong H: the two groups have the same structure.

  • \exp : (\mathbb{R}, +) \to (\mathbb{R}_{\gt 0}, \times) is an isomorphism. Its inverse is \ln. A slide rule uses this.
  • \det : GL_n(\mathbb{R}) \to (\mathbb{R} \setminus \{0\}, \times) is onto. Its kernel is SL_n(\mathbb{R}).
  • The sign map S_n \to \{1, -1\} sends even permutations to 1. Its kernel is A_n.
  • \mathbb{Z} \to \mathbb{Z}_n, a \mapsto a \bmod n. Its kernel is n\mathbb{Z}, the multiples of n.

Every homomorphism sends e to e and inverses to inverses. Its kernel is a subgroup. It is one-to-one exactly when the kernel is \{e\}: if \varphi(a) = \varphi(b), then \varphi(a^{-1}b) = e.

Same size does not mean same structure. Compare \mathbb{Z}_4 with U(8). Both have 4 elements. Look at their tables.

+0123
00123
11230
22301
33012

The element 1 has order 4. The group is cyclic.

×1357
11357
33175
55713
77531

The diagonal is all 1. Every element is its own inverse. No element has order 4.

An isomorphism keeps the order of each element. \mathbb{Z}_4 has an element of order 4 and U(8) has none. So \mathbb{Z}_4 \not\cong U(8). In fact U(8) \cong \mathbb{Z}_2 \times \mathbb{Z}_2, the Klein four-group. Notice also that each row of a group table holds every element exactly once. That is cancellation at work.

Every group G is isomorphic to a group of permutations. If |G| = n, then G is isomorphic to a subgroup of S_n.

Proof

For each g \in G, define \lambda_g(x) = gx. It is a bijection of the set G, with inverse \lambda_{g^{-1}}. So it is a permutation of G. Also \lambda_g \circ \lambda_h (x) = g(hx) = (gh)x = \lambda_{gh}(x). So g \mapsto \lambda_g is a homomorphism. If \lambda_g is the identity, then g = ge = e. So the kernel is trivial and the map is one-to-one.

In simple words: every group is a group of shuffles. Each row of the group table is a shuffle of the elements. Cayley described groups this way in a paper of 1854.

Normal subgroups and quotient groups

In \mathbb{Z}_{12} with H = \{0, 4, 8\}, we can add cosets. (1 + H) + (2 + H) = 3 + H. It does not matter which members we pick: 5 + 6 = 11 \in 3 + H too. The four cosets behave like \mathbb{Z}_4. We have built a new group whose elements are cosets.

In a group that is not abelian, this can fail. In S_3 take H = \{e, (1\,2)\}. Then

(1\,3)H = \{(1\,3),\ (1\,2\,3)\}, \qquad H(1\,3) = \{(1\,3),\ (1\,3\,2)\}.

Left and right cosets differ. Then "multiply cosets by their members" gives answers that depend on the member chosen.

A subgroup N is normal, written N \triangleleft G, if gNg^{-1} = N for every g \in G. The same: gN = Ng for every g. Then the cosets form the quotient group G/N with (aN)(bN) = (ab)N. It has |G|/|N| elements.

Where do normal subgroups come from?

  • In an abelian group every subgroup is normal.
  • Every kernel is normal: if \varphi(n) = e, then \varphi(gng^{-1}) = \varphi(g)\varphi(g)^{-1} = e.
  • Every subgroup of index 2 is normal. The two left cosets and the two right cosets are both "H and the rest".

Let \varphi : G \to H be a homomorphism. Then \ker\varphi is normal in G, and

G / \ker\varphi \;\cong\; \varphi(G).

The isomorphism sends the coset g \ker\varphi to \varphi(g).

Proof

Let K = \ker\varphi and define \Phi(gK) = \varphi(g). It is well defined: if gK = g'K, then g' = gk with k \in K, so \varphi(g') = \varphi(g)\varphi(k) = \varphi(g). It is a homomorphism: \Phi(gK \cdot g'K) = \varphi(gg') = \varphi(g)\varphi(g'). It is onto \varphi(G) by definition. It is one-to-one: if \varphi(g) = e, then g \in K, so gK = K, the identity of G/K.

In simple words: a homomorphism forgets exactly its kernel. What is left is a copy of the image. Some examples:

  • \mathbb{Z} / n\mathbb{Z} \cong \mathbb{Z}_n. Clock arithmetic is a quotient of the integers.
  • GL_n(\mathbb{R}) / SL_n(\mathbb{R}) \cong \mathbb{R} \setminus \{0\}, from the determinant.
  • S_n / A_n \cong \{1, -1\}, from the sign.
  • \mathbb{R} / \mathbb{Z} \cong the circle \{ z : |z| = 1 \}, from x \mapsto e^{2\pi i x}. Only the part after the decimal point matters, like an angle.

Do not form G/H when H is not normal. The set of cosets still exists, and Lagrange still counts it. But it is not a group in a natural way. Always check gHg^{-1} = H first.

Group actions and counting with symmetry

The square group moves the corners of the square. It also moves colourings of the corners. A group that moves the points of a set is said to act on it. This is how groups are used in practice.

An action of G on a set X gives a point g \cdot x \in X for each g \in G and x \in X, with e \cdot x = x and (gh) \cdot x = g \cdot (h \cdot x). The orbit of x is G \cdot x = \{ g \cdot x : g \in G \}. The stabiliser of x is G_x = \{ g : g \cdot x = x \}. It is a subgroup.

If a finite group G acts on X, then for every x \in X:

|G \cdot x| \cdot |G_x| = |G|.
Proof

Send the coset gG_x to the point g \cdot x. This is well defined and one-to-one: g \cdot x = h \cdot x holds exactly when h^{-1}g \in G_x, that is, when gG_x = hG_x. It is onto the orbit. So the orbit has as many points as there are cosets: |G \cdot x| = [G : G_x] = |G| / |G_x| by Lagrange.

Example: how many rotations does a cube have? A rotation can move a chosen face to any of the 6 faces. So the orbit has 6 points. The rotations that keep that face in place are the 4 turns about its axis. So the cube has 6 \times 4 = 24 rotations. Check with a corner: 8 \times 3 = 24. Check with an edge: 12 \times 2 = 24.

Burnside's lemma

A necklace has 4 beads in a circle. Each bead is red, green or blue. There are 3^4 = 81 colourings of the 4 places. But turning the necklace does not make a new necklace. How many really different necklaces are there? The answer is the number of orbits.

Let a finite group G act on a finite set X. Let \operatorname{Fix}(g) = \{ x : g \cdot x = x \}. Then

\text{number of orbits} = \frac{1}{|G|} \sum_{g \in G} |\operatorname{Fix}(g)|.

In words: the number of orbits is the average number of fixed points.

Proof (count in two ways)

Count the pairs (g, x) with g \cdot x = x. Counted by g, there are \sum_g |\operatorname{Fix}(g)|. Counted by x, there are \sum_x |G_x| = \sum_x \frac{|G|}{|G \cdot x|}. Group the points by orbit. An orbit with k points gives k \cdot \frac{|G|}{k} = |G|. So the sum is |G| times the number of orbits.

Name the group

For a necklace that may only turn: the 4 turns e, r, r^2, r^3.

Find the cycles of each move

A colouring is fixed when each cycle of places has one colour. e has 4 cycles. r and r^3 have 1 cycle. r^2 has 2 cycles: the two opposite pairs.

Count fixed colourings

With 3 colours, a move with c cycles fixes 3^c colourings. So: 81, 3, 9, 3.

Take the average

\frac{81 + 3 + 9 + 3}{4} = \frac{96}{4} = 24 different necklaces.

Allow flips too

Add 4 mirrors. Two go through opposite beads: 3^3 = 27 each. Two go between beads: 3^2 = 9 each. \frac{96 + 27 + 27 + 9 + 9}{8} = 21.

from itertools import product

n, k = 4, 3                                    # 4 beads, 3 colours
rot = [tuple((i + t) % n for i in range(n)) for t in range(n)]
mir = [tuple((t - i) % n for i in range(n)) for t in range(n)]

def act(m, c):                                 # move the beads of c by m
    return tuple(c[m[i]] for i in range(n))

def count(moves):
    colourings = list(product(range(k), repeat=n))
    orbits = {frozenset(act(m, c) for m in moves) for c in colourings}
    fixed = sum(act(m, c) == c for m in moves for c in colourings)
    return len(orbits), fixed, fixed / len(moves)

for name, moves in (("rotations", rot), ("rotations + mirrors", rot + mir)):
    orbits, fixed, average = count(moves)
    print(f"{name:20s} orbits={orbits}  fixed total={fixed}  average={average}")
rotations            orbits=24  fixed total=96  average=24.0
rotations + mirrors  orbits=21  fixed total=168  average=21.0

The brute-force count of orbits and the Burnside average agree. For a cube whose faces are painted in 2 colours, the 24 rotations give \frac{1}{24}(2^6 + 3 \cdot 2^4 + 12 \cdot 2^3 + 8 \cdot 2^2) = \frac{240}{24} = 10 different cubes. Burnside published the lemma in his 1897 book, and he credited Frobenius. Cauchy knew it in 1845. Chemists use the same counting, extended by Polya, to count molecules.

Do not divide the number of colourings by |G|. 81 / 4 is not even a whole number. Colourings with symmetry, like "all red", have small orbits. Burnside's average corrects for them.

Sylow theorems and finite abelian groups

Lagrange says what sizes subgroups may have. Sylow says which sizes they must have. First a smaller result: if a prime p divides |G|, then G has an element of order p. This is Cauchy's theorem.

Let |G| = p^k m, where p is prime and p does not divide m. A subgroup of order p^k is a Sylow p-subgroup.

  1. Existence. G has a Sylow p-subgroup.
  2. Conjugacy. Any two Sylow p-subgroups P, Q are conjugate: Q = gPg^{-1} for some g.
  3. Counting. The number n_p of Sylow p-subgroups divides m, and n_p \equiv 1 \pmod p.
Proof idea

1. Let G act by left multiplication on all subsets of size p^k. Their number is \binom{p^k m}{p^k}, and a counting argument shows p does not divide it. So some orbit has a size not divisible by p. Its stabiliser H then has order divisible by p^k, by orbit-stabiliser. Also H moves one subset S of size p^k to itself without collisions, so |H| \le p^k. Hence |H| = p^k.

3. Let a Sylow subgroup P act by conjugation on the set of all Sylow p-subgroups. Every orbit has a size that is a power of p. Only P itself is fixed. So n_p \equiv 1 \pmod p. 2 uses a similar action. Then all Sylow subgroups form one orbit under G, and orbit-stabiliser shows that n_p divides m.

Ludwig Sylow published these theorems in 1872. They make short work of many questions.

  1. 15 = 3 \cdot 5. n_3 divides 5 and n_3 \equiv 1 \pmod 3. So n_3 = 1.
  2. n_5 divides 3 and n_5 \equiv 1 \pmod 5. So n_5 = 1.
  3. So there is one subgroup P of order 3 and one subgroup Q of order 5. Being the only ones, both are normal. They meet only in e.
  4. Then G \cong P \times Q \cong \mathbb{Z}_3 \times \mathbb{Z}_5 \cong \mathbb{Z}_{15}. Every group of order 15 is cyclic.

In S_4, of order 24 = 2^3 \cdot 3, the theorems allow n_3 \in \{1, 4\} and n_2 \in \{1, 3\}. A computer search over all subgroups gives the true numbers.

from itertools import permutations

G = list(permutations(range(4)))               # the 24 elements of S4
def mul(p, q):                                 # p after q
    return tuple(p[q[i]] for i in range(4))

def generated(gens):
    """The smallest subgroup that contains gens."""
    H = {tuple(range(4))}
    while True:
        new = {mul(a, b) for a in H | set(gens) for b in H | set(gens)} | H
        if new == H:
            return frozenset(H)
        H = new

subgroups = {generated([a, b]) for a in G for b in G}   # every subgroup of S4 needs at most 2 generators
for size in (3, 8):
    print(f"subgroups of order {size}:", sum(len(H) == size for H in subgroups))
print("number of subgroups:", len(subgroups))
A4 = {g for g in G if sum(g[i] > g[j] for i in range(4) for j in range(i + 1, 4)) % 2 == 0}
print("orders of subgroups inside A4:", sorted({len(H) for H in subgroups if H <= A4}))
subgroups of order 3: 4
subgroups of order 8: 3
number of subgroups: 30
orders of subgroups inside A4: [1, 2, 3, 4, 12]

So n_3 = 4 and n_2 = 3, as Sylow allows. The last line shows that A_4 has no subgroup of order 6, as promised.

All finite abelian groups

The direct product G \times H is the set of pairs (g, h) with (g, h)(g', h') = (gg', hh'). For example \mathbb{Z}_2 \times \mathbb{Z}_3 has the element (1, 1) of order 6. So \mathbb{Z}_2 \times \mathbb{Z}_3 \cong \mathbb{Z}_6. But \mathbb{Z}_2 \times \mathbb{Z}_2 \not\cong \mathbb{Z}_4. The rule is the Chinese remainder theorem: \mathbb{Z}_m \times \mathbb{Z}_n \cong \mathbb{Z}_{mn} exactly when \gcd(m, n) = 1.

Every finite abelian group is isomorphic to a product of cyclic groups of prime power order,

\mathbb{Z}_{p_1^{a_1}} \times \mathbb{Z}_{p_2^{a_2}} \times \dots \times \mathbb{Z}_{p_r^{a_r}},

where the primes may repeat. The factors are unique up to their order. Equivalently, it is \mathbb{Z}_{d_1} \times \dots \times \mathbb{Z}_{d_s} with d_1 \mid d_2 \mid \dots \mid d_s, and these invariant factors are unique.

Proof idea

Step 1: split by primes. In an abelian group each Sylow p-subgroup is normal, so it is unique. G is the product of its Sylow subgroups, one for each prime. Step 2: in an abelian group of order p^k, take an element g of largest order. One shows that \langle g \rangle has a complement K with G = \langle g \rangle \times K. Repeat with K. Uniqueness comes from counting the elements of each order.

  1. Factor: 72 = 2^3 \cdot 3^2.
  2. The 2-part has order 8: \mathbb{Z}_8, \mathbb{Z}_4 \times \mathbb{Z}_2 or \mathbb{Z}_2 \times \mathbb{Z}_2 \times \mathbb{Z}_2. These match the ways to write 3 as a sum: 3, 2 + 1, 1 + 1 + 1.
  3. The 3-part has order 9: \mathbb{Z}_9 or \mathbb{Z}_3 \times \mathbb{Z}_3. These match 2 and 1 + 1.
  4. Combine: 3 \times 2 = 6 abelian groups of order 72, up to isomorphism.
  5. For example \mathbb{Z}_4 \times \mathbb{Z}_2 \times \mathbb{Z}_9 \cong \mathbb{Z}_2 \times \mathbb{Z}_{36} in invariant factor form, since 2 \mid 36.

Kronecker proved the result in 1870 without the language of groups. Frobenius and Stickelberger stated and proved it for groups in 1878. For groups that are not abelian, no such simple list exists. The building blocks there are the simple groups. Their classification is one of the longest proofs in mathematics. The chapter Rings, fields and Galois theory uses groups to explain why the quintic has no formula.

Patterns to remember

Patterns for group theory
PatternPurposeModelNote
Closure, associativity, identity, inversesCheck that a set is a groupU(8) = \{1, 3, 5, 7\} under \times \bmod 8Inverses must lie in the set itself.
(ab)^{-1} = b^{-1}a^{-1}Invert a productUndo "rotate, then flip" as "flip back, then rotate back"The order reverses.
Order of a in \mathbb{Z}_n is n / \gcd(a, n)Element orders in cyclic groups8 in \mathbb{Z}_{12}: 12/4 = 3The order of 0 is 1.
Order of a permutation = lcm of cycle lengthsElement orders in S_n(1\,2\,3)(4\,5) has order 6Write disjoint cycles first.
|G| = [G : H] \cdot |H|Rule out subgroup sizesNo subgroup of order 5 in a group of order 12The converse is false: A_4.
\varphi(ab) = \varphi(a)\varphi(b)Compare two groups\det(AB) = \det A \det BOne-to-one exactly when the kernel is \{e\}.
Compare element ordersProve two groups are not isomorphic\mathbb{Z}_4 has order 4, U(8) does notSame size proves nothing.
G / \ker\varphi \cong \varphi(G)Identify a quotient group\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z} \cong circleFind an onto map with the right kernel.
|G \cdot x| \cdot |G_x| = |G|Count a group or an orbitCube: 6 \times 4 = 24 rotationsThe stabiliser is a subgroup.
Orbits = average of |\operatorname{Fix}(g)|Count objects up to symmetry4 beads, 3 colours, turns: 24Never just divide by |G|.
n_p \mid m, n_p \equiv 1 \pmod pFind normal Sylow subgroupsOrder 15: n_3 = n_5 = 1n_p = 1 means the Sylow subgroup is normal.
Partitions of each exponentList abelian groups of order n72 = 2^3 3^2: 3 \times 2 = 6 groups\mathbb{Z}_m \times \mathbb{Z}_n \cong \mathbb{Z}_{mn} only if coprime.

Practice

Which of these is a group?

  • \mathbb{Z} with multiplication
  • \{0, 1, 2, 3\} with multiplication mod 4
  • \{1, 2, 3, 4\} with multiplication mod 5
  • \mathbb{N} with addition

U(5) = \{1, 2, 3, 4\} is closed and every element has an inverse mod 5. In \{0, 1, 2, 3\} mod 4, the elements 0 and 2 have no inverse.

A group has 35 elements. Which number cannot be the order of an element?

  • 1
  • 5
  • 7
  • 3

By Lagrange, element orders divide 35. The divisors are 1, 5, 7 and 35.

Which group is isomorphic to \mathbb{Z}_6?

  • S_3
  • \mathbb{Z}_2 \times \mathbb{Z}_3
  • \mathbb{Z}_2 \times \mathbb{Z}_2 \times \mathbb{Z}_2
  • D_3

\gcd(2, 3) = 1, so (1, 1) has order 6. S_3 and D_3 are not abelian. The third has 8 elements.

Which subgroup is always normal?

  • Any subgroup with 2 elements
  • The kernel of a homomorphism
  • The stabiliser of a point
  • Any cyclic subgroup

Kernels are normal. In S_3, \{e, (1\,2)\} has 2 elements, is cyclic and is a stabiliser, but it is not normal.

The order of (1\,2\,3\,4)(5\,6) in S_6 is ?.

The order of 9 in \mathbb{Z}_{12} is ?.

The rotation group of a regular tetrahedron has 4 faces in one orbit and 3 rotations fixing a face. So it has ? rotations.

The number of abelian groups of order 8, up to isomorphism, is ?.

  1. Show that \{1, -1, i, -i\} is a group under multiplication. Is it isomorphic to \mathbb{Z}_4 or to \mathbb{Z}_2 \times \mathbb{Z}_2?
    Answer

    Products stay in the set, for example i \cdot i = -1 and i \cdot (-i) = 1. Multiplication of complex numbers is associative. 1 is the identity. Inverses: 1 \leftrightarrow 1, -1 \leftrightarrow -1, i \leftrightarrow -i. The element i has order 4, so the group is cyclic: \cong \mathbb{Z}_4 by i^k \mapsto k.

  2. List the left cosets of H = \langle 3 \rangle in \mathbb{Z}_{12}. What is [\mathbb{Z}_{12} : H]?
    Answer

    H = \{0, 3, 6, 9\}. Cosets: H, 1 + H = \{1, 4, 7, 10\}, 2 + H = \{2, 5, 8, 11\}. The index is 3, and 3 \cdot 4 = 12.

  3. How many homomorphisms are there from \mathbb{Z}_6 to \mathbb{Z}_9?
    Answer

    A homomorphism is fixed by a = \varphi(1). We need 6a \equiv 0 \pmod 9, because 6 \cdot 1 = 0 in \mathbb{Z}_6. So a \in \{0, 3, 6\}. There are 3, which is \gcd(6, 9).

  4. Use the first isomorphism theorem to show \mathbb{C}^{\times} / \{ z : |z| = 1 \} \cong \mathbb{R}_{\gt 0}, where \mathbb{C}^{\times} is the nonzero complex numbers under multiplication.
    Answer

    Take \varphi(z) = |z|. It is a homomorphism because |zw| = |z||w|. It is onto \mathbb{R}_{\gt 0}, since \varphi(r) = r. Its kernel is \{ z : |z| = 1 \}, the unit circle. The theorem gives the isomorphism.

  5. How many different ways are there to colour the 4 corners of a square with 2 colours, if all 8 symmetries count as the same?
    Answer

    Fixed colourings: e: 16. Turns r, r^3: 2 each. r^2: 4. Two diagonal flips (through corners): 2^3 = 8 each. Two edge flips: 2^2 = 4 each. Sum: 16 + 2 + 2 + 4 + 8 + 8 + 4 + 4 = 48. Orbits: 48 / 8 = 6.

  6. Show that no group of order 20 is simple (has a normal subgroup other than \{e\} and G).
    Answer

    20 = 2^2 \cdot 5. n_5 divides 4 and n_5 \equiv 1 \pmod 5. The divisors of 4 are 1, 2, 4, and only 1 fits. So there is one Sylow 5-subgroup. All Sylow 5-subgroups are conjugate, so this one equals all its conjugates. It is normal, with 5 elements.

  7. Hard. List all abelian groups of order 360 in both forms.
    Answer

    360 = 2^3 \cdot 3^2 \cdot 5. 2-part: 3 choices, 3-part: 2 choices, 5-part: 1. So 6 groups. Invariant factor forms: \mathbb{Z}_{360}; \mathbb{Z}_3 \times \mathbb{Z}_{120}; \mathbb{Z}_2 \times \mathbb{Z}_{180}; \mathbb{Z}_6 \times \mathbb{Z}_{60}; \mathbb{Z}_2 \times \mathbb{Z}_2 \times \mathbb{Z}_{90}; \mathbb{Z}_2 \times \mathbb{Z}_6 \times \mathbb{Z}_{30}. For example the last one is \mathbb{Z}_2^3 \times \mathbb{Z}_3^2 \times \mathbb{Z}_5 in prime power form.

  8. Hard. Let G be a group in which g^2 = e for every g. Prove that G is abelian.
    Answer

    Every element is its own inverse. For any a, b: ab = (ab)^{-1} = b^{-1}a^{-1} = ba. So G is abelian. U(8) is an example.

Key takeaways

  • A group is a set of moves that can be combined and undone: closure, associativity, identity, inverses. Symmetries of any object form a group.
  • The main examples are \mathbb{Z}_n, U(n), S_n, matrix groups and the dihedral groups D_n.
  • Cosets cut a group into equal blocks. So subgroup sizes divide the group size (Lagrange). Euler's and Fermat's theorems follow.
  • Homomorphisms compare groups. Their kernels are normal, and G / \ker\varphi \cong \varphi(G). Every group is a group of permutations (Cayley).
  • Group actions count. Orbit size times stabiliser size is the group size. The number of orbits is the average number of fixed points (Burnside).
  • Sylow theorems force subgroups of prime power order and often prove that they are normal. Finite abelian groups are products of cyclic groups of prime power order.

Sources

  • Abstract Algebra: Theory and Applications (Thomas W. Judson). An open textbook under the GFDL, 2025 edition, used for the order of topics, examples and proofs.
  • Lagrange's theorem (Wikipedia). The statement, the history from Lagrange in 1771 to Jordan, and the A_4 counterexample.
  • Cayley's theorem (Wikipedia). The proof with left multiplication and the 1854 paper.
  • Burnside's lemma (Wikipedia). The statement, the counting proof and the history with Cauchy, Frobenius and Burnside.
  • Sylow theorems (Wikipedia). The three theorems, Sylow's 1872 paper and the groups of order 15.
  • Finitely generated abelian group (Wikipedia). The classification in both forms and its history with Kronecker, Frobenius and Stickelberger.

Rings, fields and Galois theory

Integers, polynomials and clock numbers share the same two operations: add and multiply. Algebra studies these systems as rings and fields. The story ends with two famous answers. There is no formula for the general fifth-degree equation. And you cannot trisect every angle with ruler and compass.

  • Decide if a ring is a domain, a PID, a UFD or a field, with an example of each.
  • Build quotient rings and new fields such as \mathbb{F}_p[x]/(f).
  • Prove that a polynomial is irreducible with Gauss's lemma and Eisenstein's criterion.
  • Compute degrees of field extensions with the tower law, and multiply in the AES field.
  • Explain the Galois correspondence and why the quintic has no formula.

Rings: where you can add and multiply

Look at a 12-hour clock. Nine hours after 8 o'clock it is 5 o'clock. So 8 + 9 = 5 on the clock. Also 3 \cdot 4 = 12 = 0 on the clock. Two numbers that are not zero give zero. This never happens with normal integers.

The clock numbers are written \mathbb{Z}/12. They are a ring. A ring is a set R with two operations, + and \cdot, with these rules.

  • Addition is associative and commutative. There is a zero, and every a has a negative -a.
  • Multiplication is associative. There is a one, written 1.
  • The distributive law holds: a(b + c) = ab + ac and (a + b)c = ac + bc.

In this chapter rings are commutative: ab = ba. Matrices form a ring that is not commutative. We only meet them as examples.

Four kinds of elements and rings
WordMeaningExample
unithas an inverse: ab = 1 for some b5 in \mathbb{Z}/12, since 5 \cdot 5 = 25 = 1
zero divisora \ne 0 but ab = 0 for some b \ne 03 and 4 in \mathbb{Z}/12
integral domaina ring with no zero divisors\mathbb{Z}, \mathbb{Q}[x]
fieldevery nonzero element is a unit\mathbb{Q}, \mathbb{R}, \mathbb{C}, \mathbb{Z}/7

A unit can be divided by. A zero divisor breaks cancellation. An integral domain (or just "domain") has none. A field lets you divide by anything except 0. Every field is a domain. The converse fails: \mathbb{Z} is a domain, but 2 has no inverse in \mathbb{Z}.

  1. In \mathbb{Z}/n, the element a is a unit exactly when \gcd(a, n) = 1. Bezout gives ax + ny = 1, so ax = 1 on the clock.
  2. If n = p is prime, every a = 1, \dots, p - 1 has \gcd(a, p) = 1. So \mathbb{Z}/p is a field.
  3. If n = ab with 1 \lt a, b \lt n, then a \cdot b = 0. So \mathbb{Z}/n has zero divisors.
  4. Result: \mathbb{Z}/n is a field exactly when n is prime. We write \mathbb{F}_p for it.

"ab = 0, so a = 0 or b = 0" is true only in a domain. In \mathbb{Z}/12, the equation x^2 = 0 has the solutions 0 and 6. The equation x^2 = 1 has four solutions: 1, 5, 7, 11. A polynomial can have more roots than its degree when the ring is not a domain.

Ideals and quotient rings

The even numbers 2\mathbb{Z} are closed under addition. They also "eat" multiplication: even times any integer is even. A set with these two features is an ideal.

Formally, I \subseteq R is an ideal if 0 \in I, a - b \in I for a, b \in I, and ra \in I for every r \in R and a \in I. The ideal made by one element a is (a) = \{ ra : r \in R \}. It is a principal ideal. For example (6) = 6\mathbb{Z}.

Ideals are exactly what we can "set to zero". The quotient ring R/I has the classes a + I as elements. Two elements are equal in R/I when their difference is in I. So \mathbb{Z}/12 is \mathbb{Z} with 12 set to zero.

A map \varphi : R \to S with \varphi(a + b) = \varphi(a) + \varphi(b), \varphi(ab) = \varphi(a)\varphi(b) and \varphi(1) = 1 is a ring homomorphism. Its kernel is always an ideal. The first isomorphism theorem for rings says R/\ker\varphi \cong \varphi(R). It is the ring copy of the theorem for groups.

  1. Start with \mathbb{R}[x], the polynomials with real coefficients.
  2. Set x^2 + 1 to zero. In \mathbb{R}[x]/(x^2 + 1), we get x^2 = -1.
  3. Every class has one form a + bx: divide by x^2 + 1 and keep the remainder.
  4. Multiply: (a + bx)(c + dx) = ac + (ad + bc)x + bd\,x^2 = (ac - bd) + (ad + bc)x.
  5. This is the rule for (a + bi)(c + di). So \mathbb{R}[x]/(x^2 + 1) \cong \mathbb{C}.

An ideal M \ne R is maximal if no ideal sits strictly between M and R. An ideal P \ne R is prime if ab \in P forces a \in P or b \in P.

Let R be a commutative ring and I \ne R an ideal. Then R/I is a field exactly when I is maximal. And R/I is a domain exactly when I is prime.

Proof

Let I be maximal and a \notin I. The ideal I + (a) is bigger than I, so it is all of R. Then 1 = m + ra with m \in I. In R/I this says ra = 1. So a has an inverse. Conversely, if R/I is a field and J \supsetneq I, take a \in J \setminus I. Its class has an inverse r, so 1 - ra \in I \subseteq J. Then 1 \in J, and J = R.

For prime: (a + I)(b + I) = 0 means ab \in I. "No zero divisors" in R/I is then exactly the prime condition.

In words: to build a field, divide a ring by a maximal ideal. Example: (5) is maximal in \mathbb{Z}, so \mathbb{Z}/5 is a field. The ideal (6) is not even prime, because 2 \cdot 3 \in (6).

The post-quantum standard ML-KEM (NIST FIPS 203, August 2024) computes in the quotient ring \mathbb{Z}_{3329}[X]/(X^{256} + 1). Here 3329 = 13 \cdot 256 + 1 is prime. In that field, 17^{128} = -1, so 17 is a root of unity of order 256. This lets software multiply polynomials fast with a number theoretic transform. We checked both numbers with Python.

Polynomial rings, PIDs and UFDs

In \mathbb{Z} every number above 1 splits into primes in one way: 60 = 2^2 \cdot 3 \cdot 5. Which rings have this property? Look at the ring \mathbb{Z}[\sqrt{-5}] = \{ a + b\sqrt{-5} : a, b \in \mathbb{Z} \}.

6 = 2 \cdot 3 = (1 + \sqrt{-5})(1 - \sqrt{-5}).

Use the size N(a + b\sqrt{-5}) = a^2 + 5b^2. It is multiplicative. N(2) = 4, N(3) = 9 and N(1 \pm \sqrt{-5}) = 6. No element has size 2 or 3, because a^2 + 5b^2 = 2 or 3 has no integer solution. So none of the four factors splits further. The number 6 has two truly different factorizations.

Two words make this precise. An element p (not 0, not a unit) is irreducible if p = ab forces a or b to be a unit. It is a prime element if p \mid ab forces p \mid a or p \mid b. In \mathbb{Z}[\sqrt{-5}], 2 is irreducible but not prime: 2 divides (1 + \sqrt{-5})(1 - \sqrt{-5}) but neither factor.

  • A UFD (unique factorization domain) is a domain where every nonzero non-unit is a product of irreducibles. The factors are unique up to order and units.
  • A PID (principal ideal domain) is a domain where every ideal is (a) for one a.
  • A Euclidean domain has a size function and division with remainder: a = qb + r with r = 0 or r smaller than b.

\mathbb{Z} is Euclidean with size |a|. For a field F, the ring F[x] is Euclidean with size \deg. The Gaussian integers \mathbb{Z}[i] are Euclidean with size a^2 + b^2.

If a domain has a division with remainder, then every ideal is principal. In particular \mathbb{Z} and F[x] are PIDs.

Proof

Let I \ne 0 be an ideal. Choose b \in I, not 0, of smallest size. Take any a \in I. Divide: a = qb + r. Then r = a - qb \in I. If r \ne 0, it is smaller than b, which is impossible. So r = 0 and a = qb. Thus I = (b).

In a principal ideal domain, every nonzero element that is not a unit is a product of irreducible elements. This product is unique up to the order of the factors and up to units.

Proof idea

Existence. If some a had no factorization, we could split it again and again: a = a_1 b_1, a_1 = a_2 b_2, and so on. This gives a strictly growing chain of ideals (a) \subsetneq (a_1) \subsetneq (a_2) \subsetneq \dots. The union of the chain is an ideal, so it equals (c) for some c. Then c lies in some (a_k), and the chain stops there. Contradiction.

Uniqueness. Let p be irreducible. Then (p) is maximal: if (p) \subseteq (d), then d \mid p, so d is a unit or a unit times p. By the theorem on maximal ideals, R/(p) is a field, hence a domain, so (p) is prime. So irreducible means prime, as in Euclid's lemma. Now cancel prime factors one by one from two factorizations, as in the proof for \mathbb{Z}.

The arrows go one way only. \mathbb{Z}[x] is a UFD but not a PID. The ideal (2, x) of polynomials with even constant term needs two generators. And \mathbb{Z}[\sqrt{-5}] is a domain but not a UFD.

"Irreducible" and "prime" are the same only in a UFD. In \mathbb{Z}[\sqrt{-5}], the number 3 is irreducible but not prime. Always say which ring you work in. The polynomial x^2 + 1 is irreducible in \mathbb{R}[x] but factors as (x + i)(x - i) in \mathbb{C}[x].

Is this polynomial irreducible?

Fields come from irreducible polynomials. So we need tests. Degree 2 and 3 are easy: a polynomial of degree 2 or 3 over a field is irreducible exactly when it has no root there. For \mathbb{Q}, the rational root theorem lists the possible roots. Higher degrees need more tools.

A polynomial in \mathbb{Z}[x] is primitive if the gcd of its coefficients is 1. For example 2x^2 + 3x + 4 is primitive, but 2x^2 + 4 is not.

The product of two primitive polynomials is primitive. As a result: if f \in \mathbb{Z}[x] factors into two polynomials of lower degree in \mathbb{Q}[x], then it also factors into polynomials of the same degrees in \mathbb{Z}[x].

Proof

Let g, h be primitive. Suppose a prime p divides every coefficient of gh. Reduce all coefficients mod p. We get \bar g \bar h = 0 in \mathbb{F}_p[x]. But \mathbb{F}_p[x] is a domain, so \bar g = 0 or \bar h = 0. Then p divides all coefficients of g or of h. That contradicts "primitive".

For the second part, write f = gh with rational coefficients. Pull out fractions: g = a\,g_0 and h = b\,h_0 with g_0, h_0 primitive in \mathbb{Z}[x] and a, b \in \mathbb{Q}. Then f = (ab)\,g_0 h_0. The product g_0 h_0 is primitive, so ab must be an integer. Now f = (ab\, g_0)\, h_0 is a factorization in \mathbb{Z}[x].

The same proof shows more: if R is a UFD, then R[x] is a UFD. So \mathbb{Z}[x] and \mathbb{Q}[x, y] have unique factorization.

Let f = a_n x^n + \dots + a_1 x + a_0 \in \mathbb{Z}[x]. Suppose a prime p divides a_0, a_1, \dots, a_{n-1}, does not divide a_n, and p^2 does not divide a_0. Then f is irreducible in \mathbb{Q}[x].

Proof

By Gauss's lemma, suppose f = gh in \mathbb{Z}[x] with both degrees at least 1. Reduce mod p. All coefficients but the top one vanish, so \bar g \bar h = \bar a_n x^n. In \mathbb{F}_p[x] factorization is unique, so \bar g = c\,x^k and \bar h = d\,x^{n-k}. Since p \nmid a_n, the degrees do not drop, so k \ge 1 and n - k \ge 1. Then both constant terms of g and h are divisible by p. Their product a_0 is divisible by p^2. Contradiction.

  1. x^4 + 10x + 5: use p = 5. 5 divides 10 and 5, not 1, and 25 does not divide 5. Irreducible.
  2. x^n - 2: use p = 2. So x^n - 2 is irreducible for every n. There are irreducible polynomials of every degree over \mathbb{Q}.
  3. \Phi_5(x) = x^4 + x^3 + x^2 + x + 1: no p works directly. Shift: \Phi_5(x + 1) = x^4 + 5x^3 + 10x^2 + 10x + 5. Now p = 5 works. A shift does not change irreducibility.

Another test: reduce mod a prime. If \bar f is irreducible in \mathbb{F}_p[x] and p \nmid a_n, then f is irreducible over \mathbb{Q}. Example: x^3 + x + 1 has no root in \mathbb{F}_2 (0 gives 1, 1 gives 1). So x^3 + 3x + 5, which reduces to it, is irreducible over \mathbb{Q}.

Eisenstein is a sufficient test, not a necessary one. If it fails, you learn nothing. x^2 + 1 is irreducible, but no prime works directly. Try a shift x \mapsto x + 1: x^2 + 2x + 2 works with p = 2. Also, the reduction test fails the other way: x^4 + 1 is irreducible over \mathbb{Q} but reducible mod every prime.

Field extensions and the tower law

The number \sqrt{2} is not rational. Add it to \mathbb{Q}. The smallest field that holds both is \mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{2}) = \{ a + b\sqrt{2} : a, b \in \mathbb{Q} \}. Inverses stay inside: \frac{1}{a + b\sqrt{2}} = \frac{a - b\sqrt{2}}{a^2 - 2b^2}.

A field extension L/K is a field L that contains a field K. Then L is a vector space over K. Its dimension is the degree [L:K]. For example [\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{2}):\mathbb{Q}] = 2, with basis 1, \sqrt{2}. And [\mathbb{C}:\mathbb{R}] = 2, with basis 1, i.

A number \alpha is algebraic over K if it is a root of a nonzero polynomial in K[x]. The monic one of smallest degree is the minimal polynomial. It is irreducible. If it has degree d, then

K(\alpha) \cong K[x]/(m_\alpha), \qquad [K(\alpha):K] = d, \qquad \text{basis } 1, \alpha, \dots, \alpha^{d-1}.

A number that is not algebraic over \mathbb{Q} is transcendental. Hermite proved this for e in 1873, and Lindemann for \pi in 1882.

If K \subseteq M \subseteq L are fields, then [L:K] = [L:M]\,[M:K]. This holds also when the degrees are infinite.

Proof

Let m_1, \dots, m_r be a basis of M over K and l_1, \dots, l_s a basis of L over M. We show that the rs products m_i l_j form a basis of L over K.

They span. Any x \in L is \sum_j c_j l_j with c_j \in M. Each c_j = \sum_i a_{ij} m_i with a_{ij} \in K. So x = \sum_{i,j} a_{ij} m_i l_j.

They are independent. If \sum_{i,j} a_{ij} m_i l_j = 0, group by l_j: \sum_j \big( \sum_i a_{ij} m_i \big) l_j = 0. The l_j are independent over M, so each inner sum is 0. The m_i are independent over K, so every a_{ij} = 0.

  1. [\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{2}):\mathbb{Q}] = 2, because x^2 - 2 is irreducible.
  2. Is \sqrt{3} \in \mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{2})? If (a + b\sqrt{2})^2 = 3, then 2ab = 0. With b = 0, a^2 = 3. With a = 0, 2b^2 = 3. No rational solution. So no.
  3. So x^2 - 3 stays irreducible over \mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{2}), and the next step has degree 2.
  4. Tower law: [\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{2}, \sqrt{3}):\mathbb{Q}] = 2 \cdot 2 = 4. A basis is 1, \sqrt{2}, \sqrt{3}, \sqrt{6}.

A quick use: \sqrt[3]{2} is not in \mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{2}, \sqrt{3}). Its degree 3 would have to divide 4.

The splitting field of f \in K[x] is the smallest extension where f splits into linear factors. For x^3 - 2 over \mathbb{Q}, the roots are \sqrt[3]{2}, \omega\sqrt[3]{2} and \omega^2\sqrt[3]{2}, with \omega = e^{2\pi i/3}. The splitting field is \mathbb{Q}(\sqrt[3]{2}, \omega). Its degree is 3 \cdot 2 = 6, by the tower law.

Adding one root of f does not always give the splitting field. \mathbb{Q}(\sqrt[3]{2}) lies inside \mathbb{R}. The two complex roots of x^3 - 2 are not in it. So [\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt[3]{2}):\mathbb{Q}] = 3, but the splitting field has degree 6.

Finite fields, codes and cryptography

We know the fields \mathbb{F}_p with p elements. Can a field have 4 elements? Not \mathbb{Z}/4: there 2 \cdot 2 = 0. Instead, take \mathbb{F}_2[x] and the irreducible polynomial x^2 + x + 1. By the theorem on maximal ideals, \mathbb{F}_2[x]/(x^2 + x + 1) is a field. Call the class of x by the name \alpha. Then \alpha^2 = \alpha + 1 (remember -1 = 1 here).

Multiplication in the field with 4 elements, where \alpha^2 = \alpha + 1
×01αα+1
00000
101αα+1
α0αα+11
α+10α+11α

Every nonzero row contains a 1, so every nonzero element has an inverse. Also \alpha generates the nonzero elements: \alpha^1 = \alpha, \alpha^2 = \alpha + 1, \alpha^3 = 1.

Every finite field has p^n elements for some prime p and some n \ge 1. For every prime power q = p^n there is a field with q elements. Any two fields with q elements are isomorphic. We call it \mathbb{F}_q or \mathrm{GF}(q). It is the splitting field of x^q - x over \mathbb{F}_p.

Proof idea

Size. Add 1 to itself. In a finite field, some sum 1 + \dots + 1 is 0. The smallest such count is a prime p, since a product of nonzero elements is nonzero. So the field contains \mathbb{F}_p. It is a vector space of some dimension n over \mathbb{F}_p, so it has p^n elements.

Every element is a root of x^q - x. The nonzero elements form a group of size q - 1. By Lagrange, a^{q-1} = 1 for a \ne 0. So a^q = a for all a, including 0.

Existence. Take the splitting field of x^q - x over \mathbb{F}_p. Its derivative is q x^{q-1} - 1 = -1, so the polynomial has no repeated roots: there are exactly q roots. The map a \mapsto a^p respects sums in characteristic p: (a + b)^p = a^p + b^p. So the roots are closed under +, \cdot and inverses. They form the field.

Uniqueness. A field with q elements consists of the q roots of x^q - x. So it is a splitting field of that polynomial. Splitting fields are unique up to isomorphism.

The number p is the characteristic of the field. The map a \mapsto a^p is the Frobenius map. It is important in the Galois theory below.

In \mathbb{F}_q there is an element g whose powers g, g^2, \dots, g^{q-1} are all the nonzero elements. Such g is a primitive element.

Proof idea

For each d \mid q - 1, the equation x^d = 1 has at most d roots, by the factor theorem in a field. A finite abelian group with this property must be cyclic. Count: the number of elements of order d is 0 or \varphi(d), and \sum_{d \mid q-1} \varphi(d) = q - 1. So no count can be 0. In particular some element has order q - 1.

Computers love \mathbb{F}_{2^8} = \mathbb{F}_{256}. One element is one byte. Adding is XOR. The AES cipher (NIST FIPS 197, from 2001, updated 2023) uses the irreducible polynomial m(x) = x^8 + x^4 + x^3 + x + 1. A byte with bits b_7 \dots b_0 is the polynomial b_7 x^7 + \dots + b_0. To multiply, multiply the polynomials and take the remainder mod m(x).

def gf_mul(a, b):
    """Multiply two bytes in GF(2^8), the AES field."""
    result = 0
    while b:
        if b & 1:              # this bit of b is 1: add a
            result ^= a        # adding is XOR
        a <<= 1                # multiply a by x
        if a & 0x100:          # degree 8 appeared
            a ^= 0x11B         # subtract m(x) = x^8 + x^4 + x^3 + x + 1
        b >>= 1
    return result

def gf_pow(a, n):
    r = 1
    for _ in range(n):
        r = gf_mul(r, a)
    return r

print(hex(gf_mul(0x57, 0x83)))      # the example in FIPS 197
print(hex(gf_mul(0x57, 0x13)))
inv = gf_pow(0x53, 254)              # a^254 = 1/a, because a^255 = 1
print(hex(inv), hex(gf_mul(0x53, inv)))
# 0x03 generates all 255 nonzero bytes: the group is cyclic
powers = {gf_pow(0x03, k) for k in range(255)}
print(len(powers))
/// Multiply two bytes in GF(2^8), the AES field.
fn gf_mul(mut a: u8, mut b: u8) -> u8 {
    let mut result = 0u8;
    while b != 0 {
        if b & 1 == 1 {
            result ^= a; // adding is XOR
        }
        let high = a & 0x80 != 0; // will x * a have degree 8?
        a <<= 1;
        if high {
            a ^= 0x1B; // subtract x^8 + x^4 + x^3 + x + 1
        }
        b >>= 1;
    }
    result
}

fn main() {
    println!("{:#04x}", gf_mul(0x57, 0x83));
    println!("{:#04x}", gf_mul(0x57, 0x13));
    println!("{:#04x}", gf_mul(0x53, 0xca));
}
0xc1
0xfe
0xca 0x1
255
0xc1
0xfe
0x01

The outputs match the examples in FIPS 197: \{57\} \cdot \{83\} = \{c1\} and \{57\} \cdot \{13\} = \{fe\}. The inverse of \{53\} is \{ca\}. The AES S-box starts from exactly this inverse, then applies a fixed affine map over \mathbb{F}_2.

Error-correcting codes

Reed and Solomon published their codes in 1960. A message is a polynomial over \mathbb{F}_{256}. The code stores its values at many points. A polynomial of degree below k is fixed by any k values, so lost or wrong symbols can be rebuilt. RS(255, 223) adds 32 check bytes and corrects up to 16 wrong bytes per block. CDs, DVDs, QR codes and the Voyager probes use Reed-Solomon codes.

Elliptic curve cryptography

The points of an elliptic curve over \mathbb{F}_p form a group. Adding points uses only field operations. Security rests on a hard problem: from P and kP, find k.

Secret sharing

Shamir's scheme hides a secret as f(0) of a random polynomial over \mathbb{F}_p. Any k shares f(1), f(2), \dots rebuild it by interpolation. Fewer shares tell nothing.

Lattice cryptography

ML-KEM works in a quotient of \mathbb{F}_{3329}[X], as the note above shows. Its security rests on noisy linear equations over this ring.

\mathbb{F}_4 is not \mathbb{Z}/4, and \mathbb{F}_{256} is not "bytes mod 256". Arithmetic mod 256 has zero divisors: 16 \cdot 16 = 0. The field needs polynomial arithmetic mod an irreducible polynomial.

Galois groups and the fundamental theorem

Complex conjugation a + bi \mapsto a - bi keeps sums and products. It fixes every real number. It swaps the two roots i and -i of x^2 + 1. Galois saw that such symmetries of roots explain when equations can be solved.

An automorphism of a field L is a bijective ring homomorphism L \to L. The Galois group \operatorname{Gal}(L/K) is the set of automorphisms of L that fix every element of K. The key fact: if \sigma fixes K and f(\alpha) = 0 with f \in K[x], then f(\sigma(\alpha)) = \sigma(f(\alpha)) = 0. So \sigma sends roots to roots. It permutes them.

An extension L/K is Galois if L is the splitting field of a polynomial with no repeated roots. Over \mathbb{Q} and over finite fields, no irreducible polynomial has repeated roots. For a Galois extension, |\operatorname{Gal}(L/K)| = [L:K].

  1. Any \sigma sends \sqrt{2} to a root of x^2 - 2: to \pm\sqrt{2}. The same holds for \sqrt{3}.
  2. That gives at most 4 choices. The degree is 4, so all 4 occur.
  3. Name them: \mathrm{id}, \sigma (flips \sqrt{2}), \tau (flips \sqrt{3}), \sigma\tau (flips both).
  4. Each one is its own inverse. The group is \mathbb{Z}/2 \times \mathbb{Z}/2, the Klein four group.
  5. \sigma\tau sends \sqrt{6} = \sqrt{2}\sqrt{3} to (-\sqrt{2})(-\sqrt{3}) = \sqrt{6}. So it fixes \mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{6}).

Each subgroup fixes a field in the middle. Each middle field is fixed by a subgroup. This matching is the heart of the theory.

Let L/K be a finite Galois extension with group G = \operatorname{Gal}(L/K). Then the maps

H \mapsto L^H = \{ x \in L : \sigma(x) = x \text{ for all } \sigma \in H \}, \qquad M \mapsto \operatorname{Gal}(L/M)

are inverse bijections between subgroups H \le G and middle fields K \subseteq M \subseteq L. They reverse inclusion. Also [L:L^H] = |H| and [L^H:K] = [G:H]. Finally, M/K is Galois exactly when \operatorname{Gal}(L/M) is a normal subgroup. Then \operatorname{Gal}(M/K) \cong G/\operatorname{Gal}(L/M).

Proof idea

Two facts carry the proof. First, for a Galois extension, |\operatorname{Gal}(L/M)| = [L:M] for every middle field M. This holds because L/M is again a splitting field without repeated roots, and an isomorphism extends root by root in exactly [L:M] ways. Second, Artin's lemma: for any finite group H of automorphisms, [L:L^H] = |H|. The proof uses linear independence of distinct automorphisms.

From these, \operatorname{Gal}(L/L^H) \supseteq H, and both have size [L:L^H] = |H|. So they are equal. Also L^{\operatorname{Gal}(L/M)} \supseteq M, and both have the same degree under L. So they are equal. The degree formulas follow from the tower law and Lagrange. For the last part, \sigma \operatorname{Gal}(L/M) \sigma^{-1} = \operatorname{Gal}(L/\sigma M). So the subgroup is normal exactly when every \sigma maps M to itself. Then restriction G \to \operatorname{Gal}(M/K) is onto with kernel \operatorname{Gal}(L/M). Use the first isomorphism theorem.

In words: questions about fields become questions about finite groups. Groups are much easier to list. For x^3 - 2, the group of \mathbb{Q}(\sqrt[3]{2}, \omega) is S_3, all 6 permutations of the 3 roots. S_3 has 6 subgroups, so there are exactly 6 middle fields: the two ends, \mathbb{Q}(\sqrt[3]{2}), \mathbb{Q}(\omega\sqrt[3]{2}), \mathbb{Q}(\omega^2\sqrt[3]{2}) and \mathbb{Q}(\omega). Only A_3 is normal among the proper nontrivial subgroups. It matches \mathbb{Q}(\omega), the only middle field that is Galois over \mathbb{Q}.

Finite fields have the simplest Galois groups. \operatorname{Gal}(\mathbb{F}_{p^n}/\mathbb{F}_p) is cyclic of order n. The Frobenius map a \mapsto a^p generates it. So the subfields of \mathbb{F}_{p^n} are the \mathbb{F}_{p^d} with d \mid n. For example \mathbb{F}_{256} contains \mathbb{F}_2, \mathbb{F}_4 and \mathbb{F}_{16}, but not \mathbb{F}_8.

The theorem needs a Galois extension. \mathbb{Q}(\sqrt[3]{2})/\mathbb{Q} has degree 3. But its only automorphism is the identity, because the other two roots are not real. So |\operatorname{Gal}| = 1 \ne 3. Always pass to the splitting field first.

Why the quintic has no formula

The quadratic formula is ancient. Cardano's book Ars Magna (1545) printed formulas for degree 3 and 4. They use only +, -, \times, \div and roots \sqrt[n]{\ }. For three centuries people looked for such a formula for degree 5.

An equation is solvable by radicals if its roots can be written this way. Galois turned this into group theory. Adding an n-th root \sqrt[n]{a} to a field that already has the n-th roots of unity gives a cyclic Galois group. So a formula by radicals builds a tower of fields where each step has an abelian group.

A group G is solvable if there is a chain \{e\} = G_0 \unlhd G_1 \unlhd \dots \unlhd G_k = G where each G_{i+1}/G_i is abelian. S_3 and S_4 are solvable. S_5 is not. Its only proper nontrivial normal subgroup is A_5. And A_5, of order 60, is simple and not abelian.

Galois's criterion

Over \mathbb{Q}, a polynomial is solvable by radicals exactly when the Galois group of its splitting field is solvable.

Irreducible

Eisenstein with p = 3: 3 divides 6 and 3, and 9 does not divide 3. So f = x^5 - 6x + 3 is irreducible.

A 5-cycle

Adding one root gives degree 5. So 5 divides |G|. A group of permutations of 5 roots with order divisible by 5 has an element of order 5: a 5-cycle.

Three real roots

f(-2) = -17, f(-1) = 8, f(1) = -2, f(2) = 23. Three sign changes give three real roots. f'(x) = 5x^4 - 6 has only two real zeros, so there are no more.

A transposition

The other two roots are complex conjugates. Complex conjugation swaps them and fixes the three real roots. That is a transposition.

The group is S5

A 5-cycle and a transposition generate all of S_5. S_5 is not solvable. So no formula with radicals gives the roots of f.

There is no formula, built from the coefficients with +, -, \times, \div and n-th roots, that gives the roots of every polynomial equation of degree 5. The same holds for every degree n \ge 5.

Proof idea

A general formula would solve every quintic over \mathbb{Q}, including x^5 - 6x + 3. The carousel shows that its Galois group is S_5. By Galois's criterion, a solvable-by-radicals polynomial has a solvable group. The fundamental theorem turns the tower of radical fields into a chain of normal subgroups with abelian quotients. S_5 has no such chain, because A_5 is simple and not abelian. For degree n \ge 5, multiply by x^{n-5} or use S_n, which contains A_n, also simple.

Be precise about what this says. Some quintics are solvable: x^5 - 2 has roots \sqrt[5]{2}\,\zeta^k with \zeta = e^{2\pi i/5}. Its group has order 20 and is solvable. The theorem says only that no single formula works for all quintics. The roots of x^5 - 6x + 3 exist, and a computer finds them to any precision. They just have no radical expression.

from sympy import symbols, factor_list, real_roots, Poly
from sympy.polys.numberfields.galoisgroups import galois_group

x = symbols("x")
for f in (x**5 - 6*x + 3, x**5 - 2):
    G, _ = galois_group(Poly(f, x))
    print(f)
    print("  factors over Q:", len(factor_list(f)[1]))   # 1 means irreducible
    print("  real roots:", len(real_roots(f)))
    print("  group order:", G.order(), "| solvable:", G.is_solvable)
x**5 - 6*x + 3
  factors over Q: 1
  real roots: 3
  group order: 120 | solvable: False
x**5 - 2
  factors over Q: 1
  real roots: 1
  group order: 20 | solvable: True
  1. 1545 Cardano's Ars Magna. Formulas for the cubic and the quartic appear in print.
  2. 1796 Gauss and the 17-gon. A regular polygon with 17 sides can be built with ruler and compass.
  3. 1799 Ruffini. A first, incomplete proof that the quintic has no formula.
  4. 1824 Abel. A short complete proof, with a fuller version in 1826.
  5. 1832 Galois dies at 20. His ideas on groups of roots stay unpublished.
  6. 1837 Wantzel. Doubling the cube and trisecting the angle are impossible.
  7. 1846 Liouville publishes Galois. Galois theory becomes known.
  8. 1882 Lindemann. \pi is transcendental, so the circle cannot be squared.
  9. 1960 Reed and Solomon. Codes over finite fields.
  10. 2001 AES. NIST publishes FIPS 197, with arithmetic in \mathbb{F}_{256}.

"No formula" does not mean "no roots". By the fundamental theorem of algebra, every quintic has 5 complex roots. Abel-Ruffini is about the form of the answer, not its existence.

Ruler and compass

The Greeks built shapes with two tools. A ruler with no marks draws a line through two points. A compass draws a circle with a given centre through a given point. Three problems stayed open for more than 2000 years: double a cube, trisect any angle, and square a circle.

Start with the points 0 and 1. A real number is constructible if you can reach it with the two tools. Constructible numbers form a field. They are also closed under square roots: you can draw \sqrt{a} with a half circle.

If \alpha is constructible, then [\mathbb{Q}(\alpha):\mathbb{Q}] is a power of 2.

Proof

Each new point is a crossing of two lines, a line and a circle, or two circles. The equations have coefficients in the current field K. Two lines give a linear equation, so the new point is in K. The other cases lead to a quadratic equation. So each step gives an extension of degree 1 or 2. After k steps we reach a field K_k with [K_k:\mathbb{Q}] = 2^m, by the tower law. Since \mathbb{Q}(\alpha) \subseteq K_k, the tower law says [\mathbb{Q}(\alpha):\mathbb{Q}] divides 2^m.

  1. Double a cube. A cube of volume 2 has side \sqrt[3]{2}. Its minimal polynomial x^3 - 2 has degree 3. Not a power of 2, so impossible.
  2. Trisect 60°. We need \cos 20°. From \cos 3\theta = 4\cos^3\theta - 3\cos\theta with \cos 60° = \tfrac{1}{2}, the number c = 2\cos 20° solves c^3 - 3c - 1 = 0. No rational root (try \pm 1), so it is irreducible of degree 3. Impossible.
  3. Square a circle. A square with area \pi has side \sqrt{\pi}. It is transcendental, so its degree is infinite. Impossible.

Some angles can be trisected, such as 90°: 30° is easy to build. The theorem says there is no method that works for every angle.

Regular polygons follow the same rule. The Gauss-Wantzel theorem says a regular n-gon is constructible exactly when n is a power of 2 times distinct Fermat primes. The known Fermat primes are 3, 5, 17, 257 and 65537. So the 17-gon works, but the 7-gon and the 9-gon do not. For the 17-gon, \operatorname{Gal}(\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_{17})/\mathbb{Q}) is cyclic of order 16 = 2^4. It gives a tower of four quadratic steps.

The converse of the degree theorem is false. Degree a power of 2 does not guarantee constructible. A root of an irreducible quartic with Galois group S_4 has degree 4 but is not constructible. The exact test: the Galois closure must have degree a power of 2.

Most exam questions in this area follow one plan. First, find the minimal polynomial and prove it irreducible (Eisenstein, a shift, or no rational roots). Second, read off the degree. Third, apply the tower law or the Galois correspondence. Write each step with its reason.

Patterns to remember

Patterns for rings, fields and Galois theory
PatternPurposeModelNote
\mathbb{Z}/n is a field iff n is primeSpot fields among clock rings\mathbb{Z}/7 field, \mathbb{Z}/12 not: 3 \cdot 4 = 0For p^n with n \gt 1, use polynomials, not \mathbb{Z}/p^n.
R/M field iff M maximalBuild a new field\mathbb{R}[x]/(x^2 + 1) \cong \mathbb{C}In F[x], (f) is maximal iff f is irreducible.
Euclidean ⇒ PID ⇒ UFDGet unique factorization\mathbb{Z}[i] is Euclidean, so it is a UFDThe arrows do not reverse: \mathbb{Z}[x] is a UFD, not a PID.
Use the norm NShow an element is irreducibleN(1 + \sqrt{-5}) = 6, no element has N = 2, 3N must be multiplicative.
Eisenstein at pProve irreducibility over \mathbb{Q}x^4 + 10x + 5, p = 5If no p works, try x \mapsto x + 1.
Reduce mod pFast irreducibility testx^3 + 3x + 5 mod 2 has no rootKeep the top coefficient nonzero mod p.
[L:K] = [L:M][M:K]Compute degrees, rule out inclusions[\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{2}, \sqrt{3}):\mathbb{Q}] = 4Check the second step is still irreducible.
K(\alpha) \cong K[x]/(m_\alpha)Describe a simple extension\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt[3]{2}) has basis 1, \sqrt[3]{2}, \sqrt[3]{4}Use the minimal polynomial, not any polynomial.
Byte = polynomial over \mathbb{F}_2Compute in \mathbb{F}_{256}\{57\} \cdot \{83\} = \{c1\}Add with XOR. Reduce by x^8 + x^4 + x^3 + x + 1.
