  • Probability is measure theory with total mass 1. Densities, conditional expectations and KL divergence are Radon-Nikodym derivatives.

Sources

  • Axler, Measure, Integration & Real Analysis (Springer GTM, 2020, open access). Free graduate textbook on measure, L^p, Hilbert spaces and Fourier analysis.
  • Lebesgue integral. Lebesgue's idea, his money comparison and the limits of the Riemann integral.
  • Radon-Nikodym theorem. Statement, dates (1913, 1930) and uses in probability and information theory.
  • Convergence of Fourier series. Du Bois-Reymond, Kolmogorov, Carleson and the link to uniform boundedness.
  • Probability axioms. Kolmogorov's 1933 axioms as measure theory.
  • Baire category theorem. Its role in the open mapping theorem and the uniform boundedness principle.

Logic and the foundations of mathematics

Mathematics proves things. But what is a proof, exactly? And what are numbers and sets made of? This chapter turns these questions into mathematics. You will see what proofs can do. You will also see what no proof and no program can ever do.

  • Write formulas in a formal language and check a proof with a small program.
  • Tell "provable" apart from "true in a model", and use models to show that something cannot be proved.
  • Explain the ZFC axioms and the axiom of choice in simple words.
  • Count and order beyond the finite with ordinals and cardinals.
  • State the theorems of Gödel, Tarski and Turing, and say what they do not mean.

Formal languages: symbols, terms and formulas

Here is a fact about numbers: "every number has a bigger number". In symbols it is \forall x\, \exists y\, (x \lt y). This is just a row of marks. It has no meaning yet. Logic studies the grammar first and the meaning later.

A formal language has a fixed list of symbols and strict rules. The language of arithmetic uses these symbols.

KindSymbolsMeaning we have in mind
Constant0the number zero
Function symbolsS, +, \cdotnext number, plus, times
Relation symbols\lt, =smaller than, equal
Logical symbols\neg, \land, \lor, \to, \forall, \existsnot, and, or, if-then, for all, there is
Variables and bracketsx, y, z, (, )places for objects

The non-logical symbols form the signature. Rules then build two kinds of strings.

  • A term names an object. Examples: 0, x, S0, x + SS0.
  • A formula says something. Examples: x \lt y, \forall x\, \neg(Sx = 0).
  • A variable is free if no \forall or \exists controls it. A sentence is a formula with no free variables.
  1. x and 0 are terms.
  2. So x + 0 is a term. The rule: put + between two terms.
  3. So x + 0 = x is a formula. The rule: put = between two terms.
  4. So \forall x\,(x + 0 = x) is a formula. The rule: put \forall x in front of a formula.
  5. The only variable is x, and \forall x controls it. So it is a sentence.

The rule behind this: being a formula depends only on shape. A program can check the shape. Meaning comes later, from models.

This chapter uses first-order logic. Its \forall and \exists talk about objects only. Second-order logic can also say "for all sets of numbers". It is stronger, but it loses the good theorems of this chapter.

The symbol + is not the operation of adding. It is only a mark. One model reads it as adding. Another model can read it as something else. Also keep the order of quantifiers. \forall x\, \exists y\, (x \lt y) is true for the natural numbers. \exists y\, \forall x\, (x \lt y) is false. See Logic and proofs.

Proofs a computer can check

Here is a proof of p \to p. It uses two axiom patterns and one rule. Every line is checked by a short program.

  • Axiom A1: A \to (B \to A).
  • Axiom A2: (A \to (B \to C)) \to ((A \to B) \to (A \to C)).
  • Rule MP: from A and A \to B, write B.

Here A, B, C stand for any formulas. The rule MP is called modus ponens.

# proof_check.py: check a Hilbert-style proof of p -> p.
def imp(a, b):
    return ("->", a, b)

def show(f):
    return f if isinstance(f, str) else f"({show(f[1])} -> {show(f[2])})"

def is_a1(f):  # A -> (B -> A)
    return f[0] == "->" and f[2][0] == "->" and f[2][2] == f[1]

def is_a2(f):  # (A -> (B -> C)) -> ((A -> B) -> (A -> C))
    try:
        (_, (_, a, (_, b, c)), (_, (_, a2, b2), (_, a3, c2))) = f
        return a == a2 == a3 and b == b2 and c == c2
    except (TypeError, ValueError):  # the shape does not fit
        return False

p = "p"
pp = imp(p, p)
proof = [
    (imp(imp(p, imp(pp, p)), imp(imp(p, pp), pp)), "A2"),
    (imp(p, imp(pp, p)), "A1"),
    (imp(imp(p, pp), pp), (2, 1)),  # modus ponens from lines 2 and 1
    (imp(p, pp), "A1"),
    (pp, (4, 3)),
]
all_ok = True
for n, (f, why) in enumerate(proof, start=1):
    if why == "A1":
        rule, ok = "A1", is_a1(f)
    elif why == "A2":
        rule, ok = "A2", is_a2(f)
    else:  # line i is X, line j is X -> f, both earlier
        i, j = why
        rule = f"MP {i},{j}"
        ok = i < n and j < n and proof[j - 1][0] == imp(proof[i - 1][0], f)
    print(f"{n}. {rule:<7} {'ok   ' if ok else 'WRONG'} {show(f)}")
    all_ok = all_ok and ok
print("proof accepted:", str(all_ok).lower())
// proof_check.rs: check a Hilbert-style proof of p -> p.
#[derive(Clone, PartialEq)]
enum F { V(&'static str), I(Box<F>, Box<F>) } // a variable or an implication
use F::*;

fn imp(a: &F, b: &F) -> F { I(Box::new(a.clone()), Box::new(b.clone())) }

fn show(f: &F) -> String {
    match f { V(s) => s.to_string(), I(a, b) => format!("({} -> {})", show(a), show(b)) }
}

fn is_a1(f: &F) -> bool { // A -> (B -> A)
    matches!(f, I(a, r) if matches!(&**r, I(_, a2) if a2 == a))
}

fn is_a2(f: &F) -> bool { // (A -> (B -> C)) -> ((A -> B) -> (A -> C))
    if let I(l, r) = f && let (I(a, bc), I(ab, ac)) = (&**l, &**r)
        && let (I(b, c), I(a2, b2), I(a3, c2)) = (&**bc, &**ab, &**ac) {
        return a == a2 && a == a3 && b == b2 && c == c2;
    }
    false
}

fn main() {
    let (p, pp) = (V("p"), imp(&V("p"), &V("p")));
    let proof = [ // (formula, rule): rule (0, 0) is A1, (0, 1) is A2, else MP i,j
        (imp(&imp(&p, &imp(&pp, &p)), &imp(&imp(&p, &pp), &pp)), (0, 1)),
        (imp(&p, &imp(&pp, &p)), (0, 0)),
        (imp(&imp(&p, &pp), &pp), (2, 1)),
        (imp(&p, &pp), (0, 0)),
        (pp.clone(), (4, 3)),
    ];
    let mut all_ok = true;
    for (k, (f, (i, j))) in proof.iter().enumerate() {
        let n = k + 1; // the line number
        let (rule, ok) = match (i, j) {
            (0, 0) => ("A1".to_string(), is_a1(f)),
            (0, 1) => ("A2".to_string(), is_a2(f)),
            _ => (format!("MP {},{}", i, j),
                  *i < n && *j < n && proof[j - 1].0 == imp(&proof[i - 1].0, f)),
        };
        println!("{}. {:<7} {} {}", n, rule, if ok { "ok   " } else { "WRONG" }, show(f));
        all_ok &= ok;
    }
    println!("proof accepted: {}", all_ok);
}
python3 proof_check.py
rustc --edition 2024 proof_check.rs -o proof_check && ./proof_check
1. A2      ok    ((p -> ((p -> p) -> p)) -> ((p -> (p -> p)) -> (p -> p)))
2. A1      ok    (p -> ((p -> p) -> p))
3. MP 2,1  ok    ((p -> (p -> p)) -> (p -> p))
4. A1      ok    (p -> (p -> p))
5. MP 4,3  ok    (p -> p)
proof accepted: true

Both programs print the same lines. Now the rule. A proof system has axioms and rules. A formal proof is a finite list of formulas. Each line is an axiom or comes from earlier lines by a rule.

Let T be a set of sentences, the axioms. We write T \vdash \varphi if there is a formal proof of \varphi from T. Say "T proves \varphi". A set of sentences like T is called a theory.

Checking a proof is easy and mechanical. Finding a proof is hard. Even line 1 above is not obvious to find. This gap between checking and finding comes back at the end of the chapter.

Proof assistants grow this small checker into a full tool. Examples are Lean, Isabelle and Rocq. Rocq was called Coq until its version 9.0 in March 2025. Engineers use these tools to prove that software and hardware are correct.

The order in a modus ponens step matters. "MP 2,1" means: line 2 is A and line 1 is A \to B. If you write "MP 1,2" for line 3, the checker says WRONG. A checker never guesses what you meant.

Models: where a sentence is true

The sentence \exists x\, (x \cdot x = 2) is true in some worlds and false in others. The programs below check three sentences in the clock arithmetic \mathbb{Z}_n = \{0, 1, \ldots, n - 1\}. Here + and \cdot work modulo n.

# models.py: the same sentences, checked in the structures Z_n = {0, ..., n-1}.
sentences = {
    "exists x: x*x = 2": lambda n: any(x * x % n == 2 for x in range(n)),
    "forall x: x != 0 -> exists y: x*y = 1": lambda n: all(
        any(x * y % n == 1 for y in range(n)) for x in range(1, n)),
    "exists x: x != 0 and x*x = 0": lambda n: any(
        x * x % n == 0 for x in range(1, n)),
}
print("sentence".ljust(40) + "".join(f"Z_{n:<3}" for n in range(3, 9)))
for text, holds in sentences.items():
    row = "".join(("T" if holds(n) else "F").ljust(5) for n in range(3, 9))
    print(text.ljust(40) + row.rstrip())
// models.rs: the same sentences, checked in the structures Z_n = {0, ..., n-1}.
fn main() {
    let sentences: Vec<(&str, Box<dyn Fn(u32) -> bool>)> = vec![
        ("exists x: x*x = 2", Box::new(|n| (0..n).any(|x| x * x % n == 2))),
        ("forall x: x != 0 -> exists y: x*y = 1",
         Box::new(|n| (1..n).all(|x| (0..n).any(|y| x * y % n == 1)))),
        ("exists x: x != 0 and x*x = 0", Box::new(|n| (1..n).any(|x| x * x % n == 0))),
    ];
    let head: String = (3..9).map(|n| format!("Z_{:<3}", n)).collect();
    println!("{:<40}{}", "sentence", head);
    for (text, holds) in &sentences {
        let row: String = (3..9).map(|n| format!("{:<5}", if holds(n) { "T" } else { "F" })).collect();
        println!("{:<40}{}", text, row.trim_end());
    }
}
sentence                                Z_3  Z_4  Z_5  Z_6  Z_7  Z_8
exists x: x*x = 2                       F    F    F    F    T    F
forall x: x != 0 -> exists y: x*y = 1   T    F    T    F    T    F
exists x: x != 0 and x*x = 0            F    T    F    F    F    T

In \mathbb{Z}_7 we have 3 \cdot 3 = 9 = 2. So the first sentence is true there. In \mathbb{Z}_5 the squares are only 0, 1 and 4. The second sentence holds exactly when n is prime. The third finds 2 \cdot 2 = 0 in \mathbb{Z}_4.

A structure M is a nonempty set, the domain, plus a meaning for each symbol of the signature. If the sentence \varphi is true in M, we write M \models \varphi. M is a model of T if every sentence of T is true in M. We write T \models \varphi if \varphi is true in every model of T.

The proof side: T \vdash \varphi. It is about strings and rules. A proof is finite. A program can check it.

The truth side: T \models \varphi. It is about all models. There can be infinitely many models, and each can be infinite.

If T \vdash \varphi, then T \models \varphi. A provable sentence is true in every model of the axioms.

In simple words: good rules never lead from true axioms to a false result. With numbers: every line of the proof above is true for every choice of truth values of p.

Proof idea

Use induction on the length of the proof. Every axiom is true in every model of T. Each rule keeps truth: if A and A \to B are true in M, then B is true in M. So every line of a proof is true in every model.

Soundness gives the main method to show that something cannot be proved. Find a model of T where \varphi is false. Then T \not\vdash \varphi.

  1. Take the axioms of a group: a product, a neutral element, inverses, and the law (xy)z = x(yz).
  2. The numbers \mathbb{Z}_5 with + form a group where x + y = y + x always holds.
  3. The six ways to arrange three objects also form a group. There, swapping the first two and then the last two differs from doing them in the other order.
  4. So \forall x\, \forall y\, (xy = yx) is false in one model. By soundness, the group axioms do not prove it.
  5. It is true in another model. So the axioms do not prove its negation either.

"False in one model" does not mean "false". It means "not provable from these axioms". History has a famous case. Geometry without the parallel postulate has models where the postulate fails. So the other axioms cannot prove it.

Completeness, compactness and strange models

Soundness says: provable implies true in all models. Is the other direction also true? For first-order logic, yes. Kurt Gödel proved it in his 1929 thesis. He published it in 1930.

For first-order logic: if T \models \varphi, then T \vdash \varphi. An equal form: every consistent theory has a model.

In simple words: whatever is true in all models has a proof. So \vdash and \models mean the same thing in first-order logic. With an example: every sentence true in all groups has a formal proof from the group axioms.

Proof idea (Henkin, 1949)

Start with a consistent theory T. Add new constant names, one for each sentence \exists x\, \psi(x). Each name is a witness: add \exists x\, \psi(x) \to \psi(c). Extend the theory step by step until it decides every sentence, keeping it consistent. Then build the model from the terms themselves. For a countable language this model is countable.

The word "complete" has two meanings. Gödel's completeness theorem is about the logic: the rules find every consequence. A theory is complete if it proves \varphi or \neg\varphi for every sentence. Gödel's incompleteness theorems say many theories are not complete. Both results are true at the same time.

Proofs are finite lists. So a proof uses only finitely many axioms. This simple fact gives the next theorem.

A set of first-order sentences has a model if and only if every finite part of it has a model.

Proof

If T has no model, then by completeness T proves a contradiction \psi \land \neg\psi. That proof uses only a finite part T_0 of T. So T_0 proves a contradiction. By soundness T_0 has no model. The other direction is clear.

  1. Take all sentences that are true in \mathbb{N}. Add a new constant c.
  2. Add the sentences c \gt 0, c \gt S0, c \gt SS0, and so on, one for every number.
  3. Any finite part mentions only finitely many of them, say up to c \gt 100. Read c as 101 in \mathbb{N}. This is a model of that part.
  4. By compactness, the whole set has a model M.
  5. M satisfies every true sentence of arithmetic. But its element c is bigger than every standard number. It has infinitely many numbers below it.

Such a model is a nonstandard model. The same trick with a tiny positive \varepsilon gives numbers smaller than every \frac{1}{n}. Abraham Robinson used this to make infinitely small numbers exact. This field is called nonstandard analysis.

Let T be a theory in a countable language. If T has an infinite model, then T has a model of every infinite size. In particular it has a countable model.

In simple words: first-order logic cannot fix the size of an infinite model. With an example: the true sentences about \mathbb{R} also have a countable model. Löwenheim proved the first form in 1915. Skolem improved it in 1920 and 1922. The general form is due to Maltsev in 1936, and Tarski also had it.

Proof idea

Down: the Henkin model in the proof of completeness is built from countably many terms. So it is countable. Up: add \kappa new constants and the sentences c_i \ne c_j for i \ne j. Every finite part has a model, because the old model is infinite. Compactness gives a model with at least \kappa elements. Then use the downward part to cut it to size exactly \kappa.

Set theory proves that \mathbb{R} is uncountable. But if set theory has a model, it has a countable one. How can a countable model think its reals are uncountable? The answer: the model does not contain the counting function. Seen from outside, it is countable. Seen from inside, it is not. "Countable" depends on which functions exist.

A deep result by Lindström says more. First-order logic is the strongest logic that keeps both compactness and the downward Löwenheim-Skolem theorem. This is one reason why mathematics builds its foundations in first-order logic.

Sets as the ground floor: ZFC

First idea: every property gives a set. Take the property "x is not a member of itself". Let R = \{x : x \notin x\}. Is R \in R? If yes, then by the definition R \notin R. If no, then R has the property, so R \in R. Both answers fail. Bertrand Russell found this in 1901 and wrote to Frege about it in 1902.

There is no set R such that for every set x: x \in R \iff x \notin x.

Proof

Put x = R. We get R \in R \iff R \notin R. A statement cannot be equal to its own negation. So no such R exists.

So we need careful rules for making sets. The standard rules are ZFC. Zermelo gave the first list in 1908. Fraenkel and Skolem added the replacement axiom in 1922. Here are the axioms in simple words.

AxiomIn simple wordsExample
ExtensionalitySets with the same members are equal.\{1, 2\} = \{2, 1, 1\}
PairingFor any a, b there is the set \{a, b\}.\{0, \{0\}\}
UnionThe members of members form a set.\bigcup\{\{1\}, \{2, 3\}\} = \{1, 2, 3\}
Power setAll subsets of a set form a set.\mathcal{P}(\{1, 2\}) has 4 members
SeparationYou may cut out a subset by a property.\{n \in \omega : n \text{ is even}\}
ReplacementThe image of a set under a rule is a set.\{n^2 : n \in \omega\}
InfinityThere is an infinite set.\omega = \{0, 1, 2, \ldots\}
FoundationNo set is a member of itself, and no endless chain \cdots \in x_2 \in x_1 exists.x \notin x always
ChoiceFrom any family of nonempty sets you can pick one member of each.see the next section

Everything can be built from the empty set \varnothing. John von Neumann made the numbers this way.

0 = \varnothing, \quad 1 = \{0\}, \quad 2 = \{0, 1\}, \quad 3 = \{0, 1, 2\}, \quad n + 1 = n \cup \{n\} .

So the number n is a set with exactly n members. And m \lt n means simply m \in n. The pair (a, b) is the set \{\{a\}, \{a, b\}\}. Functions are sets of pairs. Real numbers are built from sets of rationals. So all of usual mathematics lives inside ZFC.

  1. 1879 Frege. The first full formal logic with quantifiers.
  2. 1901 Russell's paradox. Naive sets lead to a contradiction.
  3. 1904 Zermelo. Every set can be well-ordered, using the axiom of choice.
  4. 1908 Zermelo's axioms. The first axioms for sets.
  5. 1922 Fraenkel and Skolem. The replacement axiom completes ZF.
  6. 1930 Gödel's completeness theorem is published.
  7. 1931 Gödel's incompleteness theorems. Arithmetic cannot prove everything.
  8. 1933 Tarski. Truth in arithmetic cannot be defined in arithmetic.
  9. 1936 Church and Turing. Some problems have no algorithm.
  10. 1938 Gödel. Choice and the continuum hypothesis cannot be disproved in ZF.
  11. 1963 Cohen. With forcing, they cannot be proved either.

ZFC has separation, not "every property gives a set". You may only write \{x \in A : \varphi(x)\} for a set A you already have. Then Russell's argument gives no contradiction. It only shows that \{x \in A : x \notin x\} is not a member of A. So there is no set of all sets.

ZFC cannot prove its own consistency, if it is consistent. This follows from Gödel's second theorem below. Almost all mathematicians believe that ZFC is consistent. But that belief is not a theorem of ZFC.

The axiom of choice and its equal forms

Russell gave this picture. You have infinitely many pairs of shoes. Pick one shoe from each pair. Easy: always take the left shoe. Now you have infinitely many pairs of socks. The two socks of a pair look the same. There is no rule. Can you still pick one from each pair?

For every family \mathcal{F} of nonempty sets, there is a function f with f(A) \in A for every A \in \mathcal{F}. This f is a choice function.

The axiom says: yes, the socks can be picked, even without a rule. It has two famous equal forms. To state them we need orders. A well-order is a total order in which every nonempty subset has a smallest member. \mathbb{N} with \lt is well-ordered. \mathbb{Z} is not: it has no smallest member. \mathbb{R} is not: the interval (0, 1) has no smallest member.

Let P be a nonempty partially ordered set. Suppose every chain in P has an upper bound in P. Then P has a maximal member.

Proof idea (from the axiom of choice)

Suppose there is no maximal member. Then above every chain there is a strictly bigger member. Use a choice function to pick one each time. Start anywhere and climb: step 1, step 2, and so on. At a limit step, pick an upper bound of everything so far. The climb never stops. It goes on through all the ordinals of the next section. But P is a set, and there are more ordinals than members of any set. This is a contradiction.

Every set can be well-ordered.

Proof (from Zorn's lemma)

Let A be a set. Look at pairs (B, \le_B) where B \subseteq A and \le_B well-orders B. Say one pair is below another if the second continues the first: same order on B, with all new members on top. A chain of such pairs has an upper bound: the union. So Zorn gives a maximal pair (B, \le_B). If some a \in A were not in B, we could put a on top. That would be bigger. So B = A.

The circle closes easily. If every set can be well-ordered, well-order the union of the family. Then let f(A) be the smallest member of A. This is a choice function. So, over the other ZF axioms, these three statements are equal in strength: the axiom of choice, Zorn's lemma and the well-ordering theorem.

  1. Let P be the set of all linearly independent subsets of a vector space V. Order them by \subseteq.
  2. P is not empty: \varnothing \in P.
  3. The union of a chain is still independent. A dependence uses only finitely many vectors, and they all lie in one member of the chain.
  4. Zorn gives a maximal independent set B.
  5. If some v were not a combination of B, then B \cup \{v\} would be independent and bigger. So B spans V. It is a basis.

For example, \mathbb{R} is a vector space over \mathbb{Q}. So it has a basis. But nobody can write one down. This is typical: choice proves that something exists without building it.

Other equal forms are Tychonoff's theorem in Topology and "any two sets can be compared in size". Choice also has strange results. It gives sets of reals with no length, as in Measure and functional analysis. It also gives the Banach-Tarski paradox: a ball can be cut into finitely many pieces and rebuilt into two balls of the same size. Gödel showed in 1938 that choice cannot be disproved in ZF. Cohen showed in 1963 that it cannot be proved in ZF. Weaker forms, like choice for countable families, are enough for most of analysis.

You do not need the axiom of choice to pick one member from one nonempty set. That is plain logic. You also do not need it for finitely many choices, or when a rule exists, like "the smallest number". You need it for infinitely many choices with no rule.

Do not mix the names. The well-ordering principle says that \mathbb{N} is well-ordered. It is easy and needs no choice. The well-ordering theorem says that every set has some well-order. It needs choice.

Ordinals and cardinals

People stand in a queue. You can ask two questions. Which place is this person in: first, second, third? How many people are there? For finite queues the answers match. For infinite ones they split into two ideas: ordinals and cardinals.

An ordinal is a set that is well-ordered by \in and that contains every member of its members. Each ordinal is the set of all smaller ordinals.

The finite ordinals are the von Neumann numbers 0, 1, 2, \ldots. The set of all of them is the first infinite ordinal, \omega = \{0, 1, 2, \ldots\}. After it comes \omega + 1 = \omega \cup \{\omega\}, then \omega + 2, and so on.

An ordinal like \omega or \omega \cdot 2 has no last ordinal before it. It is a limit ordinal. Every well-ordered set has the same shape as exactly one ordinal. Ordinals are the measuring sticks for well-orders.

To add ordinals, put the second list after the first. One extra place in front of \omega disappears into it: 1 + \omega = \omega. One extra place after \omega is a new last place: \omega + 1 \ne \omega. The programs below add ordinals below \omega^\omega. They use Cantor normal form, like \omega^2 + \omega \cdot 3 + 5. In the code, w means \omega.

# ordinals.py: ordinals below omega^omega in Cantor normal form.
# An ordinal is a list of (exponent, coefficient), biggest exponent first.
# [(2, 1), (0, 3)] means w^2 + 3.

def add(a, b):
    if not b:
        return a
    e = b[0][0]                                # the leading exponent of b
    keep = [t for t in a if t[0] > e]          # smaller terms of a are swallowed
    same = sum(c for x, c in a if x == e)      # a term with the same exponent adds
    return keep + [(e, same + b[0][1])] + b[1:]

def show(a):
    if not a:
        return "0"
    parts = []
    for e, c in a:
        base = "" if e == 0 else ("w" if e == 1 else f"w^{e}")
        parts.append(str(c) if e == 0 else (base if c == 1 else f"{base}*{c}"))
    return " + ".join(parts)

one, w = [(0, 1)], [(1, 1)]
for x, y in [(one, w), (w, one), (w, w), ([(0, 3)], [(2, 1)]),
             ([(1, 1), (0, 5)], [(1, 2), (0, 1)])]:
    print(f"({show(x)}) + ({show(y)}) = {show(add(x, y))}")
print("1 + w == w + 1 ?", add(one, w) == add(w, one))
// ordinals.rs: ordinals below omega^omega in Cantor normal form.
// An ordinal is a list of (exponent, coefficient), biggest exponent first.
// vec![(2, 1), (0, 3)] means w^2 + 3.
type Ord = Vec<(u32, u64)>;

fn add(a: &Ord, b: &Ord) -> Ord {
    let Some(&(e, c)) = b.first() else { return a.clone() };
    let mut out: Ord = a.iter().copied().filter(|t| t.0 > e).collect(); // smaller terms are swallowed
    let same: u64 = a.iter().filter(|t| t.0 == e).map(|t| t.1).sum(); // same exponent adds
    out.push((e, same + c));
    out.extend_from_slice(&b[1..]);
    out
}

fn show(a: &Ord) -> String {
    if a.is_empty() { return "0".into() }
    let parts: Vec<String> = a.iter().map(|&(e, c)| {
        let base = match e { 0 => String::new(), 1 => "w".into(), _ => format!("w^{}", e) };
        if e == 0 { c.to_string() } else if c == 1 { base } else { format!("{}*{}", base, c) }
    }).collect();
    parts.join(" + ")
}

fn main() {
    let (one, w): (Ord, Ord) = (vec![(0, 1)], vec![(1, 1)]);
    let pairs = [(one.clone(), w.clone()), (w.clone(), one.clone()), (w.clone(), w.clone()),
                 (vec![(0, 3)], vec![(2, 1)]), (vec![(1, 1), (0, 5)], vec![(1, 2), (0, 1)])];
    for (x, y) in &pairs {
        println!("({}) + ({}) = {}", show(x), show(y), show(&add(x, y)));
    }
    println!("1 + w == w + 1 ? {}", if add(&one, &w) == add(&w, &one) { "True" } else { "False" });
}
(1) + (w) = w
(w) + (1) = w + 1
(w) + (w) = w*2
(3) + (w^2) = w^2
(w + 5) + (w*2 + 1) = w*3 + 1
1 + w == w + 1 ? False

Ordinals give a stronger form of induction. Transfinite induction says: if a property passes from all ordinals below \alpha to \alpha, then every ordinal has it. It extends strong induction past \omega.

Two sets have the same size if there is a bijection between them. A cardinal is an ordinal that has no bijection with any smaller ordinal. The size |A| of a set is the cardinal in bijection with it.

With choice, every set has such a cardinal, by the well-ordering theorem. The ordinals \omega, \omega + 1 and \omega \cdot 2 are different. But they all have the same size, \aleph_0 (say "aleph zero"). The next cardinal is \aleph_1, then \aleph_2, and so on.

Cardinal factWhy
\aleph_0 + \aleph_0 = \aleph_0Even and odd numbers together are all numbers.
\aleph_0 \cdot \aleph_0 = \aleph_0Pairs of numbers can be listed. So the rationals are countable.
2^{\aleph_0} = |\mathbb{R}| \gt \aleph_0Cantor's diagonal argument.
2^{\kappa} \gt \kappa for every \kappaCantor's theorem. There is no biggest cardinal.
\kappa + \lambda = \kappa \cdot \lambda = \max(\kappa, \lambda)For infinite cardinals, with choice.

Now a famous question. Is there a size between \aleph_0 and 2^{\aleph_0}? The continuum hypothesis (CH) says no. In symbols: 2^{\aleph_0} = \aleph_1.

If ZFC is consistent, then ZFC + CH is consistent, and ZFC + \negCH is consistent. So ZFC can neither prove nor disprove CH.

Gödel announced the first half in 1938 and published the proof in 1940. He built a small model L, the constructible universe, where CH holds. Cohen proved the second half in 1963. He invented forcing to add many new reals to a model. He received the Fields Medal in 1966 for this work.

Why "if ZFC is consistent"?

By completeness, "consistent" means "has a model". Gödel and Cohen turn any model of ZFC into a model of ZFC + CH, or of ZFC + \negCH. They cannot start from nothing. By Gödel's second theorem, ZFC cannot prove that it has a model at all. So the result is relative.

"Independent" does not mean "not solved yet". It is a proved fact: the ZFC axioms alone can never settle CH. Set theorists still disagree whether CH has a true answer. Some look for new axioms. Others think there are many equally good universes of sets.

What cannot be proved: Gödel and Tarski

Read this sentence: "This sentence is not provable." Suppose it is provable. Then a false sentence is provable, which is bad. So it is not provable. But then what it says is true. So it is true and not provable. Gödel made arithmetic say exactly this, about itself.

The trick is to turn formulas into numbers. Give each symbol a code: 0 \mapsto 1, S \mapsto 2, = \mapsto 3. The string "S0=S0" has codes 2, 1, 3, 2, 1. Use them as powers of the primes:

\ulcorner S0{=}S0 \urcorner = 2^2 \cdot 3^1 \cdot 5^3 \cdot 7^2 \cdot 11^1 = 808\,500 .

This number is the Gödel number of the string. By unique factorisation, we can get the string back from the number. Now statements about formulas become statements about numbers.

Code everything

Every formula \varphi gets a number \ulcorner \varphi \urcorner. A proof is a list of formulas. So it gets a number too.

Proof checking is arithmetic

"n codes a proof of the formula with code m" is checked by a program. So it is a formula \operatorname{Prf}(n, m) of arithmetic.

Provable is a formula

Let \operatorname{Prov}(m) be \exists n\, \operatorname{Prf}(n, m). It says: "the formula with code m has a proof".

Self-reference

The diagonal lemma gives a sentence G with T \vdash G \leftrightarrow \neg\operatorname{Prov}(\ulcorner G \urcorner). So G says "I am not provable".

G is not provable

If T \vdash G, then T can check that proof, so T \vdash \operatorname{Prov}(\ulcorner G \urcorner). But G gives T \vdash \neg\operatorname{Prov}(\ulcorner G \urcorner). So T is inconsistent.

Not G is not provable

Gödel needed a slightly stronger condition here. Rosser changed G a little in 1936. Then plain consistency is enough.

Let T prove basic facts of arithmetic. For every formula F(x) with one free variable, there is a sentence D with

T \vdash D \leftrightarrow F(\ulcorner D \urcorner) .
Proof idea

Let \operatorname{diag}(n) be the code of the formula you get by putting the number n into the formula with code n. This is a computable function. So arithmetic can express it. Let A(x) = F(\operatorname{diag}(x)) and D = A(\ulcorner A \urcorner). Then \operatorname{diag}(\ulcorner A \urcorner) = \ulcorner D \urcorner. So D says F(\ulcorner D \urcorner). This is Cantor's diagonal trick again.

Let T be a consistent theory. Suppose a program can list its axioms, and T proves basic facts of arithmetic. Then there is a sentence G with T \not\vdash G and T \not\vdash \neg G.

In simple words: every such theory has gaps. Adding G as a new axiom does not help. The new theory has its own Gödel sentence. This applies to Peano arithmetic (PA) and to ZFC. Gödel published it in 1931.

Let T be as above and strong enough, for example PA or ZFC. Let \operatorname{Con}(T) be the sentence "T does not prove 0 = S0". If T is consistent, then T \not\vdash \operatorname{Con}(T).

Proof idea

Step 5 of the carousel is a proof of "if T is consistent, then G". It uses only simple arithmetic. So T can do this proof itself: T \vdash \operatorname{Con}(T) \to G. If T also proved \operatorname{Con}(T), it would prove G. The first theorem says it cannot.

There is no formula \operatorname{True}(x) of arithmetic such that for every sentence \varphi: \mathbb{N} \models \operatorname{True}(\ulcorner \varphi \urcorner) \leftrightarrow \varphi.

Proof

Suppose such a formula exists. Use the diagonal lemma with F(x) = \neg\operatorname{True}(x). We get a sentence L with L \leftrightarrow \neg\operatorname{True}(\ulcorner L \urcorner) true in \mathbb{N}. With the property of \operatorname{True}: L \leftrightarrow \neg L. This is the liar paradox, and it is impossible.

In simple words: provability can be written in arithmetic, but truth cannot. Tarski published this in 1933. Gödel had found it around 1930 too.

Gödel sentences look artificial. But there are natural examples. Write a number in base 2, also in its exponents: 4 = 2^2. Change every 2 into a 3: 3^3 = 27. Take away 1: 26. Repeat with base 3 to 4, and so on. This is a Goodstein sequence.

# goodstein.py: write n in hereditary base b, change every b to b + 1, take away 1.
def bump(n, b):
    result, power = 0, 0
    while n:
        n, digit = divmod(n, b)
        result += digit * (b + 1) ** bump(power, b)  # exponents are rewritten too
        power += 1
    return result

def goodstein(m, steps):
    seq, base = [m], 2
    while len(seq) < steps and seq[-1] > 0:
        seq.append(bump(seq[-1], base) - 1)
        base += 1
    return seq

print("start 3:", goodstein(3, 20))
print("start 4:", goodstein(4, 12))
s = goodstein(4, 1001)
print("start 4, after 1000 steps:", s[1000])
// goodstein.rs: write n in hereditary base b, change every b to b + 1, take away 1.
fn bump(mut n: u128, b: u128) -> u128 {
    let (mut result, mut power) = (0u128, 0u128);
    while n > 0 {
        let digit = n % b;
        n /= b;
        result += digit * (b + 1).pow(bump(power, b) as u32); // exponents are rewritten too
        power += 1;
    }
    result
}

fn goodstein(m: u128, steps: usize) -> Vec<u128> {
    let (mut seq, mut base) = (vec![m], 2u128);
    while seq.len() < steps && *seq.last().unwrap() > 0 {
        seq.push(bump(*seq.last().unwrap(), base) - 1);
        base += 1;
    }
    seq
}

fn main() {
    println!("start 3: {:?}", goodstein(3, 20));
    println!("start 4: {:?}", goodstein(4, 12));
    println!("start 4, after 1000 steps: {}", goodstein(4, 1001)[1000]);
}
start 3: [3, 3, 3, 2, 1, 0]
start 4: [4, 26, 41, 60, 83, 109, 139, 173, 211, 253, 299, 348]
start 4, after 1000 steps: 1022573

Start 4 seems to grow forever. Yet Goodstein proved in 1944 that every such sequence reaches 0. The sequence from 4 needs about 3 \cdot 2^{402\,653\,211} steps. His proof replaces the base by \omega. Then 4 = 2^2 becomes \omega^\omega, and 26 becomes \omega^2 \cdot 2 + \omega \cdot 2 + 2. These ordinals always go down. A well-order has no endless way down. So the sequence stops. Kirby and Paris showed in 1982 that PA cannot prove this theorem. The proof needs ordinals up to \varepsilon_0, the limit of \omega, \omega^\omega, \omega^{\omega^\omega}, \ldots.

Gödel does not say that mathematics is broken. He does not say that truth is a matter of opinion. Some theories are complete and decidable. Examples are arithmetic with only + (Presburger arithmetic) and the theory of the real numbers as an ordered field (Tarski). Also, the theorem needs a program that lists the axioms. The set of all true sentences of arithmetic is complete, but no program can list it.

In 1936 Gentzen proved that PA is consistent. This does not contradict the second theorem. His proof uses induction up to \varepsilon_0, which PA cannot do. Since then, logicians measure the strength of a theory by such ordinals.

The link to computation: the halting problem

Suppose someone sells a tool that decides whether any program stops. Below, three such tools are tested. For each tool we build a "trouble" program. Trouble asks the tool about itself and then does the opposite.

# halting.py: every claimed halting decider fails on its own "trouble" program.
import inspect

def make_trouble(decider):
    def trouble():
        if decider(trouble):       # the decider says "trouble halts"...
            while True:            # ...so trouble loops forever
                yield
        return                     # the decider says "loops", so trouble stops
        yield                      # (makes trouble a generator, run step by step)
    return trouble

def halts_within(program, steps):  # run at most `steps` steps
    gen = program()
    for _ in range(steps):
        try:
            next(gen)
        except StopIteration:
            return True
    return False

deciders = {
    "always yes": lambda prog: True,
    "always no": lambda prog: False,
    "reads the code": lambda prog: "while True" not in inspect.getsource(prog),
}
for name, decide in deciders.items():
    t = make_trouble(decide)
    said = "halts" if decide(t) else "loops"
    real = "halts" if halts_within(t, 10_000) else "still running after 10000 steps"
    print(f"{name:<15} says: {said:<6} real: {real}")
always yes      says: halts  real: still running after 10000 steps
always no       says: loops  real: halts
reads the code  says: loops  real: halts

Every tool is wrong about its own trouble program. This is not bad luck. It happens to every possible tool. A problem is decidable if one program answers it correctly for every input and always stops.

There is no program H such that, for every program P and input x, H(P, x) stops and answers correctly whether P stops on x.

Proof

Suppose H exists. Build the program D: on input P, run H(P, P). If the answer is "stops", loop forever. If the answer is "loops", stop. Now run D on itself. If D(D) stops, then H said "loops", which is wrong. If D(D) loops, then H said "stops", also wrong. So H cannot exist. It is Cantor's diagonal argument with programs instead of digits.

Turing proved this in his 1936 paper on computable numbers. He did not use the words "halting problem". The name came later, in the 1950s. Church found an equal result in 1936 with a different model. The Church-Turing thesis says that their models capture every mechanical method. It is a thesis, not a theorem, because "mechanical method" is not a formal idea.

Halting is semi-decidable. Run the program. If it stops, you know. If it runs on, you never know for sure.

The halting problem gives a version of Gödel's first theorem. Take a consistent theory T whose axioms a program can list. Suppose T proves only true facts about programs. If T proved every true sentence "P does not stop on x", we could decide halting. Run P on x and, at the same time, list all proofs of T. One of the two searches must succeed. So some true sentence of this form has no proof in T.

The same idea solves Hilbert's Entscheidungsproblem. By completeness, the valid first-order sentences are exactly the provable ones. So a program can list them. But no program decides validity. Validity is semi-decidable, like halting.

Rice's theorem extends the halting problem. Every non-trivial question about what a program does is undecidable. "Does this function ever divide by zero?" is an example. So type checkers, linters and static analysers must be careful guessers. They reject some correct programs, or they miss some errors. The Computer Science book covers Turing machines in more detail.

Undecidable does not mean "we can never know for one program". For many single programs we can prove that they stop. It means that no single program works for all programs. Also, the proof needs H to always stop. A checker that sometimes runs forever is allowed.
