Read the two tables together. HNSW reached full recall at the default setting and was about 40 times faster than the exact scan. IVFFlat needed 60 probes for 98.8 percent and was then only about 1.6 times faster. On this data HNSW wins. It pays with a bigger index and a slower build, as the memory section shows.

Filters change the maths

Suppose a query asks for the 10 nearest memories of one user, and that user owns 1 percent of the rows. The index returns about ef_search = 40 candidates, then the filter runs. On average only 40 \times 0.01 = 0.4 candidates survive. So you get fewer than 10 results. pgvector 0.8.0 added iterative index scans for this. The scan continues until enough rows pass the filter, up to a limit such as hnsw.max_scan_tuples.

SET hnsw.iterative_scan = relaxed_order;   -- keep scanning until enough rows pass
SELECT id FROM memories
WHERE user_id = 42
ORDER BY embedding <=> '[...]' LIMIT 10;

Interviews often ask: "Recall is low. What do you change?" Give the order. First raise the query setting (ef_search or probes), because it needs no rebuild. Then check filters. Only then rebuild with a larger M, ef_construction or more lists.

Compression: quantisation and its error

A 1536-number embedding in 32-bit floats takes 6,144 bytes. One million of them take 6.1 GB. Quantisation stores each vector with fewer bits. It saves memory, and it loses some accuracy. Here are three kinds.

Scalar quantisation

Round each number on its own to one of a few levels. 16-bit floats halve the memory. 8-bit integers with 256 levels use a quarter.

Product quantisation

Cut the vector into parts. Run k-means with 256 centroids on each part. Store only the number of the nearest centroid, one byte per part.

Binary quantisation

Keep one bit per number: 1 if it is above zero, else 0. Compare two codes by counting the bits that differ.

Round a number to the nearest level of a grid with step \Delta. If the rounding error is spread evenly on [-\Delta/2, \Delta/2], its mean square is \mathbb{E}[e^2] = \frac{1}{\Delta}\int_{-\Delta/2}^{\Delta/2} t^2\,dt = \frac{\Delta^2}{12}, so the typical error is \Delta / \sqrt{12} \approx 0.29\,\Delta.

Check it with real numbers. On our 128-dimension data, 8-bit scalar quantisation gave a measured typical error of 0.00082. The formula \Delta/\sqrt{12} with the average step also gave 0.00082. Each extra bit halves \Delta, so it lowers the mean square error by a factor of 4.

Binary codes are compared with the Hamming distance. Why does counting bits say anything about angles?

Let r be a random Gaussian vector. For two vectors u, v with angle \theta, P\big(\operatorname{sign}(r \cdot u) = \operatorname{sign}(r \cdot v)\big) = 1 - \frac{\theta}{\pi}.

Proof idea

Look only at the plane that holds u and v. The random vector gives a random line through 0 in this plane, at a uniform angle. The two signs differ exactly when the line falls between u and v. That happens for an angle range of 2\theta out of 2\pi.

So the expected share of different bits is \theta/\pi. This is Charikar's SimHash idea from 2002. pgvector's binary_quantize uses the fixed coordinate axes, not random ones. On our spread-out data it behaved the same. The mean share of different bits was 0.4997, and the mean of \theta/\pi was 0.4994.

Measured results

50,000 vectors, 128 dimensions, recall@10 against the exact answer
StorageBytes per vectorRecall@10After re-ranking 100
float32 (exact)5121.0001.000
float16 (halfvec)2560.9995not needed
int8 scalar1280.9915not needed
product, 16 parts160.5331.000
binary, 128 bits160.42450.939

The small codes lose a lot on their own. But they are good at making a short list. Re-ranking means this: take the best 100 by the cheap code, then sort those 100 with the exact vectors. Product quantisation then gave full recall at 16 bytes per vector. pgvector 0.8.7 offers float16 and binary indexes. It does not offer product quantisation. Libraries such as FAISS do.

CREATE INDEX ON items USING hnsw ((binary_quantize(embedding)::bit(128)) bit_hamming_ops);

SELECT id FROM (
    SELECT id, embedding FROM items
    ORDER BY binary_quantize(embedding)::bit(128) <~> binary_quantize('[...]')
    LIMIT 100                                   -- cheap short list
) shortlist
ORDER BY embedding <-> '[...]' LIMIT 10;        -- exact re-ranking

In pgvector this query gave recall 0.970 on our data with hnsw.ef_search = 100.

Binary quantisation needs data centred around zero. If every number of every vector is positive, every bit is 1, and all codes look the same. Check the mean of each dimension before you use it.

Words and ranks: BM25 and reciprocal rank fusion

A user asks the agent about "PG-17 upgrade". An embedding may match general texts about databases. A keyword search matches the exact token "PG-17". Good memory systems run both and merge the lists.

For a query with terms t and a document D of length |D|: \text{score}(D) = \sum_{t} \text{IDF}(t)\cdot \frac{f(t, D)\,(k_1 + 1)}{f(t, D) + k_1\left(1 - b + b\,\frac{|D|}{\text{avgdl}}\right)}. Here f(t, D) is the term frequency and avgdl is the average document length. Lucene uses k_1 = 1.2, b = 0.75 and \text{IDF}(t) = \ln\!\left(1 + \frac{N - n_t + 0.5}{n_t + 0.5}\right), where n_t of the N documents contain t.

Each part has a job. The inverse document frequency makes rare words count more. The fraction grows with the term frequency but never passes k_1 + 1. So the tenth "vectors" adds much less than the first. The factor with b makes long documents pay a little.

import math
docs = {
    "d1": "postgres stores vectors in a table",
    "d2": "hnsw is a graph index for vectors vectors vectors",
    "d3": "the agent remembers the user likes tea",
}
k1, b = 1.2, 0.75                                   # Lucene defaults
toks = {d: t.split() for d, t in docs.items()}
N = len(docs)
avgdl = sum(len(t) for t in toks.values()) / N

def idf(term):
    n = sum(term in t for t in toks.values())       # documents with the term
    return math.log(1 + (N - n + 0.5) / (n + 0.5))

def bm25(query, d):
    score = 0.0
    for term in query.split():
        f = toks[d].count(term)                     # term frequency
        norm = k1 * (1 - b + b * len(toks[d]) / avgdl)
        score += idf(term) * f * (k1 + 1) / (f + norm)
    return score

for d in docs:
    print(d, round(bm25("vectors graph", d), 3))
d1 0.508
d2 1.602
d3 0.0

Now we have two ranked lists with scores on different scales. Cosine scores are near 0.8. BM25 scores can be 1 or 20. Adding them is risky. Cormack, Clarke and Büttcher proposed a simple fix in 2009. It is a kind of rank fusion.

Let r_i(d) be the rank of document d in list i, with rank 1 for the best. Then \text{RRF}(d) = \sum_{i} \frac{1}{k + r_i(d)}, where a list that does not contain d adds 0. The paper fixed k = 60.

Two facts follow straight from the formula. First, it uses only ranks, so the scales of the scores do not matter. Second, agreement wins. A document at rank r in two lists beats a document at rank 1 in only one list when \frac{2}{k + r} \gt \frac{1}{k + 1}. That means r \lt k + 2. With k = 60, rank 61 in both lists still beats a single first place.

def rrf(lists, k=60):
    score = {}
    for ranked in lists:
        for rank, doc in enumerate(ranked, start=1):     # rank 1 is the best
            score[doc] = score.get(doc, 0) + 1 / (k + rank)
    return sorted(score.items(), key=lambda t: -t[1])

vector = ["m7", "m2", "m9", "m4"]        # by cosine similarity
keyword = ["m2", "m5", "m7", "m1"]       # by BM25
for k in (60, 0):
    print("k =", k, [(d, round(s, 4)) for d, s in rrf([vector, keyword], k)][:4])
k = 60 [('m2', 0.0325), ('m7', 0.0323), ('m5', 0.0161), ('m9', 0.0159)]
k = 0 [('m2', 1.5), ('m7', 1.3333), ('m5', 0.5), ('m9', 0.3333)]

A small k trusts the top ranks a lot. A large k makes the curve flat, so many lists must agree. Real projects choose differently, as we found in their code on 2026-11-15.

  • Hindsight (v1.2.1) fuses four lists with k = 60: semantic, BM25, graph and time.
  • Graphiti (v0.31.2) adds 1/(i + 1) for a position i that starts at 0. That is the formula with k = 0.
  • mem0 (v2.2.1) does not use ranks. It squeezes BM25 into 0 to 1 with a sigmoid, adds the cosine score and an entity bonus, and divides by the best possible total.
WITH v AS (
  SELECT id, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY embedding <=> '[1,0.1,0]') AS r
  FROM memories ORDER BY embedding <=> '[1,0.1,0]' LIMIT 20
), t AS (
  SELECT id, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY ts_rank_cd(to_tsvector('english', note), q) DESC) AS r
  FROM memories, plainto_tsquery('english', 'tea') q
  WHERE to_tsvector('english', note) @@ q LIMIT 20
)
SELECT m.note, v.r AS vec_rank, t.r AS text_rank,
       round(COALESCE(1.0 / (60 + v.r), 0) + COALESCE(1.0 / (60 + t.r), 0), 5) AS rrf
FROM v FULL JOIN t ON v.id = t.id
JOIN memories m ON m.id = COALESCE(v.id, t.id)
ORDER BY rrf DESC LIMIT 4;
note=User likes green tea in the morning | vec_rank=1 | text_rank=1 | rrf=0.03279
note=User is allergic to milk in tea     | vec_rank=3 | text_rank=2 | rrf=0.03200
note=The tea shop opens at nine          | vec_rank=4 | text_rank=3 | rrf=0.03150
note=User drinks coffee at work          | vec_rank=2 |             | rrf=0.01613

PostgreSQL's built-in ts_rank_cd is not BM25. It does not use document frequency across the table in the same way. If you need true BM25 inside PostgreSQL, you need an extension or a separate search engine. RRF still works, because it only needs the order.

Agent memory: caching, forgetting and time

A memory store is like a small fast desk next to a large slow archive. The desk is the cache. When the desk is full, one item must leave. Choosing it is called eviction.

If you know all future requests, the best rule is: evict the item whose next request is furthest in the future. It gives the fewest misses of all rules.

Nobody knows the future, so systems use Least Recently Used (LRU). It evicts the item unused for the longest time. To compare an online rule with the best rule, we use the competitive ratio.

Let LRU have a cache of size k. Against the best offline rule with a cache of size h \le k, LRU makes at most \frac{k}{k - h + 1} times as many misses, apart from a small constant. With h = k the ratio is k, and no deterministic online rule does better.

Proof idea

Cut the request list into blocks. Each block is as long as possible with only k different items. LRU misses at most k times per block, once per item. A block and the first request of the next block ask for k + 1 different items. So the best rule with h slots misses at least k - h + 1 times in each such window. Divide the two counts.

In simple words: give LRU twice the memory of the perfect rule, and it is at most about 2 times worse. Real traffic is kinder than the worst case. Requests often follow Zipf's law. We simulated 100,000 Zipf requests over 10,000 items.

Hit rate under Zipf requests (cache_sim.py)
Cache sizeLRUBelady
100.1330.331
1000.3900.581
10000.6730.808

A cache with only 10 percent of the items served 67 percent of the requests. This is why a small "hot" memory in RAM can make an agent feel fast.

Forgetting as a formula

Old memories often matter less. One simple model multiplies the relevance by a decay factor with a half-life h: \text{score}(t) = \text{similarity} \cdot 2^{-t/h}. With h = 7 days, a memory from two weeks ago keeps one quarter of its score.

We checked the code of three projects for this on 2026-11-15. mem0 v2.2.1 has no decay. It hides a memory only after its expiration_date. Graphiti does not forget either. It stores time on each fact instead.

Two clocks for every fact

A bi-temporal record keeps two time ranges. Valid time says when the fact was true in the world. System time says when the store learned it and when it was retired. Graphiti edges carry valid_at, invalid_at, created_at and expired_at.

  1. Fact 1: "Ana works at Acme", valid from 2023-02 to 2026-06.
  2. Fact 2: "Ana works at Beta", valid from 2026-06 with no end.
  3. The question asks about time t = 2025-05. Keep facts with \text{valid\_at} \le t and t \lt \text{invalid\_at}.
  4. Only fact 1 passes. The answer is Acme. Nothing was deleted, so the history stays correct.

Three real memory systems

mem0 (v2.2.1, Apache-2.0)

Problem. A chat assistant forgets the user between sessions. Sending the whole history costs too many tokens.

How it works. add asks an LLM to extract short facts from new messages. It looks up the 10 most similar old memories and drops exact duplicates by hash. search runs a vector search and a BM25 search with a candidate pool of \max(4 \cdot \text{top\_k}, 60), adds entity bonuses, and returns the best top_k (20 by default).

Theory. Score fusion: (\text{cosine} + \sigma(\text{BM25}) + \text{bonus}) / 2.5. For cosine 0.82, raw BM25 6.1 and bonus 0.3 we computed 0.7214.

Trade-off. Scores on different scales need hand-tuned sigmoids. The authors publish benchmark numbers for their managed platform. They say the open-source version is only "directionally similar".

Graphiti (v0.31.2, Apache-2.0)

Problem. Facts change over time. A flat list of memories cannot say what was true last March.

How it works. It builds a temporal knowledge graph of entities and fact edges. Search can use cosine similarity, BM25 and breadth-first search, then rerank with RRF, maximal marginal relevance, node distance or a cross-encoder.

Theory. Bi-temporal intervals, RRF with k = 0, and graph distance as a relevance signal. Its default minimum cosine score is 0.6 and its default search depth is 3.

Trade-off. You run a graph database (Neo4j, FalkorDB, Kuzu or Neptune). Writing needs LLM calls to extract and resolve entities.

Hindsight (v1.2.1, MIT)

Problem. The authors want agents that learn from experience, not only recall chat history.

How it works. Memories live in isolated banks. retain extracts facts, entities and times. recall runs four searches in parallel and fuses them with RRF. A cross-encoder then reranks, and the result is cut to a token budget. reflect reasons over stored memories. Storage is PostgreSQL with pgvector.

Theory. RRF with k = 60, the HNSW index from pgvector, and a token budget as a hard limit.

Trade-off. Four searches plus a reranker cost more time per recall than one vector query. The authors report top LongMemEval results. Those are their own numbers.

How much memory an index needs

Here is the question every team asks. "We have one million memories with 1536-dimension embeddings. How much RAM do we need?" Let us compute it step by step for pgvector.

  1. One vector value takes 4 \cdot 1536 + 8 = 6{,}152 bytes. The table holds about 10^6 \times 6{,}152 \approx 6.2 GB.
  2. A pgvector HNSW index also stores the vector in each node. So it needs another 6.2 GB plus the graph.
  3. Graph links: floor 0 has 2M = 32 links, and the upper floors add about 16/15 \approx 1.1 links on average. Each link is a 6-byte row pointer. That is about 33 \times 6 \approx 200 bytes per node.
  4. Page headers and free space add more. In our test the index used about 312 bytes per vector on top of the vector itself.
  5. Total HNSW index: about 10^6 \times (6{,}152 + 312) \approx 6.5 GB. Table plus index: about 12.7 GB.

Now compare cheaper storage for the index. A halfvec takes 2 \cdot 1536 + 8 = 3{,}080 bytes. A binary code takes 1536 / 8 = 192 bytes plus a small header.

Estimated HNSW index size for one million 1536-dimension vectors (M = 16)
Index onVector bytesGraph and overheadTotal
vector (float32)6,152about 312about 6.5 GB
halfvec (float16)3,080about 312about 3.4 GB
binary_quantize, bit(1536)about 200about 312about 0.5 GB

We checked the pattern on our 50,000-vector test table with 128 dimensions. The table took 29.4 MB. The float32 HNSW index took 41.6 MB, the halfvec index 28.5 MB and the binary index 15.9 MB. With small codes, the graph becomes the biggest part. Then a smaller M saves more memory than more compression.

For n vectors, \text{memory} \approx n \cdot (\text{bytes per code} + \text{bytes per node for links and headers}). For HNSW the links grow like M. For IVF they are almost free, but recall needs more probes.

An HNSW index is fast only when its pages are in RAM. If the index is twice the size of memory, most steps of the greedy walk read from disk. Then a query takes many milliseconds. Size the RAM for the index first, then for everything else.

Building an HNSW index is much faster when the graph fits in maintenance_work_mem. pgvector prints a notice when it no longer fits. Do not set this so high that the server runs out of memory.

Practice

In pgvector, which operator orders rows by cosine distance?

  • <->
  • <#>
  • <=>

<=> is cosine distance. <-> is Euclidean distance. <#> is the negative inner product.

Two unit vectors have cosine similarity 0.9. Their squared Euclidean distance is ?.

With HNSW and M = 16, the share of nodes that reach floor 2 is 1 in ?.

An IVFFlat index has recall 0.73 with one probe. What is the cheapest first fix?

  • Rebuild with twice as many lists.
  • Raise ivfflat.probes for the query.
  • Switch from float32 to binary codes.

More probes open more cells. It needs no rebuild. More lists alone make each cell smaller and often lower recall at one probe.

  1. Use RRF with k = 60. Document X is rank 1 in the vector list and missing from the keyword list. Document Y is rank 5 in both lists. Which wins?
    Answer

    X scores 1/61 \approx 0.01639. Y scores 2/65 \approx 0.03077. Y wins, because 5 \lt k + 2 = 62.

  2. A table has 4 million rows. Give a starting lists and probes for IVFFlat.
    Answer

    Above one million rows use \sqrt{\text{rows}} = \sqrt{4{,}000{,}000} = 2000 lists. Then start with \sqrt{2000} \approx 45 probes.

  3. Estimate a halfvec HNSW index for 10 million vectors with 768 dimensions and M = 16.
    Answer

    One halfvec takes 2 \cdot 768 + 8 = 1{,}544 bytes. Add about 312 bytes for links and headers. That is 1,856 bytes per vector, so about 10^7 \times 1{,}856 \approx 18.6 GB.

  4. An 8-bit scalar quantiser covers values from -0.2 to 0.2. What is the typical rounding error?
    Answer

    The step is \Delta = 0.4 / 255 \approx 0.00157. The typical error is \Delta / \sqrt{12} \approx 0.00045.

  5. Why does the Johnson-Lindenstrauss bound not depend on the original dimension d?
    Answer

    The proof looks at one difference vector at a time. Its projected squared length is a sum of k independent squared Gaussians, whatever d is. The concentration depends only on k. The union bound over the n^2/2 pairs brings in \ln n.

  6. A user filter keeps 2 percent of the rows, and hnsw.ef_search is 40. About how many candidates survive the filter without iterative scans? What do you do?
    Answer

    About 40 \times 0.02 = 0.8 rows. Turn on hnsw.iterative_scan, or use a partial index or a partition for big users.

  7. Hard. Show that Lloyd's algorithm can stop at a bad answer. Use the four points (0,0), (0,1), (4,0), (4,1) with k = 2.
    Answer

    Start with centroids (2, 0) and (2, 1). Step A gives the bottom two points to the first and the top two to the second. Step B leaves both centroids where they are. Cost: each point is 2 away, so J = 4 \cdot 4 = 16. The good split, left pair and right pair, has centroids (0, 0.5) and (4, 0.5) and cost 4 \cdot 0.25 = 1. The algorithm stopped at a local minimum.

  8. Hard. Prove that cosine distance 1 - \cos\theta breaks the triangle inequality. Use unit vectors at angles 0, 45 and 90 degrees in the plane.
    Answer

    From 0 to 90 degrees the cosine distance is 1 - 0 = 1. Each 45-degree step costs 1 - \cos 45^\circ \approx 0.293. The detour costs 0.586 \lt 1. So the direct way is longer than the detour, and it is not a metric. The angle \theta itself, or \sqrt{2 - 2\cos\theta}, is a metric.

Key takeaways

  • On unit vectors, cosine similarity, inner product and Euclidean distance give the same order, because \|u - v\|^2 = 2 - 2\cos\theta.
  • In high dimensions random distances become almost equal, but real embeddings have structure, and random projection keeps distances with only about \ln n dimensions.
  • IVF searches a few Voronoi cells found by k-means. HNSW walks a layered small-world graph. Both trade recall for speed through one query setting.
  • Quantisation error follows \Delta^2/12. Tiny codes plus exact re-ranking keep recall high with a fraction of the memory.
  • RRF merges keyword and vector lists using only ranks. Caching, decay and bi-temporal facts are the maths of what an agent keeps and forgets.

Theorem atlas and exam practice

This chapter ties the whole book together. It teaches you how to read and write proofs, ranks the 100 theorems worth knowing, and gives you four practice exams with full solutions. Use it as a map and as a gym.

  • Read a theorem by finding its hypotheses, its conclusion and its quantifiers.
  • Read a proof actively and check where each hypothesis is used.
  • Write clear proofs with the five main methods.
  • Find any of the 100 ranked theorems and the chapter that proves it.
  • Test yourself with four exams, from basic to graduate entry, and follow a study plan.

How to read a theorem

Here is a theorem from the Derivatives chapter: "If f is differentiable at a, then f is continuous at a." It has two parts. The part after "if" is the hypothesis. The part after "then" is the conclusion.

Read every theorem with the same five steps. They take two minutes, and they save hours later.

  1. Name the objects. A function f and an interval [a, b].
  2. List the hypotheses. f is continuous, and the interval is closed and bounded.
  3. Say the conclusion in your own words. f reaches a largest value and a smallest value on [a, b].
  4. Test it with an example. f(x) = x^2 on [-1, 2] has a maximum 4 at x = 2 and a minimum 0 at x = 0.
  5. Drop one hypothesis and look for a failure. On the open interval (0, 1), the function f(x) = x has no largest value. So "closed" is needed.

Step 5 is the most useful. A counterexample for each dropped hypothesis tells you why that hypothesis is there. For the intermediate value theorem, drop continuity. The step function that is -1 for x \lt 0 and 1 for x \ge 0 changes sign but never equals 0.

Quantifiers

A quantifier says how many objects a statement talks about. "For all" is written \forall. "There exists" is written \exists. Their order matters a lot.

  • \forall x\ \exists y : y \gt x. For every number there is a bigger one. True.
  • \exists y\ \forall x : y \gt x. One number is bigger than all numbers. False.

Do not read a theorem backwards. "Differentiable implies continuous" is true. The converse, "continuous implies differentiable", is false. The function |x| is continuous at 0 but has a corner there.

How to read a proof

A proof is not a story to read once. It is a machine to check part by part. Here is a short one.

  1. Method: we prove the contrapositive. If n is odd, then n^2 is odd.
  2. Let n be odd. Then n = 2k + 1 for some integer k.
  3. Square it. n^2 = 4k^2 + 4k + 1 = 2(2k^2 + 2k) + 1.
  4. This has the form "2 times an integer plus 1". So n^2 is odd.

Now read it like a checker. Ask four questions at each line.

  • Which method is this? Here it is the contrapositive.
  • Where is each hypothesis used? "Odd" is used in line 2 only.
  • Can I check this step with numbers? Try k = 3: n = 7, n^2 = 49 = 2 \cdot 24 + 1. Yes.
  • Can I say the idea in one sentence? "Odd times odd is odd."

Big proofs use smaller theorems. The book draws these links as a graph. Here is one small part of it, from the Number theory chapter.

When a proof uses a theorem you do not know, follow the link and read only its statement. Come back and finish the proof. Read the second proof later. This keeps you moving.

"I followed every line, so I understand it." Not yet. Close the book and write the proof again from the one-sentence idea. If you cannot, you have only followed it.

How to write a proof

Every proof has the same shape. State the claim. Set up the objects with "Let". Say the method. Do the steps. Say clearly that you are done.

Claim: a^2 + b^2 \ge 2ab for all real a, b. Proof: a^2 + b^2 \ge 2ab, so a^2 - 2ab + b^2 \ge 0, so (a - b)^2 \ge 0. This is true, so the claim is true.

This starts from the claim and ends with something true. That only shows "claim implies true", which proves nothing.

Claim: a^2 + b^2 \ge 2ab for all real a, b. Proof: Let a, b be real. A square is never negative, so (a - b)^2 \ge 0. Expand: a^2 - 2ab + b^2 \ge 0. Add 2ab to both sides: a^2 + b^2 \ge 2ab. Done.

This starts from a known fact and ends with the claim. Each arrow points the right way.

Direct proof

Assume the hypothesis and walk to the conclusion. Claim: the sum of two even numbers is even. Let them be 2a and 2b. Their sum is 2(a + b), which is even.

Contrapositive

To prove "if P then Q", prove "if not Q then not P". We did this above for "if n^2 is even then n is even".

Contradiction

Assume the claim is false and reach something impossible. The proof that \sqrt 2 is irrational assumes \sqrt 2 = p/q in lowest terms and shows that p and q are both even.

Cases

Split into cases that cover everything. Claim: n^2 + n is even. If n is even, n^2 + n = n(n + 1) has the even factor n. If n is odd, the factor n + 1 is even.

Induction

Claim: 2^n \ge n + 1 for n \ge 0. Base: 2^0 = 1 \ge 1. Step: if 2^n \ge n + 1, then 2^{n+1} = 2 \cdot 2^n \ge 2n + 2 \ge n + 2.

Some goals have a fixed opening move. To prove a "for all" statement, start with "Let x be any ...". To prove a "there exists" statement, build the object and check it. To prove "A if and only if B", prove both directions. To prove two sets are equal, show each is inside the other.

Examples are not proofs. "It works for 1, 2, 3 and 100" proves nothing about all numbers. The formula n^2 + n + 41 gives primes for n = 0, 1, \dots, 39, but at n = 40 it gives 41^2. One counterexample, though, does disprove a "for all" claim.

Examiners give marks for structure. Write the definition you will use in the first line, for example "n is odd means n = 2k + 1". Name the method. End with a clear last line. Even an unfinished proof with this shape gets partial marks.

The 100 theorems to know

Here is our ranking of the 100 theorems that matter most for this book. We ranked them by two things: how often an AI engineer uses the idea, and how much other mathematics stands on it. The ranking is our own choice. Another author would order them differently.

Each line gives the theorem, one sentence in simple words, and the chapter that proves it. Click the theorem to jump to its exact statement. Click the chapter to read it from the start.

A well-known list of 100 theorems from 1999 is used by Freek Wiedijk's page on formal proofs. That page tracks which theorems computer proof checkers such as Lean and Isabelle have verified. In November 2026 it reports that all 100 theorems of that list are now formalised in at least one system.

Practice exam 1: basic

This exam covers numbers, first algebra, geometry and simple chance. Give yourself 60 minutes. Write full answers, then open the solutions.

  1. Find \gcd(84, 120) and \operatorname{lcm}(84, 120).
    Solution

    Factor both numbers. 84 = 2^2 \cdot 3 \cdot 7 and 120 = 2^3 \cdot 3 \cdot 5. The gcd takes the smaller power of each shared prime: 2^2 \cdot 3 = 12. The lcm takes the larger power of every prime: 2^3 \cdot 3 \cdot 5 \cdot 7 = 840. Check: 12 \cdot 840 = 10080 = 84 \cdot 120.

  2. Compute 8^{2/3} + 27^{-1/3} as a fraction.
    Solution

    8^{1/3} = 2, so 8^{2/3} = 2^2 = 4. 27^{1/3} = 3, so 27^{-1/3} = 1/3. The sum is 4 + \frac13 = \frac{13}{3}.

  3. A price goes up by 20 percent and then down by 20 percent. What is the total change?
    Solution

    Multiply the factors: 1.2 \times 0.8 = 0.96. The final price is 96 percent of the start. It fell by 4 percent. The two changes do not cancel, because the second 20 percent is taken from a bigger number.

  4. Solve 3(x - 2) = 2x + 5.
    Solution

    Expand: 3x - 6 = 2x + 5. Take 2x from both sides: x - 6 = 5. So x = 11. Check: 3 \cdot 9 = 27 and 22 + 5 = 27.

  5. Solve x^2 - 5x + 6 = 0.
    Solution

    Find two numbers with sum 5 and product 6. They are 2 and 3. So (x - 2)(x - 3) = 0, and x = 2 or x = 3.

  6. A right triangle has legs 9 and 12. Find the longest side, the area, and the height onto the longest side.
    Solution

    By the Pythagorean theorem, c = \sqrt{81 + 144} = \sqrt{225} = 15. The area is \frac12 \cdot 9 \cdot 12 = 54. The same area is \frac12 \cdot 15 \cdot h. So h = 108 / 15 = 7.2.

  7. Prove that the sum of two odd numbers is even.
    Solution

    Let the numbers be 2a + 1 and 2b + 1 with integers a, b. Their sum is 2a + 2b + 2 = 2(a + b + 1). This is 2 times an integer, so it is even.

  8. You save 1000 euros at 5 percent interest per year, added to the balance each year. How much do you have after 3 years?
    Solution

    Each year multiplies the balance by 1.05. After 3 years: 1000 \cdot 1.05^3 = 1157.625, about 1157.63 euros. Simple interest would give only 1150, because it does not earn interest on interest.

  9. Find the line through (1, 2) and (4, 11).
    Solution

    The slope is \frac{11 - 2}{4 - 1} = 3. Use the point (1, 2): y - 2 = 3(x - 1), so y = 3x - 1. Check the other point: 3 \cdot 4 - 1 = 11.

  10. Roll two fair dice. Find the probability that the sum is 7, and the probability that the sum is at least 10.
    Solution

    There are 36 equally likely pairs. Sum 7 comes from (1,6), (2,5), (3,4), (4,3), (5,2), (6,1): 6 pairs, so 6/36 = 1/6. Sum at least 10 comes from (4,6), (5,5), (6,4), (5,6), (6,5), (6,6): also 6 pairs, so 1/6.

  11. Prove that \sqrt 3 is irrational.
    Solution

    Suppose \sqrt 3 = p/q with integers in lowest terms. Then p^2 = 3q^2, so 3 divides p^2. Since 3 is prime, Euclid's lemma gives 3 \mid p. Write p = 3k. Then 9k^2 = 3q^2, so q^2 = 3k^2, and in the same way 3 \mid q. Now 3 divides both p and q. This contradicts "lowest terms". So \sqrt 3 is irrational.

  12. Find 3 + 7 + 11 + \dots + 99.
    Solution

    This is an arithmetic sequence with first term 3 and difference 4. The number of terms is \frac{99 - 3}{4} + 1 = 25. By the arithmetic series formula the sum is \frac{25\,(3 + 99)}{2} = 1275.

Practice exam 2: intermediate

This exam covers functions, one-variable calculus, trigonometry, vectors, complex numbers and series. Give yourself 90 minutes.

  1. Find \displaystyle\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{\sin 3x}{x}.
    Solution

    Write \frac{\sin 3x}{x} = 3 \cdot \frac{\sin 3x}{3x}. Put u = 3x. As x \to 0, also u \to 0, and \frac{\sin u}{u} \to 1. So the limit is 3.

  2. Differentiate g(x) = x^2 e^{3x}.
    Solution

    Use the product rule and the chain rule. g'(x) = 2x \cdot e^{3x} + x^2 \cdot 3e^{3x} = x e^{3x}(3x + 2).

  3. Compute \int_0^1 x e^x\,dx.
    Solution

    Use integration by parts with u = x and dv = e^x dx. Then \int_0^1 x e^x dx = [x e^x]_0^1 - \int_0^1 e^x dx = e - (e - 1) = 1.

  4. Solve 2^{x+1} = 24.
    Solution

    Divide by 2: 2^x = 12. Take \log_2: x = \log_2 12 = 2 + \log_2 3 \approx 3.585. Check: 2^{4.585} \approx 24.

  5. A rectangle has perimeter 20. Which sides give the largest area?
    Solution

    Let the sides be x and 10 - x. The area is A(x) = 10x - x^2. Then A'(x) = 10 - 2x = 0 at x = 5, and A''(x) = -2 \lt 0, so it is a maximum. The best rectangle is a 5 by 5 square with area 25.

  6. Find the sum 6 + 2 + \frac23 + \frac29 + \dots.
    Solution

    This is geometric with a = 6 and r = \frac13. Since |r| \lt 1, the geometric series formula gives \frac{6}{1 - 1/3} = 9.

  7. Prove by induction that 1 + 3 + 5 + \dots + (2n - 1) = n^2 for all n \ge 1.
    Solution

    Base case: for n = 1 both sides are 1. Step: assume the sum of the first n odd numbers is n^2. Add the next odd number, 2n + 1. The new sum is n^2 + 2n + 1 = (n + 1)^2. That is the formula for n + 1. By the principle of induction, it holds for all n \ge 1.

  8. Find the exact value of \sin 75^\circ.
    Solution

    Use the angle addition formula: \sin(45^\circ + 30^\circ) = \sin 45^\circ \cos 30^\circ + \cos 45^\circ \sin 30^\circ = \frac{\sqrt2}{2}\cdot\frac{\sqrt3}{2} + \frac{\sqrt2}{2}\cdot\frac12 = \frac{\sqrt6 + \sqrt2}{4} \approx 0.9659.

  9. Find the angle between u = (1, 1, 0) and v = (1, 0, 1).
    Solution

    u \cdot v = 1. Both lengths are \sqrt 2. So \cos\theta = \frac{1}{\sqrt2 \cdot \sqrt2} = \frac12, and \theta = 60^\circ.

  10. Compute (1 + i)^8.
    Solution

    First (1 + i)^2 = 1 + 2i + i^2 = 2i. Then (1 + i)^8 = (2i)^4 = 16\, i^4 = 16. With polar form: 1 + i = \sqrt2\, e^{i\pi/4}, so the eighth power is 16\, e^{2\pi i} = 16.

  11. Write the Taylor polynomial of degree 3 for \ln(1 + x) at 0. Use it to estimate \ln 1.1, and bound the error.
    Solution

    The polynomial is x - \frac{x^2}{2} + \frac{x^3}{3}. At x = 0.1: 0.1 - 0.005 + 0.000333 = 0.095333. The series alternates with shrinking terms, so the error is below the next term, \frac{0.1^4}{4} = 0.000025. The true value is 0.0953102. The error is about 0.0000232, inside the bound.

  12. Find the inverse of A = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 5 & 3 \end{pmatrix}.
    Solution

    \det A = 6 - 5 = 1. For a 2 by 2 matrix, swap the diagonal, change the signs of the other two entries, and divide by the determinant: A^{-1} = \begin{pmatrix} 3 & -1 \\ -5 & 2 \end{pmatrix}. Check: A A^{-1} = \begin{pmatrix} 6 - 5 & -2 + 2 \\ 15 - 15 & -5 + 6 \end{pmatrix} = I.

Practice exam 3: hard

This exam covers linear algebra, many variables, probability, counting, number theory and graphs. Give yourself 2 hours.

  1. Diagonalise A = \begin{pmatrix} 4 & 1 \\ 2 & 3 \end{pmatrix}.
    Solution

    The characteristic polynomial is \lambda^2 - 7\lambda + 10 = (\lambda - 5)(\lambda - 2). For \lambda = 5, A - 5I = \begin{pmatrix} -1 & 1 \\ 2 & -2 \end{pmatrix} gives v_1 = (1, 1). For \lambda = 2, A - 2I = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 2 & 1 \end{pmatrix} gives v_2 = (1, -2). So A = PDP^{-1} with P = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & -2 \end{pmatrix} and D = \operatorname{diag}(5, 2). Check: trace 7 = 5 + 2 and determinant 10 = 5 \cdot 2.

  2. Fit the least squares line y = a + bx to the points (0, 1), (1, 3), (2, 4), (3, 4).
    Solution

    The normal equations are 4a + 6b = 12 and 6a + 14b = 23. Solve: a = 1.5, b = 1. So y = 1.5 + x. The residuals are -0.5, 0.5, 0.5, -0.5. They add to 0, as they must when the model has an intercept.

  3. Find and classify the critical points of f(x, y) = x^3 - 3x + y^2.
    Solution

    Set the partial derivatives to 0: 3x^2 - 3 = 0 and 2y = 0. So the points are (1, 0) and (-1, 0). The Hessian is \operatorname{diag}(6x, 2). At (1, 0) it is \operatorname{diag}(6, 2), positive definite, so a local minimum with f = -2. At (-1, 0) its determinant is -12 \lt 0, so it is a saddle point.

  4. Maximise xy subject to x + 2y = 8 with x, y \gt 0.
    Solution

    With Lagrange multipliers: (y, x) = \lambda (1, 2), so y = \lambda and x = 2\lambda. The constraint gives 4\lambda = 8, so \lambda = 2, x = 4, y = 2, and xy = 8. Check by substitution: (8 - 2y)y has its top at y = 2.

  5. Compute \iint_{x^2 + y^2 \le 4} e^{-(x^2 + y^2)}\,dA.
    Solution

    Change to polar coordinates. The Jacobian adds a factor r. \int_0^{2\pi}\!\int_0^2 e^{-r^2} r\,dr\,d\theta = 2\pi \left[ -\tfrac12 e^{-r^2} \right]_0^2 = \pi (1 - e^{-4}) \approx 3.084.

  6. A disease affects 1 percent of people. A test finds 95 percent of sick people and wrongly flags 5 percent of healthy people. A person tests positive. How likely is it that they are sick?
    Solution

    By Bayes' theorem: P(\text{sick} \mid +) = \frac{0.01 \cdot 0.95}{0.01 \cdot 0.95 + 0.99 \cdot 0.05} = \frac{0.0095}{0.059} = \frac{19}{118} \approx 0.161. Only about 16 percent. Most positives come from the large healthy group.

  7. Shuffle n cards numbered 1 to n at random. What is the expected number of cards that land in their own place?
    Solution

    Let I_k = 1 if card k is in place k, else 0. Then P(I_k = 1) = 1/n. By linearity of expectation, the expected count is n \cdot \frac1n = 1, for every n. The I_k depend on each other, but linearity does not need independence.

  8. How many solutions in non-negative integers does x_1 + x_2 + x_3 + x_4 = 10 have?
    Solution

    By stars and bars, put 10 stars and 3 bars in a row. Choose the places of the bars: \binom{13}{3} = 286.

  9. Solve 7x \equiv 3 \pmod{26}.
    Solution

    Find the inverse of 7 with the Euclidean algorithm. 26 = 3 \cdot 7 + 5, 7 = 1 \cdot 5 + 2, 5 = 2 \cdot 2 + 1. Backwards: 1 = 3 \cdot 26 - 11 \cdot 7. So 7^{-1} \equiv -11 \equiv 15. Then x \equiv 15 \cdot 3 = 45 \equiv 19 \pmod{26}. Check: 7 \cdot 19 = 133 = 5 \cdot 26 + 3.

  10. Prove that a finite graph in which every vertex has degree at least 2 contains a cycle.
    Solution

    Take a longest path v_0 v_1 \dots v_k. The vertex v_0 has at least two neighbours. One is v_1. Call another one w. If w were not on the path, the path w v_0 v_1 \dots v_k would be longer. So w = v_i for some i \ge 2. Then v_0 v_1 \dots v_i v_0 is a cycle.

  11. Prove that there are infinitely many primes of the form 4k + 3.
    Solution

    Suppose there are only finitely many: p_1, \dots, p_m. Let N = 4 p_1 \cdots p_m - 1. Then N \equiv 3 \pmod 4, and N is odd. A product of numbers that are all 1 \bmod 4 is 1 \bmod 4. So N has a prime factor q \equiv 3 \pmod 4. Then q is one of the p_i. It divides 4 p_1 \cdots p_m and N, so it divides their difference, 1. That is impossible.

  12. Flip a fair coin 100 times and let X be the number of heads. Bound P(|X - 50| \ge 10) with Chebyshev and with Hoeffding. Which bound is better? Repeat for a gap of 20.
    Solution

    X is a sum of 100 independent flips, each with variance \frac14. So \operatorname{Var} X = 25. Chebyshev: P \le 25 / 10^2 = 0.25. Hoeffding: P \le 2 e^{-2 \cdot 10^2 / 100} = 2e^{-2} \approx 0.271. Chebyshev wins at this small gap. For a gap of 20: Chebyshev gives 25/400 = 0.0625, Hoeffding gives 2e^{-8} \approx 0.00067. Now Hoeffding wins by far. The exact values are about 0.0569 and 0.0000785.

Practice exam 4: graduate entry

This exam has the style of graduate entry tests such as the GRE Mathematics Subject Test. In November 2026, ETS describes that test as about 66 multiple-choice questions in 2 hours and 50 minutes. About half the questions are on calculus and about a quarter on algebra. Check the official page before you book, because formats change. Our exam is shorter and mixes multiple choice with proofs. Give yourself 2 hours.

1. What is \displaystyle\lim_{n \to \infty} \left( 1 + \frac{2}{n} \right)^n?

  • 1
  • 2
  • e
  • e^2
  • \infty

Take logs: n \ln(1 + 2/n). As n \to \infty, \ln(1 + 2/n) \approx 2/n, so the product tends to 2. The limit is e^2.

2. What is the radius of convergence of \displaystyle\sum_{n \ge 1} \frac{n!}{n^n} x^n?

  • 0
  • 1
  • 1/e
  • e
  • \infty

Use the ratio test. \frac{a_{n+1}}{a_n} = \frac{(n+1)!\, n^n}{(n+1)^{n+1}\, n!} = \left( \frac{n}{n+1} \right)^n \to \frac1e. So the series converges when |x|/e \lt 1. The radius is e.

3. How many group homomorphisms are there from \mathbb{Z}_{12} to \mathbb{Z}_{18}?

  • 1
  • 3
  • 6
  • 12
  • 18

A homomorphism is fixed by the image a of 1. It needs 12a \equiv 0 \pmod{18}, so 18 \mid 12a, so 3 \mid 2a, so 3 \mid a. The choices are 0, 3, 6, 9, 12, 15. That is 6, which equals \gcd(12, 18).

4. How many elements of order 2 does the symmetric group S_4 have?

  • 3
  • 6
  • 9
  • 12
  • 24

An element of order 2 is a single swap or two disjoint swaps. Single swaps: \binom42 = 6. Two disjoint swaps: 3. Total 9.

  1. (5) Compute \int_0^\infty x^2 e^{-x}\,dx.
    Solution

    Integrate by parts twice, or use \int_0^\infty x^n e^{-x} dx = n!. The answer is 2! = 2. By parts: \int_0^\infty x^2 e^{-x} dx = [-x^2 e^{-x}]_0^\infty + 2\int_0^\infty x e^{-x} dx = 0 + 2 \cdot 1 = 2.

  2. (6) A real 3 by 3 matrix A has eigenvalues 1, 2 and 3. Find \det(A^2 + I) and \operatorname{tr}(A^2 + I).
    Solution

    If Av = \lambda v, then (A^2 + I)v = (\lambda^2 + 1)v. So the eigenvalues of A^2 + I are 2, 5 and 10. The determinant is their product, 100. The trace is their sum, 17.

  3. (7) Use residues to compute \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \frac{dx}{(x^2 + 1)^2}.
    Solution

    Close the path with a large half circle in the upper half plane. The integral over the half circle tends to 0. The only pole inside is z = i, of order 2. Its residue is \frac{d}{dz} (z + i)^{-2} at z = i, which is -2 (2i)^{-3} = \frac{-2}{-8i} = \frac{1}{4i}. The residue theorem gives 2\pi i \cdot \frac{1}{4i} = \frac{\pi}{2}.

  4. (8) Prove that every continuous f : [0, 1] \to [0, 1] has a fixed point.
    Solution

    Let g(x) = f(x) - x. It is continuous. g(0) = f(0) \ge 0 and g(1) = f(1) - 1 \le 0. By the intermediate value theorem, g(c) = 0 for some c \in [0, 1]. Then f(c) = c. This is the one-dimensional case of Brouwer's theorem.

  5. (9) Find the dimensions of the spaces of real symmetric and of real skew-symmetric 3 by 3 matrices. Show that every 3 by 3 matrix is the sum of one of each.
    Solution

    A symmetric matrix is fixed by its diagonal and the entries above it: 3 + 3 = 6. A skew-symmetric matrix has zeros on the diagonal and is fixed by the 3 entries above it: 3. Every A equals \frac{A + A^\top}{2} + \frac{A - A^\top}{2}. The first part is symmetric and the second is skew. The only matrix in both spaces is 0, and 6 + 3 = 9 is the dimension of all 3 by 3 matrices.

  6. (10) Solve y'' - 3y' + 2y = 0 with y(0) = 1 and y'(0) = 0.
    Solution

    The characteristic equation r^2 - 3r + 2 = 0 has roots 1 and 2. So y = c_1 e^t + c_2 e^{2t}. The conditions give c_1 + c_2 = 1 and c_1 + 2c_2 = 0. So c_2 = -1, c_1 = 2, and y = 2e^t - e^{2t}.

  7. (11) Let X and Y be independent and uniform on [0, 1]. Find P(X + Y \le \frac12) and E[\max(X, Y)].
    Solution

    The pair is uniform on the unit square. The region x + y \le \frac12 is a triangle with legs \frac12, so its area is \frac18. For the maximum, P(\max \le t) = P(X \le t)P(Y \le t) = t^2. Its density is 2t, so E[\max] = \int_0^1 t \cdot 2t\,dt = \frac23.

  8. (12) Prove that \sum_{n \ge 1} \frac{\sin(nx)}{n^2} converges uniformly on \mathbb{R} to a continuous function. Can you differentiate it term by term on all of \mathbb{R}?
    Solution

    Each term is bounded by \frac{1}{n^2}, and \sum \frac{1}{n^2} converges. The Weierstrass M-test gives uniform convergence. A uniform limit of continuous functions is continuous. Term-by-term derivatives give \sum \frac{\cos(nx)}{n}. At x = 0 this is the harmonic series, which diverges. So you cannot differentiate term by term on all of \mathbb{R}.

A study plan

Here is a plan for 12 weeks with about one hour a day. Each block ends with an exam from this chapter. Move faster through parts you already know.

  1. Weeks 1 to 2 Numbers, algebra and functions. Read the first two parts of the book. Take exam 1.
  2. Weeks 3 to 4 One-variable calculus. Limits, derivatives, integrals and series.
  3. Weeks 5 to 6 Linear algebra. From elimination to the SVD. Take exam 2.
  4. Week 7 Probability and statistics. Bayes, expectation and the limit theorems.
  5. Week 8 Logic, counting and graphs. Write one proof each day.
  6. Week 9 Many variables and optimisation. Gradients, Lagrange and convexity. Take exam 3.
  7. Week 10 The maths of AI. Learning theory, deep learning and vector search.
  8. Week 11 A tour of higher mathematics. Read statements and proof ideas, not every detail.
  9. Week 12 Review. Take exam 4 with a timer. Redo every problem you missed.

The daily routine

  • 10 minutes: review theorem cards. Show a card again after 1, 3, 7, 14 and 30 days if you knew it. Show it tomorrow if you did not.
  • 30 minutes: read one section and do its practice.
  • 20 minutes: write one proof from memory, from its one-sentence idea.

Chain rule

(f \circ g)'(x) = f'(g(x))\,g'(x).

Bayes' theorem

P(A \mid B) = P(B \mid A)\,P(A) / P(B).

Cauchy-Schwarz inequality

|u \cdot v| \le \|u\|\,\|v\|, with equality when one vector is a multiple of the other.

Central limit theorem

For independent copies with mean \mu and variance \sigma^2, \sqrt n (\bar X_n - \mu)/\sigma tends to a standard normal.

Spectral theorem

A real symmetric matrix is Q \Lambda Q^\top with Q orthogonal and \Lambda real diagonal.

Rank-nullity theorem

For an m \times n matrix, rank plus nullity equals n.

Markov's inequality

For X \ge 0 and a \gt 0, P(X \ge a) \le E[X]/a.

Fermat's little theorem

For a prime p and any integer a, a^p \equiv a \pmod p.

In a timed multiple-choice test, do a first pass and answer only what you can solve in two minutes. Mark the rest. Use the options. You can often rule out three of five by checking a special case, such as n = 1 or x = 0.

Patterns to remember

Patterns for reading and writing proofs
PatternPurposeModelNote
Assume P. ... Therefore Q.Prove "if P then Q" directlyLet n = 2k. Then n^2 = 2(2k^2).Never start from Q.
Assume not Q. ... Therefore not P.Prove by contrapositiveIf n is odd, then n^2 is odd.Do not confuse it with the converse.
Suppose not. ... Contradiction.Prove by contradictionSuppose \sqrt3 = p/q in lowest terms.Say clearly what the contradiction is.
Let x be arbitrary.Prove a "for all" statementLet \varepsilon \gt 0 be given.Do not pick a special x.
Take x = \dots. Check.Prove a "there exists" statementTake \delta = \varepsilon/3.Show the object really works.
One counterexampleDisprove a "for all" statement|x| is continuous but not differentiable at 0.Check the example fits every hypothesis.
Base case, then stepProve for all n \ge n_0n^2 + (2n + 1) = (n + 1)^2Use the assumption for n in the step.
Case 1 ... Case 2 ...Split a proof into easier partsn even, or n oddThe cases must cover everything.
Show both inclusionsProve two sets are equalA \subseteq B and B \subseteq AOne inclusion is only half.
Prove both directionsProve "if and only if"(\Rightarrow) ... (\Leftarrow) ...Label each direction.
Assume two, show equalProve uniquenessIf e and e' are identities, e = ee' = e'.Existence is a separate step.
Take the smallest or longestUse an extreme objectTake a longest path in the graph.Check that such an object exists.

Practice

What is the negation of "for every x there is a y with y \gt x"?

  • For every x there is a y with y \le x.
  • There is an x such that every y has y \le x.
  • There is a y such that y \gt x for every x.

Negation swaps each quantifier and negates the inside: \exists x\ \forall y : y \le x.

Which statement is the contrapositive of "if it rains, the street is wet"?

  • If the street is wet, it rains.
  • If it does not rain, the street is not wet.
  • If the street is not wet, it does not rain.

The contrapositive is "if not Q then not P". The first option is the converse, and the second is the inverse. Neither is equal to the original.

To disprove a "for all" statement, you need one ?.

In the ranked list, the theorem in place 1 is the ?.

  1. Find the error. "Let a = b. Then a^2 = ab, so a^2 - b^2 = ab - b^2, so (a + b)(a - b) = b(a - b), so a + b = b, so 2b = b, so 2 = 1."
    Answer

    The step from (a + b)(a - b) = b(a - b) to a + b = b divides by a - b. But a = b, so a - b = 0. Dividing by zero is not allowed.

  2. Write the negation of "f is continuous at a": for every \varepsilon \gt 0 there is a \delta \gt 0 such that |x - a| \lt \delta implies |f(x) - f(a)| \lt \varepsilon.
    Answer

    There is an \varepsilon \gt 0 such that for every \delta \gt 0 there is an x with |x - a| \lt \delta and |f(x) - f(a)| \ge \varepsilon.

  3. The extreme value theorem needs a continuous function on a closed bounded interval. Give a counterexample when "bounded" is dropped.
    Answer

    f(x) = x on [0, \infty) is continuous and the interval is closed, but f has no largest value.

  4. A student proves "if n^2 is odd then n is odd" by checking n = 1, 3, 5, 7. Grade the proof and fix it.
    Answer

    It is not a proof, because examples cannot cover all integers. Fix: prove the contrapositive. If n is even, n = 2k, so n^2 = 4k^2 = 2(2k^2) is even.

Key takeaways

  • Read a theorem by naming its objects, hypotheses, conclusion and quantifiers, then drop each hypothesis to see why it is needed.
  • Read a proof as a checker: find the method, find where each hypothesis is used, and rewrite it from a one-sentence idea.
  • Five methods cover most proofs: direct, contrapositive, contradiction, cases and induction.
  • The ranked atlas links each of the 100 key theorems to the chapter that proves it.
  • Practise with timed exams, review theorem cards on a spaced schedule, and write one proof a day.
